This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain <note>A legal status where a work is no longer protected by intellectual property laws and is free for public use.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>Notes or sketches written in the margins of a book by previous readers or owners.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten, or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. <margin>1</margin> It is indeed agreed upon <note>original: "Συμφωνεῖται" — The editor notes that the beginning of the work seems damaged or incomplete since Pythagoras's name has not yet appeared in the main sentence; he believes a formal preface is missing.</note> by most writers that he was the son of Mnesarchus; however, there is disagreement regarding the lineage of Mnesarchus. ---

<note>The following are scholarly annotations provided by the original editor/transcriber regarding the Greek text above.</note>

1) **It is indeed agreed upon**] Who does not see that the beginning of the work is mutilated, since the name of Pythagoras appears nowhere? I think the preface of the work is missing, to the end of which these words should be referred.

2) **From Tyre**] Thus I have restored the text in place of *Pyrrhus* and *Pyrrhan*, which were meaningless words. A similar error occurred in Number 10, where *Pyrrhinian* was previously read instead of *Tyrrhenian*. And behold, besides Diogenes Laertius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Plutarch—all witnesses worthy of trust—Clement of Alexandria (in the 5th book of the *Stromata*), Eusebius (in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 10, chapter 4), and Theodoret (in the 1st book of *Therapeutics*) all state: "Aristoxenus, Aristarchus, and Theopompus say that Pythagoras was a Tyrrhenian <note>An Etruscan or non-Greek Italian</note>. But Neanthes says he was a Tyrian <note>A native of Tyre, in modern-day Lebanon</note>."

# PORPHYRY

## ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

### BOOK.

The opinion of most authors is in agreement that Pythagoras was the son of Mnesarchus; however, regarding the lineage of Mnesarchus, not everyone is in accord. For some affirm that he was a Samian <note>A native of the island of Samos</note>. But Cleanthes, in the fifth book of his *Fabulous Matters*, recorded that he was a Syrian, from the city of Tyre in Syria. He states that when a great famine arose in Samos, Mnesarchus arrived at the island for the purpose of trade and was granted citizenship as a reward. Pythagoras, however, to whom—

---

<note>The following section appears to be a scholarly commentary on the sources used in the main text.</note>

...names <note>original Greek: ὀνομάζει</note>. Where you see things cited from Neanthes, our author cites them from Cleanthes: I observe that among other writers, the names of these two are likewise placed interchangeably. For what the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator</note> on Aristophanes’ *The Knights* relates from Cleanthes concerning the three cities which provided Themistocles with grain, wine, and meat, Plutarch affirms on the authority of Neanthes of Cyzicus in his *Life of Themistocles*. Yet I would not dare to pronounce anything certain here; since our author uses the testimony of Neanthes further below, while Athenaeus praises the *Mythical Matters* <note>original Latin: μυθικὰ</note> of Cleanthes in his thirteenth book.

# PORPHYRIUS

...being from childhood naturally gifted <note>original Greek: εὐφυοῦς (euphyous)</note> for every branch of learning, 
<margin>(4)</margin> Mnesarchus <note>Pythagoras's father</note> led him away to Tyre. 
There, having been introduced to the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian sages known for their knowledge of astronomy and occult sciences</note>, he was made to participate in their teachings more fully. Returning from there to Ionia <note>The central coast of ancient Greek Turkey</note>, Pythagoras first associated with Pherecydes of Syros; secondly, he studied with Hermodamas the Creophylian, who was already 
<margin>2</margin> growing old in Samos. But Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> says there are others who declare his father was a Tyrrhenian <note>An Etruscan or non-Greek inhabitant of the Aegean</note>, from those who colonized Lemnos. From there, having come to Samos for business, he remained and became a citizen. When 
<margin>(5)</margin> Mnesarchus sailed to Italy, Pythagoras sailed with him...

---

3) **naturally gifted** <note>original Greek: εὐφυοῦς</note> ] Plato and others properly used the term "natural giftedness" <note>original Greek: εὐφυΐαν</note> for excellence of talent, and called one endowed with it "naturally gifted" <note>original Greek: εὐφυῆ</note>; just as they used "dullness" <note>original Greek: ἀφυΐαν</note> and "dull" <note>original Greek: ἀφυῆ</note> for one who lacks such gifts. Plato clearly explains both in the *Republic*: "Did you mean that one man is naturally gifted for something, and another not, in that one learns easily, while the other with difficulty? And the one, from a little learning, is able to discover much about what he learned; while the other, despite much learning and practice, cannot even preserve what he learned," etc. The Stoics defined natural giftedness as a state originating from nature or from temperament, well-suited for virtue, through which some are easily receptive to virtue. Hence Plutarch in the *Symposiacs*, Book IX, Question 14, says that the soul, because of "natural giftedness," is easily stirred to the remembrance and love of celestial matters. Herodotus says of Homer: "He saw that the boy was intelligent and very naturally gifted." In the same place he calls it "a good nature" <note>original Greek: Φύσιν ἀγαθὴν</note>; just as Zeno does in the *Epistle to Antigonus*, calling it "a noble nature" <note>original Greek: φύσιν εὐγενῆ</note>: which passage is worth seeing. Concerning Socrates, Porphyry's words are found in Theodoret, *Series 1 on Greek Affections*: "He was dull in no respect." But regarding "dullness," see Epictetus, chapter 63, and Simplicius: and especially Arrian, Book 3, chapter 6, where he sets down a "test for the gifted and the dull" <note>original Greek: δοκιμαστήριον τῶν εὐφυῶν καὶ ἀφυῶν</note> from Rufus. Aulus Gellius, Book XIX, chapter 9, says that an Asiatic youth was of a "ready and willing talent" <note>original Latin: facili ingenio ac lubenti</note> for music. Apuleius in the *Florida* concerning Pythagoras: "A man of immense talent, and truly..."

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.
## DE VITA PYTHAGORAE.
A

the boy possessed a nature most suited for all disciplines, he was afterwards led away to Tyre by Mnesarchus <note>Pythagoras's father</note>, and there he was entrusted to the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian sages and astronomers</note>, with whose teachings he especially desired to be imbued. Having returned from there to Ionia <note>The Greek-settled coast of modern-day Turkey</note>, Pythagoras first associated himself with Pherecydes of Syros; thereafter he studied with Hermodamas the Creophylian <note>A descendant of the poet Creophylus</note>, who was then living as an old man in Samos. However, Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> writes that there are those who assert his father was a Tyrrhenian <note>An Etruscan or non-Greek inhabitant of the Aegean</note>, from the stock of those who inhabited Lemnos; and that when he had come from there to Samos for the sake of business, he remained there and was made a citizen. But when Mnesarchus was sailing to Italy, Py-

---

...more majestic than the capacity of the human mind. And elsewhere regarding Plato: *His boyish wit was sharp in perception.* But this is rather "sharpness" <note>original Greek: ὀξύτης (oxytēs)</note>, a part of "readiness to learn" <note>original Greek: εὐμαθείας (eumatheias)</note>: regarding which see below. For Arnobius <note>An early Christian apologist</note> also testifies in Book 2 <note>The Latin text says "lib. 11", but Arnobius's *Against the Heathen* only has seven books; the commentator may be citing a specific edition's numbering</note> that Pythagoras and Plato were most powerful in this regard: *Though they be the offspring of Plato or Pythagoras, or of any of those who are said to have possessed divine sharpness.*

4) **Pherecydes of Syros** <note>original Greek: Φερεκύδῃ τῷ Συρίῳ</note>] He originated from Syros, an island in the Aegean Sea, not from Syria, the eastern province. For from the former the demonym is "Syrian" <note>original Latin: Syrus</note>, and from the latter it is "Syrian" <note>original Latin: Syrius</note>. I see that people have erred in this matter six hundred times among Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, Theodoret, Diogenes Laërtius, and others: where translators always render it as "the Syrian" <note>Latin: Syrum</note>. In Theodoret's *Cure of Greek Afflictions*, Sermon 1, it is wrongly read: "For Pherecydes was a Tyrian <note>from Tyre</note>, not an Athenian" <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν γὰρ Φερεκύδης Τύριος ἦν, οὐκ Ἀθηναῖος</note>. In Diogenes Laërtius it is also faulty: "in the island of Syra" <note>original Greek: ἐν Σύρᾳ τῇ νήσῳ</note>, instead of "Syros" <note>Σύρῳ</note>; as also in Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry *Pherecydes*: "Syra is one of the Cyclades islands near Delos" <note>original Greek: ἐστὶ δὲ νῆσος μία τῶν Κυκλάδων ἡ Σύρα, πλησίον Δήλου</note>, where one should read "Syros." This error is slight, yet it has led the foremost scholars into a greater one: those who contend that all wisdom was brought from Syria into Greece using this argument—that Pythagoras, the first of the philosophers, had a "Syrian" teacher.

->PORPHYRY<-

Pythagoras, when he was still quite young and Samos was in a very prosperous state, later sailed back to it. The author lists two brothers of his, Eunostus and Tyrrhenus, who were older than him. Apollonius, in his writings *On Pythagoras*, also records that his mother was Pythais, a descendant of Ancaeus, the original founder of Samos. Apollonius says that while some report Pythagoras was the biological son of the god Apollo and Pythais, he was the son of Mnesarchus in name only. At any rate, one of the Samian poets said:

> And Pythagoras, whom Pythais, she who possessed 
> the greatest beauty among the Samians, 
> bore to Apollo, beloved of Zeus.

This author <note>Apollonius</note> states that Pythagoras studied not only under Pherecydes <note>a philosopher from Syros</note>, but also under Hermodamas, <margin>5</margin> and even under Anaximander <note>a famous pre-Socratic philosopher from Miletus</note>. Duris of Samos, in the second book of his *Annals* <term>original Greek: ὧραι (hōrai), literally "seasons" but here meaning local histories or chronicles</term>, records that Pythagoras had a son named Arimnestus, and says that this son became the teacher of Democritus <note>the philosopher famous for the atomic theory</note>. This Arimnestus, upon returning <margin>6</margin> from exile, set up a bronze <note>original Greek: χαλκοῦν (chalkoun)</note> votive offering in the temple of...

---

**5) but also under Hermod.]** It would be more correct to remove the word "but" <note>original Latin: *ἀλλὰ* (alla)</note>. Since the author already mentioned Hermodamas earlier along with Pherecydes, he is now simply adding Anaximander to the list of teachers.

**6) a bronze votive offering]** The ancient writers testify in more than one place that the discoveries of the Arts and Sciences were once publicly recorded on columns, stone pillars, and bronze tablets for the memory of posterity. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author</note> writes in Book 34, Chapter 9: *The use of copper for the permanence of monuments was long ago adopted, in the form of bronze tablets, on which public laws are engraved.* The same author says in Book 13, Chapter 11: *Public monuments began to be recorded on leaden scrolls.* Josephus <note>a Jewish-Roman historian</note> relates a very ancient example of this regarding the sons of Seth in the *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, who [recorded] the science of the stars...

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

...Pythagoras, while still quite a young man, set out together with him <note>his father, Mnesarchus</note>; and since that land was then flourishing greatly in wealth, he subsequently returned to it by ship. He <note>the author Apollonius</note> further lists his two brothers, Eunostus and Tyrrhenus, who were older than him. Apollonius, moreover, in his book *On the Life of Pythagoras*, records that his mother was Pythais, who traced her lineage from Ancaeus, the founder of Samos. Indeed, the same Apollonius asserts that some have claimed he was in reality the son of Apollo and Pythais, though in name the son of Mnesarchus. For this reason, a certain Samian poet says:

> *Pythais, the most beautiful of the Samians, bore to Phoebus* <note>Apollo</note>
> *Pythagoras, the care and delight of Jove.* <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>

The author testifies that Pythagoras did not only listen to Pherecydes <note>a philosopher from Syros</note>, but also devoted himself to the teachings of Hermodamas and Anaximander <note>a famous scientist and philosopher from Miletus</note>. Furthermore, Duris of Samos, in the second book of his *Annals* <term>original Latin: Horarum; literally "of the seasons," referring to local chronicles</term>, writes that he had a son named Arimnestus, and that Democritus <note>the philosopher famous for the atomic theory</note> was his pupil. This Arimnestus, having returned home from exile, dedicated a bronze gift in the temple of Juno <note>Hera</note>...

---

...they inscribed on two columns, one of brick and the other of stone, so that one might survive a flood and the other a fire. Among the Egyptians, Proclus <note>a late antique philosopher</note> testifies in the first book of his commentary on the *Timaeus* (p. 31) that all the admirable discoveries of the intellect and noble deeds were inscribed on columns and transmitted to posterity. 
<column-break/>
For the Egyptians, past events are always present and new through memory; and memory is maintained through history. This history comes from the pillars <note>original Greek: στηλῶν (stēlōn)</note>, on which were inscribed the marvelous things and those deeds worthy of wonder, whether they were in actions or in discoveries <note>original: Αἰγυπτίοις καὶ τὰ γεγονότα διὰ τῆς μνήμης ἀεὶ νέα πάρεστιν· ἡ δὲ μνήμη διὰ τῆς ἱστορίας. αὕτη δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν στηλῶν, ἐν αἷς ἀνεγράφοντο τὰ παράδοξα, καὶ τὰ θαύματος ἄξια τῶν πραγμάτων, εἴ τε ἐν πράξεσιν, εἴ τε ἐν εὑρέσεσιν.</note>. Indeed, even the position and circumference of the earth and sea...

# PORPHYRY

(6) ...dedicated to Hera <note>the queen of the gods, known to the Romans as Juno</note>; it had a diameter of nearly two cubits, and on it this epigram was inscribed:
> Arimnestus, the beloved son of Pythagoras, dedicated me,
> Having discovered many things in the words of wisdom.

(7) But Simon the Musician <note>literally "the Harmonic"</note>, having removed <gloss>7)</gloss> this [offering], and <gloss>8)</gloss> having claimed the **canon** <term>original Greek: κανόνα (kanona); here referring to a mathematical or musical rule or standard of measure</term> as his own, published it as his own work.

Apollonius of Rhodes, in Book IV, verse 279, is the authority for the fact that they engraved all things on these [columns]:
> They surely preserve the writings of their fathers,
> The *kyrbies*, on which are all the paths and boundaries
> For those traveling around the sea and the land.

In this passage, perhaps "written *kyrbies*" <term>original Greek: γραπτοὺς κύρβιας (graptous kyrbias); *kyrbies* were ancient triangular or four-sided pillars used for public inscriptions</term> would be a more correct reading. For while the Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> explains "writings" <note>original Greek: γράπτυς (graptus)</note> in this place as "laws," I think this by no means suits the author’s intent. You might more conveniently understand them as any inscriptions carved into stone. Iamblichus also, in *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, Section I, chapter 2, reports that all the discoveries of wisdom were inscribed on the ancient columns of Mercury <note>the Greek god Hermes, credited with inventing writing and science</note>. When Plato and Pythagoras had once read these, they established their philosophy. But no one expresses this better than the ancient and unknown author of that admirable work *On Divine Wisdom according to the Egyptians*, Book XIV, chapter 14: "The wise men of Babylon and Egypt, penetrating those hidden things of the supreme world with the sharpness of their minds, described the concepts of their souls on stones through figures <note>likely referring to hieroglyphs or symbolic images</note>, just as we ourselves are eyewitnesses. And they did the same in all the arts and sciences. Then they placed the stones on which those things were described in the temples, and displayed them like pages to be read through; such things were in use among them in place of books." Regarding the Babylonians, Pliny <note>a Roman naturalist and author</note> also notes in Book VII, chapter 56, that Epigenes teaches that there were observations of the stars for 720 years inscribed on baked bricks among the Babylonians. This same custom passed into Greece, where laws, edicts, proscriptions, treaties, and other public acts were inscribed on stone columns and pillars—that is, on **stelae** and **kyrbies** <term>original Greek: στήλαις καὶ κύρβεσιν</term>; on which matter Harpocration, the Scholiast of Apollonius, and other ancient grammarians should be consulted. Indeed, they were even inscribed in bronze; as seen in Plato's Mi--

But it is well known that Simus the Musician <note>literally "the Harmonic"</note> took this very thing and attributed the **musical canon** <term>original Latin: canonem musicum; a mathematical rule or stringed instrument used to determine musical intervals</term> to himself.

The very ancient **Arundel Chronological Marble** <note>the Parian Chronicle, a famous Greek chronological inscription brought to England in the 17th century</note>, recently brought to light for the great public benefit by most learned men, also testifies that monuments of art and genius were protected from the ravages of time in a similar way. There is also the **Paschal Canon** <note>a table used to calculate the date of Easter</note> of Hippolytus of Porto, which can be seen inscribed on his statue in the Vatican library. Hanno the Carthaginian <note>a 5th-century BC explorer</note> displayed a description of his circumnavigation of Libya in the temple of Saturn for posterity to read; and I do not doubt that this **votive offering** <note>original Greek: ἀνάθημα (anathema)</note> was expressed in bronze or marble. Fragments collected by scholars also testify that the Romans displayed the consular records <term>original Latin: fastos consulares; the official list of yearly Roman consuls</term>, various calendars, and even a **ground plan** <note>original Greek: ἰχνογραφίαν (ichnographian)</note> of the entire city—including regions, neighborhoods, streets, and all buildings—on marble tablets and pillars. Not to mention the Laws of the Twelve Tables and the remains of the Royal Law which are viewed on the Capitoline Hill: for that method of writing laws did not originate with the Romans or Greeks, but from God the Best and Greatest Himself, who promulgated the law inscribed with His own finger on stone tablets to the Hebrews through Moses. Indeed, the Sacred Scriptures express this mode of writing perfectly in Job, chapter 19, verse 24:

> *Who will grant me that my words might be written with an iron pen, or on a sheet of lead; or at least carved into flint-stone?*

You also have examples of treaties written out on bronze tablets in 1 Maccabees, chapter 8, verse 22, and chapter 15, verse 13.

I have added this for the sake of explanation: for Diogenes Laërtius <note>a biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> testifies that Pythagoras discovered the **rule** <term>original Latin: canonem; a mathematical standard or a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</term> of a single string. Nicomachus <note>a mathematician and music theorist, c. 60–120 AD</note> also mentions this in Book I of his *Manual of Harmonics*, page 79: "the so-called Pythagorean canon," the mathematical division of which he provides in that same place. This "canon" is a rule or standard containing the ratios and proportions of all musical tones. For the story of how it was discovered by Pythagoras, see the same Nicomachus on page 69 and Iamblichus, Book I, chapter 26. Ptolemy <note>the famous 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note> teaches in Book I, chapter 2 of his *Harmonics* that this canon should be used as a **standard of judgment** <note>original Greek: κριτήριον (criterion)</note> in every musical investigation: "The instrument for such a method is called the 'harmonic canon,' named from the general category and because it is employed to **standardize** <note>original Greek: κανονίζειν (kanonizein); to bring into line with a rule</note> those things where the senses fall short of the truth." On this point, a Greek scholarly note says: "A canon is a measure of the correctness of the proportions found in sounds. Or, a measure of the correctness of the harmonic differences in sounds, which are perceived through the ratios of numbers." This is according to the Greek manuscript of the musical writers which the most excellent library of the Most Illustrious **Cardinal Barberini** <note>Francesco Barberini (1597–1679), a major patron of scholarship in Rome</note> provided to me. From this source, we learn that the Pythagoreans called **single-stringed** <note>original Greek: τὰ μονόχορδα (ta monochorda)</note> musical instruments—commonly called *Panduras* <note>a long-necked lute-like instrument with three strings</note>—"Canons," as Nicomachus testifies in Book I, page 67.

---

...and that this was the only way to grasp and know the truth <note>original Greek: μόνην τὴν ἐν τούτοις κατάληψιν καὶ γνῶσιν τῆς ἀληθείας</note>. Nevertheless, every art and science is commonly called by this name [wisdom]. <margin>10) To lead the maidens <note>original Greek: ἡγεῖσθαι τῶν παρθένων</note></margin>
Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> reports the same in Book I, chapter 30: "When he had married, he educated the daughter born to him—who later married Menon of Croton—in such a way that as a maiden she would lead the choirs, and once she became a wife, she would be the first to approach the altars." This is how that passage should be understood. That she led the choirs, which preceded all others in honor and dignity, is so well known that it even gave rise to a proverb. Thus Diana <note>the goddess Artemis</note> in the Homeric hymn:

> Arranging the beautiful choir of the Muses and the Graces,
> She leads them, wearing graceful adornments upon her body,
> Leading the dance <note>original Greek: Ἐξάρχουσα χορούς</note>.

From this come the terms *choregos* <note>a choir leader</note> and *chorodektes* <note>an official who receives the chorus</note>.

For the Egyptians have been the most devoted to geometry since ancient times; the Phoenicians to numbers and proportions; and to astronomy the move— <note>the Latin text breaks here; it likely continued "movements of the stars"</note>

---
<column-break/>

...having taken its beginning, it grew to such a great size. The study of numbers began with Phoenician merchants and was eventually established among the Greeks as a distinguished branch of science. The Greeks joined the three <note>referring to geometry, arithmetic, and astronomy</note> together into one with the addition of music, weaving astronomy into geometry. By fitting numbers to both of these, and establishing the harmony inherent in them, they founded their own system of music from that basis. They discovered the limits of harmonic ratios through a perfect agreement with the sense of hearing—an agreement that is as close as possible to this mathematical truth.

*On the astrological predictions of the Chaldeans, see the same Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> in the place cited above; Julian; Aelian in On the Nature of Animals, Book 1, Chapter 22; Sextus Empiricus, Book 5, Against the Mathematicians; and Diogenes Laërtius in his Prologue:* The Chaldeans occupy themselves with astronomy and prophecy; while the Magi <note>the priestly class of ancient Persia</note> spend their time in the service of the gods, sacrifices, and prayers. *See also the following sections regarding the white garment and the manner of diet <note>referring to the ascetic Pythagorean lifestyle</note>: which Pythagoras clearly imitated. Add to these the testimony of Theophrastus from his book On Signs, as cited in Proclus, Book 4 of the Commentary on the Timaeus, page 285.*

Regarding the sacred rites of foreign nations, an example can be found in what is read about the initiations of Mithras <note>Mithras was a Persian sun god whose mystery cult involved rigorous trials</note> in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, stating that no one could be consecrated to that god unless he proved himself holy and beyond suffering through several stages of punishments. <meta>Continuity: The previous page discussed the rigorous initiations of the Persian mysteries of Mithras, emphasizing the "degrees of punishment" required to prove one’s holiness. This page connects those ancient trials to Pythagoras’s own educational methods in Egypt and their later influence on academic and monastic life.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>PORPHYRY</header>

## Pythagoras, having accepted the training of the Egyptian
## priests, and being eager to participate...

...are tormented. <note>original Latin: *excruciantur*—finishing a sentence from the previous page regarding the trials of the Mithraic mysteries.</note> Pythagoras himself later imitated the Egyptians’ policy of being difficult to approach, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras</note> testifies in Book I, chapter 17. After he had explored the nature, lineage, and character of his disciples for a long time and with great care, he was accustomed to reject them for three full years to test their constancy. When they were finally admitted to his companionship, he imposed a five-year silence as a "most difficult self-restraint" <note>original Greek: *chalepōtaton enkrateuma*</note>. He explicitly notes that this custom was transferred from the sacred mysteries; it was subsequently received into the schools of the remaining philosophers and sophists <note>professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy</note>, especially in Athens. To this kind of "hardship" <note>original Greek: *kakopatheias*</note> we should refer what Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century philosopher and historian</note> (cited in Photius, volume 80) and Gregory of Nazianzus <note>An influential 4th-century theologian</note> (in his *Oration on Basil the Great*) write regarding the "sophistic bath and cloak" <note>Rituals involving the symbolic dressing of a new student</note>. On this matter, one should consult the illustrious Heribert Rosweyd’s notes on Book VI of the *Lives of the Desert Fathers*.

In certain German Universities, similar rites—if I am not mistaken—were introduced alongside learning and are stubbornly retained; they commonly call this the <term>deposition</term> <note>original: *depositionem*—a semi-theatrical hazing ritual where a new student, or "bean-beak," was "cleansed" of his rustic horns and teeth before being admitted to the university</note>. Then there are the insolent harassments by which the newer candidates for letters are tormented for a full year by the more advanced students. Furthermore, several merchant guilds in Northern Germany receive their apprentices through similar degrees of punishment—namely whips, fire, and water.

But to return to Pythagoras: I believe that among these types of trials, circumcision was also undertaken by him, as Clement of Alexandria <note>A 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> testifies in the first book of his *Miscellanies*. However, it was not only philosophers who transferred these trials into their schools; during the era of the nascent Church, they were also received into the monasteries of monks throughout Inner Egypt. You have an eyewitness to this fact in John Cassian <note>A monk and theologian known for bringing Egyptian monasticism to the West</note> in Book IV of his *Institutes*, chapter 3: "Anyone seeking," he says, "to be received into the discipline of a monastery is not admitted at all until, staying outside the doors for ten days or more, he gives proof of his perseverance and desire, as well as his humility and patience. Having also been subjected to many insults and reproaches, he gives evidence of his constancy, and declares by his endurance of slights what he will be like in the midst of temptations." Then, in chapter 7, he says that one proven by such perseverance is not immediately...

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

He says that Pythagoras, intending to adopt the customs of the Egyptian Priests, acted with all zeal to become a participant in their rites, and requested

> to be joined to the congregation of the brothers, but was instead assigned to an elder <note>original Latin: *seniori*—a senior monk or leader</note> who, not far from the entrance of the monastery, has the care of foreigners and newcomers. And when, he says, serving in that same place for a full year without any complaint, he had shown his service toward the foreigners, he was then to be admitted to the congregation of brothers and handed over to another elder who is in charge of ten juniors. This elder will always take care to command him, as stated in chapter 8, to do things he feels are contrary to his own mind. Indeed, many things that were superfluous, unnecessary, or even impossible were frequently enjoined upon him. Of this matter, if you wish, see examples in chapters 24, 27, and 29. He then explains the reasons for this difficulty and rejection in chapter 33 and following. Almost all ascetic orders keep similar institutions accepted from the Egyptians, and they do so all the more as they depart less from the strict rigor of the primitive way of life. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> himself teaches at length in *On Abstinence*, Book IV (drawing from Flavius Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>), that the Essenes <note>A Jewish sect known for asceticism</note> among the Jewish philosophers were also once received into their communal living through similar degrees of probation. They also held many other things in common with the Pythagoreans: silence, the sharing of goods, white clothing, the hiding of their doctrines, abstinence from eating living things <note>original Latin: *animatorum esu*—refers to a vegetarian diet</note>, and similar practices. These things they themselves undoubtedly received from the Egyptians, as they did many other things. Nor should anyone wonder that I have said the institutions of sacred conversation and a more perfect life were derived from the Jews and Gentiles into the Church; since even the very names of "philosophy" <note>original Greek: *philosophias*</note> and "asceticism" <note>original Greek: *askēseōs*—meaning disciplined training</note> for the religious life were drawn from there. By no less right could Christians convert the healthier institutions of the Gentiles to their own use than the Hebrews could take the spoils of the Egyptians <note>A common theological metaphor referring to the Israelites taking gold from Egypt (Exodus 12:35-36), used here to justify adopting pagan wisdom for Christian purposes</note>. For by this argument it is clearly evident that there existed in individual nations those who, having recognized the corruption of human nature, strove for a certain degree of perfection in piety above the common people through a stricter way of living. Hence, in the writings of Clement of Alexandria <note>A prominent 2nd-century Christian theologian</note>, these institutions of the Gentiles and Jews are called "steps and foundations of the philosophy according to Christ" <note>original Greek: *bathmoi kai hypobathrai tēs kata Christon philosophias*</note>: so far is it from being the case that our people [would reject] the religious life by this name...

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.
<sig>B 2</sig>

...[he requested] the tyrant Polycrates to write to Amasis, the King of the Egyptians—who was both his friend and host—so that he might be admitted to the teachings of the priests we have mentioned. But when he had reached Amasis, he received letters from him addressed to the priests. From the people of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun," a center of solar worship</note>, whom he first encountered, he was sent away to Memphis on the grounds that they were his seniors; and the Heliopolitans truly used this as a pretext to avoid him. Having been dismissed from Memphis under the same pretext, he went to the people of Diospolis <note>Likely Thebes, the "City of Zeus"</note>. These priests, however, because they could not offer any excuse due to their fear of the King, thought he would abandon his purpose through the sheer scale of the labor and hardships involved. Therefore, they imposed very harsh rules upon him, which were entirely foreign to Greek religious practice. But because he executed these so readily, they admired him to such an extent that he was permitted both to sacrifice to the gods and to participate in their sacred studies—a privilege which is found to have been granted to no other foreigner. Returning then to Ionia, he opened a school in his fatherland,

---

...having reviewed the prayers, adds: <note>original Greek: "ὁ μὲν δὴ πόνος ὁ ἄτρυτός τε καὶ διηνεκὴς καρτερία ἀπομαρτυρεῖ τοῖς ἀνδράσι"</note> "The unwearied labor and constant endurance bear witness to the character of these men."

16) **School** <note>original Greek: "διδασκαλεῖον" (didaskaleion)</note>] This term is also used elsewhere. For they properly call the school of Pythagoras a **place of teaching**, just as they call Plato's the **Academy**, Aristotle's the **Lyceum** or the **walkway** <note>original: "peripaton," referring to the Peripatetic school where philosophers walked while discussing</note>, Epicurus's the **gardens**, and Zeno's the **porch** <note>The "Stoa," from which Stoicism gets its name</note>. From this, the followers of Pythagoras are called <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ Πυθαγορικοῦ διδασκαλείου"</note> "those from the Pythagorean school," according to Nicomachus in Book I of his *Harmonics* and Iamblichus in Book I, chapters 23 and 28, and elsewhere. But just as it is called a "place of teaching" from the act of teaching, so he calls it the "place of hearing" of Pythagoras from the act of hearing or listening in chapter 29, and more often a **place of common hearing** <note>original Greek: "ὁμακόϊον" (homakoeion)</note>: about which we will speak below.

17) **A cave suited** <note>original Greek: "ἄντρον οἰκεῖον"</note>] In this matter too, he seems to have imitated the Magi <note>The priestly caste of ancient Persia, known for their esoteric wisdom</note>, who performed their sacred rites in caves and grottoes. I believe this was so the seclusion of the place and the "sacred dread" of his teaching might inspire a certain religious awe. For this reason, we read that caves were frequented by Minos <note>The legendary King of Crete</note> and Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the second King of Rome</note>. 26) **Zalmoxis** <note>original Greek: Ζάμολξις</note>] This passage appears in Cyril, Book 6, *Against Julian*. # ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

They claim that this boy's name was Thales: whom the barbarians <note>likely referring to the Thracian tribes</note> worship in the likeness of **Hercules**. Dionysiphanes, however, says that he was indeed a slave of **Pythagoras**; but because he had been branded with marks by robbers into whose hands he had fallen, he covered his forehead on account of those burned-in marks <note>the Latin "inustas notas" refers to the tattoos or brands used to identify runaway or captured slaves</note> when Pythagoras, harassed by the factions of rebels, went into exile <note>original: solum verteret; literally "turned his soil," a common Latin idiom for leaving one's country</note>. Others say that the name **Zamolxis** signifies a "foreign man."

Furthermore, after Pythagoras had offered his assistance to **Pherecydes** <note>Pherecydes of Syros, a mythographer and early thinker considered one of Pythagoras's primary teachers</note> while he was ill in **Delos**, and had buried him after his death, he then returned to **Samos** because he longed to enjoy the companionship of **Hermodamas**, the descendant of Creophylus <note>original: Hermodamantis Creophylii; Creophylus was a legendary Samian epic poet said to have hosted Homer</note>. After he had lived with him for some time, he devoted his attention to **Eurymenes**, a Samian athlete. Although Eurymenes was of small stature, through the wisdom of Pythagoras he surpassed many who possessed tall bodies, and he won at the **Olympic Games**. For while other athletes, following the ancient custom, still fed upon cheese and figs, this man—on the advice of Pythagoras—was the first to eat a fixed daily weight of meat, thereby preparing great physical strength for himself. Gradually imbuing him with his wisdom, Pythagoras encouraged him to compete, yet in such a way that he should not seek to win: because la- <note>the text cuts off mid-word, likely "laborem" (toil) or "laudem" (praise)</note>

---

and **Diogenes Laërtius** confirms this. For the philosopher commanded his followers to abstain not only from eating, but even from the slaughter of living creatures, and, as **Hierocles** says, he ordered them to flee **"from athletic training and all so-called physical exercise"** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀθλητικὴν ἀγωγὴν καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν λεγομένην σωμασκίαν</note>.

# PORPHYRIUS

...suggesting that it was necessary to endure the physical labors of training, but to flee the envy that arises from victory <note>original: 29) φθόνους φεύγειν</note>. For it otherwise happens that those who conquer and are showered with leaves <note>the Greek tradition of *phyllobolia*, where crowds threw leaves and flowers at victorious athletes</note> are not even in a state of religious purity <note>original: μηδ' εὐαγεῖς; suggesting that the vanity and public adulation of the games could be spiritually polluting</note>. 
<margin>16</margin> After these events, when the tyranny of **Polycrates** <note>the powerful and often ruthless ruler of Samos during the mid-6th century BCE</note> took hold of the Samians, **Pythagoras** considered it unbecoming for a philosopher to live under such a political system and decided to depart for Italy. 
As he was sailing, he stopped at **Delphi**, where he inscribed an elegy upon the tomb of **Apollo**. 
<margin>(19)</margin> Through this poem, he revealed that **Apollo** was the son of **Silenus**, but was slain by **Python** and buried in the place called the **Tripod** <note>original: Τρίποδι</note>—which received this name because three daughters of Boreas <note>the North Wind</note> mourned for him there.

29) **To flee envy:** Pythagoras advises that envy must be avoided above all else, not only in this passage but elsewhere: likewise in the *Golden Verses*, line 36:

->And take care to avoid doing those things which provoke envy.<-
<note>original Greek: Καὶ πεφύλαξό γε ταῦτα ποιεῖν, ὁπόσα φθόνον ἴσχει. Original Latin: Quaecunque inuidiam pariunt, facere illo caueto.</note>

For it is necessary, as much as it lies within us, for a lover of peace to abstain from things that cause envy, and not to provoke envy like some wild beast, so that one may make progress in honorable things without being disturbed. *“A lover of tranquility must abstain from those things which produce envy, as much as possible, and not provoke it like a wild beast; so that one may advance in honorable matters without any disturbance,”* says **Hierocles** <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a famous commentary on the Pythagorean Golden Verses</note>. From this, the **Comic poet** <note>referring to Terence in his play *Andria*</note> also wisely advises that a life should be so arranged *“that you may most easily find praise without envy, and gain friends.”* For envy and rivalry, or the zeal for contention, are the "most fertile passions for breeding hatred," to use the words of **Plutarch**. But those who measure all virtue and happiness by envy—as a body is measured by its shadow—feel differently; to them, having earned envy is the very peak of happiness. Because, as a certain one of the ancients said in **Stobaeus** <note>a compiler of Greek extracts</note>, Sermon 38...

...labors <note>original: *bores*, the conclusion of *labores* from the previous page</note> indeed ought to be endured, but that the envy produced by victory should be avoided. For it generally happens that victors, and those who are showered with leaves <note>referring to the *phyllobolia*, the practice of tossing leaves and flowers at victors in the games</note>, are rendered impure <note>original: *pollutos*; meaning ritually or morally stained by the pride of victory</note>. Later, however, when the Samians were held oppressed by the tyranny of **Polycrates** <note>the ruler of Samos known for both his great power and his eventual downfall</note>, **Pythagoras**—judging it unbecoming for a man who is a philosopher to live in such a state—began to contemplate a journey to Italy. When he had put in at **Delphi** during his voyage, he inscribed certain elegiac verses upon the tomb of **Apollo**: in which he indicated that **Apollo** was the son of **Silenus**, but was slain by **Python**, and was buried in the "Tripod," as they call it. This name was given to it because:

->No one at all envies those who are nothing;<-
->All things that are noble always possess envy.<-
<note>original Greek: Τοῖς οὐδὲν οὖσιν οὐδὲ εἷς ὅλως φθονεῖ· Ἀεὶ τὰ σεμνὰ πάντα κέκτηται φθόνον.</note>

There exist in the same place most elegant verses by **Epicharmus** <note>a Greek comic playwright and philosopher often linked to the Pythagorean school</note>! The first of these, which has been fruitlessly attempted by learned men, ought to be restored to this same meaning:

->Who would wish to be a friend who is not envied?<-
->For it is clear that no man exists who is not envied.<-
<note>original Greek: Τίς δὲ βουλοίη γενέσθαι μὴ φθονούμενός φίλος, Δῆλον ὡς ἀνὴρ γὰρ οὐδείς ἐσθ᾽ ὃ μὴ φθονούμενος.</note>

*Who*, he asks, *would desire to be a friend to those whom no one envies? For it is certain that a man is a person of no account if he is envied by no one.* With similar wit, a youth in a play by **Plautus** <note>the Roman comic playwright</note> wishes that no envious person should envy his own friends. Furthermore, in accordance with the mind of his teacher, **Xystus the Pythagorean** <note>referring to the author of the *Sentences of Sextus*, a collection of moral maxims</note> also said in chapter 44: *Strive to be great indeed before God, but before men, flee envy.*

From this, the words of **Hesychius** <note>a 5th-century lexicographer</note> must be explained: *Trion*, the tripod used by the Pythagoreans at Delphi.

**32) The initiates of Morgos]** I have represented the reading of the **Vatican Manuscript**; although both **Morgos** and the "initiates of the **Morgi**" are equally unknown to me. However, **Stephanus** <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</note> mentions a certain **Morgos** under the entry for *Galarina*. As for the **Morgoi** and **Amorgoi** mentioned by **Suidas** <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>—whom **Hesychius** and the **Scholiast of Aristophanes** <note>Ancient commentators on the playwright Aristophanes</note> also call **Molgoi** and **Amolgoi**, <gloss>as those who milk the public treasury</gloss>—they have nothing to do with this passage.

**33) Idaean Dactyls]** On the **Idaean Dactyls**, one should consult **Strabo’s** digression in Book 10 <note>Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian</note> regarding the **Curetes** <note>Armed dancers who protected the infant Zeus</note> and other ministers and priests of **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note>, the **Great Mother of the Gods** <note>Cybele</note>, and **Father Liber** <note>Dionysus</note>: where he records various opinions of the ancients concerning their name, number, and homeland. For it is not sufficiently certain whether they were so named from a mountain in **Phrygia** or **Crete**, as **Hesychius** testifies. But no one is more accurate than **Apollonius of Rhodes** in Book 1 (line 1129) and his most learned **Scholiast**; where he brings forward several verses from the author of the *Phoronis* concerning them. To these add **Lylius Gyraldus** in his first *Syntagma* and *History of the Gods*, who collected almost all the passages of the ancients.

**34) The thunderstone]** The **thunderstone** <note>original: *ceraunius lapis*</note> is believed to fall from the sky together with a lightning bolt, or rather to be the tip of a three-pronged weapon, which splits and shatters whatever stands in its way with great force and truly admirable power. Regarding this, see **Anselm Boëtius** <note>Anselmus de Boodt, a 16th-century Flemish mineralogist and physician</note> in Book 2, chapter 261. Why the **Curetes** employed it in the initiations of **Jupiter the Thunderer** can be gathered from the name itself. Nor is it surprising that a stone sent down from the clouds by **Jupiter** was used in those same sacred rites, due to the symbols appropriate to those mysteries. Hence even a **Barbarian Poet** cited by **Boëtius** in the passage mentioned reports that it was commonly worn to ward off lightning strikes. For from a "sympathy" <note>an ancient scientific theory that certain objects have natural, "sympathetic" connections to celestial bodies or forces</note> of this kind, the **Seleni-** <note>the text cuts off; likely referring to "Selenite" or moonstones</note>

...three girls, daughters of **Triopas**, <note>Triopas was a legendary figure, sometimes cited as a king of Argos or Thessaly</note> were said to have lamented **Apollo** from that place. ***

...stones—**Heliotrope**, **Hephaestite**, <note>Heliotrope is "bloodstone"; Hephaestite or "Hephaestus-stone" was likely a volcanic mineral or pyrite</note> and other stones found their names. One may read many similar superstitious delusions of antiquity in **Plutarch’s** *On Rivers*, especially concerning the **Cylindrus**, **Cryphius**, **Sicyonus**, and others. Moreover, the following details regarding the ritual of purification by a sea-bath or a flowing river are well known from **Cicero’s** *On the Nature of the Gods*, **Apuleius** in Book 2 of the *Metamorphoses*, and **Virgil** in the second book of the *Aeneid*. The same poet also mentions a black animal in more than one place, in the *Georgics* (Book 4) and the *Aeneid* (Books 3 and 5).

> — — — — — — *Aeneas himself strikes with his sword*
> *A lamb of black fleece for the mother of the Furies,* <note>original: Eumenidum</note> *and her great sister.*

Then, it is also established from the same source that the head was usually veiled during sacred rites, as in the *Aeneid*, Book 3:

> *Veil your hair, covered with a purple garment.*

And shortly after:

> *And before the altars we are veiled with our heads covered in a Phrygian garment.*

Furthermore, black clothing is appropriate for serious and funeral rites, as well as rituals involving the underworld, a matter discussed by learned men regarding the aforementioned passages of the poet; and **Porphyry** himself, in **Eusebius’s** *Preparation for the Gospel* (Book 4, chapter 9), cites a verse of an Oracle:

-> Bright things for the heavenly beings, but things like the color [of darkness] for those of the earth. <-
<note>original: Φαιδρὰ μὲν οὐρανίοις, χθονίοις δ' ἐναλίγκια χροιῇ.</note>

This means *black*, <note>original: mélana</note> as **Eusebius** explains thereafter: *For such is the earth, dark by nature.* <note>original: Τοιαύτη γὰρ ἡ γῆ φύσει σκοτεινή.</note> What he adds concerning the three-times-nine days <note>original: ter nouenis diebus; 27 days</note> also pertains to these same sacred rites. For, as **Eusebius** immediately adds, *the number three is the symbol of the bodily and the earthy.* <note>original: τοῦ σωματικοῦ καὶ γεώδους τὰ τρία σύμβολα.</note> Regarding the number nine, **Proclus** writes in Book 1 of his *Commentary on the Timaeus* (page 45): *And for the dead they perform ninth-day rites, and for the newborn they likewise set names [on the ninth day].* <note>original: Καὶ τοῖς τεθνηκόσιν ἔννατα ποιοῦσι, καὶ τοῖς γεννωμένοις ὁμοίως τὰ ὀνόματα τίθενται.</note>

->**PYTHAGORAS TO ZEUS**<-

The beginning of the inscription is:

**18** When he set foot in Italy and arrived in **Croton**, **Dicearchus** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who wrote on history and geography</note> says that as a man who had traveled much and was extraordinary, and well-endowed by fortune in his own nature—for he was noble in appearance, tall, and possessed great grace and decorum in both...

...some on the ninth day: *They perform sacred rites for the dead according to the number nine, and some bestow names on the newborn on the ninth day. 35) **The Idaean Cave**] That this cave was consecrated to **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus</note> by the **Curetes** <note>Mythical armed dancers who protected the infant Zeus by clashing their shields to drown out his cries</note> is attested in the book *On the Cave of the Nymphs*: namely, because Jupiter was born there, hidden by the Curetes, and nourished by **Adrastea**, the sister of the Curetes, and by bees. As **Apollonius Rhodius** <note>The author of the Argonautica, an epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts</note> among others testifies in Book II, line 1237, and Book III, line 134. However, in this latter passage, the **Scholiast** <note>An ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes in the margins of manuscripts</note> doubts whether the name was derived from the mountain **Ida** in **Crete** or rather from the one in **Troy**, because the Trojans, he says, also claim the cradle of Jupiter for themselves. Certainly, Apollonius did not doubt it, as in the former passage he simply calls it the **Cretan cave**. **Antoninus Liberalis** <note>A Greek mythographer of the 2nd century AD</note> in chapter 19 relates that this cave was consecrated to the bees who were the nurses of Jupiter; he should be consulted regarding the nature of this cave.

->*Zan lies in this tomb, who is commonly called Jupiter.*<- <note>original: "Zan iacet hoc tumulo, qui vulgo Iupiter audit." Zan is an ancient name for Zeus. <margin>36) the customary threefold rites</margin> I have restored this passage from **Cyril** <note>Cyril of Alexandria, an influential 5th-century theologian</note> in this way, because the meaning seemed more appropriate. <margin>37) epigram</margin> **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note> mentions the same inscription in his *3rd Homily on the Epistle to Titus*: *“The Cretans possess a tomb of Zeus bearing this inscription: ‘Here lies Zan, whom they call Zeus.’ On account of this inscription, the poet <note>Callimachus</note> mocked the Cretans as liars, etc.”* The **Scholiast on Callimachus** <note>An ancient commentator on the works of the poet Callimachus</note> relates it differently: *“In Crete, it was inscribed on the tomb of Minos: **THE TOMB OF MINOS, SON OF ZEUS.** In the course of time, the name of Minos was erased, so that only **THE TOMB OF ZEUS** remained. From this, they say, the Cretans claim to have the tomb of Zeus.”* In Crete, it was inscribed on the tomb of Minos: **THE TOMB OF MINOS, SON OF JUPITER.** *However, the name of Minos was extinguished by the passage of time, so that there remained,* **THE TOMB OF JUPITER.** *Hence the Cretans say they possess the tomb of Jupiter.*

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

...both in his character and in the other gestures of his body: the city of the **Crotonians** <note>A Greek colony in southern Italy where Pythagoras founded his school</note> was so moved that, after he had captured the minds of the elders (of whom the city’s magistracy was composed) and held a long and brilliant discourse before the young boys, he then, by order of the magistrate, delivered exhortations to the youth. Afterward, he spoke to the children who flocked to him in crowds from the **literary schools** <note>original: "ludis literariis" — elementary schools where reading and writing were taught</note>; and finally even to the women, for a female assembly was also gathered for his sake. By this deed, his fame spread far and wide, and he gained many listeners—partly from that city, and not only men, but also women, the name of one of whom was **Theano**...

...concerning the assembly of the women, it was already a source of great wonder. For do you not see that when the ear is filled with the pleasure of an instrument and melodic music, it is satisfied? But when it reaches a point of satiety, it then longs for the flute and listens to the reed-pipe with pleasure. And yet, what connection is there between a flute and musical strings, or the wonderful sound of the instrument's sweetest quality? So it is with you and the **mistress** <note>original: "ἑταίρας" — a *hetaira*, or high-status female companion</note> with whom your husband lives. For your husband will care for you by relation, by nature, and by reason. But when he occasionally reaches a point of satiety, he will live with the mistress only in passing, because even in those in whom a **destructive humor** <note>original: "χυμὸς φθοροποιὸς" — a reference to the Four Humors theory of medicine, suggesting an unhealthy physical craving</note> resides, there is a certain craving for foods that are not good. May you live strongly.

### *The Letters of Theano to her Friends,*

->*Greetings to Eurydice.*<-

What grief has invaded your soul? For it is tormented by nothing else than the fact that he, with whom you live in companionship, is visiting a **common mistress** <note>original: "meretriculam" — a diminutive and disparaging term for a prostitute</note> and satisfying his bodily pleasure through her. But it is not at all fitting for you to be so affected, O glory of women—or rather, a miracle.

## (22) ...his name became widely known; and many kings and potentates from the neighboring barbarian land—

Nonne enim vides <note>This Latin passage is a commentary or translation of a lost Greek original, likely from a letter attributed to Theano regarding marital conduct.</note>, for do you not see that the ear, when it is filled with the delight of a musical instrument, is also satisfied by musical harmony? But when satiety takes hold of it, it longs for the flute and listens to the reed-pipe with pleasure. And yet, what does a flute have in common with musical strings or the wonderful sound of the sweetest instrument? You should think the same regarding yourself and the **mistress** <note>original: "meretrice" — used here to refer to a *hetaira* or outside companion</note> whom your husband enjoys. For your husband will care for you by the impulse of marital duty, nature, and reason. But if satiety should ever take hold of him, he will then turn to the company of a mistress; for those whose sense of taste for food is corrupted are also accustomed to crave even the worst things.

### To Timasonides.
And what business have I with you? Why do you constantly slander us? Or do you not know that we praise you before everyone, even if you do the opposite to us? But know this in turn: even if we praise you, there is no one who believes it; and even if you slander us, there is no one who listens. And I rejoice for this reason, because God sees us in this way, and **Truth** <note>original: "ἡ ἀλήθεια" — often personified in Pythagorean thought as the ultimate judge</note> most especially sits in judgment.

### To Timasonides.
And what business have I with you? Why do you constantly slander me? Do you not know that we praise you everywhere, even if you do the opposite? But know this: although we praise you, no one believes us; and although you slander us, no one gives you an ear. Therefore I rejoice, because God looks upon us thus, and truth most especially judges between us.

### To Eucleides the Physician.
Someone was crippled in the leg yesterday, and a messenger came to call for you. She was present as well, for the wounded man was one of our acquaintances. But the messenger returned quickly, saying that the physician himself was ill and his body was in pain. And I—I swear by the gods!—setting aside my concern for that acquaintance, kept the physician in my mind. I entreated **Panacea** <note>The Greek goddess of universal healing</note> and **Apollo of the Famed Bow** <note>original: "Κλυτότοξον Ἀπόλλωνα" — Apollo was the father of Asclepius and a god of both plague and healing</note> that nothing distressing should happen to the physician. And yet, though I am discouraged, I write these few syllables to you, wishing to learn how you are.

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

...is most illustrious: partly from the neighboring barbarian region: indeed, even the kings themselves and—

...unless the opening of your stomach has been damaged, unless your liver has lost its heat, unless some organ of yours has suffered harm. Just as I, having looked down upon many of my own limbs <note>original: "πολλῶν σκελῶν" — likely a play on words suggesting she cares more for the doctor's health than the "legs" of those seeking treatment</note>, will welcome your dear health, O good doctor.

->To Euclid the physician.<-

Yesterday, when someone had broken a leg, a messenger came to summon you; for I was present myself, since the man who had received the injury was a friend of mine. But that messenger soon returned and affirmed that the doctor himself was unwell and was afflicted by a bodily illness. There, I swear by the gods, setting aside my concern for my friend's pain, I began to be anxious for the doctor. I beseeched Panacea <note>The goddess of universal remedy</note> and Apollo, famous for his quiver, that nothing worse should happen to the physician. And now, troubled in mind, I write these things to you, desiring to be assured that you are well: whether the opening of the stomach <term>ventriculi orificium</term> <note>In ancient medicine, this referred to the "mouth" of the stomach or the cardia, often thought to be the seat of various ailments</note> is poorly affected, whether the heat of the liver is diminished, or whether any part of the body serving as an instrument is injured. Thus I, neglecting the many legs of my friends, would prefer your dear health, O best of doctors.

->To Rhodope the philosopher.<-

Are you discouraged? I too am discouraged. Are you distressed because I have not yet sent you Plato’s book, which is titled *The Ideas*, or *Parmenides* <note>The mention of Plato (c. 427–347 BCE) indicates these letters were written long after the historical Theano, who lived in the 6th century BCE</note>? But I too am most vexed that no one has yet met us to discuss the man from Ceos. For I would not have sent the book to you before someone arrived to clarify matters concerning such a man; for I am exceedingly in love with his soul—on one hand as a philosopher, and on the other because I fear the gods of the underworld—and you must not think what is being said is a mere story. For I am half-dead <note>original: "Ἡμίθνητος" — a hyperbolic expression of exhaustion or spiritual longing</note>, and I cannot bear to look upon this star of the upper air.

->To Rhodope the philosopher.<-

Are you tormented in mind? I too am tormented. You take it badly that I have not yet sent you the book of Plato which is inscribed *On Ideas*, or *Parmenides*; but I myself take it very badly that no one has yet come from Ceos who [might discuss] with me...

# PORPHYRY

...standing. What he used to say to his associates, no one can say for certain; for the silence <margin>(23)</margin> among them was no ordinary thing. However, the following <margin>(24)</margin> became most well-known to everyone: first, that he says the soul is immortal; next, that it changes into other kinds of living beings; further...

---

...would speak: for I cannot send the book to you until someone comes who can give me information about that man. For I love his soul desperately, partly as that of a wise man, partly as one who never ceases to do good, and partly because I fear the earthly gods. Do not think that what I say are mere words: for I am half-dead, and I cannot bear the sight of this daylight star <note>original: "diurni huius sideris" — a poetic reference to the sun</note>.

39) **Silence**] <note>original: "σιωπή"</note> Rittershusius has said enough about Pythagorean silence in this place, as has the illustrious Andreas Schottus in Book 2 of *On the Benefit of Silence*. From this also comes the proverb, "I shall be even more silent than those initiated by Pythagoras," <note>original: "καὶ σιωπηλότερος ἔσομαι τῶν Πυθαγόρα τελεσθέντων"</note> used for very quiet men, found in the writings of Suidas. Philostratus writes in Book 1, chapters 5 and 9, that a five-year silence was observed by Apollonius of Tyana according to the ancient Pythagorean custom; he testifies to its difficulty in these most elegant words: "this became the most laborious life for him, being practiced for five whole years; having many things to say but not saying them; hearing many things in anger but not listening; and though provoked to rebuke many, saying to himself, 'Endure, then, O heart and tongue'; and when arguments struck him, he let the refutations pass by." Where he also records this: that during the time of "vowed silence" <term>echimythia</term> <note>original: "ἐχιμυθίας" — a specific term for the Pythagorean vow of restraint in speech</note> he was accustomed to associate and converse with friends through signs and nods of the head. Diogenes Laërtius reports that the philosopher Xenocrates also dedicated an hour each day to silence and meditation. Saint Ambrose also praises this Pythagorean custom in his brilliant commentary on Psalm 119:9.

40) **The immortal soul**] <note>original: "ἀθάνατον τὴν ψυχήν"</note> Thus Porphyry himself in Stobaeus, in the *Physical Selections*, in the chapter "On the State of Souls after Death": *“The permanence and eternity of the soul is among the best known of all Pythagorean doctrines to everyone.”* <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς διαμονὴ καὶ ἀϊδιότης ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα τῶν Πυθαγορικῶν δογμάτων γνώριμόν ἐστι πᾶσιν"</note>

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

<insert><unclear>The Lords presided</unclear></insert> <note>original Latin: "Sederunt Domini" — this appears to be a later administrative or legal jotting in the margin of the manuscript, unrelated to the biography of Pythagoras.</note>

...noblemen. However, as to what he handed down to his listeners, no one can affirm with certainty. For a great and careful silence was maintained among them. But these things have become common knowledge among all: first, indeed, that he affirmed the soul to be immortal; then, that it passes into different kinds of living beings; and in addition,

this was widely celebrated. It is said that when someone told him, "I thought I saw my deceased father in my sleep," he replied, "You did not think you saw him; you actually saw him." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔδοξας, ἀλλ᾽ εἶδες"</note> *It is known to anyone that the soul's permanence and eternal nature were among the principal dogmas of Pythagoras. To a certain person who said he seemed to see his late father in a dream, they say he replied: you did not seem to see him, you saw him.* Regarding this same Pythagorean dogma, Diodorus Siculus writes in the beginning of Book 18: *Pythagoras of Samos and certain others of the ancient natural philosophers declared that the souls of humans are immortal,* etc. Cicero, in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, says that Pherecydes of Syros was the first among the Greeks to affirm this. But I shall soon show by the authority of Herodotus that Pythagoras drew this dogma, as well as those that follow, from the Magi <term>Magi: Ancient Persian priests and sages known for their astronomical and philosophical knowledge</term> and the Egyptians.

41) **Changing into other kinds of animals**] <note>original Greek: "μεταβάλλουσαν εἰς ἄλλα γένη ζώων"</note> *Thus the Vatican manuscript,* which I approve of more than "other human bodies." For Pythagoras and Plato believed that souls were introduced not only into other human bodies, but also into the bodies of brute animals. Besides others, Porphyry himself, in the place cited from Stobaeus, confirms this by the authority of Homer, where he relates that the companions of Ulysses were changed into swine. To this you may also add Macrobius, Book 1 of his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 9. Among the later Pythagoreans and Platonists, there were divergences of opinion, about which Proclus writes in Book 5 of his *Commentary on the Timaeus*, page 329. *The question is usually asked,* he says, *how souls are said to descend into brute animals. Some believe that there are certain similarities between humans and animals, which they call "feral lives" <term>feral lives: the idea that a human soul doesn't literally become an animal, but lives a life ruled by animalistic instincts</term>. For they argue that a rational substance can by no means become the soul of a wild animal.* Others, however, concede that it is actually sent into the brutes themselves, for they believe all souls are of one and the same kind; and so...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagoras's secret doctrines, transitioning from the immortality of the soul to the concepts of universal kinship and the "eternal return"—the idea that history repeats itself in cycles. # PORPHYRIUS

## (25) and besides these things, [he taught] that according to certain cycles the things that happen once happen again, and nothing is simply new; and that we must consider all living things that are born to be of the same kin. For it appears...

...into wolves, and leopards, and mongooses <note>original Latin: "ichneumones" — specifically the Egyptian mongoose, which ancient naturalists believed fought snakes and crocodiles</note> they may become. However, the true reasoning asserts that the human soul is indeed sent into brute animals, yet in such a way that those animals maintain their own proper life, and the "sent-in" soul is, as it were, "carried upon" the animal life, being bound to it by an inclination of affection and similarity. This has been proven by us with many arguments in the commentaries on the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and beauty</note>: that this is the only possible mode of entry. 

But if it is necessary to maintain that this is the opinion of Plato, one should add that in the *Republic* <term>Politia: Plato's *Republic*</term> he says that the soul of Thersites <note>In Greek mythology, a soldier known for being ugly and disruptive</note> "put on" a monkey, but not the *body* of a monkey; and in the *Phaedrus*, he says the soul descends into a "wild life," not into a "wild body." For life is joined with its own proper soul. And in this place, he says the soul is changed into a "wild nature": for a wild nature is not a wild body, but a wild life. But this, as I said, must be sought from the commentaries on the *Phaedrus*. 

I have written these things here in Latin because I know that this wonderful work is read by few, and understood by even fewer. 

The Rabbis of the Hebrews hold the same opinion concerning the "incorporation" of the soul, or its return, which is asserted in more than one place in the Talmudic book *Bava Metzia* <note>original: "Baua Meziha" — a tractate of the Talmud dealing with civil law, though here cited for its mystical passages</note>. I myself have heard them stubbornly defending this opinion through the story of Nebuchadnezzar and the words of Psalm 21, verse 21: *Deliver my soul from the sword; my only one from the hand of the dog.* By these words, they affirmed that the Prophet was seeking this from God: that his soul, once freed from the body, should not be plunged again into a dog or some other brute animal—a commentary truly worthy of those triflers! 

Furthermore, Herodotus in his second book is the authority for the claim that the Egyptians were the first to affirm that the human soul is immortal, and that it periodically migrates into one animal after another; and when it has traveled through all creatures of land, sea, and air, it enters again into a human body. He says this cycle is completed within three thousand years. He also adds that certain Greeks borrowed these opinions from the Egyptians and sold them as their own. Others defined the circuit of the soul by different periods of time. Proclus, following Porphyry, recorded in the first book of his commentary on the *Timaeus* (page 45) that the cycle lasts ten thousand years. Add to this Macrobius, in his first book on the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 9.

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

...that after certain cycles of time, the same events that once occurred happen again, and nothing is entirely new; and that all living beings are to be considered kin to one another and of the same species.

---

42) **according to cycles** <note>original Greek: *kata periodous*</note>] Pythagoras seems to have learned these things from the Magi <note>Persian priests and scholars renowned in antiquity for their knowledge of astronomy and theology</note>, to whom Diogenes Laërtius attributes this doctrine on the authority of Theopompus. For the latter says in the preface of his work: *He also asserts that, according to the Magi, men will return to life and be immortal, and that all things endure through their own revolutions.* <note>original Greek: "ὃς καὶ ἀναβιώσεσθαι κατὰ τοὺς Μάγους φηὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ἔσεσθαι ἀθανάτους καὶ τὰ ὄντα ταῖς αὐτῶν ἐπικυκλήσεσι διαμένειν."</note> This is how the passage should be read; for the word "invocations" <note>original Greek: *epiklēsesi*</note>, which appears in the common manuscripts, is a most foul reading <note>The translator is correcting a common scribal error where "revolutions" was miscopied as "invocations"</note>. Proclus, in Book I of his commentary on the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato</note>, page 39, writes: *In the universe as a whole, you might observe the same thing if you consider that all things which come into being also perish; they yield to the cosmic cycles and to the revolutions of the whole of life; and when these cycles join with one another, they produce a single, continuous life.* See also page 9 of the same work. The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy</note> also determined that similar cycles of events occur in the circuit of the Great Year <term>Magnus Annus: a vast period of time after which the planets return to the same positions and history repeats</term>; concerning these, see among others Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XV, chapter 19. The Emperor Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, in Book XI, calls this "the periodic rebirth of all things" <note>original Greek: "τὴν περιοδικὴν παλιγγενεσίαν τῶν ὅλων"</note>.

43) **living things are of the same kind** <note>original Greek: *ta empsycha homogenē*</note>] This is the foundation of the Pythagorean abstinence <term>apochē: the practice of refraining from eating animal flesh</term>, by which the philosopher exhorted his followers to the observation of justice and "every honor due to one's kin," according to the testimony of Iamblichus in Book 2. This argument is treated at great length by Porphyry himself in his work *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, especially in Book 3, where he attempts to prove—following the mind of Pythagoras—that every soul participating in sense and memory is rational. He argues that the souls of animals are of the same substance <term>homoousios: sharing the same essential nature</term> as our own, and do not differ in their essence, but only in the degree to which they participate more or less in reason. Plutarch treats the same argument in his book *On the Cleverness of Animals*. He also, in Book IV of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapter 7, records among the decrees of Pythagoras that "the soul, upon departing, withdraws into the soul of the universe toward that which is of its own kind."

<summary>This page explains two pillars of Pythagorean thought: the concept of the "eternal return" where history repeats in cosmic cycles, and the belief that all sentient beings share a rational soul, which forms the ethical basis for vegetarianism.</summary>

# PORPHYRIUS

...Pythagoras was the first to bring these doctrines to Greece. He so turned all eyes toward himself that, with only a single lecture given upon his arrival in Italy (as Nikomachos <note>A mathematician and follower of Pythagorean thought from the 1st century AD</note> says), he won over more than <margin>20</margin> two thousand people with his words. These people did not return home, but instead, along with their children and wives, they established a massive <margin>(26)</margin> **communal auditorium** <term>homakoeion: a place for gathered listening or a shared lecture hall</term> and settled that part of Italy which became known by all as "Great Greece" <note>original Latin: *Magna Graecia*</note>. ---

44) **communal auditorium** <note>original Greek: *homakoeion*</note>] This was the specific name given to the school of the Pythagoreans. Clement of Alexandria, in Book I of his *Miscellanies* <note>original Latin: *Stromata*</note>, says regarding Pythagoras: *And even the assembly called by that name today is an allusion to his communal auditorium.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν νῦν οὕτω καλουμένην τὸ παρ’ αὐτῷ ὁμακόϊον αἰνίττεται."</note> Hierocles, at the end of his commentary on Pythagoras, says that the *Golden Poem* is not the memoir of a single Pythagorean, but of the whole sacred gathering—or, as they themselves would say, the common utterance of the entire **communal auditorium**. For this is how translators correctly read the text, instead of "common union." Also, Proclus in Book I of his commentary on the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato</note>: *Is it not a Pythagorean trait that different levels of hearing were defined? For among those who attended the communal auditorium, some grasped the deeper doctrines, while others touched upon those closer to the surface.* *Is it not also a Pythagorean practice that distinct levels of listening were established? For among those who frequented the common lecture hall, some perceived more profound teachings, and others more superficial ones.* From this, the listeners of Pythagoras themselves were called by the common name "fellow listeners" <note>original Greek: *homakoöi*</note>, according to Iamblichus in Book I, chapter 17: *For this is what all those around the man were called.* For it should be read as "called" <note>original Greek: *ekalounto*</note> rather than "were spoken" <note>original Greek: *elalounto*</note>, which spoils the meaning.

45) **possessions in common** <note>original Greek: *tas ousias koinas*</note>] This institution he also transferred from foreign peoples <note>The author uses "barbarians" to mean non-Greeks, likely referring to Egyptian or Babylonian influences</note> to his own way of life. For almost all those in any nation who have striven for a more perfect way of life above the common crowd have abdicated the private use of goods and made them common with others. Examples and reasons for this matter from sacred and profane [history]...
