# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

For Pythagoras was the first of all, it seems, to bring these doctrines into Greece. And he so turned all people toward himself that, according to the account of Nicomachus <note>A mathematician and Pythagorean biographer from the 1st century AD</note>, by a single discourse which he delivered upon his first arrival in Italy, he captured more than two thousand people with his oratory. So that they would no longer be away from home, they established, together with their children and wives, a certain communal auditorium <term>homakoeion: a shared space for learning and living</term> of vast size; and they occupied that part of Italy which is commonly called "Great Greece," having founded cities there. They also received laws and statutes from him as if they were divine precepts, and it was considered a sin to do anything contrary to them. These same people [held] their goods... <note>The sentence concludes on the next page, likely referring to communal property.</note>

<note>The following section appears in a smaller typeface, functioning as a commentary or footnote block.</note>

...[evidence from] antiquity is available. And indeed, if we must begin with the myths, the poets count this also among the other benefits of the Golden Age: that there was a common use of all things, and that this was not entirely abolished even under the Silver Age of Jupiter. For this reason, Jupiter is also believed to be the leader and protector of "those living as citizens according to the best constitution, which makes all things common" <note>original Greek: τῶν πολιτικῶς ζώντων κατὰ τὴν ἀρίστην πολιτείαν τὴν πάντα κοινὰ τιθεμένην</note>, as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> testifies in his commentary on Hesiod's *Works and Days*, Book I. The philosophers do not stray far from the opinion of the poets: for Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle</note>, cited in Porphyry's *On Abstinence*, Book IV, catalogs three types of life in the same manner. The first of these he himself calls "Golden"; the second he calls the nomadic [life] <note>original Greek: τὸ νομαδικὸν</note>, and the third the agricultural [life] <note>original Greek: τὸ γεωργικόν</note>. But although he asserts that in the second type of life, the desire for possession turned public wealth into private property, it is nevertheless well-established that many nomadic peoples maintained the shared use of resources. Concerning the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note> beyond the Maeotian Lake <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, there are beautiful verses by Scymnus of Chios, an ancient geographer, which—along with many others—have not been published until now:

> For one crossing the Panticapes river <note>A river in ancient Scythia</note>, there is a nation of marsh-dwellers,
> And many others besides, who remain unnamed,
> They are called "Nomads," and they are truly pious,
> So much so that they would never harm any living soul <note>original Greek: Τὸν Παντικάπη διαβάντι λιμναίων ἔθνος... Ὡς οὐδὲν ἐμψύχων ἀδικῆσαί ποτ᾽ ἄν</note>.

*Which I have translated as follows:*
> *Both groups dwell near the Panticapes marsh,*
> *And many others not known by their own names:*
> *The common folk call them Nomads, exceedingly pious,*
> *So that they bring no harm even to living creatures:*
> *And in wagons, as he asserts, they drag their wandering homes:*
> *And in the Scythian rite they live on the milk of mares:*
> *They lead a life sustained by communal goods,*
> *And hold all wealth in public for the use of all:*

Regarding the Essenes <note>A Jewish sect known for their asceticism and communal lifestyle</note>, Porphyry himself writes in Book IV of *On Abstinence*, quoting Flavius Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>. "They despise riches," he says, "and the communion of all things among them is wonderful; nor will you find anyone who excels others in wealth. For whoever enters the sect is ordered by law to make his goods public. Hence it happens that neither the filth of poverty nor the splendor of riches appears among them, since with the resources of individuals mixed together, there is one and the same possession for all as if for brothers."

The customs of the Samanaeans among the Indians <note>A group of ancient Indian wandering ascetics</note> and the Egyptian priests were not dissimilar; our author mentions them in the quoted passage, and others should also be consulted. Among the Greeks, Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> introduced, if not a total communion of goods, at least an equal possession of them. He also established public and communal meals, which were called *syssitia* <term>communal meals intended to foster civic unity</term> and *phiditia* <term>spartan "frugal meals" or "friendship meals"</term>, "so as to dine meeting with one another over common and prescribed side-dishes and foods," <note>original Greek: ὥστε δειπνεῖν μετ' ἀλλήλων συνιόντας ἐπὶ κοινοῖς καὶ τεταγμένοις ὄψοις καὶ σιτίοις</note> says Porphyry. Furthermore, *phiditia* were so named, according to the same witness, "as being the causes of friendship and kindliness" <note>original Greek: ὡς φιλίας καὶ φιλοφροσύνης ὑπάρχοντα αἴτια</note>; for which each month individuals contributed equally from their own goods.

But Plato, since he had proposed to himself the doctrine and institutions of Pythagoras to be imitated in almost everything, also brought the communion of goods into his Republic—that is, into [the life] of men [dedicated to] wisdom... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.
1.

->...they contributed to the common fund; and among the followers of Pythagoras...<-

...he admitted a society of those dedicated to studies, established according to a divine model and in the likeness of the entire universe. For those are mistaken who think that Plato <note>The famous Greek philosopher and student of Socrates</note> wished to introduce the common use of all things in just any state. They are mistaken, I say, because Plato’s purpose was to present to mortals a model of a life as happy as possible and most like God, conceived through the reflections of the mind. Therefore, since he had learned that God is not only content with himself and self-sufficient, requiring no external thing—being, in other words, the most fertile fountain of all good—but also spreads himself and his goodness to others and, as he himself says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>, shares them without envy; so he believed a man would be most blessed, both in public and in private, if he were conformed to the example of divine goodness and held his goods in common with as many as possible. He judged that through this communion, one approaches most closely to the likeness of divine unity. From this unity, one departs further the more each person is drawn toward some particular and private good. Thus Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato</note> writes in Book 1 of his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 14: *Why then is there such striving for particular goods among men? Because they possess a life immersed in material things, and falling away from the whole, they are carried toward the particular. For because of this, the terms "mine" and "not mine" are frequent among them, while the union and communion of life has failed.* <note>original Greek: Διὰ τί οὖν παρ’ ἀνθρώποις μεριστῶς ταῦτα σπουδάζεται; διότι ζωὴν ἔχουσιν ἔνυλον, καὶ πρὸς τὸ μερικὸν ἀποτείνονται τοῦ ὅλου ἀποστάντες. Διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο τὸ ἐμὸν καὶ οὐκ ἐμὸν πολὺ παρ’ αὐτοῖς, ἕνωσις δὲ καὶ κοινωνία ζωῆς ἐκλέλοιπεν.</note> More can be read in his work, by which Plato’s mind is clearly explained. And indeed, if we weigh the matter correctly, we shall see that every human society is all the happier and more peaceful the greater the equality and communion of goods flourishes among all; where not just a few overflow with wealth while the rest are oppressed by want—which is usually the most certain sign of an unjust and tyrannical rule. I say nothing of the community of wives <note>A reference to a controversial proposal in Plato's "Republic" regarding the shared families of the guardian class</note>. It will be worthwhile, however, to see what Cardinal Bessarion <note>A 15th-century titular Latin Patriarch of Constantinople and a key figure in the revival of Greek letters in the West</note> wrote in Book IV, Chapter 3, of his never-sufficiently-praised work against Trapezuntius <note>George of Trebizond, a scholar who criticized Plato</note>, the *Scourge of Plato* <note>original: Πλατωνομάστιγα (Platonomastiga)</note>. Furthermore, among Christians, no less...

### To Timasonides.

And what business do I have with you? Why do you always slander us? Do you not know that we praise you before all people, even if you do the contrary? But know this in turn: even if we praise you, there is no one who believes us; and even if you slander us, there is no one who listens. And I rejoice because of this, because God sees it thus, and Truth especially judges.

### *To Euclid the physician.*

Yesterday, when a certain man had broken his leg, someone came to fetch you. I was present myself, as the man who suffered the wound was a friend of mine. But the messenger soon returned and stated that the doctor himself was unwell and distressed by physical sickness. At that point—I swear by the gods—dismissing my friend’s pain, I began to be worried about the doctor. I prayed to **Panacea** <note>The goddess of universal remedy.</note> and to **Apollo**, famous for his quiver <note>Apollo was both the god of healing and the god whose arrows brought plague; the writer appeals to both sides of his power.</note>, that nothing worse should happen to the physician. And now, distressed in spirit, I write these things to you, desiring to be certain of your health: whether the opening of your stomach is poorly affected, whether the heat of your liver is diminished, or if some part of the body serving its functions is injured. Thus I, neglecting many legs of my friends, would prefer your dear health, O best of doctors.

### To Rhodope the philosopher.

Are you discouraged? I too am discouraged. You are distressed because I have not yet sent you Plato’s book, which is titled *On Ideas*, or *Parmenides*. But I too am most distressed that no one from **Keos** <note>An island in the Cyclades associated with the philosopher Prodicus and the poet Simonides.</note> has yet come to discuss things with us. For I would not have sent the book to you before someone arrived to clarify the words of such a man; for I love his soul exceedingly, both as a philosopher and out of fear of the gods of the underworld. Do not think what I say is a mere tale. For I am **half-dead**, and I cannot bear to look upon this star of airy light <note>Referring to the sun; the writer is so overwhelmed by illness or melancholy that light itself is painful.</note>.

39) **Silence** <note>original Greek: *σιωπή*</note>] Concerning Pythagorean silence, Rittershusius <note>Conrad Rittershusius (1560–1613), a German jurist and scholar who commented on Porphyry.</note> provides enough detail in this passage, as does the illustrious Andreas Schott in Book 2 of *On the Benefit of Silence*. Diogenes Laërtius records that the philosopher Xenocrates also dedicated an hour each day to silence and meditation. Saint Ambrose also praises this Pythagorean institution in his brilliant commentary on Psalm 119:9.

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

But these points are common knowledge to all: first indeed, that he affirmed the **soul is immortal**; second, that it **enters into different kinds of living beings**; additionally,

---

it is widely renowned. To a man who said, "I seemed to see my deceased father in my sleep," they say he replied, "You did not seem, but you actually saw him." *That the soul endures and is eternal is known to everyone as being among the principal doctrines of Pythagoras. It is reported that he answered a certain man who said he seemed to see his father, who had departed life, in his dreams: "You did not seem to see him, but you saw him."* <note>The text provides this anecdote in both Greek and Latin to emphasize the Pythagorean belief that the "spirit" seen in dreams is a real, persisting entity, not a mere hallucination.</note> Regarding the same Pythagorean doctrine, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> says at the beginning of Book 18: *Pythagoras the Samian and certain others of the ancient natural philosophers declared that the souls of men exist as immortal,* etc. Cicero, in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, says that Pherecydes of Syros <note>An early Greek thinker often cited as Pythagoras' teacher.</note> was the first among the Greeks to affirm this. But I will soon show, by the authority of Herodotus <note>The famous Greek historian who suggested Greek religious ideas often originated in the East.</note>, that Pythagoras also drew this doctrine, along with those that follow, from the Magi <note>Persian priests/scholars.</note> and the Egyptians.

**41)** **changing into other kinds of animals** <note>original Greek: "μεταβάλλουσαν εἰς ἄλλα γένη ζώων"</note>] This is the reading in the Vatican Manuscript, which I approve of more than "other human bodies." For Pythagoras and Plato believed that souls were introduced not only into other human bodies, but also into the bodies of brute animals. Porphyry himself, in the passage cited from Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of Greek wisdom.</note>, confirms this even by the authority of Homer, where he recounts the companions of Ulysses being changed into swine. To this you may also add Macrobius <note>A Roman writer whose work on the "Dream of Scipio" preserved much Neoplatonic thought.</note> in Book 1 of his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 9. Among later Pythagoreans and Platonists there were diversions of opinion, concerning which Proclus <note>A late antique philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy.</note> says in Book 5 of his *Commentary on the Timaeus*, page 329: "It is usually asked," he says, "how souls are said to descend into brute animals. Some indeed think there are certain likenesses of humans to animals, which they call **ferine lives** <note>Lives characterized by wild or animalistic behavior rather than actual animal bodies.</note>. For a rational substance can in no way become the soul of a wild animal. Others, however, grant that it is actually sent into the brutes themselves: for all souls are of one and the same genus; so that also..."

# PORPHYRY

...to these doctrines he adds, that after certain periods of time, the events which once occurred happen again, and nothing is ever absolutely new; and that we must believe all living things brought into being are of the same kind. For it appears that into...

---

...wolves, leopards, and mongooses they may become. <note>The commentator is discussing the various animal forms a soul might inhabit.</note> However, the true explanation asserts that the human soul is indeed sent into brute animals, yet in such a way that those animals maintain their own proper life, and the infused soul is, as it were, carried upon it <note>original Latin: "superinuehatur"</note>, and is linked to it by an inclination and similarity of disposition. We have proven this by many arguments in our commentaries on the *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato’s dialogues concerning the soul and its journey.</note>: namely, that this is the only mode of entry. 

Moreover, if it is necessary to maintain that this was Plato's view, it should be added that in the *Republic* <note>original Latin: "Politia"</note> he says the soul of Thersites <note>A Greek soldier in the Trojan War, often depicted as ugly and low-born.</note> "put on" the character of an ape, but not the physical body of an ape; and in the *Phaedrus*, that it descends into a "wild life," not into a "wild body." For life is joined with its own soul. And in this passage, he says it changes into a "wild nature" <note>original Latin: "ferinam naturam"</note>; for a "wild nature" is not a physical wild body, but a wild way of living. 

But as I said, this must be sought from the commentaries on the *Phaedrus*. I have written these things here in Latin because I know that magnificent work is read by few, and understood by even fewer. 

The Hebrew Rabbis hold the same opinion concerning the embodiment of the soul, or its return, which is asserted in more than one place in the Talmudic book *Bava Metzia* <note>original Latin: "Baua Meziha"; a section of the Talmud primarily dealing with civil law, though the commentator here cites it for mystical traditions.</note>. I myself have heard them tenaciously <note>original Latin: "mordicus", literally 'with the teeth'.</note> defending this opinion using the story of Nebuchadnezzar and the words of Psalm 21, verse 21: *Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog.* <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 22:20. The commentator is using the Vulgate numbering.</note> They affirmed by these words that the Prophet was seeking from God that his soul, once released from the body, should not be plunged again into a dog or some other brute animal—a fabrication surely worthy of such triflers. 

Furthermore, Herodotus in his second book is the authority for the claim that the Egyptians were the first to declare the human soul is immortal, and that it subsequently migrates from one animal to another; and when it has traveled through all creatures of the land, sea, and air, it enters again into a human body. He adds that this circuit is completed by the soul within three thousand years, and notes that some Greeks borrowed these opinions from the Egyptians and sold them as their own. Others defined the circuit of the soul by different spans of time. Proclus, citing Porphyry, recorded it as being ten thousand years in the first book of his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 45. See also Macrobius, Book 1 of his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 9.

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

...that after certain cycles of time, the same things that once were happen again, and nothing is completely new; and all living things should be considered related to one another and of the same kind.

---

42) **According to the periods** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ περιόδους"</note>] Pythagoras seems to have learned these things from the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and sages</note>, to whom Diogenes Laërtius attributes this doctrine on the authority of Theopompus. For the latter says in the preface of his work: **Who also says that, according to the Magi, men shall live again and be immortal, and that all things endure through their revolutions.** <note>original Greek: "ὃς καὶ ἀναβιώσεσθαι κατὰ τοὺς Μάγους φησὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ἔσεσθαι ἀθανάτους καὶ τὰ ὄντα ταῖς αὐτῶν ἐπικυκλήσεσι διαμένειν"</note> This is how the passage should be read: for the word **by invocation** <note>original Greek: "ἐπικλήσει"</note>, which appears in the common manuscripts, is utterly nonsensical. Proclus, in Book I of his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 39, says: **In the whole of the universe, you might observe the same thing, considering that everything brought into being also perishes; it yields to the cosmic periods and to the cycles of the whole of life; and when the periods join together, they produce one continuous life.** <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ παντὸς τὸ αὐτο θεωρήσειας ἂν... καὶ μίαν καὶ συνεχῆ ζωὴν ἀποτελοῦσι"</note> See also the same author on page 9. The **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy</note> also maintained that similar cycles of events occur within the circuit of a Great Year: concerning which, see among others Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XV, chapter 19. The Emperor Marcus Antoninus, in Book XI, calls this **the periodic rebirth of all things.** <note>original Greek: "τὴν περιοδικὴν παλιγγενεσίαν τῶν ὅλων"</note>

43) **Living things of the same kind** <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἔμψυχα ὁμογενῆ"</note>] This is the foundation of the Pythagorean **abstinence** <note>original Greek: "ἀποχῆς," referring to their famous vegetarianism</note>, by which the philosopher exhorted his followers to the observation of justice and **every honor due to kindred life,** as Iamblichus witnesses in Book 2. This argument is treated at great length by Porphyry himself in his work *On Abstinence from Animal Food*: especially in Book 3, where he attempts to prove, following the mind of Pythagoras, that every soul participating in sense and memory is rational; and that the souls of living creatures are **of the same substance** <note>original Greek: "ὁμοουσίους"</note> as ours, differing not in essence, but only in the degree to which they participate more or less in reason. Plutarch treats the same argument in his book *On the Cleverness of Animals*. He also, in Book IV of *Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapter 7, records among the decrees of Pythagoras that **the soul, upon departing, withdraws into the soul of the universe toward that which is of its own kind.** <note>original Greek: "τὴν ψυχὴν ἐξιοῦσαν εἰς τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ἀναχωρεῖν πρὸς τὸ ὁμογενές"</note>

44) **Shared auditorium** <note>original Greek: "ὁμακόϊον" (homakoion)</note>] This was the specific name given to the school of the Pythagoreans. Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromata"</note>, says regarding Pythagoras: **"And he hints at the assembly now so-called by his own 'shared auditorium.'"** <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν νῦν οὕτω καλουμένην τὸ παρ’ αὐτῷ ὁμακόϊον αἰνίττεται"</note> Hierocles, near the end of his commentary on the *Pythagorean Golden Verses*, states that the *Golden Poem* is not the memoir of any single Pythagorean, but **"of the whole sacred gathering and, as they themselves would say, the common utterance of the entire shared auditorium."** <note>original Greek: "ὅλου δὲ τοῦ ἱεροῦ συλλόγου... ὁμακοΐου παντὸς ἀπόφθεγμα κοινόν"</note> For the editor correctly reads *homakoion* here, where previous interpreters read *homaiou*. And Proclus, in Book I of his commentary on the *Timaeus*, writes: **"How is it not Pythagorean that different levels of listening were defined? For among those attending the shared auditorium, some grasped the deeper doctrines, while others touched upon the more superficial ones."** <note>original Greek: "πῶς δὲ οὐ Πυθαγόρειον τὸ διάφορα μέτρα τῶν ἀκροάσεων ἀφωρίσθαι..."</note> Is this not also Pythagorean, that different grades of hearing were distinguished? For among those who frequented the common lecture hall, some perceived the more profound teachings, while others grasped the lighter ones. Consequently, the listeners of Pythagoras themselves were called by the common name **shared listeners** <note>original Greek: "ὁμάκοοι" (homakooi)</note>, according to the testimony of Iamblichus in Book I, chapter 17: **"For in this way, everyone around the man was named."** <note>original Greek: "οὕτω γὰρ ἐκαλοῦντο πάντες οἱ περὶ τὸν ἄνδρα"</note> This is the correct reading instead of "spoken of" <note>original Greek: "ἐλαλοῦντο"</note>, which ruins the sense.

45) **Communal property** <note>original Greek: "τὰς οὐσίας κοινὰς"</note>] This practice he also transferred from foreign peoples <note>original Latin: "barbaris," referring to non-Greeks such as the Egyptians or Persians</note> to his own **way of life** <note>original Greek: "διαγωγὴν"</note>. For almost as many as have striven for a more perfect kind of life above the common crowd in any nation, they abdicated the private use of goods and made them common with others. Examples and reasons for this matter from sacred and secular history...

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

For Pythagoras seems to have been the first of all to bring these doctrines into Greece. And he turned everyone toward himself to such an extent that, according to Nicomachus, in a single lecture which he held upon his first arrival in Italy, he captured more than two thousand people with his speech. So that they would no longer be away from home, they, together with their children and wives, established a certain communal auditorium of immense size; and they occupied that part of Italy which is commonly called **Great Greece** <note>original: "Magna Graecia," the name given by the Romans to the coastal areas of Southern Italy which were heavily populated by Greek settlers</note>, founding cities there. They also received laws and statutes from him as if they were divine commands, beyond which it was a sin to do anything. These same people [held] their goods...

<column-break/>

...[an]tiquity are available. And indeed, if we are to begin with myths, the poets, among other advantages of the **Golden Age** <note>a mythological period of peace, harmony, and prosperity when humanity lived in a state of nature</note>, also count this: that there was a communal use of all things, nor was this practice entirely abolished under the Silver Age of Jupiter. Hence Jupiter is also believed to be the leader and presiding officer **of those living a social life according to the best constitution, which sets all things in common** <note>original Greek: "τῶν πολιτικῶς ζώντων κατὰ τὴν ἀρίστην πολιτείαν τὴν πάντα κοινὰ τιθεμένην"</note>, according to the testimony of Proclus <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his commentary on Hesiod’s *Works and Days*, Book I. Philosophers do not stray far from the opinion of the poets: for Dicaearchus <note>a student of Aristotle</note>, as cited in the fourth book of Porphyry’s *On Abstinence*, reviews three types of life in the same way. Of these, he calls the first the **Golden** age; the second the **nomadic** <note>original Greek: "τὸ νομαδικὸν"</note>; and the third the **agricultural** <note>original Greek: "τὸ γεωργικόν"</note>. But although he asserts that in the second type, the desire for possession turned public wealth into private property, it is nevertheless well known that many nomadic nations maintained the shared use of things. Regarding the Scythians <note>ancient nomadic people of central Eurasia</note> beyond Lake Maeotis <note>the modern-day Sea of Azov</note>, there are beautiful verses by Scymnus of Chios <note>a Greek geographer from the 2nd century BCE</note>, which, along with many others, have not been published until now:

->Crossing the Panticapes river, one finds a nation of marsh-dwellers,<-
->And many others besides, not individually named,<-
->But whom we call **Nomads**, a most pious people,<-
->Inasmuch as they would never harm any living creature.<-

# PORPHYRY

...and [they regarded] Pythagoras after the gods.

->They are house-carriers, as has been said, and nourished<-
->By milk from the milking of Scythian horses.<-
->They live having declared their possessions<-
->Common to all, as well as their entire substance;<-
->And the wise Anacharsis <note>a 6th-century BCE Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens and became a symbol of the "noble savage" to the Greeks</note> from among the Nomads<-

Which I have translated thus:

->*Inhabitants on both sides of the Panticapen marsh,*<-
->*And many others not known by their own name;*<-
->*The common folk call them Nomads, a very pious people,*<-
->*Who bring no injury even to living creatures:*<-
->*And in wagons, as he asserts, they pull their wandering homes:*<-
->*In the Scythian fashion they live upon the milk of mares:*<-
->*They lead a life from communal goods,*<-
->*And hold all their resources as public for everyone:*<-
->*From these Nomads, a race most pious,*<-
->*Anacharsis is said to have been born, a wise man.*<-

Regarding the Essenes <note>a Jewish sect known for communal living and asceticism during the Second Temple period</note>, Porphyry himself says in Book IV of *On Abstinence*, drawing from Flavius Josephus: "They despise riches," he says, "and the sharing of all things among them is admirable; nor will you find anyone who surpasses the others in wealth. For whoever enters the sect is commanded by law to make his goods public. Thus it happens that neither the filth of poverty nor the splendor of riches appears among them, since the resources of individuals are mixed together and there is one and the same possession for all, just as for brothers." 

The institutions of the Samanaeans <note>a term used by Greek writers to describe Indian ascetics, likely Buddhist or Jain monks</note> among the Indians and of the Egyptian priests were not dissimilar, concerning whom our author should be consulted in the aforementioned place, and others as well. Among the Greeks, Lycurgus <note>the legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> introduced, if not a total sharing of goods, at least an equal possession, as well as a public and communal way of eating, which were called *communal meals* and *meals of friendship* <note>original: συσσίτια (syssitia) and φιδίτια (phiditia), the Spartan practice of common mess halls intended to foster equality and military camaraderie</note>, "so that they might dine together, meeting over common and prescribed portions of meat and grain," as Porphyry says. Moreover, they were called *phiditia*, according to the same witness, "as being the causes of friendship and kindliness" <note>original: ὡς φιλίας καὶ φιλοφροσύνης ὑπάρχοντα αἴτια</note>; for which each individual contributed equally from his own goods every month. 

But Plato, since he had proposed to himself that the teaching and institutions of Pythagoras should be imitated in almost all things, also introduced the sharing of goods into his own Republic—that is, into the lives of men of wisdom...

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

...they shared in common; and Pythagoras received among the society of those dedicated to studies a way of life established according to the divine model and the likeness of the entire universe.

For those people are mistaken who think that Plato <note>the famous Greek philosopher and student of Socrates</note> wished to introduce the common use of all things into just any city-state. They are mistaken, I say, because Plato’s purpose was to propose to mortals a model of a life as happy as possible and most like to God, conceived through the reflections of the mind. And therefore, since he had learned that God is not only content with himself and sufficient unto himself—needing no external thing, being the most abundant fountain of all good things—but that He also spreads Himself and His goods and, as Plato himself says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>, communicates them to others without envy; so he believed that a man would be most blessed, both publicly and privately, if he were conformed to the example of divine goodness and held his goods in common with as many people as possible. He believed that through this communion, one approaches most closely to the likeness of divine unity. One departs further from this unity the more each individual is drawn toward some particular and private good.

Thus Proclus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Plato’s works</note> says in Book 1 of his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 14: *Why then is there such zealous pursuit of these divided things among men? It is because they possess a life immersed in matter, and they reach for the particular part because they have stood apart from the whole. For this reason, the concepts of "mine" and "not mine" are frequent among them, while the union and communion of life has failed.* <note>original Greek: Διά τί οὖν παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις μεριστῶς ταῦτα σπουδάζεται; διότι ζωὴν ἔχουσιν ἔνυλον, καὶ πρὸς τὸ μερικόν ἀποτείνονται τοῦ ὅλου ἀποστάντες. Διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο τὸ ἐμὸν καὶ οὐκ ἐμὸν πολὺ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ἕνωσις δὲ καὶ κοινωνία ζωῆς ἐκλέλοιπεν.</note> More can be read in Proclus's own work, by which Plato’s mind is clearly explained. 

And indeed, if we weigh the matter correctly, we will certainly see that every human society is more happy and tranquil the more a greater equality and communion of goods flourishes among everyone; where it is not the case that a few overflow with riches while the rest are oppressed by poverty—which is usually the most certain mark of an unjust and tyrannical rule. I say nothing here about the communion of wives <note>a controversial proposal in Plato’s Republic that women and children should be shared by the guardian class to ensure total social cohesion</note>. However, it will be worthwhile to see what Cardinal Bessarion <note>a 15th-century scholar and Catholic cardinal who defended Platonism</note> wrote in Book IV, chapter 3 of his never-sufficiently-praised work against George of Trebizond, the <term>Platonomastix</term> <note>meaning "Scourge of Plato"; George of Trebizond was a fierce critic of Plato and Bessarion's intellectual rival</note>. Moreover, among Christians, it is not much dif—

# PORPHYRY

**(29) ...they counted. Therefore, one of the things among them...** <note>original Greek: κατηρίθμουν. διόπερ ἕν τι τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς. This is a fragment of the source text being commented upon.</note>

A similar sharing of goods seems not to have been introduced later, but was born together with religion itself, since it is certain that Christ our Savior had external means of life in common with his disciples. The sacred scriptures explicitly testify to this same institution in the primitive Church. The use or likeness of this communal living remained only among the <term>ascetics</term> <note>monks or those living a life of strict self-denial</note> as the fervor of charity cooled. I would not hesitate to affirm that this communion is no less a foundation of our religion than it was of the Pythagorean school; for we are commanded to pursue our neighbor with the same affection of union as ourselves. We believe that we have been appointed by God as both possessors and distributors of goods, and we place pious generosity toward others as the head of our profession and its chief virtue. Indeed, the many pious foundations and so many outstanding monuments of Christian charity, in which our religion glories above others, have no other origin or cause. But perhaps this is **"to throw one's foot beyond the steps,"** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ βαθμῶν πόδα ῥίπτειν. A Greek proverb meaning to overreach or to wander outside the bounds of the current argument.</note> according to the Greek proverb. Certainly, no one would deny that the Pythagoreans came very close to our religion through this sharing of goods, if one reads what Iamblichus <note>a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher</note> recorded in Book 1, chapter 33. Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer of Greek philosophers</note> testifies in Book 10 that Epicurus disapproved of this Pythagorean institution, because it seemed to be a practice of those who distrusted each other rather than friends. **"Epicurus did not think it right to put property into a common fund, as Pythagoras did, who said 'the things of friends are common.' For he held that such a thing belongs to those who distrust; and if to the distrustful, then not to friends."** <note>original Greek: Τόν τε Ἐπίκουρον μὴ ἀξιοῦν εἰς τὸ κοινὸν κατατίθεσθαι τὰς οὐσίας, καθάπερ τὸν Πυθαγόραν, κοινὰ τὰ τῶν φίλων λέγοντα. ἀπιστούντων γὰρ εἶναι τοιοῦτον, εἰ δ᾽ ἀπίστων, οὐ φίλων.</note> I confess I do not sufficiently see the force of this argument: for they brought their things together into a common pool so that there might be the opportunity for everyone to use them indiscriminately, not so they would be kept like a deposit on public faith. For one who distrusts another, like the comic character Euclio <note>the miserly protagonist of Plautus's play *Aulularia*</note>, hides his things at home and, like a dragon, broods alone over his treasures.

And Lucretius, in Book 5, shows that divine honors are owed by a better right to the inventors of wisdom than to others like Bacchus, or Hercules, and the like. Regarding Pythagoras, the same is testified by

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

...they counted as gods. And therefore, whenever—

Philostratus, at the beginning of his work *On the Life of Apollonius*, writes: "Whatever Pythagoras declared, his followers considered it a law, and they honored him as one come from Zeus." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὅτι ἀποφήναιτο Πυθαγόρας, νόμον τοῦτο οἱ ὁμιληταὶ ἡγοῦντο, καὶ ἐτίμων αὐτὸν ὡς ἐκ Διὸς ἥκοντα.</note> Furthermore, concerning the oath taken by the Pythagoreans by their teacher, Hierocles writes thus in his commentary on the *Golden Verses*, page 225: "Moreover, the oath itself becomes a doctrine for him, for the teacher of truth ought to be so honored that one should even swear by him, if there were ever a need to confirm the doctrines. And one should not only say of him, 'He himself said it' <note>The famous phrase <term>Ipse dixit</term> or original Greek: Αὐτὸς ἔφα, used to denote an unchallengeable authority.</note>, but also affirm that things are so by swearing 'Yes, by him.'" <note>original Greek: Ἔπειτα καὶ ὁ ὅρκος αὐτῷ γίνεται δόγμα, ὅτι τὸν διδάσκαλον τῆς ἀληθείας οὕτω δέοι τιμᾷν, ὡς καὶ ὀμνύναι αὐτὸν, εἴ του δέοι πρὸς βεβαίωσιν τῶν δογμάτων. καὶ μὴ μόνον τὸ Αὐτὸς ἔφα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει, Νὴ τὸν αὐτόν.</note> Furthermore, the oath is held as a doctrine for them: for such honor is to be granted to the teacher of truth that one swears by him, if ever there is a need for the confirmation of the doctrines: it is not enough to merely use the phrase "He himself said it" concerning him, but to affirm that the matter stands so by his very name. 

And on page 230, he says that the Pythagoreans observed oaths by the immortal gods with singular religious devotion; but they specifically swore by the master who had delivered the <term>quaternary</term> <note>the number four, known as the Tetractys, which Pythagoreans viewed as the root of all nature</note> to them; although he was neither of the number of the gods nor the heroes, "but a man adorned by a likeness to God, and preserving a divine image for those who came after him." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄνθρωπος ὁμοιώσει Θεοῦ κοσμηθεὶς, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ θείαν ἀποσῴζων εἰκόνα.</note> And by this oath, he says, it is silently implied in what great veneration Pythagoras was held by his listeners, and how much dignity he had won for himself through the disciplines he delivered. 

But since Hierocles explicitly says that the disciples swore "by the teacher who delivered the <term>tetractys</term> to them," which Iamblichus also confirms in Book I, chapter 28, I was of the opinion that in verse 53, one should read "by him" instead of "by it," <note>a philological note: the author suggests changing the Greek gender from feminine (referring to the Tetractys) to masculine (referring to Pythagoras himself)</note> which the sense of the passage clearly seems to require. However, lest I change anything, I am stayed by the authority of Plutarch, Lucian, Macrobius, and other authors, who affirm that they swore by the quaternary, and not by Pythagoras. Regarding this disagreement among the ancient writers, see the commentary of Marcilius on the *Golden Verses*, which Nicetas (the commentator on Gregory of Nazianzus's Fifth Homily on Pentecost) strives to reconcile. 

Theon the Platonist affirms that they swore by both, in his book *On Mathematical Places in Plato’s Timaeus*, in the chapter "On the Quaternary and the Decade," which I read in a manuscript in the library of the most illustrious Cardinal Barberini. <note>Francesco Barberini, a 17th-century cardinal and famous collector of manuscripts.</note> For after he shows that all musical harmonies are found within the quaternary, he adds: "And it is not only for this reason that it is preferred by all the Pythagoreans, but because it also seems to contain the nature of the whole. Wherefore it was also an oath for them—" <note>original Greek: οὐ διὰ τοῦτο δὲ μόνον πᾶσι τοῖς Πυθαγορικοῖς προτετίμηται, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπεὶ καὶ δοκεῖ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν συνέχειν. διὸ καὶ ὅρκος ἦν αὐ-</note>

When, near **Tarentum** <note>a major Greek colony in southern Italy, modern Taranto</note>, he saw an ox grazing at random and indiscriminately upon green beans, he approached the herdsman and advised him to tell the ox to abstain from the beans. But when the herdsman mockingly replied that he did not know how to <gloss>speak like an ox</gloss> <note>original Latin: bouinari</note>, Pythagoras himself approached and whispered into the ox’s ear. He did this so effectively that the animal not only withdrew from the field sown with beans, but never touched beans again for the rest of its life. This ox remained for many years afterward around the **Temple of Juno** <note>the Roman name for Hera, Queen of the Gods</note> in Tarentum until it grew old; it was commonly called the **Sacred Ox**, and it lived on the foods offered to it by everyone it encountered. 

Furthermore, it is said that during the **Olympic Games**, as an eagle was flying over his head while he happened to be discussing omens, symbols, and divine signs with his companions—explaining that the gods signal and foretell certain things to men endowed with true piety—he drew the bird down from the sky, and after stroking it with his hand, he released it again.

This last name was given because Abaris traveled upon an arrow given to him by the **Hyperborean Apollo**, riding it across rivers, seas, and impassable terrain, essentially walking through the air. Some suspected that **Pythagoras** experienced this as well when he conversed with his friends in **Metapontum** and **Tauromenium** on the <margin>30</margin> very same day. He did not take his walks in a conspicuous manner with many people, but with one or two companions in temples or groves, choosing those places that were the quietest and most beautiful.

<margin>33</margin> He loved his friends exceedingly, being the first to declare that "the things of friends are common property" <note>A famous Pythagorean maxim: "koina ta tōn philōn"</note> and that "a friend is another self." While they were in good health, he spent his time with them constantly; when their bodies were ailing, he cared for them; and when their souls were sick, he comforted them, as we have said, some with incantations and charms, and others with music. For he possessed melodies that were healing <note>original: "paiōnia," acting as a physician or healer</note> for the diseases of the body, which he would sing to restore those who were suffering. There were also melodies that brought about a forgetfulness of grief, soothed anger, and purged unseemly desires.

<margin>34</margin> Regarding his diet: for breakfast he had honeycomb or honey; for dinner, bread made of millet, or a barley-cake <term>maza: a staple Greek food, a kneaded dough of barley-meal, water, and oil</term>, and vegetables, both boiled and raw. He rarely ate the meat of sacrificed animals, and even then, not from every part of the victim.

...should he expect to delay for any length of time in a place, he made use of foods that prevent hunger and thirst. The hunger-staving food <note>original: "alimos"</note> he prepared from poppy seed and sesame, and the skin of squill <term>squill: a bulbous Mediterranean plant, often used in ancient medicine for its diuretic and heart-stimulating properties</term> thoroughly washed until it was cleared of its bitter juice. After pounding all these ingredients in equal weight, he mixed them together with Hymettian honey <note>original: "Hymettio" – honey from Mount Hymettus near Athens, legendary for its superior quality and aroma</note>.

The thirst-quenching food <note>original: "adipsos"</note> he made from cucumber seed and plump raisins, from which he had removed the pits, as well as coriander flower, mallow seed, purslane, grated cheese, fine flour, and cream. All these he likewise mixed with honey from the islands. He used to say that **Heracles** learned these recipes from **Demeter** <note>The goddess of agriculture and the harvest</note> when he was being sent into the waterless regions of Libya.

Because of this regimen, his body was maintained in a constant condition as if measured by a plumb-line. He was never healthy at one moment and sickly at another; nor was he at one time gaining weight and growing stout, and at another becoming thin and wasted. <margin>35</margin> His soul likewise displayed a consistent character through his outward appearance. For he was never expanded too far by pleasure, nor contracted by distress; he never appeared to be gripped by either joy or grief. Indeed, no one ever saw him <margin>(59)</margin> laughing or weeping.

<margin>40</margin> He also recommended paying the greatest attention to two specific times: (41) one, when turning to sleep; the other, when rising from sleep. For he believed it was fitting in each of these moments to examine the things already done, and the things yet to be done.

...to step over <note>This continues the precept "Do not step over the balance," meaning do not violate justice.</note>; that is, not to be greedy. **Do not stir the fire with a sword**; which meant, do not provoke a person who is already swelling with pride and anger by using sharp words. **Do not pluck the crown**; that is, do not violate the laws, for these are the "crowns" of cities. Again, there are other such sayings, such as: **Do not eat the heart**; meaning, do not wear yourself down with grief. **Do not sit upon a bushel measure** <term>choenix</term> <note>A *choenix* was a Greek dry measure, roughly a daily ration of grain. Pythagoras uses a pun here; the handle of a Greek drinking cup was called its "ear" (*ous*). Pythagoras himself, along with his friends and associates, was for a long time held in such high admiration in Italy that the cities even entrusted the management of their republics to his disciples. Eventually, however, they began to suffer from envy, and a rebellion was stirred up against them for the following reason.

Cylon of Croton <note>A wealthy and influential citizen who eventually led the violent uprising against the Pythagorean community.</note> was a man who, by his lineage and the fame and wealth of his ancestors, was easily the leading citizen of the entire city. While he considered himself worthy of every other distinguished honor, he judged himself especially worthy of being a participant in the Pythagorean philosophy. <summary>A title page for an anonymous biographical account of the philosopher Pythagoras, sourced from the 9th-century "Library" of Photius and translated by the scholar Lucas Holstenius.</summary>

--- Page 119 ---
<meta>This page continues from the title page of the biography of Pythagoras, derived from Photius’s 9th-century library and translated by Holstenius. The original page bears a stamp reading "IMPRIMÉS" (Printed).</meta>

<margin>1 (56)</margin>It is said that Plato became the ninth successor in the lineage starting from Pythagoras, having been a student of Archytas the Elder; Aristotle, in turn, was the tenth. Among the followers of Pythagoras, some were dedicated to contemplation—these were called the <term>Sebastikoi</term> <note>original: *Sebastikoi*. This term implies those who are "reverent" or "venerable," focused on the divine or theoretical aspects of philosophy.</note>; others were concerned with human affairs—these were called the <term>Politikoi</term> <note>original: *Politikoi*. From "polis," referring to those engaged in the social and political life of the community.</note>; and others focused on the sciences, such as geometry and astronomy—these were called the <term>Mathematikoi</term> <note>original: *Mathematikoi*. In the ancient world, "mathematics" referred more broadly to "things learned," including all the sciences.</note>. Furthermore, those who lived during the time of Pythagoras himself were called the <term>Pythagorikoi</term>; those who were students of his followers were called the <term>Pythagoreioi</term>; and those from the outside who merely emulated his way of life were called the <term>Pythagoristai</term>. They abstained from eating living creatures <note>This refers to the famous Pythagorean vegetarianism, rooted in the belief in the transmigration of souls.</note> and only tasted the meat of sacrifices on the proper occasions.

<margin>2</margin>Pythagoras is said to have lived to the age of one hundred and four. One of his sons, Mnesarchus, is said to have died while still quite young. Telauges, his other son, became his successor. <margin>(57)</margin> His daughters were Sara and Myia. It is also said that Theano was not only a student of his but was actually one of his daughters. <note>While this text lists Theano as a daughter, most other ancient traditions identify her as the wife of Pythagoras.</note>

3 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The followers of Pythagoras said that the <term>monad</term> <note>original: *monas*. In Pythagorean thought, the Monad represents the first principle, unity, or the "One" from which all things arise.</note> and the "one" differ. For among them, the monad was considered to exist in the realm of the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" or "noetic" refers to the world of pure ideas or forms, accessible only to the mind rather than the physical senses.</note>, while the "one" exists among numbers. Similarly, the "two" exists among things that are counted, but they called the <term>dyad</term> <note>original: *dyas*. Representing duality, division, or the "other."</note> <term>indefinite</term> <note>original: *aoristos*. Often called the "Indefinite Dyad," this represents the principle of multiplicity or flux.</note>.

4 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The monad is understood according to equality and measure, whereas the dyad is understood according to excess and deficiency. Now, a middle point or a measure cannot become "more" or "less," but excess and deficiency can proceed toward infinity. For this reason, they called the dyad "indefinite." And since they traced all things back to numbers—originating from the monad and the dyad—they called all existing things "numbers." A number is completed at the ten; and the ten is the sum of the first four numbers, when we count them in order <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.</note>. Because of this, they called the whole of number the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>original: *tetraktys*. A triangular figure consisting of ten points; it was a sacred symbol upon which Pythagoreans swore their oaths.</note>.

<margin>(58)</margin>
5 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; They said that a human being becomes better than themselves in three ways. First, through communion with the gods; for it is necessary that as one approaches them, at that moment, one must separate oneself from all vice, making oneself like God as much as possible <note>This refers to *homoiosis theo*, the philosophical goal of becoming like the divine.</note>. Second, by doing good; for this is a quality of God and a divine imitation. Third, through death. For if, to some degree, the soul becomes better than itself when separated from the body while the creature is alive—as happens in sleep during dreams—<insert>then it must be much more so after death.</insert>

# ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

The Pythagoreans used to say that <term>unity</term> <note>original: *vnitas*. Also known as the Monad, representing the divine source of all things.</note> and the "one" differ. For they considered unity to be that which exists among things of the intellect <note>In this context, the "intellectuals" or "intelligibles" refer to pure ideas or forms that exist beyond the physical world.</note>; but the "one" to be that which exists among numbers. In the same way, the "two" exists among numbers, but they called <term>duality</term> <note>original: *dualitas*. Also known as the Dyad, representing division or "otherness."</note> the infinite.

Unity is understood in terms of equality and measure, while duality is understood in terms of excess and deficiency. Therefore, a middle point or a measure cannot accept "more" or "less." But excess and deficiency, since they proceed toward the infinite, do accept this. For this reason, they called duality itself the infinite. And since they traced all things from unity and duality back to numbers—for they called all existing beings "numbers"—number is completed at the <term>decade</term> <note>original: *denarius*. The number ten.</note>. The decade is composed when we count the first four numbers in order <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.</note>. And for this reason, they called all number the <term>quaternary</term> <note>original: *quaternarium*. This refers to the Tetractys, the sacred Pythagorean figure where four levels of points add up to the perfect number ten.</note>.

They affirmed that there are three ways a human may become better than themselves. First, through <term>communion with the gods</term> <note>original: *colloquio deorum*. Literally "conversation" or "discourse" with the divine.</note>. For it is necessary that one approaching them at that time must abstain from every evil deed, making themselves as like to God as their strength allows. Second, by doing good. For this is a quality proper to God, and in this, one imitates God. Finally, third, by dying. For if the soul, while this life is being lived, becomes better than itself when it is even slightly separated from the body—as happens in sleep through dreams, and in the ecstasies of dy- <note>The text breaks off mid-word (likely *moriendo*, "dying"), suggesting the soul's full potential is reached when entirely freed from the body.</note>

Next in order is the sphere of air; after it comes that of water; and finally, at the base of everything, is the earth. Since there are twelve ranks <term>ranks</term> <note>original: *taxeôn*, referring to the levels or layers of the cosmos.</note> in total, the First Cause resides in the "unwandering" sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which does not move independently like the planets.</note>. They say that whatever is close to this cause is ordered in a stable and excellent manner, while those things further away are less so. This perfect order is preserved as far down as the Moon; however, the things beneath the Moon are no longer ordered in the same way.

<margin>11</margin> Out of necessity, vice also exists in the region around the earth; since the earth holds the position of the "bottom" <note>original: *pythmên*, literally a "foundation" or the "dregs" at the bottom of a cup.</note> in relation to the whole cosmos, it is a suitable place for the reception of sediment <term>sediment</term> <note>original: *hypostathmês*, the residue or dregs that settle at the bottom of a liquid.</note>. They say that all the other parts of the universe are governed according to divine Providence <term>Providence</term> <note>original: *pronoian*, the foresight and care of the divine.</note>, stable order, and the fate of God, which follows His will. However, the affairs below the Moon are governed by four types of causes: by God, by Fate, by our own Choice <term>Choice</term> <note>original: *proairesin*, referring to the human faculty of moral decision-making.</note>, and by Chance. For example: whether to board a ship or not is within our own power. Yet, for a storm

<margin>(61)</margin> and a surge to suddenly arise during calm weather happens by Chance. Furthermore, for a sinking ship to be saved against all hope is the result of the Providence of God. There are many forms and variations of Fate, and it differs from Chance in this way: Fate possesses a chain <note>original: *heirmon*, a linked sequence of events.</note>, an order, and a sequence. Chance, on the other hand, is characterized by spontaneity and "whatever happens." For instance, passing from childhood into youth and moving through the successive stages of life in their proper time is one example of the workings of Fate.

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

...next is the sphere of air; then that of water; and finally, beneath all of these, lies the globe of the earth. In the highest of these twelve spheres, or the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, the outermost shell of the universe in the Pythagorean system.</note>, resides the First Cause <term>First Cause</term> <note>original: *prima causa*, the ultimate source of motion and existence, often identified with God or the Monad.</note>. They affirm that whatever is near to that Cause is established firmly and in the best possible way; however, those things that are further away are the least stable. A constant order is maintained as far down as the Moon; but below the Moon, all things are carried along in a confused manner.

For this reason, evil also necessarily exists around the region of the earth; since the earth serves as the "bottom" <note>original: *fundi*, meaning the base or the dregs at the bottom of a container.</note> for the whole world—the natural and most convenient receptacle for those things that sink to the lowest point. They say that while all the other parts of the universe are governed by providence, stable order, and fate—all of which obey the divine will—the things below the Moon are ruled by four specific causes: God, fate, our own choice <term>choice</term> <note>original: *consilio*, referring to human deliberation and will.</note>, and fortune.

For example: whether to board a ship or not is within our power. But for gales and a storm to suddenly arise in clear weather depends on fortune. That a sunken ship might be saved beyond all hope occurs through divine providence. 

Furthermore, there are many and diverse modes of fate. Fate differs from fortune because the former follows a series, a structured order, and a logical sequence; fortune, however, happens by reckless chance. For example, growing from a boy into a young man, and then passing through the remaining ages of life in their proper order—this happens according to one mode of fate.

# A N O N Y M U S

And from these factors arise the **Etesian winds** <term>Etesian winds: Derived from the Greek word "etos" (year); these are strong, periodic northern winds of the Aegean Sea that blow annually during the summer.</term>, caused by the currents of air produced by the melting of northern moistures <note>The author refers to the melting of snow and ice in the "arctic" or northern regions as the source of these air currents.</note>. These winds are then carried toward the opposite regions in the south. Once they are carried there, they strike against the highest mountains of *Ethiopia*; as they gather in great and concentrated masses, they produce heavy rains. It is from these rains that the Nile overflows during the summer, even though it flows from southern and arid regions. *Aristotle* investigated this phenomenon himself. He came to understand it through the study of nature’s workings, <margin>(67)</margin> after requesting that *Alexander the Great* <note>original: *Alexander the Macedonian*.</note> send an expedition to those regions so that he could learn the cause of the Nile’s rising through direct observation. For this reason, he says that this is no longer a "problem" <note>original: *problema*. In ancient science, a "problem" was a specific paradox or unanswered question that required a logical solution.</note>. For it was clearly observed that the river increases its flow because of the rains. The paradox is that in the driest parts of *Ethiopia*—where there is otherwise neither winter nor water—it happens that the heaviest rains occur during the summer.

### ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS <note>Although the header names Pythagoras, the text on this page focuses on Aristotle’s findings regarding the Nile's flooding.</note>

...is changed, from which the **Etesian winds** <term>Etesian winds: Strong, periodic northern winds of the Mediterranean, named from the Greek word for "annual."</term> arise. They originate from the spirit <note>original: *spiritu*; here referring to air currents or atmospheric pressure.</note> that is produced when moisture is released in the northern regions. These winds are then carried toward the opposite southern regions; having been driven there, they become trapped against the highest mountains of **Ethiopia**. Once they have been gathered and condensed, they produce rains. It is from these rains that the **Nile** increases in volume during the summer, even though it flows out from southern and arid lands.

**Aristotle** discovered this through his own investigations. He deduced this from the nature of the matter itself, having requested that **Alexander the Macedonian** <note>Alexander the Great, who was a pupil of Aristotle.</note> send people to those places so that they might learn the cause of the Nile’s rising through direct observation. For this reason, he says, we should no longer seek further answers regarding this matter. It is clearly evident that the river increases because of the rains. It is indeed a great marvel that in the most parched places of Ethiopia—where there is neither winter nor any other water—the heaviest rains occur during the summer season.

# TO DANIEL HEINSIUS

->CONRAD RITTERSHUYS SENDS HIS WARMEST GREETINGS TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN <note>original Latin: *V. C. S. P. D. C. R.*, an abbreviation for *Viro Clarissimo Salutem Plurimam Dicit Conradus Rittershusius*</note><-

You may remember, most learned man, that I long ago gave you hope of receiving this work of Malchus <note>Malchus was the original name of the philosopher Porphyry.</note> from me. I would have presented it to you from my own manuscript much earlier, had various obstacles not delayed me. Among these, you may count the fact that I had intended to add a translation into English <note>original: *Latinam*</note> and an explanation of certain more obscure passages. 

But manifold distractions <note>original Greek: *ἀσχολίαι* (*ascholiai*), meaning a lack of leisure or being occupied with business</note> forced me to cast aside this plan, to say nothing for now of my poor health. However, lest I should remain indebted to you for the promised gift for too long, and lest this little book should perhaps be lost to us in the meantime, I have given it—just as it is—to our printer during these past few days to be published. It happened to come to hand while I was searching for other things among my scraps and trifles. 

As for the brief notes I have added, I hope you will receive them as an invitation for you to produce more substantial scholarly commentary <term>Scholia: Explanatory notes or remarks written in the margins of ancient manuscripts by early scholars to clarify the text.</term> and a full translation of the volume yourself. But...

### *A conjecture concerning the author of this little book.*

<margin>
*Compare the Introduction by Rittershusius, preface between [pages] 3-175-17*
</margin>

This Malchus, whom we are now the first to present to the public, as to his family and from what home he came, I do not indeed have sufficiently certain or documented information. If there is room for conjecture, perhaps he is that same sophist <note>A "sophist" in this late antique context refers to a professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy.</note> and historian from Philadelphia <note>Philadelphia was a city in ancient Lydia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>, from whose seven books of Byzantine history Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, included several excerpts in his *Library* <note>The *Bibliotheca* or *Library* of Photius is a 9th-century collection of summaries and excerpts from 279 books, many of which are now lost.</note> on page 100 and following, in the Greek edition published at Augsburg by our distinguished friend David Hoeschelius <note>Hoeschelius (1556–1617) was a prominent German humanist and editor of Greek texts.</note>, where a notable praise of him is also added, which I shall write down: 

<note>original Greek: ἔστι δ’ ὁ συγγραφεὺς, εἴ τις ἄλλος, κατὰ συγγραφὴν ἱστορίας ἄριστος, καθαρὸς, ἀπέριττος, εὐκρινὴς, λέξεων ταῖς ἀνθηροτάταις καὶ εὐσήμοις, καὶ εἰς ὄγκον τινὰ ἀνηγμέναις, χρώμενος. καὶ οὐδὲ αἱ καινοπρεπεῖς αὐτῷ, ὅσαι τὸ ἐμφατικὸν καὶ ἔνηχον καὶ μεγαλεῖον ἔχουσι, παραβλέπονται, καὶ ὅλος (fort. ὅλως legend·) κανών ἐστιν ἱστορικοῦ λόγου. Σοφιστὴς δ’ ἦν τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα, καὶ ῥητορικῆς εἰς ἄκρον ἐληλακὼς, καὶ τὴν θρησκείαν οὐκ ἔξω τοῦ χριστιανικοῦ θιάσου.</note>

"The writer is, if anyone ever was, excellent in the writing of history: clear, concise, and lucid, using words most flowery and significant, and elevated to a certain grandeur. Nor are new or unusual words overlooked by him, provided they have emphasis, resonance, and majesty; he is entirely [or perhaps "generally"] a standard for historical prose. He was a sophist by profession, having reached the pinnacle of rhetoric, and his religion was not outside the Christian fold." 

These words of Photius seem to me to fit our Malchus as well; as do those of the *Suda* <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia that serves as a vital source for ancient history and literature.</note>: "Malchus, a Byzantine Sophist, wrote a history from the reign of..." <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSIUS

<note>original Greek: ...Κωνσταντίνου, καὶ ἕως Ἀναστασίου, ἐν ᾗ τὰ κατὰ Ζήνωνα καὶ Βασιλίσκον, καὶ τὸν ἐμπρησμὸν τῆς δημοσίας βιβλιοθήκης, καὶ τῶν ἀγαλμάτων τοῦ Αὐγουσταίου, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ διεξέρχεται, μάλα σεμνῶς, καὶ τραγῳδίας δίκην ἀποθρηνῶν αὐτά.</note> ...from the time of Constantine until the reign of Anastasius, in which he recounts the events concerning Zeno and Basiliscus, the fire of the public library, the statues of the Augusteum <note>A ceremonial square in Constantinople.</note>, and certain other things, doing so quite solemnly and mourning these events like a tragic drama. If anyone knows anything more accurate regarding these matters and might teach us, he will find us to be grateful debtors of the tuition fee.

But whoever this Malchus was, it is easily apparent—and the work itself will show—that he was a very learned and ancient writer who read many authors whose works we no longer possess today. Since many things occur here which you may read in the exact same words, or certainly with very little change, in Iamblichus’s *Life of Pythagoras*, one might rightly wonder which of the two borrowed from the other. I am of the opinion that Malchus lived later than Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, and was therefore a sort of epitomizer <note>An author who produces a summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note> of his writing. Whatever the case may be, a comparison of these two will be useful for the <term>restoration</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπανόρθωσιν (epanorthosin)</note> of certain passages in Iamblichus. Quite a few of these passages still lie suffering from "disease" and errors, even after the "Machaonian treatment" <note>A reference to Machaon, the legendary healer of the Greeks at Troy; here used as a metaphor for the scholarly editing and "healing" of a corrupted text.</note> performed by the most learned Desiderius Heraldus <note>Didier Hérauld (1579–1649), a French jurist and classical scholar.</note>; we shall demonstrate this in more than one place below.

The manuscript book included the addition **"or of the King"** <note>original Greek: ἢ Βασιλέως (ē Basileōs)</note>: by which we suspect the scribe intended to indicate that the name Malchus (which is of Hebrew origin) means "King." <note>The name Porphyry—the author to whom this work is usually attributed—is a Greek play on the Semitic name "Malchus" (king), as purple (porphyra) was the royal color.</note>

### THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

Those who have written down the lives of the philosophers are many. We have heard that the first example of this genre proceeded from Xenophon, about whom Suidas <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> writes as follows: *Xenophon, son of Gryllus, an Athenian, a Socratic philosopher, who was the first to write the lives of philosophers.* However, this work does not survive today.

Besides our Malchus, several others have recorded the life of Pythagoras in literature: chief among these is Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who specialized in music and ethics.</note>, who lived in the time of Dionysius of Syracuse and indicates in his own writings that he was an intimate of that tyrant. For it is from that famous story that we learned of the bail of Damon, which he provided for his friend Phintias when the latter was condemned to death <note>The classic story of Damon and Pythias (Phintias), where one friend offers his life as security so the other can settle his affairs before execution.</note>—about which see Iamblichus No. 234 and 235, and Malchus No. 60 and 61. Cicero, in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, calls him a contemporary and fellow student of Dicaearchus and a learned man. Aulus Gellius also makes use of this Aristoxenus’s testimony regarding Pythagoras in Book IV, Chapter 11, and not without significant praise for the man: *Aristoxenus (he says)...*

<summary>Rittershusius argues that Malchus (Porphyry) likely summarized Iamblichus's work and explains that the name "Malchus" is a Semitic term for "King." He then begins a history of Pythagorean biography, citing early sources like Xenophon and Aristoxenus.</summary>
<keywords>Malchus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Pythagoras, Desiderius Heraldus, Xenophon, Suidas, Aristoxenus, Damon and Phintias, textual criticism, etymology</keywords>

->### ON PORPHYRY<-

...[Clear]chus <note>Probably Clearchus of Soli, a disciple of Aristotle.</note>, a man most diligent in ancient literature and a student of the philosopher *Aristotle*, in the book which he left concerning *Pythagoras*, etc.

Then there is *Hermippus*, of whom a very honorable mention exists in the work of *Josephus*, that most illustrious writer of Jewish history, in Book I of *Against Apion*. *Pythagoras of Samos*, (he says) *though ancient in age, yet excelling all philosophers in wisdom and divine piety, is clearly shown not only to have recognized our customs, but it is also apparent that he emulated them in many respects.* And indeed, no writing of his <note>Meaning Pythagoras himself.</note> is found: yet many have reported on it: the most distinguished of whom is *Hermippus*, a man who was a most diligent investigator of all history. He reports, therefore, in his first book on *Pythagoras*, that *Pythagoras*, upon the death of one of his close associates named *Calliphon*, a native of *Croton*, used to say that the man's soul lived with him day and night: and that it instructed him not to pass by a place where a donkey had fallen, to abstain from foul water, and to shrink from all blasphemy. Then follows: *He did and said these things by imitating the opinions of the Jews and Thracians, and transferring them to himself. For it is truly said that that man transferred many Jewish laws into his own philosophy.* *Diogenes Laertius* praises the second book of this same *Hermippus* regarding *Pythagoras* in Book VIII, page 574, and the most learned *Origen* mentions him in Book I of *Against Celsus*, page 13. <note>original Greek: Λέγεται δὲ καὶ ῎Ερμιππον ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ περὶ νομοθετῶν ἱστορηκέναι, Πυθαγόραν τὴν αὑτοῦ φιλοσοφίαν ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων εἰς ῎Ελληνας ἀγαγεῖν.</note> <note>Translation: "It is said that Hermippus, in his first book On Lawgivers, recorded that Pythagoras brought his own philosophy from the Jews to the Greeks."</note> *Didymus* also wrote a book on Pythagorean philosophy, as I learned from *Clement of Alexandria*, *Miscellanies* Book I, page 113. The poet *Alexis* even wrote a comedy which he titled *The Life of Pythagoras*: as indicated by *Aulus Gellius* <note>The text uses the Greek form "Agellius."</note> in Book [blank], chapter 11, in addition to *Athenaeus*. Testimonies from *Nicomachus* concerning *Pythagoras* are also frequently cited by *Malchus* <note>Porphyry.</note> and others: just as *Apollonius* is praised by *Malchus* in Section 2, and *Lycus* in Section 4. There is furthermore *Iamblichus of Chalcis* from Coele-Syria, who lived in the times of the *Emperor Julian* and was held in the highest esteem by him. Twelve years ago, *Johannes Arcerius Theodoreti Frisius* was the first to bring this author into the light <note>i.e., published the first printed edition.</note>, and he earned great favor among scholars with that edition; however, he would have deserved even greater favor and praise if he had kept his most unfortunate hand away from both his corrections—which were for the most part rash—and his Latin translation, and had instead presented *Iamblichus* exactly as he had found him in the manuscript, however corrupted, leaving the correction of the text free to anyone. There is likewise *Lycon of Iasos*, whose book concerning...

<meta>Continuing the enumeration of ancient sources for the life of Pythagoras, Rittershusius expands his list beyond Hermippus and Porphyry to include Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus, and various classical biographers, while discussing the semi-divine status attributed to Pythagoras by his followers.</meta>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

Athenaeus praises Pythagoras in Book I. There is also Diogenes Laertius, who began the eighth book of his *philosophical biographies* <note>original: βιογραφίας</note> with Pythagoras. We learn from Malchus <note>Malchus is the original name of the philosopher Porphyry.</note>, entry number 10, that another man named Diogenes—in his *Commentaries on Incredible Things Beyond Thule*—also made mention of Pythagoras. Regarding Moderatus, who wrote several books on the Pythagorean Schools, I will speak below.

Similarly, I will speak of Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote on the soul and Greek history.</note> below. Finally, there is a certain *anonymous* <note>original: ἀνώνυμος</note> writer of a life of Pythagoras, whose excerpts can be seen in the *Library* of Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, on page 712 and the following four pages.

We have learned from the cited passages of Iamblichus, Malchus, Athenaeus, Agellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of *Attic Nights*.</note>, Clement of Alexandria, and others, that many wrote concerning Pythagorean philosophy and its symbols, including Aristotle, Androcydes, Antiphanes, and Alexander. And indeed Iamblichus, in entry number 31, records from that highest peak of philosophers this *classification* <note>original: διαίρεσιν</note> of the Pythagoreans, which they held as a secret among themselves: *Of rational beings, one kind is God, another is man, and another is such as Pythagoras.* It is as if they established the leader of their sect as possessing a middle nature between the divine and the human. It will be worthwhile to note here the true etymology of his name as well. For Aristippus of Cyrene thought Pythagoras was so named *because he spoke the truth no less than the Pythian oracle* <note>original: ὅτι τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἠγόρευεν οὐχ ἧττον τοῦ Πυθίου; a pun on "Pythios" (Apollo) and "agoreuein" (to speak)</note>, as recorded by Diogenes Laertius in the aforementioned Book VIII, page 581, and from him Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> under the entry for *Pythagoras the Samian*. Using a *circumlocution* <note>original: περιφράζοντες</note>, they also used to call him *the long-haired one from Samos*, that is, the *long-haired Samian*; this is according to Iamblichus, entries 11 and 30, where he teaches that this title became a proverb that lasted even until his own time, used to designate a man of the highest gravity and religious devotion.

*Wherefore even now,* he says, *the proverb proclaims 'the long-haired one from Samos' in reference to the most venerable man.* It seems that even this should not be kept silent: that his followers did not call Pythagoras by his own name, but either *divine* <note>original: ϑεῖον</note> while he was among the living, or *that man* <note>original: ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἄνδρα</note> once he had been removed from human affairs. This they did (as is easy to perceive) out of the highest veneration for their master. Iamblichus taught us this mystery in several places, such as entries 53, 88, and 255.

<summary>This page catalogs the diverse ancient sources for the life of Pythagoras, including Diogenes Laertius and Photius, and highlights the Pythagorean belief that their master was a semi-divine figure bridging the gap between humanity and God.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus, Porphyry, etymology, Samian, divinity, ancient biographies</keywords>
