<meta>Continuing the discussion on the reputation of Pythagoras, this page addresses the historical misconceptions regarding his influence on early Roman leaders, specifically King Numa Pompilius, and uses chronological evidence from classical historians to correct the timeline.</meta>

### ON PORPHYRY

One can judge how much the Romans esteemed Pythagoras from several facts: first, they granted him citizenship in their own city; second, they honored him with a bronze statue, just as they did for Alcibiades. (They did so to honor the one as the bravest of Greece, and the other as the wisest.) Finally, it was commonly believed that King Numa—who they say was an intimate friend of Pythagoras—imitated many of his teachings as if Pythagoras were his own master. See Plutarch in his *Life of Numa*.

But Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in Book 2 of the *Roman Antiquities*, refutes this opinion as a fabrication. Some had handed down the story that Numa was a disciple of Pythagoras and had been summoned to Rome to take up the kingship from Croton <note>A Greek city in southern Italy where Pythagoras established his school.</note>, where he was then studying philosophy under this master. Dionysius denies that this was possible based on the calculation of the dates. First, because the city of the Crotonians was first founded by Myscelus four full years after Numa took the throne; second, because Pythagoras lived four whole generations after Numa. For Numa gained his kingdom around the middle of the 16th Olympiad <note>An Olympiad was a four-year period used by the Greeks to track time; the 16th Olympiad began in 716 BCE.</note>, whereas Pythagoras taught in Italy only after the 50th Olympiad <note>Starting in 580 BCE.</note>.

Cicero also refutes the same error in the preface of the 4th book of the *Tusculan Disputations* and in the 2nd book *On the Orator*. It is worth the effort to hear the very words of both these great authors. Thus says Cicero: *Indeed, I believe that because of their admiration for the Pythagoreans, King Numa was also thought to be a Pythagorean by later generations. For when they became acquainted with the discipline and institutions of Pythagoras, and had heard from their ancestors of the king's fairness and wisdom—yet remained ignorant of the dates and times because of their antiquity—they believed that he who excelled in wisdom had been a student of Pythagoras.*

Then the same Cicero says in another place: *Philosophy, he says, has never been scorned by this city. For Italy was once filled with Pythagoreans at the time when that region was called Great Greece <note>original: Magna Graecia</note>. Because of this, some say that our king Numa Pompilius was a Pythagorean—though he lived many years before Pythagoras himself. On this account, he should be considered an even greater man, since he understood the wisdom of establishing a state nearly two centuries before the Greeks realized that such wisdom had even been born.*

Livy, however, in Book 1, chapter 18, says: *The author of his teaching <note>referring to Numa</note> (whom he calls the most learned man in every divine and human law, as much as anyone could be in that age...)*

<summary>This page examines the Roman tradition that King Numa Pompilius was a student of Pythagoras, a claim refuted by historians like Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Cicero using chronological evidence. The text highlights how the Romans' high regard for both Numa and Pythagoras led to this historical myth.</summary>

<keywords>Pythagoras, Numa Pompilius, Cicero, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, Roman history, chronology, Magna Graecia, Croton, Olympiads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philological notes of Konrad Rittershuis, specifically focusing on the chronological arguments of Titus Livy and other classical authors to prove that King Numa Pompilius could not have been a student of Pythagoras due to the significant gap in time between their lives.</meta>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUIS

...it could be) because no other exists, they falsely present the Samian Pythagoras: whom it is well established held gatherings of students eager to emulate his studies in the farthest coast of Italy around Metapontum, Heraclea, and Croton, more than a hundred years later, during the reign of Servius Tullius <note>The sixth king of Rome, reigning roughly 578–535 BCE.</note> at Rome. From these places, even if he had lived at the same time, by what fame could he have reached the Sabines, or by what exchange of language could he have stirred anyone to a desire for learning? And by what protection could a single man have traveled through so many nations differing in speech and customs? The same author <note>Livy</note> in Book 40, chapter 29, adds that Valerius Antias wrote that the books of Numa were Pythagorean—the books which he writes were found under the Janiculum Hill in one of two stone chests bound with lead, and were then burned—accommodating a belief in a probable lie based on the popular opinion which holds that Numa was a student of Pythagoras.

To this may be added the authority of Cicero, who writes in Book 1 of the *Tusculan Disputations* that Pythagoras came to Italy during the reign of Tarquinius Superbus <note>Tarquin the Proud, the last king of Rome.</note>, and held that Great Greece <note>original: "Magnam illam Graeciam"; the Greek-speaking coastal areas of Southern Italy.</note> with honor and discipline, as well as authority, etc. Aulus Gellius chimes in with Cicero in the last chapter of Book 17: *After those events, Pythagoras the Samian came to Italy while the son of Tarquinius—who was surnamed the Proud—held the kingdom.*

The chronology of Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop known for his "Chronicle," which aligned world histories.</note> mostly agrees with the testimony of Dionysius of Halicarnassus regarding the 50th Olympiad. On page 149, at the 60th Olympiad, he noted these words: "Pherecydes the historian was becoming known, the teacher of Pythagoras" <note>original: Φερεκύδης ἱστορικὸς ἐγνωρίζετο, Πυθαγόρου διδάσκαλος</note>. Although the same Eusebius, on page 42 of the previous book, makes Theognis the teacher of Pythagoras: "Theognis the poet was becoming known, the teacher of Pythagoras" <note>original: Θέογνις ποιητὴς ἐγνωρίζετο, Πυθαγόρου διδάσκαλος</note> (unless perhaps something is missing); and at the 64th Olympiad: "The tyrants of Samos—Polycrates, Syloson, and Pantagnotus—were brothers"; and at the 65th Olympiad: "Pythagoras the natural philosopher was becoming known" <note>original: Πυθαγόρας φυσικὸς φιλόσοφος ἐγνωρίζετο</note>. Saint Jerome, in the first book of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* on page 30, says: *Pherecydes the historian is held to be famous.* And shortly after: *In Samos, three brothers exercise tyranny: Polycrates, Syloson, and Pantagnotus.* And on page 31: *The 65th Olympiad, in which was the second year of Darius, son of Hystaspes, King of the Persians: Pythagoras the natural philosopher is held to be famous.*

He repeats the same things on pages 128 and 129 of the later book. However, Clement of Alexandria, who is older than Eusebius, in *Stromata* Book 1, page 130, pushes Pythagoras back by some anticipation to the 62nd Olympiad along with Polycrates: "Pythagoras is found to be during the time of Polycrates the tyrant, around the 62nd Olympiad" <note>original: Πυθαγόρας δὲ κατὰ Πολυκράτη τὸν τύραννον, περὶ τὴν ἑξηκοστὴν δευτέραν Ὀλυμπιάδα εὑρίσκεται</note>.

<summary>This page presents a scholarly refutation of the legend that King Numa Pompilius was a student of Pythagoras by citing the conflicting timelines of Cicero, Livy, Eusebius, and St. Jerome. These authors place Pythagoras's arrival in Italy during the reign of Tarquinius Superbus, long after Numa's death.</summary>

# ON PORPHYRY

The death of Pythagoras is reported by Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Roman historian and Christian bishop, known for his "Chronicle."</note> at the last year of the 70th Olympiad <note>Approx. 497/496 BCE.</note>. See the Greek edition, pages 43 and 152: "Pythagoras the philosopher died aged 95, others say 71." <note>original Greek: "Πυθαγόρας ὁ φιλόσοφος τέθνηκεν ἐτῶν λέ, οἱ δὲ οά"—the OCR's 'λέ' (35) is likely a transcription error for 'ϟε' (95) as confirmed by the Latin 'XCV' below.</note> And in the Latin version of Jerome, page 130, where he omitted the philosopher's age, who completed 95 years, or according to others 75, in living.

But in Photius’s *Library* <note>Photius was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople who compiled summaries of hundreds of books.</note> page 712, in the *Excerpts from an unknown writer of the Life of Pythagoras*, we read that he reached his one hundred and fourth year. "That Pythagoras is said to have lived one hundred and four years." <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι ρ' καὶ τεσσάρων ἐτῶν λέγεται ἑξηκέναι τὸν Πυθαγόραν."</note> But perhaps in Photius, the number 70 or 30 was corrupted into 100. Finally, in Diogenes Laertius <note>Author of "Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers."</note> page 595, only eighty years, and by others ninety, are attributed to him: "Pythagoras at any rate (as Heraclides the son of Sarapion says) died as an octogenarian, according to his own description of the stages of life; but according to most, having lived ninety years." <note>original Greek: "Ὁ γοῦν Πυθαγ... ἔτη βιοὺς ἐννενήκοντα."</note> Thus far regarding the title of this small work. There follows the text itself.

**Num. 1. [To have been born the son of Mnesarchus]** Herodotus also calls Pythagoras the son of Mnesarchus in his fourth book, *Melpomene*, as do Clement of Alexandria, Justin, Origen, Iamblichus, and others everywhere. In Iamblichus, Section 146, I restore the reading: "to Pythagoras the son of Mnesarchus," namely "son" <note>original Greek: "υἱῷ"</note>, instead of "to Mnesarchus," which was published. But why is it that in Iamblichus, Section 4, we read "Mnemarchus and Pythais were those who gave birth to Pythagoras"? I think that there "Mnesarchus" was erroneously changed into "Mnemarchus." Yet Justin, in Book 20, makes the father of Pythagoras Demaratus of Samos, a wealthy businessman. In the writer who copied Justin, John of Salisbury <note>A 12th-century English philosopher and bishop.</note> in Book 7 of the *Policraticus*, chapter 4, we read "Maratus": but I think the name was curtailed <note>Latin: "capite minutum," a play on the legal term for a loss of status, here meaning the first part of the name "Demaratus" was cut off.</note>, and that even there "Demaratus" ought to be restored. Of the sons of Pythagoras himself, one is said to have been called Mnesarchus, and the other Telauges. The unknown author of the *Life of Pythagoras* in Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, *Library* page 712, says: "And Mnesarchus, one of his sons, is said to have died younger; but Telauges, the other, succeeded him." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ὁ μὲν Μνήσαρχος... Τηλαυγὴς δὲ ὁ ἕτερος διεδέξατο."</note> In the same place he names two daughters of Pythagoras, Sara and Myia. Mention of Telauges occurs elsewhere, as well as in Iamblichus, Section 146.

Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> in his *Description of Greece: Corinth*, makes Pythagoras the great-grandson of Hippasus, the grandson of Euphron, and the son of Mnesarchus; and he says that Hippasus fled from Phlius to Samos because of certain disagreements with Regnida. This genealogy from an excellent historian...

### NOTES BY CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS <note>Conrad Rittershusius (1560–1613) was a German jurist and classical scholar known for his detailed commentaries on ancient texts.</note>

**And Cleanthes]** <note>original Greek: "Κλεάνθης δὲ"</note> I think this is that Cleanthes, the Stoic philosopher, of whom they write that he earned a wage by drawing water from a well at night so that he could devote his days to his studies. Because of this, he was nicknamed *the well-drawer* <note>original Greek: "φρεάντλης" (phreantles), a play on his name and his labor.</note> as an allusion to his name. From this passage by Malchus <note>Another name for Porphyry, the author of the biography being discussed.</note> we understand that he wrote books on mythical matters, at least five in number. Nothing of his survives today except for certain fragments of poems. Among these, the four heroic verses preserved by Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the 2nd century.</note> in the fifth book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original Latin title: "Stromat."</note> are especially memorable; they concern the contempt one should hold for the tasteless and foolish opinions and judgments of the common people. The same author, in two iambic lines elsewhere, does not hesitate to pronounce a man "illiberal" <note>In this context, meaning unrefined or lacking the character of a free man.</note> if he looks toward public opinion, as if anything good could come to him from there. Those first verses are very well known, even from the *Chronicles* of Philip Melanchthon <note>A major figure in the Protestant Reformation and a renowned scholar of the 16th century.</note>, and should therefore be omitted here. I will only add the iambic ones:

->Every man is illiberal who looks to public opinion,<-
->As if he were to obtain something beautiful from it.<-
<note>original Greek: "Ἀνελεύθερος πᾶς, ὅστις εἰς δόξαν βλέπει, Ὡς δὴ παρ’ ἐκείνης τευξόμενος καλοῦ τινος."</note>

That is to say:

->*Whoever is fixed upon opinions,*<-
->*As if something of good could happen to him from here,*<-
->*I say he is endowed with an illiberal nature.*<-

Concerning the same Cleanthes, it is worth remembering what I read in Simplicius's <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator.</note> *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Epictetus*: that such honor was paid to him by the Roman Senate that, by a decree of the Senate, a statue was erected for him at Assos <note>A city in Asia Minor where Cleanthes was born.</note>, which Simplicius himself testifies to having seen. There is also his etymology and a saying regarding the pig which is worthy of note and memory, recorded by Clement of Alexandria in the second book of his *Miscellanies*, page 174. The etymology is this: *That the pig (hys) is called thys, as being suitable only for sacrifice (thysis) and slaughter.* <note>original Greek: "Τὴν ὗν, θῦν εἶναι, ὡς εἰς θύσιν καὶ σφαγὴν μόνον ἐπιτήδειον." Rittershusius notes that "only" should perhaps be read in the feminine form to agree with the pig.</note> It seems the pig was named by the Greeks after the act of sacrificing, because it is destined and fit for this use alone: to be slaughtered. The saying is this: *The soul of the pig was given in place of salt, so that the meat would not rot:* <note>original Latin: "Sui animam pro sale datam esse, ne caro putresceret."</note> *To this animal, a soul was given for no other purpose than to keep its flesh firm.* <note>original Greek: "δεδόσθαι τῷδε τῷ ζῴῳ ψυχὴν πρὸς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ἢ ἕνεκα τοῦ τὰς σάρκας σφριγᾶν."</note> Clement records this same insight of Cleanthes again in the seventh book of the *Miscellanies*, page 304, in slightly different words: *Aesop said, not without wit, that pigs cry out the loudest because they are conscious of being useful for nothing else when they are being dragged away* (these two words, *when they are being dragged*, I think...

# ON PORPHYRY,

<note>This section continues a technical discussion on the placement of a phrase in the Greek text.</note> it is more rightly placed after the phrase "having cried out very loudly") or "except" (read as "except that," or by deleting the "or" entirely) "for the sacrifice." Therefore Cleanthes also says that pigs have a soul instead of salt, so that their meat does not rot. <note>original Greek: "Διὸ καὶ Κλεάνθης φησὶν, ἀνθ’ ἁλῶν αὐτοὺς ἔχειν τὴν ψυχὴν..." This was a famous Stoic joke suggesting that a pig's soul serves only the biological function of keeping its carcass fresh until it is eaten.</note> Note here in passing that "sacrifice" <note>original Greek: "θυσίαν" (thysian)</note> means nothing other than "slaughter" <note>original Greek: "θύσιν" (thysin)</note>—that is, a killing or butchery—lest anyone think that by this name a religious sacrifice is meant, for which a pig is not typically used. But let us now return to the main path from this not unpleasant digression.

**Being naturally gifted in every kind of learning]** <note>original Greek: "Εἰς πᾶσαν μάθησιν ὄντος εὐφυοῦς"</note> One who is born with such a character was elegantly described by Herodotus as having "a soul swelling with desire for learning." <note>original Greek: "ἔχειν ψυχὴν ὀργῶσαν πρὸς τὰ μαθήματα"</note> And the old man Herodotus himself recognized such a disposition in the young Thucydides <note>The famous historian of the Peloponnesian War.</note> and proclaimed it to his father, Olorus. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> notes under the entry "To Swell with Desire": "Herodotus, seeing Thucydides crying out of a sort of divine inspiration, said: 'I congratulate you, Olorus, on your fine child; for your son has a soul swelling with desire for learning.'" The same Suidas, under the entry "Natural Talent" <note>original Greek: "Εὐφυΐα" (Euphyia)</note> noted these things from some unknown commentator on Aristotle: "It is the mark of a gifted person to feel at home with the truth, but to turn away from falsehood; and he who possesses this also has the ability to judge the truth well." See the many points that follow in that same source concerning the dexterity of judgment.

**To Pherecydes the Syrian]** <note>original Greek: "Φερεκύδῃ τῷ Συρίῳ"</note> To the two teachers of Pythagoras—Pherecydes and Hermodamas—the author will soon add a third in section Number 2: Anaximander the physicist. Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who also wrote a life of Pythagoras.</note> also joined these three together in Chapter 2, Number 11. How this most grateful disciple, Pythagoras, did not desert Pherecydes either during his most foul illness or in death will be discussed below. <note>Pherecydes was said to have died of a gruesome disease involving an infestation of lice; Pythagoras supposedly stayed by his side until the end.</note>

**To Hermodamas the Creophylian]** <note>original Greek: "Ἑρμοδάμαντι τῷ Κρεοφυλίῳ"</note> There were, of course, several men named Hermodamas: one of whom Pythagoras had as a teacher, and another as an intimate friend and companion in his flight. Regarding the latter, see Malchus <note>An alternative name for Porphyry.</note> below in Number 15. The author Apuleius <note>The Roman novelist and philosopher.</note> also mentions the former in his work *Florida*; but there the copyists have corrupted "Hermodamas" into "Leodamas" in our texts. The words are: *And likewise Leodamas, the disciple of Creophylus* (namely, that Pythagoras followed him for the sake of instruction), *which Creophylus is remembered to have been the host of the poet Homer and his rival in singing.* See also Strabo, <note>The ancient Greek geographer.</note> Book 14 of his *Geography*, where he also records a four-line epigram by Callimachus regarding the work of Creophylus of Samos, which was attributed by some to his guest, Homer.

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSIUS

by which Teutagora, whom I find mentioned nowhere else. However, I suspect that other parts of this passage are also not quite sound <note>Meaning the Greek text appears corrupted or miscopied in the original manuscript.</note>.

**Ancaeus]** <note>original Greek: "Ἀγγαίου"</note> In the work of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous "Life of Pythagoras."</note> (Chapter 2, Number 5), he is called Ancaeus. After previously inhabiting Samos in Cephalonia, he later led a colony—by order of Apollo’s oracle—to an island which was called *Melamphyllos* <note>meaning "Black-leaf"</note> because of the richness and fertility of its soil; it is as if you were to say "Nigrifolia" <note>original Latin: "Nigrifoliam"</note>. In that island, Ancaeus founded a city which he named Samos, after the example of that other Samos in Cephalonia. This Ancaeus was believed to be a son of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note>, "either because of his virtue, or because of some greatness of soul," <note>original Greek: "εἴτε δι᾿ ἀρετὴν, εἴτε διὰ ψυχῆς τι... μέγεθος"</note> as he had gained this reputation for himself, according to Iamblichus. However, Pausanias <note>A famous Greek traveler and geographer.</note> in his *Description of Greece* (specifically the book on Achaia, page 208 in my edition), makes Ancaeus the son of Neptune <note>Poseidon.</note> and Astypalaea. In the version by the translator Arcerius, it is written *Melamphylos*, which would mean *black tribe* <note>original Latin: "nigra tribus"</note>, as if a "black tribe" <note>original Greek: "μέλαιna φυλὴ"</note> were implied in the word *melamphylos*. Indeed, it is written this way in some editions of Strabo <note>A prominent Greek geographer.</note> (Book 14), with only one 'l'. But it truly ought to be read with an additional letter as *melamphyllos* <note>with two 'l's, referring to leaves rather than tribes.</note>. This is clearly proven by the later verse of the Delphic oracle cited by Iamblichus in the same place: "And she is named Leafy." <note>original Greek: "Φυλλὰς δ᾿ ὀνομάζεται αὐτή."</note> Therefore, the island took its name from its black leaves, not from a black tribe or race; from the "leaves" <note>original Greek: "φύλλων"</note>, not from the "tribe" <note>original Greek: "φυλῆς"</note>. Besides, what does a tribe or race have to do with the fertility of the soil? For humans are not born from the earth like trees and leaves—"like a piece of beet," as Varro <note>A Roman scholar and writer.</note> says. In the aforementioned Book 14 of Strabo, among the various names of Samos (which it changed often), *Melamphyllos* is also listed. And that most noble Geographer says that because of the island's excellent fertility, a proverb was applied to it: "it even bears bird’s milk" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι φέρει καὶ ὀρνίθων γάλα"</note>—meaning it produces even the most impossible or rarest luxuries.

**A certain one of the Samian poets]** <note>original Greek: "Ποιητῶν τῶν Σαμίων τινὰ"</note> The mention of this anonymous Samian poet, and those two verses of his, are also found in Iamblichus, in the cited Chapter 2.

<margin>3</margin> **Simos the Harmonicist]** <note>original Greek: "Σῖμον τὸν Ἁρμονικὸν"</note> In Pliny’s *Natural History* (Book 35, Chapter 11), I find a Simos among the famous painters. But he hardly seems to be the same person as this one mentioned by Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus.</note>.

<margin>4</margin> **From Theano]** <note>original Greek: "Ἐκ Θεανοῦς"</note> Regarding Theano <note>A female philosopher and student (or wife) of Pythagoras.</note>, see the things I shall say below.

**Timaeus records]** <note>original Greek: "Τίμαιος δ᾿ ἱστορεῖ"</note> This is Timaeus the historian, who, because of his excessive zeal for criticizing others, was nicknamed *Epitimaeus* <note>The Fault-finder</note>, from the Greek word for "finding fault" <note>original Greek: "ἐπιτιμᾶν"</note>.

### ON PORPHYRY

**To make the house a sanctuary of Demeter]** <note>original Greek: "τὴν δ᾽ οἰκίαν Δήμητρος ἱερὸν ποιῆσαι"</note> That the house of Pythagoras was converted into a sacred temple of Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter.</note> has been recorded by many authors. However, some mention that this was done by the people of Metapontum, while others say it was the people of Crotona <note>Both were Greek colonial cities in Southern Italy where Pythagoras lived and taught.</note>. Justin <note>A Roman historian.</note> writes in Book 20: *Pythagoras (he says), having spent twenty years at Crotona, moved to Metapontum and died there. Such was the admiration for him that they made a temple out of his house and worshiped him as a god.* (Understand here: the people of Metapontum). Diogenes Laërtius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> on page 577 also expressly attests to this: *The Metapontines indeed called his house a sanctuary of Demeter, and the alleyway the Museum, as Favorinus says in his "Miscellaneous Histories."* <note>original Greek: "Μεταποντῖνοί γε μὲν τὴν μὲν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ Δήμητρος ἱερὸν ἐκάλουν, τὸν στενωπὸν δὲ, Μουσεῖον..."</note> Valerius Maximus, however, attributes this to the people of Crotona in Book 8, Chapter 15: *The Crotoniates earnestly requested of him that he allow their Senate, which consisted of a thousand men, to use his counsel. That most wealthy city, having frequently venerated him, made his house a shrine of Ceres after his death; as long as that city flourished, the goddess was honored in the memory of the man, and the man was honored in the religious worship of the goddess.*

**Leucus]** <note>original Greek: "Λεῦκος"</note> Who this Leucus is, whose fourth book of histories Malchus <note>The author Porphyry.</note> praises here, I have not yet been able to find.

**The Egyptians applied themselves to Geometry]** <note>original Greek: "Γεωμετρίας ἐπιμεληθῆναι Αἰγυπτίους"</note> I find this reason indicated by others as to why the ancient Egyptians devoted so much labor to geometry: that this science was necessary for them to redraw boundaries when the ownership of fields was confused by the flooding of the Nile.

**The Chaldeans [applied themselves] to heavenly observations]** <note>original Greek: "Χαλδαίους δὲ τὰ περὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν θεωρήματα"</note> Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> says: *Chaldeans: the name of a nation, perfected in astronomy.* <note>original Greek: "Χαλδαῖοι, ὄνομα ἔθνους, περὶ τὴν ἀστρονομίαν ἠκριβωμένοι"</note> Where he says "perfected," I think it should be read as a genitive <note>original Latin: "ἠκριβωμένου"</note> so that it refers to the "nation." It seems that with these words Malchus equally encompasses both astronomy and astrology. It is known to anyone even slightly educated that the "Chaldeans" were so called not only for those who observed the motions and revolutions of the heavenly bodies, but also for those who promised to predict the fates of men from the gathering and motions of the stars and the positions and aspects of the planets. The Chaldeans are even mentioned by the Emperors Constantine and Julian <margin>|</margin> in Law 5, "Let no one [consult] a soothsayer," in the *Code on Evildoers and Mathematicians* <note>original Latin: "C. de Malefic. et Mathemat." In Roman law, "mathematician" was often a technical term for an astrologer.</note> and similar places; the curiosity of these people for divining is ordered to remain perpetually silent for everyone, under the penalty of the avenging sword. Favorinus argued extensively against this class of people at Rome, as Aulus Gellius testifies in Book 14, Chapter 1. See also Cicero in the second book of *On Divination*, whose words I will quote a little later when mentioning Eudoxus. See also Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in several books against prediction...

# NOTES BY CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...fighting against astrological predictions, as does Francisco Valles in *On Sacred Philosophy, chapter 31,* and, older than both of them, John of Salisbury in *Policraticus, book 2, chapter 19.* <note>John of Salisbury (c. 1115–1180) was an English philosopher and bishop; Francisco Valles (1524–1592) was a Spanish physician known as "the divine Valles." Both were critical of superstitious astrology.</note>

**Agistiae**] <note>original Greek: Ἁγιστίας</note> This should be written as *agisteias*. For it is derived from the verb *agisteuein*, which Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon.</note> explains as "to sanctify" or "to hallow." And "having performed the rites," that is, "having completed the duties of the sacrifice." The same author defines *Agisteias* as "holiness, purity, or religious worship." Hesychius <note>An 5th or 6th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> says: "He performs rites" means "he reveres"; "Performing rites" means "being pious."

<margin>7</margin>
**Eudoxus in the seventh book of the Circuit of the Earth**] <note>original Greek: Εὔδοξος ἐν τῇ ἑβδόμῃ τῆς γῆς περιόδῳ</note> The name of this Eudoxus is most celebrated, becoming famous primarily for that most beautiful achievement by which he was the first to attempt to establish the calendar year among the Greeks. Hence, in the poet Lucan, Julius Caesar says: *Nor shall my Eudoxian year be surpassed by the calendars.* <note>original Latin: "Nec meus Eudoxi vincetur fastibus annus." Caesar is claiming his reformed calendar is superior even to that of the great Eudoxus.</note> He was a native of Cnidus, the son of Aeschines, one of the students of Socrates, and a contemporary of Plato, with whom he traveled to Egypt and stayed for thirteen years. He was an excellent physician, astronomer, and geometer. Cicero writes in *On Divination, book 2*: *Let us come to the delusions of the Chaldeans; regarding them, Eudoxus, a student of Plato (I would prefer to say of Socrates) and easily the leader in astrology in the judgment of the most learned men, gave this opinion, which he left in writing: that the Chaldeans are not to be believed at all in their predictions and in their marking of each person's life from their day of birth.* Suidas records: *Eudoxus, son of Aeschines, of Cnidus, a philosopher, a contemporary of Plato* (if a contemporary, as Strabo also testifies, writing that he was Plato’s companion on the Egyptian journey, then he was not his student, as it appeared in Cicero) *who had three daughters, Actis, Delphis, and Philtis. He had a supernatural talent for philosophy; he wrote many works of this kind, as well as an eight-year cycle; and furthermore, a work on astronomy in verse.* Strabo often uses the testimony of Eudoxus and attributes much to him. I will cite only one or two passages. In Book 14, where in the description of Cnidus he mentions the famous men who originated from there, he puts Eudoxus in the first place: *The notable men of Cnidus are, first, Eudoxus the mathematician, one of the companions of Plato; then Agatharchides, etc.* <note>original Greek: Ἄνδρες δ' ἀξιόλογοι Κνίδιοι, πρῶτον μὲν Εὔδοξος...</note> The same author says in Book 17 that he saw the places in Egypt where Eudoxus and Plato had stayed: *There they showed us the houses of the priests, and the lodgings of Plato and Eudoxus; for Eudoxus traveled there with Plato, and they stayed there with the priests for thirteen years, as some have said. For since these priests were eminent in their knowledge of the heavenly bodies, but were secretive and reluctant to share their knowledge, they [Plato and Eudoxus] eventually won them over through time and attentive service, so that they were taught some of the principles; however, the barbarians kept most things hidden.* In Book 9, he calls him...

# ON PORPHYRY

...a mathematical man, and most skilled in figures and climates. From this passage of Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Syriac name of Porphyry, the author whose work is being commented upon.</note> we learn that Eudoxus also wrote a *Circuit of the Earth* <note>original Greek: γῆς περίοδον</note>, in at least seven books. It was a geographical work: a genre in which we have today (to say nothing of more recent authors) not only Ptolemy and the books of Strabo, illustrated by the illustrious Isaac Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar and a contemporary of the author.</note>, but also several minor authors like Marcian of Heraclea, Scylax of Caryanda, Artemidorus of Ephesus, Dicaearchus of Messana, and Isidore of Charax, which were published together by David Hoeschel at Augsburg ten years ago.

**Never approach hunters**] <note>original Greek: Θηράτορσι μηδέποτε πλησιάζειν</note> That the Pythagoreans were strangers to hunting is also testified by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who also wrote a biography of Pythagoras.</note> in chapter 21: **Regarding hunting, they do not approve of engaging in it, nor of using such a form of exercise.** So also in canon law, clerics are forbidden from hunting, as well as from giving donations to hunters. See Canon 8, *Those who [give] to hunters*, and the following 5th section in Distinction 86; however, these canons, like many others, are poorly observed today. Otherwise, how much value should be placed on the exercise of hunting by those for whom it is not prohibited—provided it is used in moderation—I have previously proved by the testimonies of the most excellent authors in my *Commentaries on Oppian’s Cynegetica* <note>Oppian’s "Cynegetica" is an ancient Greek poem on hunting; Rittershusius published a commentary on it in 1597.</note>.

**Endurance**] <note>original Greek: Τὴν καρτερίαν</note> This, a little later in Number 8, he will call **hardship** <note>original Greek: κακοπάθειαν</note>; or rather, endurance is concerned with the endurance of hardship.

**Having accepted the training of the Egyptian priests**] <note>original Greek: Ἀποδεξάμενον τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἱερέων τὴν ἀγωγήν</note> Thales kindled this zeal and love for the Egyptian priests in the mind of Pythagoras. When Pythagoras came to him desiring to learn, Thales pleaded his extreme old age and the weakness of his strength, which prevented him from assisting him. Instead, he became the advisor for Pythagoras to undertake a journey to Egypt, specifically to the priests of Memphis and Diospolis. It was from them, of course, that Thales himself had carried away whatever wisdom he possessed, as if it were travel-provisions for his life. How much more would this come to Pythagoras, whom Thales saw was far better equipped, not only by natural gifts but also by the benefit of his training, than Thales himself had been? Thales, therefore, did not hesitate to predict concerning Pythagoras that, if he were to associate with those priests, he would become more divine and wiser than all other mortals. So writes Iamblichus at the end of chapter 2 regarding this most wise counsel and prophecy of Thales. But in the Greek text there, some things must be corrected: **He urged him to sail to Egypt, and to those in Mem-**

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...and especially to meet with the priests of Diospolis <note>original Greek: Διοσπόλει. This refers to the "City of Zeus," the Greek name for the Egyptian city of Thebes.</note>. For he <note>Pythagoras</note> provided himself with these things from them.

**To write to Amasis**] Diogenes Laertius (page 568) also testifies that Pythagoras traveled to Egypt, furnished with letters of recommendation from Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, to Amasis, the King of Egypt. Herodotus also records in his third book (*Thalia*) that Amasis was a friend of Polycrates, but that he eventually renounced the rights of friendship because he was troubled by Polycrates's extraordinary good fortune. Amasis feared that such extreme luck would eventually turn into extreme misery, resulting in a wretched end—which is exactly what happened <note>Polycrates was eventually lured into a trap and crucified by a Persian satrap.</note>. Diogenes writes: **He was in Egypt, therefore, at the time when Polycrates introduced him to Amasis by letter.**

**To the Heliopolitans**] Strabo, in his seventeenth book, writes that when he was in Egypt, he saw large houses in Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun."</note> where priests used to live; these priests were both philosophers and astronomers. However, by Strabo's time, that specific order and their way of life had vanished, so much so that not a single leader of those ancient studies and exercises could be shown to him. There were only certain minor sacrificial officials there who would explain the rites of their sacred ceremonies to foreigners. His own words are these: **In Heliopolis we saw large houses in which the priests lived; for they say that in ancient times this was especially the residence of men of philosophy and astronomy. But this community and its discipline have now disappeared. There, no one was shown to us who presided over such training, but only the temple-performers and those who interpret the sacred matters to strangers.**

**Of those examining** <note>original Greek: Σκεπτομένων (skeptomenōn)</note>] This is how it appeared in the manuscript. But without a doubt, the true reading is **making excuses** <note>original Greek: σκηπτομένων (skēptomenōn)</note>. This participle indicates the "pretext" of a matter, which is more commonly called a *prophasis* <term>prophasis: a stated reason or excuse that hides the true motive</term>, when something is offered as a cause that is not the real cause—or when one thing is pretended while another is being done. The lexicographer Hesychius says: *Skēptetai* means he makes an excuse. *Skēptoi* means he might make an excuse. *Skēpsas* means having made an excuse. *Skēpsis* means a pretext. Suidas says similarly: *Skēptetai* means he makes an excuse. *Skēpsis* means a cover or a pretext. And later: "I make an excuse" is used instead of "I pretend," where he also cites the playwright Aristophanes's *Plutus*. This correction of ours is confirmed by the words that follow shortly in Malchus: **By a similar pretext** <note>original Greek: σκῆψιν</note> and **to put forward causes**. For these terms—making excuses, pretending, and putting forward causes—all have the same meaning. But regarding the word "examining"...

### ON PORPHYRY

...there can be no place for this. We should note here the spiteful and crafty nature of the Egyptian priests, whom Strabo also testifies were **mystical and reluctant to share their knowledge** <note>original Greek: μυστικοὺς καὶ δυσμεταδότους</note>; that is, they were accustomed to hiding their secrets out of envy and did not easily communicate them to others. They demonstrated this clearly enough toward Pythagoras as well; treating him like a ball, as the saying goes, they sent him from one place to another. The Heliopolitans sent him to the people of Memphis on the pretext that they were their seniors; the Memphites, in turn, sent him to the people of Diospolis <note>Thebes</note> under the same excuse. These last ones finally admitted him out of fear of the King's <note>Amasis's</note> anger, but they treated him with extreme harshness, hoping that by such ill-treatment they might drive him away and make him a stranger to them.

<margin>8</margin>
**It is not found to have happened**] <note>original Greek: Γεγονὸς οὐχ’ εὑρίσκεται</note> This was surely due to the envious concealment practiced by the priests, or their **mystical and reluctant nature**, to use Strabo's phrasing.

<margin>9</margin>
**To establish a school in his fatherland**] <note>original Greek: Κατασκευάσαι ἐν τῇ πατρίδι διδασκαλεῖον</note> See Iamblichus, Chapter 5, Number 26: **And first he established a school in the city, which is even now called the Hemicycle of Pythagoras, in which the Samians now meet to deliberate on public affairs, believing that they should hold inquiries into what is noble and useful in that place which was established by the man who took care for all things.** Where perhaps the text should read **settled** <note>original Latin: κατεσκήνωσεν</note> instead of **established** <note>original Latin: κατεσκεύασεν</note>.

**The Cave**] <note>original Greek: Ἄντρον</note> Regarding the cave of Pythagoras, see also Iamblichus, Chapter 5, Number 27, where he compares Pythagoras to Minos, the son of Zeus, who they say similarly lived in a cave for nine years and devoted himself to the service of Zeus.

**Having reached forty years**] <note>original Greek: Γεγονότα δ’ ἐτῶν μ’</note> If it is true, as Iamblichus writes in the aforementioned Chapter 5, that Pythagoras returned to Samos from his Egyptian and other travels when he was already about fifty-six years old, I do not see by what reasoning it is said here that he left Samos when he was only forty years old. Perhaps the number is corrupted, which is a common occurrence in manuscript notes.

**The tyranny of Polycrates becoming more intense**] <note>original Greek: Τὴν τοῦ Πολυκράτους τυραννίδα συντονωτέραν οὖσαν</note> Concerning this same flight of Pythagoras from his native Samos—which was oppressed by the tyranny of Polycrates (who, after a brief period of incredible good fortune, was finally crucified)—Dio Chrysostomus also writes in his 47th Oration, the words of which I shall quote below. Tertullian interprets this flight quite unfavorably and unfairly in his book *On the Soul*, Chapter 31, as if he had fled out of mere cowardice to avoid the burdens of war. In this matter, Tertullian argues, Pythagoras showed himself to be far different from Euphorbus <note>A Trojan hero in the Iliad</note>, whose soul Pythagoras used to claim had migrated into his own body...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

<note>Rittershusius is here responding to an ancient critic—likely the Christian author Tertullian—who argued that Pythagoras could not have been the reincarnation of the Trojan hero Euphorbus because their personalities were too different.</note> ...wanted him to be the heir. **For behold (he says), it is well established that Euphorbus possessed a military and warlike soul, as is clear from the very fame of the consecrated shields; but Pythagoras was so slothful and unwarlike that, avoiding the battles of Greece at that time, he preferred the peace of Italy, devoted to geometry, astrology, and music, and was a stranger to the zeal and disposition of Euphorbus, etc.** <note>Pythagoras famously claimed to remember his past life as Euphorbus, a warrior in the Trojan War. The critic uses this to mock the doctrine of the "transmigration of souls."</note> As if, forsooth, those who prefer to follow and cultivate the studies and arts of peace deserve reproach more than those who pursue horrific wars. In this same vein, our Saint Isidore of Pelusium <note>A 5th-century monk and prolific letter writer</note> writes in Book 4 of his *Epistles*—which I was the first to bring to light when they were previously unpublished <note>original Latin: ἀνέκδοτον (anecdote/unpublished)</note>—in Epistle 205, that Pythagoras recoiled from the company of Phalaris because his teaching could not turn the man away from his tyrannical purpose. **But Pythagoras, who thought so highly of his own wisdom, why did he leap away from the company of Phalaris? Was it not because that man remained a tyrant even after such great instruction?** <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόρας δὲ, ὁ μέγα ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ φρονήσας, τῆς Φαλάριδος συνουσίας διὰ τί ἀπεπήδησεν; οὐκ ἐπειδὴ μετὰ τὴν τοσαύτην διδασκαλίαν ἐκεῖνος πάλιν τύραννος ἦν;</note> 

Although one might suspect that Isidore suffered a lapse in memory by naming Phalaris <note>A notoriously cruel tyrant of Sicily known for his "brazen bull"</note> when he meant or ought to have spoken of Polycrates <note>The tyrant of Samos</note>, I nevertheless believe he can easily be excused from any error. I know that Phalaris was indeed tested by Pythagoras and his follower Abaris the Hyperborean <note>A legendary priest of Apollo</note> to see if he would desist from tyranny, cruelty, and impiety—but he was tested in vain. This is witnessed by Iamblichus in Chapter 32, where in Number 221 he writes something especially memorable: that on the very day Phalaris plotted the death of Pythagoras and Abaris, he himself was slaughtered by others. Thus, even here, the proverb (or rather the verse) proved true:

->**The man who devises evil for another, devises evil for himself.**<-
<note>original Greek: Οἷ αὐτῷ κακὰ τεύχει ἀνὴρ, ἄλλῳ κακὰ τεύχων. This is a variation of a famous line by the poet Hesiod.</note>

But let us return for a moment to the mention of his flight due to the tyranny of Polycrates. Regarding this, Strabo writes in Book 14 of his *Geography*: **Regarding him (Polycrates), they record that Pythagoras, seeing the tyranny growing, left the city and departed for Egypt and Babylon for the sake of learning; returning from there and seeing the tyranny still persisting, he sailed to Italy and spent the rest of his life there.** <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τούτου δὲ (τοῦ Πολυκράτους) καὶ Πυθαγόραν ἱστοροῦσι φυομένην ἰδόντα τὴν τυραννίδα, ἐκλιπεῖν τὴν πόλιν...</note> Compare also Iamblichus, Chapter 2, Number 11, where he writes that at the very first rise of Polycrates' tyranny, when Pythagoras was about eighteen years old, he stole away from Samos by night without anyone knowing. Taking Hermodamas as a companion, he crossed over to visit the philosophers Pherecydes, Anaximander, and Thales. Thales, that wise old man, was the one who advised him to undertake the journey to the Egyptian priests, from whom he would draw more wisdom. Thus, Pythagoras fled his homeland of Samos twice: once before visiting Egypt and other foreign lands...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

"...all the younger men desire to be his disciples, and the elders more gladly see their own children associating with him than tending to their own affairs." <note>original: "νεωτέρους ἅπαντας ἐπιθυμεῖν αὐτοῦ μαθητὰς εἶναι..."</note> etc. The things which follow in that same place I have used below to illustrate another passage of Malchus <note>Malchus was the birth name of the philosopher Porphyry, the author of the biography being commented upon</note>. Strabo, in book 17, testifies that he saw large houses in Heliopolis <note>A major city of ancient Egypt, center of the sun-cult</note> in which priests formerly lived; however, their order had entirely failed by then, as had their knowledge. Clement of Alexandria, in *Stromata* Book I, page 131, names the Egyptian "arch-prophet" Sonchedes, whose disciple Pythagoras was said to be. There he also adds who were the teachers of Plato and Eudoxus in Egypt: "It is recorded that Pythagoras studied under Sonchedes the Egyptian arch-prophet; Plato under Sechnuphis of Heliopolis; and Eudoxus the Cnidian under Conuphis, who was also an Egyptian." <note>original: "ἱστορεῖται δὲ Πυθαγόρας μὲν Σώγχηδι... Κονούφιδι, τῷ καὶ αὐτῷ Αἰγυπτίῳ."</note> I am correcting Clement here in passing in the words shortly following: "He introduces the most wise Solon learning from the barbarian." <note>original: "Τὸν σοφώτατον Σόλωνα μανθάνοντα εἰσάγει πρὸς τοῦ βαρβάρου."</note> For it should be read as "from *a certain*" (*pros tou*) instead of "from *the*" (*pros tou* with a definite article); this has the force of "from someone." This is just as in St. Paul’s First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, verse 6: "in *a* matter," which has the force of "in *some* matter." For it should be read thus where the common versions say "in *the* matter." In the same way, in 1 Corinthians 15:8, instead of what is in the common books, "as if to *the* untimely birth," we should undoubtedly restore it more correctly from John Chrysostom as "as if to *some* [untimely birth]," that is, "as if to a certain one." But these things are mentioned in passing.

<margin>12</margin> **And three differences of letters**] This is a memorable passage concerning the threefold difference of letters which existed among the Egyptians. It can be illustrated by a comparison of the things which Clement of Alexandria has in *Stromata* Book 5, page 237: "Immediately, those being educated among the Egyptians learn first of all the method of Egyptian letters called <term>epistolographic</term> <note>The "common" script used for everyday correspondence, now known as Demotic</note>; second, the <term>hieratic</term> <note>A cursive form of hieroglyphs used by priests for religious documents</note>, which the sacred scribes use; and last and final, the <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>The famous "sacred carvings" used on monuments</note>. Of the hieroglyphic, one kind is literal through the first elements <note>Meaning phonetic or alphabetic signs</note>, and the other is symbolic. Of the symbolic, one kind is literal through imitation <note>For example, drawing a literal picture of an object</note>; another is written figuratively; and another is directly allegorical through certain enigmas. For instance, wishing to write 'Sun,' they make a circle; and for 'Moon,' a crescent shape, according to the literal form. But figuratively, they draw by transferring and shifting according to a particular quality, sometimes changing things, sometimes reshaping them in many ways. Indeed, they record the praises of kings through theological myths, inscribing them through reliefs. Of the third kind, regarding enigmas, let this be an example: they likened the path of the other stars, because of their oblique course, to the bodies of snakes; but the Sun they likened to a beetle, because [the beetle rolls] a circular..." <note>The text ends mid-sentence here as the page turns; it refers to the Egyptian belief that the dung beetle rolling its ball represented the movement of the sun.</note>

...having fashioned a shape from cow dung, [the beetle] rolls it forward while facing it. They say it lives beneath the earth for six months, and for the other half of the year, this creature lives above ground, casting its seed into the sphere and generating offspring; they claim that no female beetle exists. <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τῆς βοείας..." This passage describes the scarab beetle, which in Egyptian symbolism represented the sun and the concept of self-creation or rebirth.</note>

**Hieroglyphics]** Many authors have mentioned hieroglyphic letters, such as Philo in Book 1 of *The Life of Moses*, Clement of Alexandria in *Miscellanies* <note>Latin: *Stromata*</note> Books 1 and 5, Cornelius Tacitus in *Annals* Book 2, Lucan in Book 3, Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 16, and Apuleius in Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*. The scholar Suidas also praises a certain Chaeremon who wrote on hieroglyphics. His book has not survived to our time, but we do have Horapollo (called by others Horus of the Nile), a writer on hieroglyphics whose work was published in Greek and Latin with highly learned notes by our friend David Hoeschel at Augsburg; I also possess a version translated into the French language. See also Francisco Valles in *On Sacred Philosophy*, Chapter 16, at the end.

**To Zabratas]** Regarding this Zabratas—who he might have been—I have not yet been able to find anything else elsewhere. However, we may infer from this passage that he was a certain Babylonian priest who initiated and instructed Pythagoras in the sacred rites.

**Wandering]** Note the purpose for which Pythagoras's travels served him: namely, that he might return home as if from a marketplace, having acquired for himself the most beautiful and precious "merchandise" of wisdom. This is the force of the word *eneporeusato* <note>original: "ἐνεπορεύσατο"</note> which Malchus <note>The birth name of Porphyry</note> uses here. For it comes from *emporos*, the Greek word for a merchant. Clement of Alexandria uses the same word with similar elegance in *Miscellanies* Book 1, page 130: "Plato does not deny that he imported the finest elements of philosophy from the barbarians, and he admits to having traveled to Egypt." <note>original: "Πλάτων δὲ οὐκ ἀρνεῖται..."</note> Let us also note here the golden rule of study which Nicolaus Damascenus handed down through a very elegant comparison regarding the method of travel, as can be seen in the encyclopedia of Suidas under the entry "Nicolaus."

Therefore, let our own youth, if they are wise, set this same goal for their own travels.

<margin>15</margin> **For he was the first to make an exact science of this study of men]** This refers to <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face</note>, which is the art of deducing the mind, nature, and character of any man from the features of his face and the condition and gestures of his body. Pythagoras was the first to treat this art with precision, and according to this art, he either admitted certain people into his inner circle or rejected them. For this very reason, he turned away Cylon, a nobleman of Croton, because from the features of his body, the mind lurking within him...

...had discovered him to be so cruel: as is seen below, in Number 74. Subsequently, many others refined and practiced this art: such as Zopyrus (who, as we learn from Cicero, lived in the age of Socrates), and others like Polemo and Adamantius. Even Aristotle, that genius and counselor of nature, did not leave the subject untouched. Indeed, his commentary on this matter survives, from which I will note a few points here, so that the principles of his art may be understood. These principles consist in the fact that the habits of the soul follow the temperament of the body—a point which Galen also demonstrates in an entire book. 

Thus, Aristotle states right at the beginning: <note>original Greek: Αἱ διάνοιαι ἕπονται τοῖς σώμασι...</note> "Mental characteristics follow the bodies, and they are not independent in themselves, as if they were unaffected by the movements of the body. This becomes quite clear in both states of drunkenness and in illnesses. For mental characteristics appear to be greatly altered by the affections of the body; and conversely, it is clear that the body sympathizes with the affections of the soul, as seen in cases of love, fears, griefs, and pleasures." And shortly after: "Thus it is necessary that such a disposition follows such a body."

The same author says in Chapter 4: "It seems to me that the soul and the body sympathize with one another; and when the condition of the soul is altered, it simultaneously alters the form of the body; and again, when the form of the body is altered, it simultaneously alters the condition of the soul. For since it belongs to the soul to be pained and to be glad, it is manifest that those who are pained are more gloomy, and those who are glad are cheerful," etc. More follows in the same place regarding this opinion, <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἑκάτερον ἑκατέρῳ ἕπεται</note> "that each follows the other": that is, both the soul is affected by the body, and in turn, the body by the soul. He says this becomes evident even in those suffering from mania. 

Similarly, Cassius in *Problem 51*, responding to the question: <note>original Greek: Διὰ τί οἱ τερατόμορφοι, καὶ ἄφρονες;</note> "Why are those of monstrous form also senseless?" answers from the same principle: "Because the things of the soul sympathize with the things of the body, just as the things of the body do with the soul." 

Nevertheless, that this art—being based on conjecture—sometimes fails is shown by the very famous example of Socrates. In his case, the art of Zopyrus went astray, because Socrates himself had corrected the wicked natural inclinations of his nature (of which his bodily features provided signs) through the diligence of discipline and habit: as recorded in the works of Cicero.

To this belongs that passage from our Phaedrus, in Book 3 of his *Aesopic Fables*: *“And I have often found the beautiful to be the worst: And I have known many with an ugly face to be the best.”* And as the same author says elsewhere: *“Things are not always what they seem. The first appearance <note>Latin: "frons prima", literally "the first forehead" or "the front facade"</note> deceives many.”* I noted more on this most elegant writer some 14 years ago. Regarding Pythagorean <term>physiognomonia</term> <note>the art of judging character from physical features</note>, I shall note more below.

He uses the example of Socrates to show that while physical traits may suggest certain character flaws, personal discipline can overcome natural inclinations.</summary>

<margin>14</margin>**[Whose name was Zamolxis]** Regarding this man, Iamblichus writes thus in Chapter 30, Number 173: **"Zamolxis, being a Thracian and having been a slave of Pythagoras, and having heard the teachings of Pythagoras, was set free. Arriving among the Getae <note>a Thracian tribe</note>, he established laws for them and exhorted the citizens to courage, having persuaded them that the soul is immortal."** (*I read* **having persuaded** <note>original Greek: πείσας</note>, *unless perhaps Iamblichus wrote,* **by persuading them that the soul is immortal**.) **"Even now the Galatians and the Triballians"** (*so I think it should be read*) **"and many other barbarians persuade their sons that the soul cannot be destroyed, but remains for those who have died; and that death is not to be feared, but one must hold firm against dangers. And having taught these things to the Getae, and having written laws for them, he is the greatest of the gods among them."** Concerning the same man, Diogenes Laertius says in Book 8, page 568: **"He also had a slave Zamolxis, to whom the Getae sacrifice, thinking him to be Cronus, as Herodotus says."** The passage of Herodotus, which Diogenes praises here, is in *The Muse* Book 4, or *Melpomene*, where he calls the Getae **"those who act as immortals"** <note>original Greek: ἀθανατίζοντας</note>, from the immortality of souls which they were taught by Zamolxis; and he describes at length the ritual by which every fifth year they send to him someone from among them chosen by lot, whom they bind by hands and feet. However, in the same place near the end, Herodotus adds that he believes Zamolxis existed many years before Pythagoras. This same Zamolxis is also mentioned several times by Origen in Books 2 and 3 of *Against Celsus*.

<margin>15</margin>**[And when Pherecydes fell ill]** Apuleius writes in his *Florida*: *"Furthermore, Pherecydes, originating from the island of Syros, was the first who, having rejected the binding of verses, dared to write in spreading words, with loose speech, and free oration."* (This is prose, as we commonly call it.) *"Pythagoras also honored him as a teacher, and when he was dissolved into a scabies of serpents by the rot of an unspeakable disease, he religiously buried him, etc."* In this passage, Apuleius uses the phrase *"rot of an unspeakable disease, etc."* as a roundabout way of describing **phthiriasis** <note>original Greek: φθειρίασιν</note>, which is the lice-infestation disease. We read that Sulla, Herod, and others were consumed by this kind of ailment—usually men who were cruel or lustful. Regarding Pherecydes, see also below, Number 55, and Iamblichus Chapter 30, Number 184.

**[And after he died, having buried him]** Iamblichus records these things more fully in the aforementioned place: **"And tending to him, he remained by him until his end, and fulfilled the sacred duty <note>original Greek: τὴν ὁσίαν ἀπεπλήρωσε</note> concerning his own leader. Thus he held his devotion to his teacher in high regard."** <unclear>Where</unclear> that phrase, **"fulfilled the sacred duty,"** Arcerius correctly translates as *he performed the funeral rites.* For so also Suidas interprets **sacred duty** <note>original Greek: ὁσίαν</note> among—

...interprets the term <term>kēdeian</term> <note>original Greek: κηδείαν</note> as "honor paid to the dead." I restored and defended this reading for Isidore of Pelusium <note>a 5th-century ascetic and prolific letter writer</note>, as the name had been corrupted in more than one place in his works. See our Notes on Letter 57, Book 4.

**[To Hermodamas, the descendant of Creophylus]** Our author Malchus <note>Rittershusius refers to Porphyry by his original Syrian name, Malchus</note> also mentions this Hermodamas above; so does Iamblichus in Chapter 2, Number 11. There, he says Hermodamas held the surname "Creophylian" because he was a descendant of that Creophylus who was Homer’s host, friend, and teacher. Strabo also mentions him in Book 14 of his *Geography* (in the section on Samos), reporting that Homer, out of gratitude for his hospitality, once dedicated a poem to him titled *The Capture of Oechalia* <note>original: Οἰχαλίας ἅλωσις</note>. However, the poet Callimachus and others believed the poem was actually written by Creophylus himself and merely attributed to his guest, Homer. Furthermore, in Strabo’s text, the name is spelled *Kreōphylos* (with an omega) rather than *Kreophylos*.

**[Of Eurymenes the Samian athlete]** This Samian athlete Eurymenes is distinct from the Eurymenes of Syracuse, the brother of Dion, whom Iamblichus mentions in Chapter 31, Number 189. Regarding this athlete—whom Pythagoras was the first to strengthen by recommending a moderate diet of meat, whereas he had previously followed a different regimen—Diogenes Laertius writes an account similar to Malchus in Book 8, page 575: **"It is said that he was the first to train athletes on meat, and specifically Eurymenes first,"** etc. Therefore, Pythagoras did not entirely abhor the eating of meat himself, nor did he wish all of his followers to abstain from it. <note>This comment addresses the famous debate over whether Pythagoras was a strict vegetarian or allowed meat for certain groups like athletes.</note>

**[Those who feed on cheese and figs]** In the same passage, Diogenes Laertius testifies that in ancient times, athletes used dried figs, soft cheeses, and wheat <note>original Greek: ἰσχάσι ξηραῖς, καὶ τυροῖς ὑγροῖς, καὶ πυροῖς</note>.

**[To flee the envy that comes from winning]** This is an ancient proverb: **"To win is good; but to over-win brings envy."** Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> in Book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 21, discusses the Emperor Julian. The Emperor had spurned the frequent embassies and pleas of the Persian King, who was begging for an end to the war and the siege of Ctesiphon (a great city in Persia), even offering a portion of the territory. But Julian did not pay attention, nor did he pity the supplication; rather, as the proverb says, he did not consider that **"it is good to win; but to over-win is invidious."**

**[Of the Idaean Dactyls]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν Ἰδαίων Δακτύλων; these were mythical ancient metalworkers and magicians associated with Mount Ida</note> Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: *Idaean Dactyl*. *Idaean* comes from Mount Ida.

<margin>18</margin>
**[Dicaearchus]** <note>original Greek: Ὁ Δικαίαρχος</note> This man was a famous Peripatetic <note>a member of the philosophical school founded by Aristotle</note>, a disciple of Aristotle, and a contemporary and fellow student of Aristoxenus (of whom I speak elsewhere). Diogenes Laertius also makes use of his testimony in his biography of Pythagoras. Cicero mentions him very often, and almost never without a glowing eulogy, at one time calling him an "excellent man," at another "most skilled in history," and elsewhere a "great and eloquent Peripatetic," etc. All of these things strongly confirm the judgment of our Malchus concerning him, who below counts him among the "more accurate" <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀκριβεστέροις</note> writers. There exists today a small book titled *The Life of Greece* <note>original Greek: Βίος Ἑλλάδος; just as the Roman scholar Varro wrote *The Life of the Roman People*</note>, bearing the name of Dicaearchus and addressed to Theophrastus, written partly in iambic senarii <note>a common meter in ancient drama</note> and partly in prose, which the Illustrious Henri Estienne first published, and then our own David Hoeschel. If anyone should ask me what I think of that book, I would say it seems to me to be more of a summary <note>term: epitome; a condensed version of a larger work</note> of Dicaearchus rather than the work of Dicaearchus himself. For we have learned from Suidas and from Stephanus of Byzantium’s *On Cities* that he wrote several books on this subject—specifically three. However, that book I mentioned is a single, continuous work. Furthermore, not everything cited from Dicaearchus by others is found in it today. Moreover, there is a memorable eulogy of the city of Athens reported there, adding also a testimony taken from the verses of Lysippus. I will transcribe the passage from a little earlier, so that it may appear at the same time what distinction that author makes between *Attics* and *Athenians*, which is not easily found elsewhere; at the same time, I will supply a missing part. "Of the inhabitants, some are Attics, and some are Athenians. The Attics are meddlesome in their speech, deceitful, slanderous, and observers of the lives of foreigners. But the Athenians are high-minded, simple in their ways, and genuine guardians of friendship. Certain speech-writers run through the city, shaking down those visiting and the wealthy foreigners; whom, when the people catch them, they punish with harsh penalties. But the sincere Athenians are sharp listeners to the arts, because of their constant (it seems *schools*, or *conversations*, or *exercises* should be supplied)..."

-> ### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSII ### <-

In general, just as other cities differ from the countryside regarding pleasure and the correction of life, so does the city of the Athenians surpass the rest of the cities. One must guard against the courtesans as much as possible, lest one perish pleasantly without noticing. The verse of Lysippus <note>a comic poet of the 5th century BCE</note> says:

> If you have not seen Athens, you are a log.
> If you have seen it, but were not captivated, you are an ass.
> If you depart satisfied, you are a pack-mule.

We shall exchange these for as many Latin iambic verses in this form:

> *If Athens you have never seen, a trunk you be.*
> *If seen but not enthralled, a mere ass you see.*
> *Leaving your visit at a run? To me, a mule you be.*

**[Much-wandering]** <note>original Greek: Πολυπλάγου</note> Thus Homer calls **Ulysses** <note>original: Vlyssem</note> **much-wandering** <note>original Greek: πολύπλαγκτον</note>.

**[Extraordinary]** <note>original Greek: Περιττοῦ</note> For the most part, **superfluous** things <note>original Greek: Περιττὰ</note> are *unnecessary*: (from which also the physicians' term **residue** <note>original Greek: περιττώματα; meaning waste products or bodily excretions</note> is derived) which are called by another name **the excesses** <note>original Greek: τὰ ὑπερβάλλοντα</note>, as in that noble philosophical precept, which Simplicius <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> emphasizes more than others: **Let superfluous things be silenced** <note>original Greek: Σιγάσθω τὰ περιττά</note>; that is: *Let the unnecessary things be left unsaid.* Likewise in the verses of the comic poet Alexis found in Athenaeus, book 10,

> I hate the superfluous. For in things that exceed
> There is no pleasure, but only great expense.

That is:
> *I loathe the unnecessary. For no joy*
> *Dwells in the superfluous: it is only empty cost.*

So it is found everywhere else. But here, an **extraordinary man** <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ περιττὸς</note> is one who is eminent, remarkable, and excellent: who elsewhere is called **select** <note>original Greek: ἐξαίρετος</note>: as is very frequent in Aristotle. To provide proof, I will bring forward several examples. Thus in the *Problems*, Book 1, Section 30, page 212: **Extraordinary men are melancholic.** And on page 216: **Having nothing extraordinary**: *Possessing nothing remarkable or distinguished.* Thus in the *Ethics*, Book 6, chapter 7, he joins **extraordinary and wonderful, and difficult, and divine.** <note>original Greek: περιττὰ καὶ θαυμαστὰ, καὶ χαλεπὰ, καὶ δαιμόνια</note> Likewise in the *Politics*, Book 8, he joins in parallel **the extraordinary and wonderful works.** <note>original Greek: τὰ περιττὰ καὶ θαυμάσια τῶν ἔργων</note> Thus in the *Metaphysics*, Book 1, chapter 2: **that extraordinary men are unfortunate.** Also in the same work, Book 10, chapter 1: **Saying nothing extraordinary, they seem to say something.** Thus in the *Politics*, Book 5, chapter 10, it is called an **extraordinary action** <note>original Greek: περιττὴ πρᾶξις</note>. Other most excellent authors use it this way as well, such as Theognis <note>an archaic Greek poet</note>:

> A servant and messenger of the Muses should, if he knows
> Anything extraordinary in wisdom, not be begrudging, etc.

<summary>This page features a linguistic and cultural commentary on the city of Athens and the Greek term "perittos." Rittershusius explores the double meaning of the word as both "superfluous" and "extraordinary," citing numerous classical authorities like Aristotle and Simplicius.</summary>
<keywords>Athens, Lysippus, Ulysses, Aristotle, Philology, Greek Etymology, perittos, Superfluous vs. Extraordinary, Classical Commentary</keywords>

<header>ON PORPHYRY. 153</header>

So in Plato’s *Axiochus* <note>a dialogue formerly attributed to Plato</note> there are **extraordinary words** <note>original Greek: περιττοὶ λόγοι</note>. And in the same place **common things** are contrasted with **extraordinary things**. So Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher</note> in his book *On Joseph* says: "he kindled the nature of the boy with **exceptional and extraordinary care**" <note>original Greek: ἐξαιρέτοις καὶ περιτταῖς ἐπιμελείαις</note> etc. Behold, he joins **exceptional** and **extraordinary** in parallel, as being equivalent in meaning. So Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry, the author being commented upon</note> himself below joins "the **more extraordinary** account" <note>original Greek: τὸν περιττότερον λόγον</note> and "the account of science worked out with **precision**." So Simplicius <note>a late antique commentator on Aristotle and Epictetus</note> in his *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Epictetus*, page 8, column b: "those having something **extraordinary** in the arts are able to distinguish the results from the instruments." That is, those who have something **excellent** in the arts, etc. So in Suidas <note>the Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, Sallustius the Palace Prefect is called by some historian "a man **exceptionally extraordinary** in philanthropy" <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ διαφερόντως περιττὸς εἰς φιλανθρωπίαν</note>: *A man endowed with a certain exceptional and singular humanity.* And shortly after in the same place, he writes that the so-called "golden apples" were not named so because they were truly made of gold, but because they were **more extraordinary than the others** <note>original Greek: περιττώτερα τῶν ἄλλων</note>, that is, superior to the others. For I would prefer to explain it this way rather than, as Suidas does, as **larger** <note>original Greek: μείζονα</note>, that is, greater in size.

**[The city of the Crotoniates]** Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist biographer of Pythagoras</note> calls this a **most distinguished city** in chapter 6. And Valerius Maximus <note>a Roman historian</note> in Book 8, chapter 15, calls it a "most wealthy city, whose Senate (unprecedentedly) consisted of a thousand men." Pythagoras was a counselor to this great and truly most honorable Senate at their own request, as we learn from the same testimony of Valerius. From this, one can estimate the high opinion and trust the people of Croton had in his wisdom.

**[The assembly of elders: and soon: to the youths: and again: to the children]** To this pertains what Isocrates <note>an Athenian rhetorician</note> writes in *Busiris* about Pythagoras returning from Egypt: that he so excelled others in nobility that all the young men desired to be his disciples, and the elders preferred their children to live with him rather than tend to family business. I will record the Greek words in another place.

<margin>19</margin>
**[Not only men, but also women]** That women also ought to be cultivated in the study of learning, and indeed that this can be done without detriment or danger to their modesty, is demonstrated with both reasons and examples by Juan Luis Vives <note>a Spanish Renaissance humanist</note> in his *On the Education of a Christian Woman*, Book 1. Also in his book *On the Office of a Husband*, in the chapter on the discipline of a woman.

**[And the name of Theano was spread abroad]** Instead of "was spread abroad" <note>original Greek: καὶ διεβοήθη</note>, perhaps we should more correctly read "was famous all around" <note>original Greek: περιεβοήθη</note>. Moreover, this **Theano** is also listed by Iamblichus in the catalog of illustrious women—

<header>NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS</header>

...of those who followed the Pythagorean sect. And Didymus <note>a Greek scholar and grammarian of the 1st century BC</note>, in the book he wrote on Pythagorean philosophy, testifies in Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*, Book 1, page 133, that **Theano of Croton was the first of women to practice philosophy and write poems.** <note>original Greek: Θεανὼ τὴν Κροτωνιᾶτιν πρώτην γυναικῶν φιλοσοφῆσαι, καὶ ποιήματα γράψαι</note> So Ausonius <note>a Roman poet</note> says: *Those virtues which Tanaquil <note>the legendary queen of Rome</note> possessed, and those of the Pythagorean Theano.* But as to who she actually was, I see it is not sufficiently established among authors. For some make her the daughter of Brontinus of Croton and the wife of Pythagoras; others, however, make her the wife of Brontinus and a student of Pythagoras. Diogenes Laertius, Book 8, page 594, says: **Pythagoras also had a wife named Theano, the daughter of Brontinus of Croton; but others say she was the wife of Brontinus and a student of Pythagoras.** <note>original Greek: Ἦν δὲ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ καὶ γυνὴ, Θεανὼ ὄνομα, Βροντίνου τοῦ Κροτωνιάτου θυγάτηρ· οἱ δὲ γυναῖκα μὲν εἶναι Βροντίνου, μαθήτριαν δὲ Πυθαγόρου.</note> Theodoretus <note>a 5th-century Christian bishop and theologian</note> also writes in his second discourse, *On the First Principle, Against the Gentiles*, that Theano was the wife of Pythagoras, and that after her husband’s death she took up the governance of the schools along with his sons Telauges and Mnesarchus. The words of Theodoretus, repeated from a little earlier, are these:

> Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, said the Monad <note>the "One" or the fundamental unit</note> was the beginning of all things. At the same time, Anaxagoras and Pythagoras lived. But Pythagoras’s school was inherited by his wife Theano, and Telauges and Mnesarchus, his sons. Empedocles of Acragas became a student of Telauges. Archelaus was a student of Anaxagoras, and Socrates the Athenian was a student of Archelaus. Both Anaxagoras and Pythagoras, having arrived in Egypt, met with the wise men of the Egyptians and Hebrews there, and gleaned their knowledge concerning Being. <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόρας δὲ ὁ Μνησάρχου ἀρχὴν τῶν πάντων ἔφησε τὴν μονάδα. κτλ.</note>

But we learn from Iamblichus, Book 1, chapter 27, that two different women possessed the name Theano; one of whom was the wife of Pythagoras, the other of Brontinus. Indeed, there are even those who make one of the daughters of Pythagoras a Theano; among these is the unnamed **biographer** <term>biographer</term> <note>original Greek: βιογράφος</note> in Photius, page 712 of the *Library*: **And Theano is said to be not only a student, but also one of his daughters.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἡ Θεανὼ δὲ λέγεται οὐ μαθήτρια μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μία τῶν θυγατέρων αὐτοῦ εἶναι.</note> One or the other of these women is said to have uttered this famous and beautiful maxim (Iamblichus calls it "the beautiful and much-admired saying" <note>original Greek: τὸ καλὸν καὶ περίβλεπτον ῥῆμα</note> in chapter 27 and "the world-renowned apophthegm" <note>original Greek: τὸ περιβόητον γενόμενον ἀπόφθεγμα</note> in chapter 11): **that a woman rising from her cohabiting husband is holy and may approach the temples and offer sacrifice the same day; but from a man not her own, never.**

Moreover, the Latin translation of this chapter 11 in Iamblichus is of no value <note>Rittershusius is criticizing a previous translator's work here</note>, which says: *Regarding these things, that famous story was widely known, that she spoke freely in a public assembly, saying it is pious to go to the rites on the same day as rising from a husband sharing the same home; but from one who is not a relative or kinsman, to go by no means.*
