For the interpreter thought that Pythagoras had brought this forth in a public assembly regarding the duty of a wife, whereas Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras</note> intends that the wife herself—following the mind and opinion of Theano—speaks or thinks this during marital union. For this is how I understand "the meeting" <note>original Greek: τὴν σύνοδον (tēn synodon)</note>, which in the same chapter was previously called "conversation with husbands" <note>original Greek: ἡ πρὸς τοὺς ἄνδρας ὁμιλία (hē pros tous andras homilia)</note>, and is more commonly called "being together" <note>original Greek: συνουσία (synousia)</note>; in Ausonius's *Summaries of Homer* <note>original Latin: Periochis Homericis; Ausonius was a 4th-century Roman poet</note> it is "a gathering into an assembly." Nor did the interpreter correctly translate the little word *never* <note>original Greek: μηδέποτε (mēdepote)</note> as "by no means," as if it were the same as *not at all* <note>original Greek: μηδαμῶς (mēdamōs)</note>. But *mēdepote* means *never*. Furthermore, "he who does not belong" <note>original Greek: ὁ μὴ προσήκων (ho mē prosēkōn)</note> simply means an outside man, or *another's husband*. For Diogenes Laertius <note>a 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> also calls him "another’s" <note>original Greek: ἀλλότριον (allotrion)</note> in Book 8, page 595, where he writes that Theano uttered this famous decree in response to someone else's question: "They say that when she was asked how many days it takes for a woman to be pure after being with a man, she said: 'From her own husband, immediately; from another’s, never.'" <note>original Greek: φασὶν αὐτὴν ἐρωτηθεῖσαν, ποσταία γυνὴ ἀπ’ ἀνδρὸς καθαρεύει, φάναι· Ἀπὸ μὲν τοῦ ἰδίου παραχρῆμα· ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου οὐδέποτε.</note> Theodoretus <note>a 5th-century Christian bishop and theologian</note> in Discourse 12, *On Active Virtue*, reports the same with these words: "When asked how many days it takes for a woman to go down to the Thesmophorion <note>a temple or festival of Demeter, where ritual purity was required</note> after being with a man, she said: 'From her own husband, immediately'; she said, 'from another’s, never.'" <note>original Greek: Ἐρωτηθεῖσα, ποσταία γυνὴ ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς εἰς τὸ Θεσμοφόριον κάτεισιν· Ἀπὸ μὲν τοῦ ἰδίου παραχρῆμα ἔφη. Ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου οὐδέποτε.</note> In short, Theano wished to indicate that marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled: but that fornicators and adulterers will be condemned by divine judgment; which is the sentiment of St. Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, the last chapter, verse 4. See what I have said in the Notes to Isidore's Epistle 129, Book 4.

There is also another memorable decree of Theano, in which she said that she who enters into her husband's presence ought to put off her modesty along with her garments, and upon rising again, take it up again along with her garments. Diogenes Laertius says: "She (Theano) used to advise a woman about to go to her own husband to put off her modesty along with her clothes; and when rising, to take it up again with them." <note>original Greek: Τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα μελλούσῃ πορεύεσθαι, παρῄνει (ἡ Θεανὼ) ἅμα τοῖς ἐνδύμασι καὶ τὴν αἰσχύνην ἀποτίθεσθαι· ἀνισταμένην τε πάλιν ἅμα αὐτοῖσιν ἀναλαμβάνειν.</note> Theodoretus relates a third saying <note>original Greek: ἀπόφθεγμα (apophthegm)</note> of hers in the aforementioned Discourse 12. For when some man or other, looking at her and admiring her beauty, said, "**A beautiful forearm!**" <note>original Greek: Καλὸς ὁ πῆχυς (Kalos ho pēchys)</note> she replied: "**But not for the public!**" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐ δημόσιον (All’ ou dēmousion)</note>—that is, *But not common* (just as a *common woman* is described by Ulpian <note>a 2nd-century Roman jurist</note> in Law 13, *If a wife*, section *but also in her*, Digest *on the Julian law regarding adultery*, who publicly prostitutes herself).

**Nor was their silence of an ordinary kind**] Concerning the Pythagorean silence, which was commanded of the disciples, it is a most celebrated matter. They also called it "restraint of speech" <note>original Greek: ἐχεμυθίαν (echemythian)</note>, according to Aulus Gellius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author, often called Agellius in early modern texts</note> in Book 1, chapter 9. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> says: "He practices restraint of speech; he keeps his words within himself. Restraint of speech: silence, mysteries. One who restrains speech: one who guards a hidden mystery, or one who is prudent." <note>original Greek: Ἐχεμυθεῖ, ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον. Ἐχεμυθία, σιωπὴ, μυστήρια. Ἐχέμυθος, μυστήριον κρυπτὸν φυλάττων, ἢ φρόνιμος.</note>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

Then, from an anonymous author, he adds the following: "He was extremely secretive and kept his thoughts hidden, etc." <note>original Greek: Ἦν δὲ ἐχέμυθος ἐς τὰ μάλιστα καὶ κρυψίνους</note> And shortly after: "The most secretive is the most prudent." <note>original Greek: Ἐχεμυθότατος, ὁ φρονιμώτατος</note> Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> says: "He keeps silence; he holds the word within himself in stillness." <note>original Greek: Ἐχεμυθεῖ, ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον σιωπῇ</note> "To keep silence is to be still, to conceal one's words." <note>original Greek: Ἐχεμυθεῖν, σιωπᾶν, λόγους στέγειν</note> "A silent person is one who holds the word within himself, or rather restrains the word in silence." <note>original Greek: Ἐχέμυθος, ἔχων ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἤτοι κρατῶν τὸν λόγον σιωπῇ</note> They also used the term *secretiveness* <note>original Greek: ἐχεμυθοσύνην (echemythosynēn)</note>, though it was a rarer word. See Iamblichus, Book 1, chapters 16, 20, 25, 31, and 32. Likewise, Book 2, the final chapter.

There also exists an epigram by Palladas <note>a 4th-century Greek poet known for his biting wit</note> on this Pythagorean silence in the first book of the *Anthology*, under the title *On Silence*, which I will provide here along with my own Latin translation.

->*Silence is a great part of education among men;*<-
->*I have the wise Pythagoras himself as my witness.*<-
->*He, though knowing how to speak, taught others to be silent,*<-
->*Having discovered a powerful remedy in quiet.*<-
<note>Translated from the original Greek: Ἡ μεγάλη παίδευσις ἐν ἀνθρώποισι σιωπή... (Hē megalē paideusis en anthrōpoisi siōpē...)</note>

->*To be able to keep silent is no small part of learning:*<-
->*Pythagoras the wise is my witness in this matter.*<-
->*He, being skilled in speaking, taught others to hold their tongues,*<-
->*And applied a suitable remedy to the mouth.*<-
<note>Translated from Rittershusius's Latin verse: Doctrinae pars haud postrema est, posse tacere...</note>

Simplicius, in his most learned commentary on Epictetus’s *Enchiridion* <note>Simplicius was a 6th-century Neoplatonist; the Enchiridion is a "handbook" of Stoic ethics</note> (on page 81 and following in my Venetian edition), discusses the precept: "Let silence be the rule for the most part, or let only necessary things be spoken, and in few words." <note>original Greek: Ἡ σιωπὴ τὸ πολὺ ἔστω, ἢ λαλείσθω τὰ ἀναγκαῖα, καὶ δι’ ὀλίγων</note> He also mentions this Pythagorean silence and gives the reason for it in these words: "Among the traits proper to such a character, the first and most sovereign is, he says, 'let silence be the rule.' For the entire aim of educational discourses is to turn the soul back into itself, away from external things and from the irrational passions within it and from the body, so that it may always live its own life. Silence contributes the most to this. Wherefore the Pythagoreans also prescribed the five-year silence as the most effective beginning of their way of life, etc." <note>original Greek: Τῶν δὲ οἰκείων τῷ τοιούτῳ χαρακτῆρι... (Tōn de oikeiōn tō toioutō charaktēri...)</note>

However, there is no agreement among all authors regarding the duration of this silence, specifically how long it lasted. It is commonly believed by most that it was five years for everyone without distinction. Hence, Servius <note>a 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> (in the edition of Pierre Daniel) on Book 10 of the *Aeneid*, page 602, speaks of "silent Amyclae," <note>original Latin: Amyclas tacitas; a legendary city in Italy said to have been destroyed because a law of silence prevented citizens from warning of the enemy's approach</note> that is, "Pythagorean" Amyclae. "For the Pythagorean virtue," he says, "is a five-year silence." Diogenes Laertius, in Book 8, page 573, says: "And they remained silent for a period of five years <note><term>quinquennale silentium</term>: the famous five-year vow of silence required of Pythagorean initiates</note>, only listening to the discourses and not yet seeing Pythagoras, until they were sufficiently tested. From that point on, they became members of the household..." <note>original Greek: Πενταετίαν τε ἡσύχαζον... (Pentaetian te hēsychazon...)</note>

# ON PORPHYRY

...of him, and they shared in the vision. Hence Lucian <note>a 2nd-century Syrian satirist who wrote in Greek</note> also, in his work *The Sale of Lives* <note>original Greek: βίων πράσει (biōn prasei)</note>, when the question is asked: "What is the method of reminiscence?" <note>original Greek: τίς ὁ τρόπος τῆς ἀναμνήσεως; (tis ho tropos tēs anam nēseōs?)</note> By this I mean, how did Pythagoras call back to the memory of men those things which they had known before? (For he used to say that learning was nothing other than remembering, a doctrine that later pleased Plato as well). To this, Pythagoras is made to answer in the Ionic dialect in this manner: "First, a long quiet, and speechlessness, and to say nothing for five whole years." <note>original Greek: Τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἡσυχίη μακρὴ, καὶ ἀφωνίη, καὶ πέντε ὅλων ἐτέων λαλέειν μηδέν.</note> 

This claim, however, is refuted by those words of Aulus Gellius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author, here called "Agellius" following a common older spelling</note> in the aforementioned Chapter 9: "Pythagoras ordered a certain time to be silent: not the same for everyone, but different times for different people, according to his estimate of their natural cleverness." And shortly after: "But no one was silent for less than two years, etc." Therefore, a five-year silence <note>original Greek: πενταετὴς ἐχεμυθία (pentaetēs echemythia)</note> was not imposed on everyone without distinction; rather, for some it was of much shorter duration, if we are to believe Gellius. 

The reason for this commanded silence should also be noted, which was so that they might be exercised in difficult matters. For, as Aristotle also says, virtue and art are concerned with what is difficult. "Of all forms of self-restraint, the hardest is to control the tongue," <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ πάντων χαλεπώτατον ἐγκρατευμάτων, τὸ γλώττης κρατεῖν</note> as Iamblichus says in Book 1, Chapter 31. Whence Socrates also used to say that it was easier to hold a burning coal upon the tongue than a secret word. Aristotle, too, when he was asked what was the most difficult of all things in life, replied: "To be silent about things that ought not be spoken." <note>original Greek: Σιωπᾷν ἃ μὴ δεῖ λαλεῖν</note> See Stobaeus <note>a 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts</note>, Discourse 30, *On Secrets*. And, as Dionysius Cato <note>supposed author of a popular collection of Latin moral proverbs</note> says: "He is nearest to God who knows how to keep silent with reason." Ovid says in the second book of *The Art of Love*:

->*It is an exceptional virtue to keep silence about things;*<-
->*But on the other hand, it is a heavy fault to speak what should be hidden.*<-

To this also pertain those words of Gellius in the place mentioned: "When they had learned the most difficult of all things—to keep silent and to listen—and had now begun to be educated by silence, which was called *echemythia* <term>echemythia: the Pythagorean practice of secrecy or "holding one's speech"</term> etc." Clement of Alexandria <note>a Christian theologian of the 2nd century</note>, in his *Stromata* <note>meaning "Miscellanies"</note>, Book 5, page 247, gives this reason for the imposed silence: "So that the associates of Pythagoras, having turned away from sensible things <note>objects perceived by the physical senses</note>, might contemplate the divine power with the mind alone." This is therefore what the five-year silence means, which Pythagoras enjoined upon his followers: that having turned away from the things of the senses, they might behold the divine with the pure mind. <note>original Greek: Τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπὴ... ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν.</note>

I observe, however, a twofold Pythagorean silence: one of the disciples, which was limited to a certain time, such that it was not less than two years, nor more than five; the other was that of those who had already completed the legitimate years of discipleship, which they practiced not among themselves, but toward others who were not Pythagoreans or were outsiders. And this was perpetual. Thus it happened—

The author explains that silence was a spiritual exercise intended to restrain the tongue and redirect the mind from physical sensations toward the contemplation of the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological discussion of the Pythagorean discipline of silence. On the previous page, the author was likely discussing the duration and nature of this silence. The text resumes mid-sentence, concluding a point about the "proper" term for "complete silence" used by the Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus.</meta>

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...properly <note>The text begins mid-word, likely continuing "proprio" from the previous page.</note> in Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> in more than one place as "complete silence" <note>original Greek: παντελῆ σιωπὴν (pantelē siōpēn)</note>: where Desiderius Heraldus <note>A 17th-century French scholar known for his editions of ancient texts.</note>, in my judgment, incorrectly attempts to substitute "five-year silence" <note>original Greek: πενταετῆ σιωπήν (pentaetē siōpēn)</note>. I say we must retain "complete." See Numbers 68 and 188. For it is not likely that in so many places the adjective "complete" was corrupted into "five-year." This latter kind of silence, which we have said is called "complete" or "total," provides us an opportunity to remove one or two notable errors of writing from two passages of Iamblichus. 

One is in Book I, chapter 23, number 104, where it is published thus: *But according to the ritual silence <note>original Greek: ἐχεμυθίαν (echemythian)</note> commanded for them by Pythagoras regarding divine mysteries and secret ways from the uninitiated, they touched upon [the subjects], and through symbols they examined <note>original Greek: ἐπεσκόπουν (epeskopoun)</note> their mutual discourses or even writings.* From which the later words were translated quite wordily and defectively by the Frisian Interpreter <note>likely referring to a previous Latin translator of Iamblichus</note>: *And so through symbols they considered their mutual communications and colloquies or even commentaries and writings.* But either I see nothing at all, or in place of *epeskopoun* ("they examined") we must restore *epeskotoun* <note>original Greek: ἐπεσκότουν</note>, which is, *they involved in darkness, they obscured.* 

The other place needing emendation is in the *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original Latin: Protrepticus</note>, chapter 21, page 131, where it reads: *But according to the ritual silence commanded for them by Pythagoras regarding mysteries and secret ways from the more uninitiated (I think it should read "uninitiated in secret ways") they touched upon [the subjects], and through symbols they covered <note>original Greek: ἐπέσκεπον (epeskepon)</note> the discourses or writings toward others.* Someone might perhaps think that here too we should read "they obscured" <note>original Greek: ἐπεσκότουν</note> instead of "they covered." But nothing should be changed. For Iamblichus seems to have used "to obscure" and "to cover" for the same thing. *Skepo* <note>original Greek: σκέπω</note>, from which comes *skepas* ("a shelter"), is *to cover*; *episkepo* is *to cover over*. Furthermore, I think "one another" <note>original Greek: ἀλλήλους (allēlous)</note> should be restored instead of "others" <note>original Greek: ἄλλας (allas)</note>, as it was read in the previous passage. Or should we rather read "others" <note>original Greek: ἄλλους (allous)</note> in both places? This does not seem right to me. 

But let us return for a moment to the Pythagorean silence: about which I cannot restrain myself from adding the words of Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman orator and author of "The Golden Ass."</note> in his *Florida*: which I do all the more gladly because they contain a notable eulogy of Pythagoras. 

*Having been educated by so many teachers, having drunk from so many and such various fountains of disciplines throughout the whole world—a man especially of immense talent and a spirit more august than the grasp of a human—the first namer and founder of philosophy, he taught his disciples nothing before he taught them to be silent; and the first meditation for the future wise man was to restrain the whole tongue (perhaps "entirely"), and those words, which the poet calls "winged," to press those words, with their feathers clipped, within the wall of gleaming teeth. Entirely, I say, this was the first rudiment of wisdom: to learn to meditate, and to unlearn how to babble. They did not, however, lose their voice entirely, nor did everyone follow the master as if speechless for an equal amount of time; but...*

He supports his analysis of the pedagogical necessity of silence by quoting a high-praise passage from Apuleius.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological discussion of the Pythagorean discipline of silence. On the previous page, the author began discussing the duration of the silence imposed on students, contrasting "complete silence" with the specific five-year period often cited by ancient authors.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY.

To more serious men, a shorter period of modified silence seemed sufficient. More talkative men, however, were punished with a "voice exile" for nearly five years. <note>The Latin text includes a suggested reading here: "as if by an exile of the voice."</note> So says that Platonist from Madaura <note>Apuleius of Madaura (c. 124–170 AD), a philosopher and rhetorician</note>, who himself, just like Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author who described the Pythagorean silence in his "Attic Nights."</note>, testifies that a five-year silence was not commanded for everyone, but for some even a shorter time was ordered. I will not omit here the perverse imitation <note>original Greek: κακοζηλίαν (kakozēlian), referring to a poor or misguided imitation of a style or practice</note> of the heretic Basilides <note>An early Gnostic religious teacher in Alexandria.</note>, whom they write also commanded silence for his followers for five years in the Pythagorean manner. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, Chapter 7. Nor will I leave unmentioned what I read in Saint Jerome’s *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, Chapter 3, on the words: *A time to be silent, and a time to speak.* That most learned man notes the following:

> I believe the Pythagoreans—whose discipline involves keeping silent for five years and then, once educated, speaking—drew the origin of their decree from here. Let us also learn, therefore, first not to speak, so that later we may open our mouths for speaking. Let us be silent for a fixed time and hang upon the eloquence of our teacher. Let nothing seem right to us except what we learn, so that after much silence we may be transformed from disciples into masters. But now, because of the vice of an age daily sliding toward the worse, we teach in churches what we do not know. And if, through the arrangement of words or by the prompting of the Devil (who is the favorer of errors), we have stirred up the applause of the people, we think we know something against our own conscience, simply because we were able to persuade others of it. We do not learn any arts without a teacher; yet this art [of theology] is considered so cheap and easy that it supposedly requires no instructor. Thus far Saint Jerome.

Concerning the latter kind of Pythagorean silence, which we called "complete silence" <note>original Greek: παντελῆ σιωπὴν (pantelē siōpēn)</note> or "restraint of speech" <note>original Greek: ἐχεμυθίαν (echemythian)</note>, I also observe a passage from Iamblichus, Chapter 32, Number 226: *All the Pythagoreans always preserved the most important and essential of the doctrines among themselves in secret, maintaining them with strict silence toward outsiders, keeping them unwritten in memory, handing them down to their successors like the mysteries of the gods. For this reason, nothing worthy of mention reached the public, though they were taught and learned for a long time; they were known only within the school’s walls.* etc. Cicero alluded to this same thing when he wrote in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*: *Nor do you hide things from me, as Pythagoras was accustomed to do from strangers.* Where we should understand "strangers" to mean the uninitiated <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἀμυήτους (tous amyētous)</note>, whom Iamblichus calls sometimes "the unperfected" <note>original Greek: ἀτελέστους (atelestous)</note>, sometimes "outsiders" <note>original Greek: ἐξωτερικοὺς (exōterikous)</note>, sometimes "those at the door" <note>original Greek: θυραίους (thyraious)</note>, and sometimes "the profane" <note>original Greek: βεβήλους (bebēlous)</note>—that is, those not initiated into the Pythagorean mysteries. To Virgil, Horace, and others, these are the "profane."

### **That he says the soul is immortal]** 
Pythagoras drew his opinion regarding the immortality of the soul from his teacher...

->### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUIS<-

**On Pherecydes.** Cicero, in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 1, writes: *“Pherecydes of Syros was the first to state that human souls are eternal. He was ancient indeed, for he lived while my kinsman was reigning.”* <note>original Latin: *meo regnante gentili*. Cicero refers to Servius Tullius, the sixth king of Rome (reigned 578–535 BC), with whom he shared the name 'Tullius'.</note> *“Pythagoras, his student, greatly confirmed this opinion,”* and so on. In another place, the same Cicero testifies that Pythagoras himself asserted that souls possess immortality.

However, he corrupted this most true sentiment with a most foolish and false addition, teaching—if indeed he taught it—**transmigration of souls** <note>original Greek: μετεμψύχωσιν (*metempsychosis*)</note>, or rather **re-embodiment** <note>original Greek: μετενσωμάτωσιν (*metensomatosis*)</note>, which is the idea that souls pass into other bodies of humans or even of irrational animals. The most learned Tertullian <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage.</note> calls this the soul’s **"re-occurrence"** <note>original Latin: *recidiuatum*, implying a recurring fall or relapse back into a body.</note>. Diogenes Laërtius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> on page 570 calls it "the wandering of the soul." The same Diogenes on page 576 says: *“They say that he [Pythagoras] was the first to declare that the soul, changing through the circle of necessity, is bound at different times to different animals.”*

So also Saint Jerome <note>A Latin priest and theologian, best known for translating the Bible into the Vulgate.</note> in his *Apology against Rufinus*: *“And because I said I had read Pythagorean dogmas, listen to what Pythagoras first discovered among the Greeks: that he himself was first Euphorbus, second Callides, third Hermotimus, fourth Pyrrhus, and finally Pythagoras.”* <note>Pythagoras claimed to remember his past lives, most famously as Euphorbus, a hero of the Trojan War.</note>

Lactantius <note>A counselor to Constantine the Great and an apologist who often used pagan philosophy to argue for Christian truths.</note> also mentions these Pythagorean dogmas several times, as in Book 3, Chapter 18: *“Others, however,”* he says, *“discuss the opposite—that souls survive after death; these are especially the Pythagoreans and Stoics. Although they should be forgiven because they sense what is true, I cannot help but rebuke them, for they stumbled upon the truth by chance rather than by knowledge. Therefore, in the very thing they thought correctly, they erred somewhat. For since they feared the argument which concludes that souls must perish with bodies because they are born with bodies, they said that souls are not born, but rather slip into bodies and migrate from one to another. Nor did they think it possible for souls to survive after bodies unless they were seen to have existed before bodies. Thus the error of both parties is equal and nearly identical,”* etc.

The same author in Chapter 19: *“But clearly he [Plato] believed Pythagoras—while saying he gave thanks to nature, among other things, that he was born a human rather than a mute animal—who, to forbid men from eating animals, said that souls pass from their bodies into the bodies of other animals. This is both vain and impossible. Vain, because it was not necessary to lead old souls into new bodies, since the same Craftsman <note>Lactantius uses the term *artifex*, referring to the Creator.</note> who once made the first souls could always make new ones. Impossible, because the soul of right reason cannot change the nature of its state any more than fire can strive downward or spread its flame sideways like a lightning bolt,”* etc.

So too Saint Ambrose <note>The influential 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> in his book *On the Good of Death*, Chapter 10: *“So that the Pagans might know...”*

<summary>This page discusses the ancient origins of the belief in the soul's immortality, attributed to Pherecydes of Syros, and critiques Pythagoras for "corrupting" this truth with the doctrine of transmigration (metempsychosis).</summary>

# ON PORPHYRY <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and a famous critic of Christianity. These notes likely engage with his "Life of Pythagoras."</note>

...those things which they admire in the books of the philosophers are translated from our own <note>i.e., borrowed from Christian or Hebrew scriptures</note>. And would that they had not mixed in superfluous and useless things, such as saying that the souls of humans and beasts are shared in common, and that the highest reward for these souls would be if the souls of great philosophers migrated into bees or nightingales—so that those who previously fed the human race with speech might later soothe them with the sweetness of honey or the delight of song. It would have been enough for them to have said that souls, once freed from their bodies, sought *Hades* <note>original Greek: ᾅδην</note>, which is to say, "the place which is not seen"—a place we call "the underworld" in English <note>original Latin: *infernum*</note>. Indeed, the Scripture also called those habitations "storehouses" of souls, etc. 

So John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "golden-mouthed" eloquence.</note> pronounces that dogma full of filth in his first Homily on John: that the Pythagoreans taught that the souls of men even migrate into flies, gnats, and shrubs: <note>original Greek: Δογμάτων δὲ ἕνεκεν... "Regarding their dogmas about the soul, they have left no excess of shame remaining, saying that the souls of men become mice [or flies], gnats, and shrubs, and claiming that God himself is the soul, and committing other such indecencies."</note> (Here it is commonly read as "mice" [*mues*]; which the translator *Aretinus* <note>Leonardo Bruni (1370–1444), a humanist scholar from Arezzo.</note> accepted, since he translated it as "mice" [*mures*]. I think it should be corrected to "flies" [*muias*], for "mice" would be *mues*.) ...and claiming that God himself is a soul, and other such shameful things. 

In the same place, a little further on (which I mention in passing), it seems the same Chrysostom should be emended where the text is published as follows: "For just as they are carried here and there in the Euripus <note>A narrow channel of water in Greece famous for its violent and unpredictable currents.</note>, so they never stood upon the same ground, since they speak everything from manifest and precarious reasonings." Because the translator rendered the last part as: *speaking all things from an uncertain and fragile opinion,* he seems to have read, or had in mind, the word for "uncertain" <note>original Greek: *adēlōn*</note>. But I say the true reading is "timid" <note>original Greek: *deilōn*</note>. For Chrysostom calls the fluctuating opinions of philosophers regarding things "timid and slippery reasonings."

Theodoretus <note>A 5th-century theologian and bishop of Cyrrhus.</note> also more than once refutes this vanity of **transmigration** <note>original Greek: *metempsychosis*</note>; as in his *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, where he speaks of the heretic Carpocrates: "While they [the Carpocratians] accepted the Pythagorean passages from bodies into bodies, they did not accept what was connected to them by Pythagoras. For Pythagoras said that souls which sinned were sent into bodies so that they might pay the penalty and be rightly purified. But these people [the Carpocratians] offer a reason for that transition into bodies which is diametrically opposed to the Pythagorean view. For they say that souls are sent into bodies so that they may perform every kind of lust and insolence. Therefore, those souls which have fulfilled this in one descent do not need another mission. But those which have sinned too little are sent a second, third, and even more times."

<meta>This page continues the critique of Pythagorean and Platonic theories regarding the soul, specifically focusing on the rejection of the doctrine of transmigration (metempsychosis). ### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUISEN <note>Conrad Rittershuisen (1560–1613) was a celebrated German scholar and jurist known for his commentaries on classical and patristic texts.</note>

...until they have filled up every kind of vice, etc. Theodoret <note>A 5th-century Bishop and influential theologian of the Eastern Christian Church.</note> says the same in his *Summary of Divine Decrees*, under the title *On Man*:

> "We say that the soul is simple, endowed with reason, and immortal; however, it does not exist before the body. For Pythagoras, Plato, and Plotinus, and those of their sect, while confessing that souls are immortal, claimed that they exist before bodies and constitute a certain innumerable population of souls. They claimed that those which sin are sent down into bodies so that, having been purged by such discipline, they might return to their proper place. However, they also claimed that those which, even while in bodies, have embraced an unjust and wicked life, are sent down into animals devoid of reason: those who are full of bitter bile and the poison of wrath into snakes; the rapacious into wolves; the bold into lions; the deceitful into foxes; and they have fashioned other such senseless fables, etc." 

Finally, in the same book, in the chapter *On Judgment*: 

> "Pythagoras told fables of the passage of souls into bodies, saying that they pass not only into the bodies of brutes, but even into trees. Likewise, Plato also followed this fable in some manner. From this, Mani <note>The founder of Manichaeism.</note> and the heresy of the impious Gnostics which preceded him, taking the opportunity, said that this was a form of punishment. Furthermore, the wicked Carpocrates, Epiphanes, Prodicus, and the Cainites—establishing what was plainly the life of a pig—said that souls are transmitted into bodies so that through lust and every kind of intemperance they might worship each of the angels who created the world. But the Church of the faithful detests these and similar fables," etc.

But regarding that fabulous migration of souls into other bodies, and the "transformation" <note>original Latin: *metamorphosi*</note> of Pythagoras himself, there will be a place to say more below. I will add only this in this place, which I read in Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21: that even Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), who rejected Christianity in favor of Neoplatonic paganism.</note> was so maddened by this most vain opinion that he persuaded himself, according to the sentiment of Pythagoras, that through transformation he possessed the soul of **Alexander the Great**; indeed, that he himself was Alexander in another body. Whence, even through dreams, he allowed himself to be led into the hope that he would be not only equal to Alexander of Macedon in his achievements, but even superior to him. But this opinion and hope seduced him and brought it about that he rejected the supplication of the Persian King. While he was mingling in the battle that had commenced, even though he was unarmed—relying solely on his hope for good fortune—he perished, pierced by a javelin, the author of his death remaining uncertain.

<summary>This page cites the Church Father Theodoret to condemn the Pythagorean and Gnostic belief in the transmigration of souls into animals as "senseless fables," and illustrates the danger of this belief through the hubris and death of Emperor Julian the Apostate.</summary>

# ON PORPHYRY.

**"According to certain cycles, the things that once happened occur again"** <note>original: Κατὰ περιόδους τινὰς τὰ γινόμενα ποτὲ, πάλιν γίνεται</note>] 8. Jerome says in his *Apology against Rufinus*: *“After certain cycles of time, those things which had been happen again, and nothing new happens in the world, etc.”* This is also the opinion of the most wise Solomon in *Ecclesiastes, chapter 1*: **"What is that which has been? That which shall be. And what is that which has been done? That which shall be done; and there is nothing entirely fresh under the sun. Who shall speak and say: Look, this is new? It has already happened in the ages that were before us, etc."** <note>original: Τί τὸ γεγονός; αὐτὸ τὸ γενησόμενον. Καὶ τί τὸ πεποιημένον; αὐτὸ τὸ ποιηθησόμενον· καὶ οὐκ ἔστι πᾶν πρόσφατον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιον. Ὅς λαλήσει, καὶ ἐρεῖ· Ἰδὲ τοῦτο καινόν ἐστιν. Ἤδη γέγονεν ἐν τοῖς αἰῶσι τοῖς γενομένοις ἀπὸ ἔμπροσθεν ἡμῶν, etc.</note> See the same place in Jerome's Commentary, where explaining this more broadly, he simultaneously refutes the opinion of Epicurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who founded a school of thought based on atomism and the pursuit of pleasure (tranquility).</note>, who asserted that through innumerable cycles the same things occur in the same places and through the same people. From the same source, Jerome also thinks that famous line from the comic playwright Terence flowed: *“Nothing is said that has not been said before”*; and after he praised his teacher Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a great 4th-century grammarian and Jerome's tutor.</note>, he adds: *“But if nothing new can be said in speeches, how much more so in the administration of the world, which was so perfected from the beginning that God rested from his works on his seventh day, etc.”* In Malchus <note>The birth name of the philosopher Porphyry.</note>, however, here after the word **"simply"** <note>original: ἁπλῶς</note> there was a gap in the manuscript: so it is believable that many excellent things concerning the dogmas of Pythagoras have perished from this section.

**"So as no longer to depart homeward"** <note>original: Ὡς μηκέτι οἴκαδ’ ἀποστῆναι</note>] I guessed it should be read as **"to return home"** <note>original: ἀπονοστῆσαι</note>. But perhaps nothing should be changed. However, these four words seem entirely necessary to be supplied in Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note>, chapter 6, page 43, after **"they were held fast"** <note>original: ἐνεσχήθησαν</note> (which is clearly corrupt) and before **"but together with children,"** where based on Malchus it should be read as **"with children"** <note>original: σὺν παισί</note>.

**"A certain very large meeting-place"** <note>original: Ὁμακόϊόν τι παμμέγεθες</note>] In Iamblichus in the said place, where these same things are read, it is written: **"a very large meeting-place"** <note>original: ὁμακόειον παμμέγεθες</note>. Nevertheless, you may find **"meeting-place"** written elsewhere in the same author with an **iota** [ι], not an **epsilon-iota** [ει].

**"Commands as if they were divine instructions"** <note>original: Προστάγματα ὡσανεὶ θείας ὑποθήκας</note>] So says Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note>, page 576: **"He was so admired that they said his acquaintances were all kinds of voices of God."** <note>original: Οὕτω δὲ ἐθαυμάσθη, ὥστε ἔλεγον τοὺς γνωρίμους αὐτοῦ παντοίας θεοῦ φωνάς.</note> Regarding which passage our illustrious Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), one of the greatest classical scholars of the Renaissance.</note> noted thus: *“Something is missing here, which Ambrosius concealed, etc.”* Yet he does not add what he thinks is missing. In my mind, nothing is missing there, but I say that instead of **"the acquaintances"** <note>original: τοὺς γνωρίμους</note>, we should read: **"the opinions"** <note>original: τὰς γνώμας</note>. Thus all things will be complete, healthy, and plain. Should we also replace **"so that they said"** <note>original: ὥστε ἔλεγον</note> with **"so as to say"** <note>original: ὥστε λέγειν</note>?

**"That which was called by everyone Great Greece [Magna Graecia]"** <note>original: Τὴν πρὸς πάντων ἐπικληθεῖσαν μεγάλην Ἑλλάδα</note>] Iamblichus, chapter 29: **"And from these practices it happened that the..."**

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershuisen’s commentary on the life of Pythagoras. # NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUISEN

**"...that all of Italy was filled with philosophers; and whereas it was previously unknown, it was later called 'Great Greece' because of Pythagoras; and many philosophers, poets, and lawmakers came from it; for the rhetorical arts and demonstrative speeches, and the written laws from those men happened to be brought into Greece, etc."** <note>original: Ἰταλίαν πᾶσαν φιλοσόφων ἀνδρῶν ἐμπλησθῆναι· καὶ πρότερον ἀγνοουμένης αὐτῆς, ὕστερον διὰ Πυθαγόραν μεγάλην Ἑλλάδα κληθῆναι... etc.</note> I wanted to include this passage all the more willingly because the reason for the name appears from it—why such a small portion of Italy was called **"Great"** or **"Greater Greece"** <note>original: Magna sive Maior Graecia</note>: it was even called **"Greatest"** <note>original: Maxima / μεγίστη</note> by Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> in his first *Homily on John*. However, Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae'.</note> in Book 12 gives another reason for this title: namely, that because of the fertility and abundance of that region, a great multitude of people flocked there. **"And not a little toward the luxury and prosperity of this entire region was also the multitude of people; wherefore almost all the settlement throughout Italy was called Great Greece."** <note>original: Οὐκ ὀλίγον δὲ πρὸς τὴν τρυφὴν καὶ τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν τοῦ σύμπαντος τούτου κλίματος... etc.</note>

**"And they made their property common"** <note>original: Καὶ τὰς οὐσίας κοινὰς ἔθεντο</note>] Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note>, Section 168. Similarly, Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> on page 573: **"And his disciples deposited their belongings, making them into one."** <note>original: Καὶ αὐτοῦ οἱ μαθηταὶ κατέθεντο τὰς οὐσίας εἰς ἓν ποιούμενοι</note> Where it seems to me the preposition "into" <note>original: εἰς</note> is redundant. Likewise, on page 581, among the dogmas of Pythagoras he lists this too: **"To consider nothing as one's own."** <note>original: Ἴδιον μηδὲν ἡγεῖσθαι</note> And this practice too, like many others, Plato appropriated—that is, he made it his own. But Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> in Book III, Chapter 21 and following, argues extensively against this "community of all things."

Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of 'Attic Nights'; Rittershuisen uses the variant spelling 'Agellius'.</note>, Book I, Chapter 4: *"All those together who had been received by Pythagoras into that band of studies* (Isaac Casaubon <note>A renowned classical scholar of the Renaissance.</note> prefers "disciples," with whom I easily agree), *what each had of family and money, they put into the middle, and an inseparable society was entered into: as if that were the ancient partnership which in Roman law and speech was called a* <term>coenobium</term> <note>original: κοινόβιον; a term for communal living, often used later for monastic communities.</note>.*"* But what Gellius says—that an inseparable society was entered into among the Pythagoreans—seems to be contradicted by a passage in Iamblichus, Book I, Chapter 30, Section 168, where he writes that if anyone did not like remaining in that society, he was free to depart, having received back the goods he had contributed to the common pool, and indeed with some addition. The words of Iamblichus are these: **"Thus he established this best among men in their customs, banishing everything private and increasing the common, even down to the ultimate possessions, which are causes of discord and disturbance. For all things were common to everyone, and these things were too; no one possessed anything as their own. And if he was pleased with the community, he used the common goods according to what was most just; but if not, he [received back...]"** <note>original: Τοῦτο τοίνυν ἄριστα ἀνδρῶν κατεσκεύασεν ἐν τοῖς ἤθεσι... etc.</note>

# ON PORPHYRY.

...having taken back his own property, and even more than he had contributed to the common fund, he departed. <note>original Greek: λαβών ἂν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ οὐσίαν, καὶ πλείονα ἧς εἰσενηνόχει εἰς τὸ κοινόν, ἀπηλλάττετο.</note> *And indeed this matches those principles of our law:* <note>The author refers to Roman Law, specifically the Digest and the Code of Justinian.</note> *No joining of a partnership is for eternity. And: No one is compelled to remain in a communion or partnership against their will, etc. Law 4, section 1; Law 63, "it is true," the last section; and Law 65, "by action," section 2, "we say," and several following; Law 70, "none," in the Digest 'on the partner.' Law 14, "into this judgment," the section "if it is agreed," in the Digest 'on dividing common property.' The final law in the Code under the same title.*

**"They numbered Pythagoras among the gods"** <note>original Greek: Μετὰ τῶν Θεῶν τὸν Πυθαγόραν κατηρίθμουν</note>] *Iamblichus also often writes that Pythagoras was worshipped as a god, especially in Chapter 6:* "And they thereafter numbered Pythagoras among the gods as a certain good and most philanthropic <term>daemon<gloss>in the ancient sense: a benevolent spiritual being mediating between gods and men</gloss></term>; some called him the Pythian [Apollo], others the Apollo from the Hyperboreans, others the Paean, and others one of the spirits inhabiting the moon; while still others spoke of him as another of the Olympian gods, saying that he appeared to those of that time in human form for the benefit and correction of mortal life, so that he might grant the saving spark of happiness and philosophy to mortal nature—a greater good than which neither has come nor ever will come, granted by the gods through this Pythagoras, etc." <note>original Greek: Καὶ μετὰ τῶν θεῶν τὸν Πυθαγόραν λοιπὸν κατηρίθμουν... etc.</note> *Dio Chrysostomus testifies to this same thing in Oration 47 (on page 524 of my Paris edition):* "Pythagoras fled Samos voluntarily when it was under a tyranny. Among all other men, however, and especially I believe around Italy, he was honored as a god." <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόρας ἐκ Σάμου μὲν ἔφυγεν... etc.</note> *Justin (Book 20) testifies to the same. But he says this happened after he died, so that he was worshipped as a god: others indicate he was held as a god even while living. In both cases, however, the idolatry was equal and the same. For there is only one God, as we know by the benefit of God through many testimonies of the Sacred Scriptures.*

**"No, by him who [gave to our soul the tetractys]"** <note>original Greek: Οὐ μὰ τὸν ἁμετ.</note>] Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> in the entry 'Number': "That the Pythagoreans called every number a <term>tetractys<gloss>a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, representing the organization of space and the universe</gloss></term>. The number is completed at ten. And ten is the composition of the four [1+2+3+4], and because of this they said every number was a tetractys." <note>original Greek: Ὅτι οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι πάντα ἀριθμὸν τετρακτὺν προσηγόρευον... etc.</note> *Macrobius, Book 1 on Scipio's Dream, Chapter 6: 'But the Pythagoreans venerate the number four, which they call the* **tetractys**, *as pertaining to the perfection of the soul, so much so among their secrets that they even made it a religious oath for themselves:* "No, by him who gives to our soul the tetractys." *I swear to you by him who gives the fourfold number to our soul.' See Iamblichus, Chapter 28, number 150, where he writes thus:* "Such an oath is attributed to the Pythagoreans, as they were reverent about naming Pythagoras (just as they were very sparing in using the names of the gods), so through the..."

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...of the discovery of the <term>tetractys<gloss>a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows (1, 2, 3, and 4), which the Pythagoreans viewed as a symbol of the organization of the universe</gloss></term>, manifesting the man. He then adds those two noble verses, though the former with some variation: *Yes, by the one who found the tetractys of our wisdom,* etc. <note>original Greek: Ναὶ μὰ τὸν ἁμετέρας σοφίας εὑρόντα τετρακτύν</note> Iamblichus says the same in chapter 29, number 162: "All these things, and other greater things like them, Pythagoras devised as fictions and poems for the benefit and correction of those living with him; and they were so revered, and he was so deified by those who understood <note>Latin: "ab intelligentibus"; the author notes that one might instead read "those who were present" (συνόντων) implying his close associates</note> that they turned into forms of oaths for his listeners: *No, by him who handed down the tetractys to our generation,* etc." <note>original Greek: οὐ μὰ τὸν ἁμετέρᾳ γενεᾷ παραδόντα τετρακτύν</note> From this comparison it appears how variously this formula of the Pythagorean oath is reported; concerning which see also Caelius Rhodiginus, book 22, *Ancient Lessons*, chapter 9. Thus Lucian, in his defense of a mistake made in a greeting, alluded to this: "There are some who also called the tetractys their greatest oath (meaning those following Pythagoras) and the one that completes the perfect number for them. Others also called it the beginning of health," etc. <note>original Greek: Εἰσὶ δὲ, οἳ καὶ τὴν τετρακτὺν, τὸν μέγιστον ὅρκου αὐτῶν... τὸν ἐντελῆ αὐτοῖς ἀριθμὸν ἀποτελεῖν.</note> Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian, one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> also mentions this oath in his *Homily on the Holy Pentecost* in these words: "The children of the Hebrews honor the week <note>The number seven, rooted in the seven days of creation.</note>, from the lawgiving of Moses; just as the Pythagoreans later honored the tetractys, which indeed they made into an oath." Where Nicetas, in his paraphrase, brings forward these points: "The Samian philosopher Pythagoras was born later than Moses; his students swore in this way, as he says in his so-called Golden Verses: *Yes, by him who handed down the tetractys to our soul, the fountain of ever-flowing nature*; they called the tetractys the 'fountain of ever-flowing nature' because of the four elements from which all worldly nature is composed. And indeed, did the students swear by Pythagoras himself because of the tetractys? Yes, he says, but they swore by deifying Pythagoras on account of the tetractys, as he handed down to them its secret and mystical power; so that for them Pythagoras was second in honor to the tetractys, and they swore by it directly through him."

<margin>21</margin> **"Having filled with a free-minded spirit"** <note>original Greek: Φρονήματος ἐξελευθερίου πλήσας</note>] Iamblichus, in chapter 7, says on the same matter: "Having filled these with a free-minded spirit." Compare that whole passage to the present one. For one will be clarified by the other.

**"Tauromenon"**] Read it with one additional letter, **Tauromenium**, or even as **Tauromeneion** <note>A famous ancient city in Sicily, modern-day Taormina.</note>. For it is written both ways. And from this, Iamblichus should be corrected in the mentioned place, where it was published incorrectly and without sense as *Taramenas*. Nor any better...

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershusius’s philological commentary on Porphyry’s *Life of Pythagoras*. While the previous page focused on the sacred "tetractys" and the various forms of the Pythagorean oath, this page shifts to correcting geographical names and the biographies of famous Pythagorean lawgivers like Charondas and Zaleucus, as well as fixing errors in the Greek text of Iamblichus.</meta>

### ON PORPHYRY.

The corrector Fris. thought the word **Tyrrhenia** <note>A region in central Italy, home of the Etruscans</note> should be read here. On the contrary, I say that **Tauromenium** <note>Modern-day Taormina in Sicily</note> should be restored from Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus, which Rittershusius uses to refer to him</note>. For it is a city of Sicily, according to the testimony of Stephanus: *Tauromenium, a city of Sicily; the citizen is a Tauromenite, or a Tauromenian.* <note>original Greek: Ταυρομένιον, πόλις Σικελίας. ὁ πολίτης, Ταυρομενίτης, καὶ Ταυρομένιος</note> Strabo also reviews the same city in Book 6 among other Sicilian cities and joins it with Catana. Suidas says: *Tauromeneion, a small town; and Tauromenite.* <note>original Greek: Ταυρομένειον, πολίχνιον· καὶ Ταυρομενείτης</note> Therefore, we should understand that the man originating from there is written in both ways: *Tauromenite*, as in Suidas, and *Tauromenite*, as in Stephanus and Iamblichus in chapter 25. In that chapter, the story is told of a young **Tauromenite** whose fury—inflamed by drunkenness as well as love and rivalry—Pythagoras extinguished through Phrygian song and melody.

**"For whom he also established laws through Charondas of Catana and Zaleucus of Locri"** <note>original Greek: Αἷς καὶ νόμους ἔθετο διὰ Χαρώνδα τε τοῦ Καταναίου, καὶ Ζαλεύκου τοῦ Λοκροῦ</note> Iamblichus also mentions this same pair of most famous Pythagorean legislators in more than one place, such as in chapters 7, 27, and 30: *The best lawmakers of all were those who approached Pythagoras: first Charondas the Catanian; then Zaleucus and Timaratus, the Locrians who wrote the laws for their people, etc.* <note>original Greek: Νομοθέται πάντων ἄριστοι γεγόνασιν οἱ Πυθαγόρᾳ προσελθόντες, πρῶτον μὲν Χαρώνδας ὁ Καταναίος· ἔπειτα δὲ Ζάλευκος, καὶ Τιμάρατος, οἱ Λοκροῖς γράψαντες τοὺς νόμους</note> He mentions them again in chapter 25. Regarding the <term>nomothesia<gloss>the system or act of lawgiving</gloss></term> of both men, about twenty years ago I delivered and published an oration in which I diligently collected whatever is memorable regarding these two most famous legislators found among the best authors of both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>, pertaining both to their lives and their legislation. Regarding Charondas, see also Pietro Vettori, Book 26 of *Variations*, chapter 21.

But since we just happened upon Iamblichus chapter 30, we shall do the text a service by removing two notable—or rather, ugly—errors. Because they were not noticed, the translator Arcerius stumbled. In the first place, where Iamblichus compares the **legislative aspect of justice** with the **judicial aspect**—that is, the part of politics concerned with making laws versus the part concerned with court trials—he compares them in such a way that he prefers the former to the latter. He argues that legislation prohibits and takes precautions far in advance so that the soul does not fall into the "disease" of injustice at all, but ensures its health remains intact, while the judicial aspect provides medicine only to one who is already sick. In that passage, the text was published as: **"but to not even perceive the beginning"** <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ νοεῖν</note>. Arcerius translates this as: *That one indeed cannot even perceive the beginning in thought,* etc., which makes no sense. I would bet anything that it should be read: **"not even to be sick at all"** <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ νοσεῖν</note>; and that the phrase *tēn archēn* <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν</note> here does not mean "the beginning," but **"at all"** or **"entirely."** How truly this...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...should be established by me. To make it more manifest, come, let us write out the whole passage, especially since it may also be useful for other matters: **"In addition to these things, he (Pythagoras) established another most beautiful form of justice, the <term>legislative</term> <note>original Greek: νομοθετικὸν (nomothetikon)</note> kind, which commands what one must do and forbids what one must not do. This is superior even to the <term>judicial</term> <note>original Greek: δικαστικοῦ (dikastikou)</note> kind. For the latter resembles medicine and heals those who have fallen ill. But the former [the legislative] does not even consider falling ill in the first place <note>original: οὐδὲ νοεῖν; Rittershusius suggests reading οἷο νοσεῖν (hoio nosein), "to be sick"</note>, but rather looks after the health of the soul from a distance."**

I illustrate this remarkable sentiment of Iamblichus regarding the difference between the two parts of politics—or, as he calls it, justice—namely the legislative and the judicial, in a brief digression by employing the dialogue of Plato with Dionysius of Syracuse. When that most divine of philosophers was asked by the tyrant what the duty of a politician was, he replied: **"To make the citizens good."** (The tyrant, however, was expecting Plato to say "to exercise judgments well," for he prided himself on this virtue.) When asked again by the same man whose duty he thought it was to judge correctly, Plato replied: **"Judging correctly is only a small part of being a politician."** <note>original Greek: Μόριόν τι μικρὸν πολιτικοῦ τὸ δικάζειν ὀρθῶς. Rittershusius suggests reading "of politics" (πολιτικῆς) instead of "of a politician" (πολιτικοῦ)</note> **"For they are like menders <note>original Greek: ἀκεσταῖς (akestais)</note>, who re-weave torn garments."** See Eusebius Pamphilus, *Chronicle*, Book I, page 46.

Clement of Alexandria also agrees with Plato in *Stromata*, Book I, page 151, when he defines the **judicial** art as **"the science that corrects errors for the sake of justice"**; and he adds, **"parallel to it is the <term>punitive</term> <note>original Greek: κολαστική (kolastike)</note> art, which is a kind of science of the proper measure in punishments. For punishment is the correction of the soul."**

But let us return from these matters to the correction of Iamblichus. There follows, therefore, another cited passage from the same author, which is itself no less faulty than the previous one. In that passage, Iamblichus compares the Pythagorean legislators with Heraclitus of Ephesus. He notes that the former approached the passing of laws with great benevolence and political science; but the latter [Heraclitus] was most harsh and vehement toward the Ephesians, declaring that all were worthy of having their necks broken <note>original Latin: gula frangeretur</note> (evidently on account of their expulsion of Hermodorus, an excellent man, from their city, as is clear from Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, Strabo, and others). And this should be done **"from youth"** <note>original Greek: ἡβηδὸν (hebedon)</note>, that is, from the beginning of age or from the first onset of puberty <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς ἥβης (apo tes hebes)</note>; not, as Arcerius translates it, "petulantly and wantonly," through all ages, etc.

It is read in the same place: **"with much intelligence"** <note>original Greek: μετὰ πολλῆς ἐννοίας (meta polles ennoias)</note> (which the translator rendered as "with all understanding") **"and political science he attempted to legislate"**; whereas the true reading is **"with much benevolence"** <note>original Greek: εὐνοίας (eunoias)</note>, and **"they attempted"** <note>plural: ἐπεχείρησαν (epecheiresan)</note>. Thus, I believe no one will doubt that the most true reading has been restored by us in a passage that was twice corrupted: first, if one notices that the **great benevolence** <note>original: εὔνοιαν πολλὴν</note> of the Pythagorean legislators is contrasted with the obstinate and...

# ON PORPHYRY

...to the better severity of Heraclitus <note>original: *meliosae seueritati Heracliti*; "meliosae" may be a corruption in the transcription for *meliori* (better)</note>. Second: one who has noticed that the word **"they attempted"** <note>original: ἐπεχείρησαν (*epecheirēsan*)</note> refers to what preceded it: **"all these legislators received honors equal to the gods."** For the following words provide the reason why the Pythagorean legislators were held in such high honor—namely, because of their **"great goodwill"** <note>original: πολλὴν εὔνοιαν (*pollēn eunoian*)</note> and the **"political science"** <note>original: πολιτικὴν ἐπιστήμην (*politikēn epistēmēn*)</note> with which they set about to establish laws: **"they attempted to legislate."** I shall say nothing of the fact that the phrase "he attempted" has no nominative subject to govern it or upon which it might depend. But let us finally return from Iamblichus to Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus; Rittershusius uses it here to refer to the author of the biography.</note>.

**"Enviable to their neighbors"**] In the edition of Iamblichus, it is incorrectly published as **"the inhabitants above"** <note>original: τοὺς ὑπεροίκους (*tous hyperoikous*)</note>. However, it should be read there also as **"to their neighbors"** <note>original: τοῖς περιοίκοις (*tois perioikois*)</note>, a conclusion which Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius Theodoretus, a 16th-century Frisian scholar.</note> finally reached correctly by conjecture. Perhaps, however, in both Malchus and Iamblichus, one should read **"by the neighboring [cities]"** <note>original: ταῖς περιοίκοις (*tais perioikois*)</note>, specifically referring to the city-states. Who the "neighbors" <term>perioikoi: literally "those dwelling around," often used in a technical sense in geography or social hierarchy</term> are in the doctrine of the world's position and the sphere must be sought elsewhere.

**"And Symichus, the tyrant of the Centoropians"**] Who this Symichus was, and likewise who the Centoropians <note>An ancient people of Sicily, from the town of Centuripe.</note> were—over whom he voluntarily laid down the absolute power he had obtained after hearing Pythagoras—requires further inquiry. Iamblichus certainly says nothing about him. There are, however, examples even in Roman history of emperors who voluntarily abdicated their command, changing from monarchs into private citizens.

**"Having heard her"**] Read **"having heard him"** <note>Latin: *audito Pythagorā*; the Greek text likely had a gender error in the pronoun, which Rittershusius is correcting.</note>.

<margin>22</margin>
**"The Romans"**] How much the Romans esteemed Pythagoras is sufficiently declared by what Plutarch wrote in his *Life of Numa*. See also what I noted above regarding the title of this work, drawing from Cicero, Livy, and others.

**"He utterly destroyed factionalism, not only from those in Italy..."**] I have always suspected this passage of being mutilated, since the phrase **"not only"** ought to be followed by **"but also,"** etc., which is missing here to the detriment of the meaning. Finally, having inspected Iamblichus, chapter 7, I discovered it to be thus, and the following words should be supplied here after "not only": **"from his acquaintances and even their descendants for many generations, as it is told; but also universally"** <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν γνωρίμων καὶ τῶν ἀπογόνων δὲ αὐτῶν μέχρι πολλῶν, ὡς ἱστορεῖται, γενεῶν. ἀλλὰ καὶ καθόλου</note>, so that it may then follow: "from those in Italy," etc.

**"One must expel"**] This frequent and most weighty <term>apophthegm: a pithy saying or maxim</term> of Pythagoras, or decree, is recorded in almost the exact same words in Iamblichus’s *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 7, except that at the end there one reads **"lack of parts"** <note>original: ἀμερίαν (*amerian*)</note>, which Arcerius translates as "partisan zeal." But it should be restored from this passage of our Malchus...

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry’s life of Pythagoras. On the previous page, Rittershusius was discussing the "enviable" nature of Pythagorean communities and correcting textual errors in the manuscripts of Iamblichus and Porphyry (Malchus) regarding neighboring peoples. This page moves into a specific analysis of a famous Pythagorean maxim about "cutting away" excess, comparing various ancient sources like Iamblichus and St. Jerome.</meta>

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...lack of measure <note>original: *ametria*</note>. Iamblichus most truly judges this Pythagorean decree to be "like a divine advisory oracle <note>original: *chrēsmō Theou symbouleutikou*</note>, a sort of summary and recap of his views, through which he most affectionately reminded everyone of the best teachings." *St. Jerome, in his Apology against Rufinus*, records the same maxim, although with slightly changed words, yet keeping the same sense. I will transcribe it here for the sake of comparison, beginning a bit earlier with the words of that most learned Father: *“Look at the whole coast of Italy, which was once called Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia</note>: and you will recognize the Pythagorean doctrines engraved on public bronze tablets. For whose are those **Golden Precepts** <note>original: *chrysa parangelmata*</note>? Are they not Pythagoras’s? In them, all his doctrines are briefly contained. Iamblichus wrote a commentary on these in a very extensive work, partly imitating Moderatus—a most eloquent man—as well as Archippus and Lysis, students of Pythagoras. Archippus and Lysis held schools in Greece, specifically in Thebes; keeping the teacher's precepts by memory, they used their own minds instead of books. From them comes this saying:* **One must flee entirely and cut away: sickness from the body, ignorance from the soul, luxury from the belly, rebellion from the city, discord from the home, and universally from all things, excess.** <note>original Greek: *Pheukteon pantapasi kai ekkopteon, astheneian men tou sōmatos, apaideusian de tēs psychēs, akolasian de tēs gastros, stasin de tēs poleōs, tēn de diaphonian apo tēs oikias, kai koinē apo pantōn to akrates.*</note> *Which we can translate into Latin as follows: We must put to flight by all means and prune away: weakness from the body, lack of skill from the mind, luxury from the stomach, sedition from the city, discord from the house, and in common from all things, intemperance.”* **These are the words of Jerome (in my Plantin edition, Volume 1, page 261).**

The word "excess" <note>original: *to akrates*</note> is used here, whereas in Iamblichus and Malchus it is "lack of measure" <note>original: *ametria*</note>. Iamblichus elsewhere also calls these things "the unmeasured" <note>original: *asymmetra*</note>, as in chapter 51: "The general precepts concerning temperance have already been stated, in which it is ordained to cut away all unmeasured things with fire and steel." By these words, he hints at nothing other than this very maxim, which he had reported earlier in chapter 7, and which Malchus has here. 

I suggest we should see whether, in Jerome's text, we should read **"must be put to flight"** <note>original: *phygadeuteon*</note> instead of **"one must flee"** <note>original: *pheukteon*</note>, or perhaps **"fleeing"** <note>original: *fugienda*</note> instead of **"putting to flight"** <note>original: *fuganda*</note>; for the Greek word *pheukteon* carries the meaning of "that which must be avoided." I had written these notes when I later returned to a very old edition of Jerome, which I have in a version printed in Lyon in the year 1508 by Jacobus Saccon. In that edition, I discovered the Greek varies slightly from the more recent editions: for instead of **"discord"** <note>original: *diaphonian*</note> it reads **"strife"** <note>original: *dichonoian*</note>; and instead of **"universally from all things, excess,"** it is written, **"and simply, the lack of measure in every single thing."** I did not think this variation in the readings should be ignored.

### ON PORPHYRY

<margin>23</margin>
**If it is necessary to believe]** These same stories regarding the Daunian bear and the Tarentine bull—which were tamed and made gentle by Pythagoras—and about the eagle flying overhead while he happened to be discussing omens with his companions, which he reportedly drew down from the air and stroked with his hand (by which it is proved, if it is right to believe it, that even wild beasts were obedient to his word and understood his speech), also exist, and indeed in almost as many words, in *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras</note> chapter 13, numbers 61 and 62. However, they appear in such a way that certain parts in Iamblichus can be restored to their integrity using this passage from Malchus <note>Malchus is the original name of Porphyry</note>. It seems to me, however, that these stories (like the one about the river that greeted Pythagoras with a clear and human voice as he crossed it, as well as the story of him being seen in two very distant cities on the same day, etc.) are of the sort that could easily hold their place among the *True Histories* of Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata wrote "True Histories" as a satire of the tall tales and lies found in ancient travelogues and histories</note>. For "what does lying Greece not dare in history?" to use the words of the Satirist <note>Juvenal, Satire 10.174</note>. I think it is of the same sort <note>original Greek: *tou autou kommatos*, literally "of the same minting/stamp"</note> what they write about Ammonianus the philosopher (a relative of Syrianus), that he had a donkey who was a "listener of wisdom" <note>original: *sophias akroatēn*</note>; I suppose they believed the donkey's soul had previously inhabited the body of some philosopher. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says under the entry *Ammonianus*: "This was Ammonianus, who happened to possess a donkey that was a listener of wisdom." Furthermore, St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father</note> also mentions this "bovine conversation," as well as the eagle with whom Pythagoras supposedly discussed matters. Taking these stories as true, he brings them forward as an argument to prove that Pythagoras was a magus <note>a sorcerer or practitioner of magic</note> and a charlatan. I will write down his very words from *Homily 1 on the Gospel of John*, where he brilliantly demonstrates how the most learned doctrines of the highest philosophers (such as Pythagoras and Plato) were forced to yield and fall silent before the Gospel truth and the simple "fisherman’s simplicity" of the Apostles—to the point that the authors of those doctrines are now scarcely known by name among the common Christian people. Concerning Pythagoras, he then adds the following:

"Pythagoras, having taken over Greater Greece <note>Southern Italy</note> and displayed ten thousand forms of sorcery <note>original Greek: *goēteias*</note>—for talking to bulls (for they say he did this) was nothing other than sorcery—is clearly exposed from this: he who spoke to irrational creatures in this way did no benefit to the human race, but rather did the greatest harm. Yet the nature of humans is much better suited for philosophical discourse. Nevertheless, he spoke to eagles and bulls, as they say, practicing sorcery. For he did not make the irrational nature rational (since that is impossible for a man), but he deceived the ignorant with magic tricks <note>original: *manganeiais*</note>. And neglecting to teach humans anything useful, he taught them that it was the same thing to eat beans and to eat the heads of..." <note>The text likely ends with the famous Pythagorean taboo comparing eating beans to eating the heads of one's parents or human flesh</note>

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...the heads of those who begat them. And he persuaded his companions that the teacher’s soul had once become a bush, once a girl, and once a fish. Is it not reasonable, then, that all those teachings were extinguished and vanished completely? It was reasonable and consistent with logic. <note>original Greek: This quote is from St. John Chrysostom, *Homilies on the Gospel of John*, 2.3, where he ridicules the absurdity of Pythagorean reincarnation.</note>

Regarding what St. John Chrysostom says first—that in the doctrine of Pythagoras it is the same thing and an equal crime to eat beans as it is to eat the heads of one’s parents—he was alluding to these verses by Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who was a follower of Pythagorean ideas</note> (who was a student of Pythagoras, as will be discussed below):

> Wretched ones, utterly wretched, keep your hands away from beans!
> It is the same, truly, to eat beans and the heads of your parents.

The first of these verses appears in Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author</note> Book 4, Chapter 11; the second is found in Clement of Alexandria’s *Miscellanies* <term>Stromata</term>, Book 3, page 187. Elsewhere, however, the word "to feed upon" <note>original Greek: *phagein*</note> is read instead of "to eat" <note>original Greek: *trōgein*</note>, though the meaning remains the same. 

Next, where the same St. Chrysostom writes that Pythagoras wanted to persuade his listeners that his own soul had once been a shrub, once a girl, and once a fish: in this, it is clear to me that he was looking at those verses of Empedocles which are preserved in Athenaeus and others:

> For I have already been, once, a boy and a girl,
> A bush, a bird, and a speechless fish in the sea.

Here I should not hide the fact that instead of "speechless" <note>original Greek: *ellopos*</note>, the word "fiery" <note>original Greek: *empyros*</note> is read in the *Greek Anthology of Epigrams*, Book 1, Chapter 86, in the section "on philosophers." 

Finally, regarding this illustrious passage from Chrysostom, one might also usefully observe: he acts most holily when he prefers heavenly truth far above all the dogmas of the philosophers (even the most excellent ones), for this truth surpasses them by its brilliance as much as the sun at high noon in a clear sky outshines a lamp. However, he is acting as a rhetorician <note>In this context, meaning he is using persuasive but perhaps biased speech to make a point</note> when he selects only the "foulest" or most absurd of Pythagoras’s views—those most vulnerable to attack—while omitting his saner teachings. In this way, he completely belittles, mocks, and misrepresents him, as if Pythagoras had contributed nothing at all to the common benefit of the human race and never taught men anything healthy or true. 

Other writers have demonstrated that the reality is quite different, including the Church Father Clement of Alexandria. While Clement grants the Greek philosophers some degree of dignity and attributes to them a certain "image of the truth" (which he believed was drawn from Moses and the teachings of the Hebrews), he also holds a slightly more merciful opinion of Pythagoras—at least regarding those things he taught which were more sensible. What I have noted about this passage in Chrysostom applies more broadly; similar things can be said of Tertullian, Lactantius, Justin Martyr, and other Saints...

He notes that while the Church Fathers championed Christian truth, they often used rhetorical strategies to highlight only the most absurd aspects of pagan philosophy.</summary>

...to the Church Fathers, when they speak somewhat harshly of the philosophers, and perhaps in some instances undeservingly.

**"No longer was seen"** <note>original Greek: *Ouketi ōphthē*</note>. Iamblichus <note>A later biographer of Pythagoras</note> writes more fully, **"no longer from then on was seen"** <note>original Greek: *ouketi ektote ōphthē*</note>. In my judgment, there is no reason why anyone should change this to **"from this"** <note>original Greek: *ek toutou*</note>.

**"In a mixed pasture"** <note>original Greek: *Pammigē nomē*</note>. Iamblichus, in Chapter 13, writes **"in a mixed pasture"** <note>original Greek: *en pammigei nomē*</note>. And so I think Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original Syrian name was Malchus; Rittershusius uses it to refer to the text of Porphyry he is editing</note> should also be corrected here.

**"And when he said he did not know how to speak in Ox-language"** <note>original Greek: *Kai phēsantos, ouk eidenai boisti lalein*</note>. In the aforementioned passage in Iamblichus, it is written, **"and when he said he did not know how to speak Ox-language"** <note>original Greek: *kai ou phēsantos eidenai boisti eipein*</note>. Regarding this elegant transposition of the negation <note>shifting "not" to a different part of the sentence</note>, which was familiar to good authors, see Desiderius Heraldus’s <note>A 17th-century French scholar</note> *Observations on Iamblichus*, Chapter 6.

**"To stop"** <note>original Greek: *Aposiēsai*</note>. Iamblichus adds **"without practice"** <note>original Greek: *ameleti*</note>; where perhaps one should read **"without care"** <note>original Greek: *amelēti*</note>.

**"The so-called sacred ox"** <note>original Greek: *Ton hieron kaloumenon boun*</note>. Iamblichus adds, **"of Pythagoras"**; so that it was called "The Sacred Ox of Pythagoras." <note>This refers to a famous legend where Pythagoras whispered into the ear of an ox to stop it from eating beans; the ox allegedly obeyed and lived out its days at a temple.</note>

**"Nourishment"** <note>original Greek: *Trophas*</note>. Iamblichus says, **"feeding on human food"** <note>original Greek: *anthrōpinais trophais sitoumenon*</note>.

<margin>25</margin>
**"An eagle flying over"** <note>original Greek: *Aeton de hyperiptamenon*</note>. Besides Iamblichus, Malchus, and Chrysostom, etc., Plutarch also mentions this eagle in his *Life of Numa*. <note>Pythagoras was said to have the power to call down a white eagle from the sky to his hand.</note>

**"While he was conversing with his acquaintances"** <note>original Greek: *Prosomilountos autou tois gnōrimois*</note>. This passage clearly confirms the correction made by Heraldus in Iamblichus, Section 62. In that text, the reading **"to him"** <note>original Greek: *autō*</note> was worthless; even more worthless was the interpretation: "those who were most famous by fortune." In fact, that phrase **"by chance"** <note>original Greek: *apo tychēs*</note> should be connected with the word **"conversing"**, and not at all with the word **"acquaintances"**.

**"Divination signs"** <note>original Greek: *Diosēmeiōn*</note>. In Iamblichus, it is wrongly read as **"through signs"** <note>original Greek: *dia sēmeiōn*</note>. What **"divination signs"** <note>original Greek: *diosēmeia*</note> actually are is well known, even from Aratus <note>A Greek poet</note>, who described in verse not only the *Appearances* <term>Phaenomena</term>, but also the *Divination Signs* <term>Diosēmeia</term>. These are signs by which one may foreknow future changes in the weather, either from the stars (especially the moon and sun), or from certain living creatures, or even from inanimate things. Different from these is the word **"divine omen"** <note>original Greek: *diosēmia*</note>, which is explained by Suidas <note>A famous 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> as **"divine wrath"** <note>original Greek: *theomēnia*</note>. For I say it should be read that way there, instead of **"divine omen"** <note>original Greek: *theomnia*</note>. **"Divine wrath"** <note>original Greek: *theomēnia*</note> is **"the anger of God"** <note>original Greek: *mēnis theou*</note>. You could call it "the wrath of Jove" with Ovid at the end of his *Metamorphoses*. Suidas cites an example from some historian: **"And there were present two thousand Scythians, swifter than any divine omen—that is, lightning, or a fire-wind, or a thunderbolt, or a storm-bolt, or a shooting star."** He then adds another descri-
