# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...interpretation of **"signs from the sky"** <note>original Greek: diosemias</note>, which is to say, **"a storm out of season"** <note>original Greek: ho para kairon cheimōn</note>. (Such was the weather when I was writing this, at the beginning of the year 1610.) He also adds in the same place the custom of the Athenians, who were used to dismissing the assembly, or pausing their business, if any sign from the sky occurred: **"The Athenians used to watch for signs from the sky, and they would dissolve the assemblies when a sign occurred, or if they were about to accomplish anything else."** <note>original Greek: Parephylatton de Athēnaioi tas diosemias, kai dielyon tas ekklēsias diosemias genomenēs, ē allo ti mellontes anyein.</note> From these things it is possible to gather that a "sign from the sky" has the same meaning as **"the violence of God"** <note>original Latin: theou bia</note> mentioned by the jurist Ulpian in Book 15 of his work *On Leases*, under the section *If goods*, regarding **"major force"** <note>original Latin: vis maior; a legal term for an "Act of God" or unavoidable accident</note>.

**"That [they come] from the gods"** <note>original Greek: Hoti para theōn</note>] From this, Iamblichus <note>A later biographer of Pythagoras</note> should be corrected, in whose work it was incorrectly published as **"concerning"** <note>original Greek: peri</note>, which I have observed scribes have substituted for **"from"** <note>original Greek: para</note> more than once elsewhere in the same author's work.

**"The same ones"** <note>original Greek: Hai autai</note>] Based on Iamblichus, the word **"and"** <note>original Greek: kai</note> should be restored here. And conversely, in Iamblichus, instead of the masculine **"themselves"** <note>original Greek: autoi</note>, one should read the feminine **"themselves"** <note>original Greek: autai</note>: namely, referring to **"the announcements"** <note>original Greek: hai angeliai</note>.

**"To bring down"** <note>original Greek: Katagagein</note>] Iamblichus writes **"to lead across"** <note>original Greek: metagagein</note>. Finally, in the same Chapter 13 of Iamblichus, instead of **"Pythagoras possessed something analytical and admonishing,"** I think it would be more correctly read as **"Pythagoras possessed something encouraging and admonishing."** Let this excellent sentiment from the same chapter be noted: *Since even brute animals are capable of discipline and can be tamed, much more should humans—to whom mind and reason have been given—lend patient ears to discipline and cultivation.* **"Instruction is achieved for those who have a mind, just as it is for those who are considered wild and lacking in reason."** <note>original Greek: Didaskalia periginetai tois noun echousin, hopou kai tois anēmerois te kai amoirein logou nomizomenois.</note> There was no need for the previous editors to add marks here as if the text were missing something. For the phrase **"instruction is achieved"** <note>original Greek: didaskalia periginetai</note> is meant to be understood as applying to both parts of the sentence.

**"Standing by the net-casters"** <note>original Greek: Diktyobolois t’ epistanta</note>] When it was incorrectly read as *diktyoulaois* in the manuscript, I restored it to **"net-casters"** <note>original Greek: diktyobolois</note>. But later, having inspected Iamblichus, I noticed that here too one should read **"net-haulers"** <note>original Greek: diktyoulkois</note>. For "net-haulers" are fishermen, named from **"drawing the nets"** <note>original Greek: para to helkein ta diktya</note>. Plutarch also mentions this story in *Table Talk* <note>original Latin: Sympos.</note>, Book 8, Problem 8, in these words: **"And yet they say Pythagoras once bought a catch of fish, then ordered them to release the net; not as one who disregarded the fish as being of another race or as enemies, but as one paying a ransom for prisoners who had become friends and kin."** He also alluded to the same story in his commentary *On how to benefit from one's enemies*, in these words: **"And buying catches of fish, he ordered them to be released."** See also Iamblichus Book 1, Chapter 8; a comparison will teach the reader that some things are to be corrected from Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name, here used for his text</note> using Iamblichus, and vice versa. I will therefore write them down:

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUIS
### Page 176

...that the biographer is Porphyry himself. For he was called by his own name "King" <note>original Greek: Basileus</note>, as witnessed by Suidas <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note>, which is "Malchus" in the Syrophoenician language <note>Malchus is derived from the Semitic root *mlk*, meaning king; Porphyry was born in Tyre</note>. For his homeland was Tyre. Suidas says: *Porphyry, the one who wrote against the Christians, who was properly called King, a Tyrian philosopher, a student of Amelius (who was a student of Plotinus), and the teacher of Iamblichus, living during the times of Aurelian,* etc. Therefore, there is no reason for us to look around for some other "Malchus," as I was doing earlier before I had examined Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, who quoted Porphyry in his polemics</note> more closely. Let this little work now be attributed by us to Porphyry himself, based on arguments that are, in my opinion, by no means doubtful or trivial. It is also possible that Porphyry's own name was at one time added to the title, which later scribes omitted: *The Life of Pythagoras, by Porphyry, also known as Malchus or King.* This is the first point regarding the author of our little work.

Next, I observe that this work was divided into at least two books by Porphyry himself, of which the second, and indeed the end of the first, has been lost. It is easy to gather this from another passage in Cyril, Book 9 of the same work *Against Julian*, a passage I will quote elsewhere in these Notes. For since he names there the "first book of Porphyry's history of Pythagoras," he implies that there were more than one, and at least two books. For "first" is usually said in respect to a "second," and so on.

It follows from this that we should say—since Iamblichus was a student of Porphyry (Suidas: *Iamblichus, from Chalcis in Syria, a philosopher, student of Porphyry the philosopher, who heard Plotinus, living during the times of the Emperor Constantine,* etc.)—that Iamblichus wrote later, and expanded upon the brevity of his master with a more fertile commentary. That this is true will be easily apparent to anyone from a comparison of the texts. Therefore, I also retract what I said above: that this Malchus seemed to be a sort of epitomizer <note>a creator of summaries or abridgments</note> who compiled his work from Iamblichus. 

Furthermore, a comparison of Malchus with Cyril is useful for correcting the Latin translation. For while Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), a prominent humanist and Reformer who translated many Greek patristic texts into Latin</note> translates it this way:

> (Therefore Porphyry, his companion [Julian’s] and the father of slanders against us, describing the life of Pythagoras, says thus: *For the things that are recited about that which resides at Mycenae, among the Trojan spoils at the temple of Argive Juno. When we had passed the monument of Euphorbus the Phrygian and his shield, as if it were very cheap, they said the river Causas, when he was crossing with many others, spoke to him in the hearing of all the others: HAIL, PYTHAGORAS!*)

...the translator indicates enough that he either had a faulty manuscript, or, if he had a corrected one, he did not grasp the sense of the true reading.

We can therefore restore Cyril’s Latin translation in this manner: *For those things narrated about the shield of Euphorbus the Phrygian <note>Euphorbus was a Trojan hero said to be a previous incarnation of Pythagoras</note>, which was said to have been hung up for Juno of Argos at Mycenae among the Trojan spoils, we pass over as being less well known. However, they said that the river Causus <note>original: Causum</note>, while Pythagoras himself was once crossing it with many companions, spoke to him in the hearing of everyone: "Greetings, Pythagoras," etc.* Note these things as well: first, it seems that Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius, a 16th-century Protestant reformer and translator</note> read "others" <note>original Greek: heteron</note> instead of "companions" <note>original Greek: hetairon</note>, since he translated it as *others*; second, that the phrase: *and the river, having become something* (this is how it should be read, just as I find it clearly written in Iamblichus, not *having become someone*) *and spoke out clearly,* is not found in Cyril’s Latin version.

**Of this shield of Euphorbus the Phrygian]** The shield of Euphorbus, hung as a votive offering <term>anathema: a gift dedicated to a god and displayed in a temple</term> in the temple of Juno of Argos at Mycenae, though worn away by age, was said to have been recognized by Pythagoras. He claimed that his own soul had previously inhabited the body of Euphorbus. Hyginus, the freedman of Augustus, in his *Fables* <note>original: Fabulis</note> chapter 112, writes: *Menelaus fought with Euphorbus. Euphorbus is killed. He later became Pythagoras, and remembers that his soul passed into other bodies.* Tertullian, in *On the Soul* <note>original: de Anima</note> chapter 28, says: *But he recognized the shield of Euphorbus, which had once been consecrated at Delphi, and said it was his own, and proved it by signs commonly unknown, etc.* Here one may notice a lapse of memory in this most learned writer. For if that shield was hung in the temple of Juno of Argos at Mycenae (as is said here, and in Iamblichus chapter 14, as well as Ovid in Book 15 of the *Metamorphoses*), then it was not at Delphi in the shrine of Pythian Apollo. See also what I shall note below. Furthermore, that word "this" <note>original Greek: toutou</note> is very suspicious to me: although it is also read in Iamblichus, where Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius, a 16th-century editor of Iamblichus</note> tries to change it to "this thing" <note>original Greek: touto</note>, which I do not approve of.

**We pass over]** In Iamblichus, in the same chapter 14, the word "we are present" <note>original Greek: paresmen</note> is read, which makes no sense; hence it should be corrected to "we pass over" <note>original Greek: pariemen</note>: that is, *we omit*. Nor do I like Arcerius’s reading, "the mark of the shield" <note>original: touto asp. parasemon</note>, nor his translation: *the insignia of the shield, etc.* There are also several things in that same place that could either be filled in, amended, or even defended against the interpreter's "over-corrections" <term>paradiorthoseis: excessive or mistaken textual emendations</term>. For first, Iamblichus lacks the word "dedicated" <note>original Greek: anakeimenes</note>, which should be restored after "at Mycenae"; instead of "concerning the ones who" <note>original Greek: peri ton</note> one should not read "they placed around" <note>original Greek: perithetan</note>, but "concerning the [shield]" <note>original Greek: peri tes</note>, which refers back to "the shield." Finally, instead of "with fellow Trojans" <note>original Greek: suntroikois</note> it should be rewritten separately as "with the Trojan [spoils]" <note>original Greek: sun Troikois</note>; although Arcerius also saw this last point, his translation here is full of errors. ### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS ###

To accomplish, to finish, to carry out, to help, to demand (I suspect these last two words are errors in the text). The Suda <note>original: Suidas; a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note> defines the term as: Effectively, actively, practically, completely. And "most effectively." For "accomplishment" <note>original: ánysis</note> means "completion." And a little before: "To accomplish" means "to complete" or "to do." Likewise again: "To achieve something" <note>original: anýsasthaí ti</note> means "to get it done" among rulers. And similarly again, for rulers to "give orders to subjects." And "to finish" is "to complete." Again the same Suda says: "It is finished" or "it has been finished." And "one must finish." "More effective" <note>original: anystikōtéra</note> instead of "most active" (one should either read "most effective" or "more active"). 

He then cites a passage from Polybius, which deserves to be recorded here because of its excellent sentiment: "One soul is more effective than the many hands of many men in certain moments; just as Archimedes <note>the famous Greek mathematician and inventor</note> alone in Syracuse was more effective than many Romans." These words are not found today in the surviving works of Polybius that we have; however, a similar concluding thought is found in the *Excerpts*, where he discusses the cleverness and machines of Archimedes in Book 8, page 518 of the new Paris edition: "Thus one man and one art, properly applied to certain affairs, appears to become a great and wonderful thing." But these things are a side-note <note>original: hodoú párergon</note>.

<margin>28</margin> **He showed his golden thigh**] There is much mention among authors of this golden thigh shown by Pythagoras on his own body. See, besides Plutarch in his *Life of Numa*, also Iamblichus Book 1, Chapter 28, and Diogenes Laertius Book 8, page 574: "It is said that once when he was partially stripped, his thigh was seen to be golden" <note>original: Legétai dè autoú poté paragymnōthéntos tòn mērón ophthēnai chrysoún</note>. That writer of *Lives* <note>Diogenes Laertius</note> speaks as if Pythagoras's thigh appeared golden by some accidental chance of being naked. But other authors record that he uncovered his thigh on purpose to show it was golden, and by that argument to prove that he was the "Hyperborean Apollo" <note>a title for the god Apollo as he was worshipped by a legendary people of the far north</note>. And indeed, he did this not only for Abaris, the priest of the Hyperborean Apollo, but also publicly to many men at the Olympic games—that is, in a very large and crowded gathering—when he stood up for this very purpose and walked around. 

Truly a strange conclusion and method of reasoning: "Pythagoras has a golden thigh. Therefore, he is that Apollo whom the Hyperboreans worship as a god." But putting aside these "nonsense of nonsenses" <note>original: lḗrōn lḗrois</note>, let us remove an error or two from the already mentioned Chapter 28 of Iamblichus. In section 135, we read: "confirming that this is true" <note>original: bebaioún hōs toúto alēthés</note>, where the reader rightly pauses to ask what that "confirming" refers to. Does it refer to Pythagoras and the verb "showed"? But then Iamblichus should have written "while confirming" <note>original: bebaiōn</note>. Does it refer to "thigh"? Then "confirming" <note>original: bebaioúnta</note> should have been written. We learn that this latter form is correct from this passage of Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry, the author of this biography</note>, where "confirming" <note>original: bebaioúnta</note> is read, which refers to the golden thigh...

<summary>Rittershusius provides philological definitions for "accomplishment" and discusses the legend of Pythagoras's golden thigh, debating whether it was revealed by accident or as a deliberate claim to divinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on the biography of Pythagoras. Having discussed the terminology of "completing" or "achieving" on the previous page, the author now moves to one of the most famous legends of Pythagoras: the "golden thigh" which was used to prove his divine nature as the Hyperborean Apollo.</meta>

### ON PORPHYRY ###

...must be referred to entirely. For this thigh was held **as a piece of evidence** <note>original: antì tekmēríou</note>, by which that opinion about Pythagoras might be confirmed: that he was, indeed, the very same person as the Hyperborean Apollo <note>the sun-god Apollo was said to visit a mythical, blessed land in the far North called Hyperborea</note>. Iamblichus certainly calls these very things **proofs** <note>original: Tekmḗria</note> in section 140, a passage we are now approaching to correct. Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius, a 16th-century editor of Iamblichus</note> published it there as: "that rising up in his life, he showed his golden thigh." And he translated it thus: *because when he had arisen in this life, etc.* It should have been noticed that instead of "life" <note>original: aiōni</note> (which has no place here), one should read "contest" <note>original: agōni</note>; and by "contest" we should understand the Olympic games specifically. For Plutarch explicitly writes in his *Life of Numa* that these things happened at the Olympic assembly: "that he showed his thigh to be golden at the Olympics, while passing through the festival." Besides Lucian in his *Dream*, or *The Cock*, Apollonius also mentions this golden thigh in chapter 6 of his *Wonderful Histories*; he writes, following Aristotle, that this **demonstration** <note>original: epídeixin</note> was made in a theater: "Once while sitting in a theater he rose up, as Aristotle says, and showed his own thigh to those sitting there as golden" (I think the text should be corrected here). Finally, he concludes that chapter (which was entirely about Pythagoras) with these words: "certain other wonders <note>original: parádoxa</note> are also told about him. But we, not wishing to do the work of copyists, will end the account here." However, others have handed down that the thigh was made of ivory; such as Origen in book 6 of *Against Celsus*: "What should even be said about Pythagoras, who practiced so many wonders, and showed his ivory thigh in a festival of the Greeks, and claimed to have recognized the shield he used when he was Euphorbus?" <note>Pythagoras claimed to remember his past lives, including being the Trojan hero Euphorbus</note>.

**It is, then**] Perhaps it should be read, "Let it be, then." Apollonius has the same story about a ship carrying a dead man in chapter 6 of his *Wonderful Histories*, from which I transcribe these things: "Following these (namely Pherecydes, Abaris, and Hermotimus), Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, at first applied himself to mathematics and numbers. But later he did not abstain from the wonder-working <note>original: teratopoïïas</note> of Pherecydes. For when a ship from the sea was coming in carrying cargo, and the bystanders were praying for it to be saved, though it was sinking due to the load, he stood and said: 'A small body will appear to you to be what is leading this ship.'" <note>The "small body" refers to a corpse on the ship, suggesting Pythagoras had supernatural perception</note>.

<margin>29</margin>
**For both predictions**] Concerning Pythagoras's predictions of the future, Clement of Alexandria writes thus in his *Miscellanies* <note>original: Stromata</note>, book 1: "Pythagoras the Great always devoted himself to foreknowledge, as did Abaris the Hyperborean and Aristeas of Proconnesus, etc." Apollonius also writes in chapter 4 of his *Wonderful Histories* that Abaris was skilled in the art of divination and recorded oracles in writing.

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS ###

...entirely in these words: "Abaris the Hyperborean <note>Abaris was a legendary priest of Apollo said to have traveled on a golden arrow and lived without food</note> was himself one of the **Theologians** <term>theologoi: those who wrote about the nature of the gods and the origins of the world</term>. He also wrote oracles as he traveled through various lands, which remain in existence until the present day. He predicted earthquakes, plagues, and similar disasters, as well as celestial phenomena. It is said that when he arrived in Lacedaemon <note>the region of Sparta</note>, he told the Spartans to perform 'averting' sacrifices to the gods; as a result, no plague occurred in Lacedaemon afterward." **An uncertain author of a Life of Pythagoras** in the excerpts found in **Photius, p. 713 of the *Library*** <note>Photius was a 9th-century scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople who summarized hundreds of books now lost to us</note>: "That they say (others read: he says) that Pythagoras predicted many things, and they all came to pass." Undoubtedly, he had drawn this art of **divination** <term>divinatio: the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</term> from his teacher Pherecydes, of whom we read that he predicted storms and many other things to which the events corresponded. **Cicero, Book 1 of *On Divination***: *Not even Pherecydes, that teacher of Pythagoras, will be considered a diviner rather than a physicist, who, when he had seen* <gloss>read: had drunk</gloss> *water drawn from a deep well, said that earthquakes were imminent, etc.* That it is more correct to read "had drunk" in Cicero is confirmed by these words of Apollonius, which I will add from Chapter 5 of his book *Wonderful Histories*: "The stories concerning Pherecydes are of this sort <gloss>read: such things</gloss>. Once on the island of Scyros, being thirsty, he requested a little water from one of his acquaintances. After drinking it, he said that an earthquake would occur on the island after the third day. When this happened, he gained a great reputation. Again, while traveling to Samos to the temple of Hera, he saw a ship being brought into the harbor and said to those standing with him that it would not enter within the harbor; even as he was speaking, a storm-cloud broke, and finally the ship vanished." But let me return from the teacher to the pupil, whose name **Pythagoras** would seem to have been earned by right if his predictions were true. I referred to the etymology of this name above in the Title of this book from **Diogenes Laertius** and **Suidas**: namely, that because he was accustomed to speaking the truth no less than the **Pythian** <note>referring to the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle at Delphi</note> priestess or the Pythian Apollo, he thus obtained the name Pythagoras. What of the fact that he also predicted long in advance that sedition which proved fatal to the Pythagoreans, which we discuss below? **Apollonius, Chapter 6 of *Wonderful Histories***: "And he predicted the uprising that was occurring <gloss>read: having occurred</gloss> against the Pythagoreans. Therefore he departed for **Metapontum**, seen by no one." **The same Pythagoras**, among many other precepts, also handed down this one, according to the testimony of **Diogenes, p. 582**: "To honor all forms of prophecy." And **Iamblichus, Chapter 28**, testifies that the Pythagoreans diligently exercised themselves in the art of divination, as it was the only way they could use an interpreter for the kind and propitious will of the gods. For this reason, concerning prophecy...

Having previously discussed the prophetic abilities Pythagoras inherited from Pherecydes, the author now examines the specific disciplines the Pythagoreans valued—music, medicine, and divination—and defends the original Greek terminology used by Porphyry and Iamblichus against earlier editors.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY

"...they strive for this; for this alone is the interpretation of the favor of the gods." <note>original Greek: σπουδάζουσι· μόνη γὰρ αὕτη ἑρμηνεία τῆς παρὰ τῶν θεῶν εὐμενείας</note> For that is how it should be read in that passage. Again, the same Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras</note> writes in chapter 29, number 163, that they held those three things especially in high esteem: music, the art of healing (especially through **diet** or an accurate regime of living, which is *diaitetike* to the Greeks), and finally **divination**. "And of the sciences, they say the Pythagoreans themselves honored not least music, and medicine (especially accepting the dietary form of it), and divination." <note>original Greek: Τῶν δ' ἐπιστημῶν οὐχ ἥκιστα φασὶν αὐτοὺς τοὺς Πυθαγορείους τιμᾷν, μουσικήν τε, καὶ ἰατρικὴν (μάλιστα δ' ἀποδέχεσθαι ταύτης τὸ διαιτητικὸν εἶδος) καὶ μαντικήν</note>

**Effusion**] <note>Greek: Ἐκχύσεως (*Ekchyseōs*), referring to an outpouring or release of emotion</note> In the passage of Iamblichus mentioned at No. 135, the prefix "ek" has disappeared and should be restored from here. For it is read there incorrectly as *chyseōs* [pourings]. Furthermore, what are here called "calmings" <note>Greek: καταστολαὶ (*katastolai*)</note> by Malchus <note>the original Syrian name of Porphyry</note> are called "lullings" or "soothings" <note>Greek: κατευνήσεις (*kateunēseis*)</note> by Iamblichus.

**Serenations**] <note>Greek: Ἀπευδιασμοὶ (*Apeudiasmoi*)</note> Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius Theodoretus, a 16th-century editor of Iamblichus</note> stirs up a "storm in a teacup" <note>literally "waves in a ladle"</note> without cause in his *Corrections to Iamblichus*, while he thinks this reading is faulty and that it would be more correct if we read *apōthismoi* [pushings away]; or he professes that he does not know what the author means, and therefore did not translate it. On the contrary, the word *apeudiasmoi* is most correctly retained in both places, both here and in Iamblichus (for one has borrowed from the other, as in many other things), which you could translate as *serenations* <term>serenatio: the act of making the mind clear or calm, like the clearing of weather</term>. For *eudia* is "serenity" or "calm weather": hence *eudiazō* [to be calm], and the compound *apeudiazō* [to make calm]: and the noun *apeudiasmos*. I had to give this warning so that we do not go about changing things with rash audacity just because we do not grasp something in writers immediately at the first step, treating it as faulty; nothing is more harmful for corrupting good authors.

**Empedocles**] <note>Greek: Ἐμπεδοκλέα</note> That Empedocles was a Pythagorean is sufficiently shown, besides the testimony of Diogenes Laertius in Book 8, by other fragments of his works as well as a couplet encompassing the doctrine of **metempsychosis** <term>metempsychosis: the transmigration of souls; the belief that the soul moves into a new body after death</term>, which Athenaeus preserved for us at the end of Book 8 (among others), and which I recorded above on another occasion. In it, he professes about himself (if anyone is to be believed about themselves) that he was previously a girl, and a boy, and a shrub, and a bird, and a fish. See below at No. 30 for six magnificent verses composed by the same man in praise of his master [Pythagoras]. Cicero also mentions Empedocles with praise more than once: as in *On the Orator*, where he calls him a **physicist** <term>physicus: a natural philosopher or scientist</term> who also wrote an excellent poem. Again in the *Academic Questions*, Book 4: *And yet those philosophers of yours, when they are stuck in some spot, quite often cry out as if driven by inspiration—Empedocles indeed, so that he sometimes seems to me to be raving: "That we perceive nothing, we see nothing..."*

He also identifies the philosopher Empedocles as a Pythagorean follower, citing his belief in the transmigration of souls.</summary>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...nothing at all can be discovered of what kind it is, etc., where Cicero expresses those verses of Empedocles which survive in the works of Sextus Empiricus: "Thus these things are neither to be seen by men, nor heard, nor grasped by the mind." <note>original Greek: Οὕτως οὔτ᾽ ἐπιδερκτὰ τάδ᾽ ἀνδράσιν, οὔτ᾽ ἐπακουστά, Οὔτε νόῳ περιληπτά</note> Later in the same fourth book, he responds to the earlier points in this way: *Does Empedocles seem to you to be mad? But to me, he seems to produce a sound most worthy of the matters of which he speaks. Does he then blind us, or rob us of our senses, if he thinks there is not enough power in them to judge those things which are subjected to them?* To this same Empedocles belong those words in Cicero's *Laelius* <note>a dialogue by Cicero also known as "On Friendship"</note>: *They say a certain learned man of Agrigentum <note>Empedocles, who lived in the Sicilian city of Akragas, known in Latin as Agrigentum</note> prophesied in Greek verses: that whatever things in the nature of things and the whole world stood firm, or whatever moved, friendship drew them together and discord scattered them. And this indeed all mortals both understand and prove in practice, etc.* Cicero is hinting at these poems of Empedocles, which I shall add here from Plutarch's *On the Opinions of the Philosophers, Book 1*, and other sources:

> Hear first the four roots of all things... <note>original Greek: Τέσσαρα τῶν πάντων ῥιζώματα πρῶτον ἄκουε — referring to the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>
> At one time all things come together into one by Love;
> At another, they are each carried apart by the hatred of Strife.

And again:

> And baneful Strife, apart from these, balanced in every way,
> And Love among them, equal in length and breadth.

*It will also be worth the effort to add here the verses written about* Empedocles himself as an <term>ethopoeia</term> <note>a rhetorical exercise of "character-making," where a writer composes a speech in the voice of a specific person</note>; namely, the kind of words he might have used when he was just about to bid farewell to human affairs, and—desiring to be considered an immortal god (as Horace says)—*chilled to the bone, he prepared to leap into burning* Aetna <note>Mount Etna, the volcano in Sicily. Legend says Empedocles jumped into the crater to prove his divinity</note>. *These are found in* Diogenes Laertius, *page 606, and the first five are also in Book 1 of the Anthology regarding Philosophers:*

> O friends, who dwell in the great city by the yellow Akragas,
> Up on the heights of the town, you who care for good works,
> Hail! I walk among you as an immortal god, no longer mortal,
> Honored by all, as is fitting,
> And crowned with headbands and blooming wreaths.
> Whenever I come with these to flourishing cities,
> I am revered by both men and women; they follow me
> In their thousands, asking where the path to profit lies;
> Some in need of prophecies, while others
> Seek to hear a healing <note>reading "euēchea" (clear-sounding) for "euēkea" (well-pointed)</note> word for all kinds of diseases.

### ON PORPHYRY

Regarding the same Empedocles, see also Athenaeus at the end of Book 8, where he recites those two verses (noted by me elsewhere) in which that philosopher of Akragas <note>original Latin: Acragantinus; Akragas was a major Greek city in Sicily, now Agrigento</note> confesses that he was once a boy, and a girl, and a bush, and a bird, and a fish of the sea. Also see Book 1 at the beginning, where he speaks of the bull he fashioned from various spices, which he, as the victor of the equestrian contest at the Olympic games, distributed among the spectators.

**And Epimenides]** <note>original Greek: Καὶ Ἐπιμενίδην</note> Iamblichus also testifies in Book 1, Chapter 32, that Epimenides of Crete was a disciple of Pythagoras. He says that Epimenides fell in with certain ambushers, upon whom he called down the Furies <note>avenging spirits of the underworld</note> to avenge his death; by those curses, he brought it about that they finished each other off in mutual slaughter. I will transcribe the words of Iamblichus so that I may simultaneously remove a textual error: *Epimenides, the student of Pythagoras, when he was about to be killed by certain people, because he called upon the Furies and the avenging gods, caused all those plotting against him to be slaughtered by one another...* <note>original Greek: Ἐπιμενίδης ὁ Πυθαγόρου μαθητὴς... The commentator notes a correction from "around themselves" to "by one another."</note> Plato also mentions this same Epimenides in Book 1 of the *Laws*, as do Pausanias and Cicero in Book 1 of *On Divination*, where he counts him among those *who prophesied through divine frenzy*. And in Book 2 of *On Laws*, Cicero says that for the sake of expiating the crime of Cylon <note>Cylon was an Athenian who attempted to seize power as a tyrant after winning at the Olympics; his followers were later murdered in a way that brought a religious curse upon the city</note>, Epimenides advised the Athenians to build and consecrate a shrine to Contumely and Impudence. Certain fragments of his poems survive, of which the most famous is the one quoted by Saint Paul in the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus: *Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.* <note>original Greek: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί.</note>

Callimachus, in his *Hymn to Jove* <note>the Roman name for Zeus</note>, reveals the reason why the Cretans should be considered liars: namely, because they constructed a tomb for the immortal Jove. *Cretans are always liars* (a half-line which Callimachus borrowed from Epimenides), *for they even built a tomb for you, O Lord, but you did not die; for you exist forever.* <note>original Greek: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται... καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα, σεῖο / Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο, σὺ δ᾿ οὐ θάνες· ἔσσι γὰρ αἰεί.</note> Saint Chrysostom also cites these verses of Callimachus in his third Homily on the same Epistle to Titus, where he also recites the epitaph of Jove itself: *The Cretans have a tomb of Zeus, bearing this inscription: Here Zan lies, whom they call Zeus.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ Κρῆτες τάφον ἔχουσι τοῦ Διὸς... Zan is an archaic or dialectal form of the name Zeus.</note> That is to say: *Zan is situated here, who is called Jupiter.*

Furthermore, I wonder why Epicharmus of Sicily was not added by Malchus <note>the original name of Porphyry, the author of the biography being discussed</note> alongside Empedocles and Epimenides. For it is well established that he too was a follower of Pythagoras, and no less an excellent poet than a philosopher, by whose testimony...

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on the life and legacy of Pythagoras. Having previously discussed the miraculous deeds and lineage of figures like Epimenides, the author now turns to Epicharmus of Kos, a philosopher and dramatist frequently associated with the Pythagorean school, examining fragments of his work preserved by later authors.</meta>

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSIUS

Cicero also uses him quite often, and almost never without a word of praise. I once pointed out in my commentary on the first book of Oppian's *Halieutica* <note>A 2nd-century Greek poem about fishing</note> that Epicharmus was greatly delighted by trochaic verses <note>A poetic meter consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one, often associated with a quick or conversational pace</note>, and in that same place, I collected and partially corrected many fragments from here and there, like planks scattered from a shipwreck. To those I will now add some others, so that I may at the same time correct them in certain places. I will begin with his noble precept on choosing friends cautiously, which both Isocrates impressed upon his pupil Demonicus in his *Exhortation*, and Cicero upon his brother Quintus in Book 3, Letter 1: *Find out how he has treated others before you make someone your friend.* <note>original Greek: Γνῶθι, πῶς ἄλλῳ κέχρηται, πρὶν φίλον ποιῇς τινα</note> For the verse seems to me to be completed in this way, though Cicero, in his usual manner, quotes only the beginning. You could express the sentiment in the same meter as follows: *Before you join anyone to you as a friend, explore how he was toward others.* Absolutely divine are the verses of the same man concerning the providence and omnipotence of God, which I will add from Theodoret’s *Cure of Greek Maladies* <note>original Latin: Therapeut. ad Gentes; a work by the 5th-century bishop Theodoret of Cyrus</note>, Oration 6, page 88. "Epicharmus the Pythagorean, knowing these things clearly, commands us to look down upon all these material things; and he urges us to fear the Overseer of all things. He speaks thus:"

> *Nothing escapes the divine; this you must know.*
> *He is our observer; and nothing is impossible for God.*
> <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲν διαφεύγει τὸ θεῖον. τοῦτο γινώσκειν σε δεῖ. Αὐτὸς ἔσθ᾽ ἡμῶν ἐπόπτης· ἀδυνατεῖ δ᾽ οὐδὲν θεῷ.</note>

->That is to say:<-

> *Nothing escapes the divine power: let this be your conviction,*
> *He himself is our overseer: and there is nothing God cannot do.*

These same verses also exist in Clement of Alexandria, from whom Theodoret borrowed them, as he did many other things. But instead of "escapes" <note>original Greek: διαφεύγει</note>, it is read there as "flees from" <note>original Greek: ἐκφεύγει</note>—and I do not know if that is not more correct. Cicero also rendered another of Epicharmus’s thoughts on death into Latin in Book 1 of his *Tusculan Disputations*, likewise in trochaic verse:

> *I do not wish to die, but being dead I count as nothing.*
> *I indeed do not wish to die, but having died, it is of no concern to me.* <note>original Greek: Βούλομαι μὲν οὐκ ἀποθνήσκειν, ἀλλὰ θανόντ᾽ οὔ μοι μέλει</note>

There is also this very famous line by Epicharmus, which appears in Plato’s *Axiochus* and partially in Stobaeus's *Sermon 10 on Injustice*: *One hand washes the other; give something, and receive something.* <note>original Greek: Ἁ δὲ χεὶρ τὰν χεῖρα νίζει· δός τι, καὶ τι καὶ λάβε</note> For it must be read this way as required by the meter. See the explanation of Erasmus in his *Adages* <note>A famous collection of Greek and Latin proverbs compiled by the Renaissance scholar Erasmus</note>, Collection 1, Century 1, Proverb 33. Again, the same Epicharmus in Stobaeus’s *Sermon 37 on Goodness*: *Character is a good spirit to men; but to some it is also an evil one.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ τρόπος ἀνθρώποισι δαίμων ἀγαθός· οἷς δὲ καὶ κακός</note> In Stobaeus, the word "and" <note>Greek: καὶ</note> is missing, which I have restored as the meter requires. This clearly agrees with that famous saying of Heraclitus: *A man's character is his destiny* <note>original Greek: Ἦθος ἀνθρώπου δαίμων</note>; by which it is meant that each man's own habits shape his for- [tune]...

Having previously discussed fragments by the philosopher and playwright Epicharmus, Rittershusius now proceeds to analyze specific ethical maxims and textual corrections from classical sources such as Plutarch, Stobaeus, and Iamblichus, focusing on friendship, virtue, and the legendary figure Abaris.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY

...whether good or bad. See Erasmus, *Adages* [Chiliades] 2, Century 4, Proverb 30. There is also a noble verse by the same Sicilian <note>Epicharmus, who was from Sicily</note>, with which he is said to have rebuked a certain spendthrift nephew; it is related by Plutarch in the *Life of Publicola*:

> You are not a lover of humanity; you have a disease: you delight in giving. <note>original Greek: Οὐ φιλάνθρωπός τύ γ’ ἐσσί· νόσον ἔχεις, χαίρεις διδούς.</note>

That is:

->I would not call you a lover of humanity; you have a disease, you who are so ready to give.<-

There is also another verse by the same man, but it is corrupted in Stobaeus <note>A 5th-century compiler of Greek excerpts</note>, Discourse 38, *On Envy*: "Who would complain that a friend is not envied?" <note>original Greek: Τίς ἐγκαλοίη, γενέσθαι μὴ φθονούμενος φίλος.</note> The most learned Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a 16th-century Swiss scholar</note> preferred the reading: "Who would wish?" <note>original Greek: Τίς ἂν βουλοίη.</note> But even so, anyone can see that the meter remains incorrect—not to mention the fault in the Latin translation: *Who is there who would desire that his friends not envy him.* I thought the correct reading should be: "Who then could complain," etc., and "by friends" <note>original: φίλοις</note> rather than "friend" <note>original: φίλος</note>; so that the author intended this: *Who, after all, is there who would find fault with anyone for not being envied by his friends?* Let someone else bring forward better suggestions. Nor should we pass over the verse containing an admonition regarding the duty of a good wife, which is to harm her husband in no way: *The virtue of a prudent woman is to do no wrong to her partner.* <note>original Greek: Σώφρονος γυναικὸς ἀρετὰ, τὸν συνόντα μὴ ἀδικεῖν.</note> For I think it should be read thus in Stobaeus, Discourse 72, *On Nuptial Precepts*, where the word "man" [husband] is redundant: unless someone should say that it was the beginning of a new verse. Finally, to break off these "Epicharmic" notes, there is also this line by Epicharmus of no despicable sentiment (though it is not Trochaic, but Sotadic <note>A rare ancient meter named after the poet Sotades</note>) concerning the gifts of friends, which should be held in esteem even if they are small: *The gift may be small, but all things coming from friends are honored.* <note>original Greek: Δῶρον μέν φ’ ὀλίγον· πάντα δὲ τιμᾶντα τὰ πὰρ φίλων.</note> "Honored" <note>original: Τιμᾶντα</note> is in the Doric dialect for the standard Greek "timienta" <note>original: τιμηέντα</note>.

**Alexamenos**] Our manuscript <term>MS [Codex]</term> had it this way. But based on Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a biography of Pythagoras</note>, chapter 28, number 136, it should be rewritten as **Alexanemos**: namely, from "warding off" or "driving away the winds" <note>From the Greek 'alexein' (to ward off) and 'anemos' (wind)</note>; just as *alexikakos* is said of one who drives away evils; likewise *alexipharmakon* <note>An antidote or "medicine that wards off poison"</note>.

**Purifier** <note>original: Καθαρτὴς</note>] From here Iamblichus should be corrected in the same section, number 136, where it was poorly edited as *Katharles*: which the translator renders as *Catharies*, that is, "clean" or "pure"—wrongly. Rather, *Kathartes*, from "to purify" <note>original: καθαίρειν</note>, is a "purifier."

**Because** <note>original: Ὅτι</note>] In Iamblichus it is "when" <note>original: ὅτε</note>. But "because" is better.

**With an arrow** <note>original: Ὀϊστῷ</note>] Famous is this arrow of Abaris the Hyperborean <note>A legendary priest of Apollo said to have traveled the world on a golden arrow without eating</note>, and we have received word that it was golden. See also Iamblichus, book 1, chapter 28, number 136.

**In both places** <note>original: Ἑκατέρωθι</note>] From here Iamblichus should be amended in the same section, number 156, where it was poorly edited as "from both sides" <note>original: ἑκατέρωθεν</note>.

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

<margin>50</margin> **And he charmed them with rhythms and melodies]** <note>original Greek: Κατεκήλει δὲ ῥυθμοῖς καὶ μέλεσι</note> To charm <term>is</term> "to enchant or to calm" <note>original Greek: θέλγειν, πραΰνειν</note>: to soothe or to make gentle. Thus Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> explains "charming" <note>κατακηλοῦσαν</note> as "enchanting or calming." And Hesychius <note>a 5th-century lexicographer</note> defines "those being charmed" as "those being inspired or enchanted." From this, Suidas explains the word "unsoothable" <note>ἀκήλητον</note> as "cruel," and brings forward a couplet from an Epigram about Orpheus:

-> Who even the heavy mind of the unmerciful Clymenus <- <note>Clymenus, meaning "the Renowned," is a common euphemism for Hades, the god of the Underworld</note>
-> And his unsoothable soul enchanted with the lyre. <-

Truly wonderful was the power of music among Pythagoras and his followers in composing and calming the emotions of the mind. Seneca writes of this in Book 3 of *On Anger*, chapter 9: *Pythagoras used to settle the disturbances of the soul with the lyre. For who does not know that bugles and trumpets are incitements, just as certain songs are inducements by which the mind is released.* Likewise, Plutarch, in his book *On Isis and Osiris*, where he had previously spoken about fragrant and sweet-smelling spices—noting that through them daily cares and troubles are relaxed for us toward nightfall, and the imagination, which is the receptacle of dreams, is smoothed and polished like a mirror—adds a comparison between these and the playing of the lyre, which the Pythagoreans were accustomed to use before sleep to drive away cares and to heal and calm the disturbances of the soul. I will write down a few words of many from that most learned author: > And it possesses a seductive quality; it loosens and dissolves the painful and tense daily cares like knots, without the need for intoxication; it polishes the imaginative and dream-receiving part of the soul, like a mirror, and makes it clearer—no less than the strumming of the lyre which the Pythagoreans used before sleep, thus enchanting and healing the passionate and irrational part of the soul. < Quintilian also writes excellently regarding this Pythagorean custom in Book 9, chapter 4: *It was certainly the custom of the Pythagoreans that when they woke up, they would stir their minds with the lyre so that they might be more alert for action; and when they sought sleep, they would first soften their minds with the same instrument, so that if there were any turbulent thoughts, they might compose them. For if there is a certain silent power in rhythms and melodies, it is most powerful in speech, etc.*

Cicero also mentions this same custom in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4, in the introduction: namely, that the Pythagoreans were accustomed to transmit certain teachings more secretly through songs, and to lead their minds away from the intensity of thought toward tranquility through singing and stringed instruments. He adds there that the ancient Romans introduced this same custom into their banquets as well. But even our own Mal-
<meta>The catchword "Mal-" refers to Malchus, the original name of Porphyry, whose biography of Pythagoras is the subject of this commentary.</meta>

He explains how music was used both as a morning stimulant for alertness and an evening sedative to clear the mind for peaceful dreams.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on the life and practices of Pythagoras. Having discussed the calming effects of music on the previous page, the author now focuses on why Pythagoras specifically chose the lyre over the flute, citing various classical authorities to explain the moral and social implications of different musical instruments.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY.

<note>Iambli</note>chus writes about Pythagoras that he was accustomed in the morning to compose and tame his soul to the lyre, singing along to the poems and paeans <note>hymns of praise or healing</note> of either Thales, Homer, or Hesiod. It should be noted that Seneca, Quintilian, Plutarch, Iamblichus, and others constantly testify that Pythagoras used the instrument of the lyre; Cicero also writes about his singing and playing of stringed instruments. 

If anyone should ask me why he wished to use the lyre rather than the flute <note>Latin: *tibia*, a double-reed pipe often associated with wilder emotions</note>, let Iamblichus answer for me in Chapter 25, Number 111: <note>original Greek: Τοὺς γὰρ αὐλοὺς ὑπελάμβανεν ὑβριστικόν τε καὶ πανηγυρικὸν καὶ οὐδαμῶς ἐλευθέριον τὸν ἦχον ἔχειν.</note> "For he supposed that flutes had a sound that was insolent, fit for a vulgar festival, and in no way gentlemanly." 

Clearly, he considered the flute an unrefined musical instrument, just as Pallas <note>Athena</note> judged it. They say that once, while playing the flute, she happened to see her reflection in the water as if in a mirror; seeing her face puffed up with swollen cheeks and rendered quite ugly, she became so estranged from it that she cast it away immediately, and never again wished to take up that kind of "breath-driven" <note>original Greek: ἔμπνευστον</note> musical instrument. 

The Romans, however, did not reject the flute. Indeed, among them, there was an ancient custom at banquets where those reclining at the table would, in turn, *sing the praises and virtues of famous men to the accompaniment of the flute. This is recorded by Cicero in the prologue of the fourth book of the Tusculan Disputations, citing Cato’s book of "Origins." Unless, perhaps, we should also read "to the lyre" in that passage.* 

The Greeks certainly employed the lyre at their banquets. When Themistocles <note>a famous Athenian general</note> refused the lyre, he was considered rather unlearned, as Cicero wrote in the prologue to the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. 

Before I depart from this illustrious topic regarding the power of music, I cannot help but recommend to the reader what Athenaeus writes in the 14th book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>"The Banquet of the Learned," a sprawling ancient collection of table talk</note>, especially since he mentions our Pythagoras there: <note>original Greek: Καὶ γὰρ Πυθαγόρας ὁ Σάμιος τηλικαύτην δόξαν ἔχων ἐπὶ φιλοσοφίᾳ, καταφανής ἐστιν ἐκ πολλῶν οὐ παρέργως ἁψάμενος μουσικῆς, ὅς γε καὶ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς οὐσίαν διὰ μουσικῆς ἀποφαίνει συγκειμένην. Τὸ δὲ ὅλον ἔοικεν ἡ παλαιὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων σοφία τῇ μουσικῇ μάλιστα εἶναι δεδεμένη... καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τῶν μὲν θεῶν Ἀπόλλωνα, τῶν δὲ ἡμιθέων Ὀρφέα, μουσικώτατον καὶ σοφώτατον ἔκρινον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς χρωμένους τῇ τέχνῃ ταύτῃ σοφιστὰς ἀπεκάλουν.</note> "For Pythagoras the Samian, who had such a great reputation for philosophy, is shown by many things to have taken up music not as a side-interest, for he even declared that the very essence of the universe was composed through music. In general, it seems that the ancient wisdom of the Greeks was especially bound to music; because of this, they judged Apollo among the gods, and Orpheus among the demigods, to be the most musical and the wisest, and they called all those who practiced this art 'sophists' <note>here meaning 'wise experts' rather than the later negative sense of 'word-twisters'</note>." 

Next, he says the Spartans <note>Lacedaemonians</note> made the greatest use of music, and tempered the austerity of their life and habits with its sweetness: <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ βίου σωφροσύνης καὶ αὐστηρίας μετέβαινον ἀσμένως ἐπὶ τὴν μουσικὴν, ἐχούσης τὸ κηλητικὸν τῆς ἐπιστήμης.</note> "For from the sobriety and austerity of their life, they gladly moved toward music, since the science of it possesses a certain charming power." (Athenaeus also attributes to music here the power of soothing the mind sweetly, just as Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> does here with the word "charmed.") "It was natural, therefore, that those listening should be filled with joy." Finally, he deplores in the same place—both in the preceding and following words—the unhappy...

Rittershusius compiles evidence from numerous classical authors to show that music was central to ancient Greek wisdom and even the structure of the universe.</summary>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...the degeneration of music from its former ancient excellence. <note>original Greek: Νῦν δὲ εἰκῆ καὶ ἀλόγως ἅπτονται τῆς μουσικῆς</note> "But now people take up music randomly and without reason," etc. Also: "After these events, disorder arose; nearly all the ancient customs grew old and this original purpose was destroyed. Base modes of music were introduced, through which those who used them gained softness instead of gentleness, and licentiousness and laxity instead of self-control. This will perhaps happen even more, and will be carried even further," etc.

I have transcribed this passage all the more willingly because it partly pertains to the customs of our own age, in which music is often forced to serve luxury, frivolity, and insolence—whereas **Pythagoras** and his followers used it for quite different purposes. It is no wonder, then, that our own republic has long been corrupted. For **Plato** taught that when musical modes change, the minds of men and the character of the state typically change as well. But since the Spartans <note>Lacedaemonians</note> have been mentioned, and how much zeal they devoted to music, let us relate a story by way of a "side-trip" <note>original Greek: ὁδοῦ παρέργως</note> about them, which is found in **Suidas** <note>The Suda, a famous 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note> under the proverb "After the Lesbian singer."

The Spartans were suffering from internal rebellion and discord. To be freed from this evil, they were warned by an oracle to summon a "Lesbian singer." Thus they called for **Terpander**, an excellent musician from Antissa. When they heard him singing at their public banquets or *common meals* <note>original Greek: συσσιτίοις — these were the 'syssitia,' mandatory communal meals for Spartan citizens designed to foster unity</note>, they bid farewell to their rebellion and internal discord and returned to harmony.

> "The Spartans used to call upon the Lesbian lyre-players first. For when their city was in a state of unrest, an oracle was given to send for a Lesbian singer; and they, having sent for **Terpander** of Antissa—who was in exile for a killing—listened to him in their common meals, and they were calmed." And again: "The Spartans, being in a state of civil war, sent for the musician Terpander from Lesbos, who harmonized their souls and ended the conflict," etc.

Let us conclude these remarks with that eulogy for music which **Athenaeus** cites from Theophilus the lyre-player in Book 14: "Music is a great and lasting treasure for all who have learned it and been educated. For it trains the character, and calms both the high-spirited and those with differing opinions." However, I believe we must by no means omit the illustrious passage by **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century philosopher who wrote on the works of Porphyry and Aristotle</note> on the power of music, which appears in his commentary on the *Five Voices* <note>A technical term for the 'Isagoge,' Porphyry's introduction to logic</note>, page 12 and following in the Venice edition, especially since a certain story regarding Pythagoras is touched upon there.

> "Music examines the harmonies of the strings; it also practices certain melodies that lull the passions of the soul, while awakening it toward virtue. That this is so is demonstrated by the traces still preserved, which are like the 'falling-away' or remnants of ancient music. For when we hear a trumpet, we are moved to a more spirited state; and for this reason..."

<meta>This page continues Rittershusius's discourse on the moral and spiritual power of music. Following the previous page's discussion on the Spartans using music to quell rebellion, this section focuses on the psychological effects of different musical modes—specifically the "relaxed" versus "disciplined" styles—and transitions into the Christian perspective of music as a weapon against spiritual evil.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY <note>Referring to the 3rd-century philosopher Porphyry of Tyre, who wrote a famous commentary on the musical theories of the mathematician Ptolemy.</note>

In times of war, the trumpet is employed to rouse the spirit. Yet when we listen to theatrical melodies, our souls are cast into a more dissolute and relaxed state. A story is told that **Pythagoras**, having seen a certain young man following a flute-girl who was playing a "relaxed" melody, ordered her to turn the flute and play a different way <note>In ancient music, "turning the flute" or changing the finger-holes could shift the mode from a wild, passionate one (like the Phrygian) to a more solemn, calming one (like the Spondaic).</note>. Once this was done, the young man’s lustful desire was brought to an end. Therefore, one should not disbelieve the claims made about divine music. For this reason, the divine **Plato** also commands that the youth should progress through both music and gymnastics: so that through music they may bring order and beauty to the soul, and through gymnastics, to the body.

But there is nothing among all things that can be stated more clearly or more divinely in praise and recommendation of music than the fact that it is effective even in driving away an evil demon, as is well known from the sacred history concerning **Saul** and **David** <note>Referring to 1 Samuel 16, where David’s harp-playing soothed King Saul’s "evil spirit."</note>. To this end, the author of this eight-line poem, written in praise of music, also looks:

> Hail, most holy music of the goddesses,
> Delight of the chaste mind and the virginal choir.
> You drive away cares and put to flight the ranks of the Furies:
> You grant the holy joys of the angelic choir.
> As a day is sad without the sun, and a night without a star,
> So without you, the life of men would be nothing but grief.
> No pleasure is more chaste than that which you offer the soul:
> Let anyone who hates your gifts perish.

Look into the reasons for this matter—namely, *why music should put an evil demon to flight*—which are learnedly investigated by **John of Salisbury** in Book 1, Chapter 6 of his *Policraticus* <note>A 12th-century work of political and ethical philosophy</note> and by **Francisco Vallés** in Chapter 28 of his *On Sacred Philosophy* <note>A 16th-century work exploring the scientific and medical realities behind biblical events</note>. However, let us attribute this power to the honor of David's lyre and his music, which, being divinely inspired <note>original Greek: θεόπνευστος (theopneustos)</note>, still resounds today in the Psalms. We include here, along with our Latin translation, ten Greek iambic verses found in the ancient Menology <note>A liturgical book of the Orthodox Church containing lives of the saints and verses for each day</note>, under this heading: *Verses upon the Divine David:*

> Be silent, **Orpheus**! **Hermes**, cast away your lyre!
> Let the tripod at **Delphi** sleep further in forgetfulness.
> For we have **David**, striking the lyre of the Spirit,
> Who makes clear the hidden mysteries of God.
> He recounts a multitude of ancient wonders,
> And moves all of creation to a hymn for its Creator.
> Saving everyone, he initiates them into the mysteries;
> He leads those who sin back toward repentance.
> Along with many other things, by revealing the Judge’s judgment,
> He teaches us to wash away the sins of the soul.

<meta>This page continues Rittershusius’s commentary on the philosophical and religious dimensions of music. Having previously discussed the "divine music" of David in contrast to the secular music of Greece, he now moves into a critique of ancient "incantations" (healing chants) and magical practices, contrasting them with Christian spiritual healing.</meta>

### NOTES BY CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS <note>Conrad Rittershusius (1560–1613) was a German jurist and classical scholar known for his extensive commentaries on Greek and Latin texts.</note>

Finally, the poet—whoever he may have been—adds this hexameter verse:
->The honey-sweet songs of David belong to a sacred harmony.<- <note>original Greek: Ἁρμονίης ἱερῆς μελιηδέα ᾄσματα Δαβίδ.</note>

**An interpretation of the preceding lines:**
> *Orpheus, be silent; Mercury, lay aside your lyre:*
> *Let the Delphic tripod <note>The three-legged stool used by the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi, here representing pagan prophecy.</note> be drowned in oblivion.*
> *For us, David, striking the lyre of the Spirit,*
> *Brings the hidden mysteries of God into the light:*
> *He tells of ancient miracles in great abundance:*
> *He moves all created things to celebrate their Creator:*
> *He writes and teaches what leads to salvation for all:*
> *He promotes the conversion of sinners:*
> *He marks the day and the final moment of the supreme Judge,*
> *And teaches how to wipe away the impure stain from the mind.*
> *The honey-sweet songs of David belong to a sacred harmony.*

**But enough of this digression.** Let us return to Malchus. <note>Malchus was the original name of the philosopher Porphyry of Tyre. Rittershusius is returning to the main subject of his commentary.</note>

**"And with incantations"**] Below, in section 33, he joins together **"incantations and magic."** Indeed, the method of healing through <term>epodae</term> <note>From the Greek 'epode', meaning a song or chant used for healing or magic.</note>—that is, incantations and magical whispers—is extremely ancient. It was already in use in the times of **Chiron the Thessalian** <note>The centaur Chiron was famous in mythology as a healer and the tutor of heroes.</note>, surnamed the Centaur (from whom the name of the herb <term>Centaurium</term> was given in botanical works), and **Aesculapius**, the son of Apollo <note>The god of medicine.</note>. The *Etymologicum Magnum* <note>A famous 12th-century Greek encyclopedia and dictionary.</note> says under the entry **Incantation**: *It must be known that healing through incantation is ancient.* **Homer** says: *He stopped the dark blood with an incantation.* <note>original: Παῦεν δ᾽ ἐπαοιδῇ αἷμα κελαινόν. From the Odyssey, referring to the healing of Odysseus’s wound.</note> (Notice how the blood is stayed by a chant.) **Pindar** also says regarding Aesculapius: *...tending some with soft incantations...* <note>original: τοὺς μὲν μαλακαῖς ἐπαοιδαῖς ἀμφέπων. This is found in Pindar’s 3rd Pythian Ode.</note> Pindar says the same in his 8th Nemean Ode: *By incantations, a man makes even labor painless.* **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century lexicographer.</note> defines "Incantators" as: *Mixers of drugs, sorcerers.* **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> writes: *An incantator is a woman who sings over sick children* (Hesychius says the same), *and incantation is sorcery.* **Polybius** <note>A Greek historian.</note> notes: *They tried every kind of incantation, sorcery, and amulet.* He also cites **Sophocles** there, who nonetheless denies that it is fitting for a wise doctor to use incantations when the ailment requires surgery: *It is not the part of a wise doctor to sing charms over a wound that needs the knife.* <note>original: Οὐ πρὸς ἰατροῦ σοφοῦ, θρηνεῖν ἐπῳδὰς πρὸς τομῶντι πήματι. From Sophocles' 'Ajax'.</note> Just as in many other matters, so too in this business of "incantations," we may use a parody of **Ovid** like this: *Ancient antiquity does not possess only things we should praise; vice resides even in the long-passing years.* <note>A play on Ovid's 'Fasti'. Rittershusius argues that just because a practice is old does not make it good.</note> For even if the method of healing through chants, magical incantations, and the amulets of certain characters is very ancient, it is not for that reason to be approved. I have always preferred the judgment of the most gravity-filled **John Chrysostom** <note>An influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>: that it is more desirable for a Christian to face both illness and death than to recover health or prolong life through the benefit of incantations—

<summary>This page concludes a poetic tribute to King David as the supreme musician of God and begins a scholarly critique of "incantations" (healing chants). Rittershusius argues that while healing through magic and chants is ancient, it is a pagan "vice" that should be rejected by Christians.</summary>

### ON PORPHYRY <note>Conrad Rittershusius is commenting on the biography of Pythagoras written by the Neoplatonist Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD).</note>

...of spells or amulets, which are called <term>periamma</term> <note>From the Greek word for "things tied around," referring to charms worn to ward off evil or disease.</note> by the Greeks. I have spoken more on this subject in my *Sacred Commentary Readings* and in the *Scholia on Quintus Serenus Sammonicus* <note>A Roman physician from the 2nd century AD.</note>, where he babbles some nonsense about curing a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day.</note> by means of the word **ABRACADABRA**, written on paper in a specific way and hung around the neck! See also the most learned physician and philosopher Francisco Vallés <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish physician known as "the Divine Vallés."</note> in his *Sacred Philosophy, chapter 3*, where he discusses at length the power of words and argues against the use of incantations.

**Understanding** <note>original Greek: Συνεὶς</note>] This should be restored to "perceiving" <note>original Greek: συνιεὶς</note>, as it appears also in Iamblichus <note>Another biographer of Pythagoras.</note>, section 65.

**According to these** <note>original Greek: Κατὰ ταύτας</note>] Iamblichus has "according to them" <note>original Greek: κατ' αὐτάς</note>, which seems to be the truer reading.

**Harmony of the stars** <note>original Greek: Ἀστέρων ἁρμονίας</note>] See Cicero in *The Dream of Scipio*, and Macrobius in his *Commentary* on that work. Likewise, see Pliny, book 2, chapter 21 and following, where he calls Pythagoras a man of sagacious mind and says he observed both the intervals of the stars and their musical concord. In chapter 8 of the same book, he writes that Pythagoras of Samos was the first to discover the nature of Lucifer <note>The "Light-Bringer," or the planet Venus appearing in the morning.</note> (which is also called Vesper, or Vesperugo, when it appears in the evening). He also adds a note on the time, namely around the forty-second Olympiad—that is, the year 142 from the founding of the city of Rome.

**Uttering an insatiable (or, as Arcerius prefers, an unwearying) melody**] Iamblichus writes of this harmony in chapter 15, section 65 of his *Life of Pythagoras*. It is a melody that one cannot be satisfied with hearing because of its immense sweetness. Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> explains this brilliantly in his book *On Dreams Sent by God*:
> *There are two things capable of praising and celebrating their Father with hymns: heaven and the mind. For man was granted this chief honor above all other animals—that he worships God. But heaven, through the perpetual concord of its movements, produces a most sweet harmony. If this could reach our ears, it would stir in us uncontrollable loves and an insane desire; spurred by this, we would forget the things necessary for our daily survival. We would not be fed by food and drink passed through the throat, but as candidates for immortality, we would be nourished by the divine songs of perfect music, etc.*
And soon after: *Therefore heaven, the archetypal musical instrument, seems to me to have been crafted for no other reason than that the hymns and praises of the Father of all things might be sung skillfully and musically, etc.*

**Having understood the universal [harmony] of the spheres, etc.** <note>original Greek: Συνεὶς τῆς καθολικῆς τῶν σφαιρῶν</note>] Read "perceiving." Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of celestial things, to which he [Pythagoras] applied himself intensely...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSII

Since Pythagoras was so devoted to the study of the stars and the heavens, it is worth the effort to add the sonorous verses of Christodorus of Thebes <note>A Greek poet of the 5th–6th century AD known for describing statues in the gymnasium of Zeuxippus.</note>, which appear in the 5th book of the *Greek Anthology* under the title *On Pythagoras*; on page 277 of my Aldine edition <note>The Aldine Press was a famous Venetian printing house known for its editions of Greek and Latin classics.</note>:

->It was fitting for Pythagoras to be the wise Samian; but in Olympus<-
->He seemed to dwell, and his bronze nature was forced,<-
->Overflowing with intellectual melodies. For as I think,<-
->He measured the heaven with pure eyes alone.<-
<note>These verses describe a statue of Pythagoras; the "bronze nature" refers to the material of the statue, which the poet suggests is almost overwhelmed by the "melodies" of the philosopher's mind.</note>

**There was a certain man** <note>original Greek: Ἦν δέ τις</note>] The first two of these verses by Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who was a follower of Pythagorean ideas.</note>, composed in praise of his master Pythagoras, are also found in Diogenes Laërtius's *Life of Empedocles*, page 602. I do not think the remaining four verses are found anywhere else except in Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Phoenician name of Porphyry, the author of the biography being commented upon.</note> and Iamblichus, chapter 15. However, in those texts, they are wretchedly distorted, and must be restored from this source.

**Wealth of the mind** <note>original Greek: Πραπίδων πλοῦτον. The word "prapides" literally refers to the diaphragm or midriff, considered by the ancients to be the seat of the mental faculties.</note>] Similarly, the same Empedocles says in another poem, quoted by Clement of Alexandria in the fifth book of his *Miscellanies*:

->Blessed is he who has acquired the wealth of divine thoughts,<-
->But wretched is he whose mind is occupied with a dark opinion about the gods.<-

In the same vein, Solon <note>An Athenian statesman and poet, one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> spoke of the "wealth of virtue" in the verses recorded by Plutarch in his *Life of Solon*. Indeed, the truth is this: the riches of the soul—that is, virtue and learning—far surpass all external riches, and even all the gold found above or beneath the earth, as Plato says. Regarding this best and most excellent kind of wealth, I will add the verses of Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician.</note> found in the first book of the *Anthology*, title 67, because I have a correction and a warning to offer regarding them:

->The wealth of the soul is the only true wealth,<-
->But other things have more harm than the possessions themselves.<-

In this passage, instead of the word for "her/it" <note>original Greek: αὐτὴν</note>, I believe we should read the word for "harm" or "bane" <note>original Greek: ἄτην (atēn)</note>, rather than the reading of Henri Estienne <note>A famous 16th-century scholar and printer, also known as Henricus Stephanus.</note>, who refers the word back to the "soul." For the poet means this: other possessions—namely, external riches—bring much greater harm than benefit. Other "goods" or external resources, which are commonly called the gifts of fortune, bring almost more injury than utility to their owners. As for the six-line poem that follows immediately in the *Anthology*, it seems to me to constitute a new and separate epigram, and has been poorly joined to the preceding two-line verse. In the first epigram, the poet completed one thought: namely, what true riches are—those of the soul or mind—adding a reason based on contrast: because the "goods" of fortune harm many more people than they help. There follows a second and distinct epigram...

# ON PORPHYRY

...of this argument: Who should rightfully be called wealthy? Clearly, it is not the man who, always sitting at his counting-tables, piles up one set of riches upon another and heaps them together, like bees packing honey into their cells more for the use of others than for their own. Rather, it is the man who knows how to use his resources correctly, to whom the gods have given wealth and the art of enjoyment, to speak along with Horace <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace, *Epistles* 1.4.7: "The gods gave you wealth and the art of enjoyment."</note>. It also moves me and confirms me in this opinion that I see no article <note>original Greek: ἄρθρον (arthron)</note> by which the third verse is joined to the preceding ones. For this reason, I think this Epigram is new and distinct from the one above:

> *It is right to call him a man of many possessions and wealthy,*
> *Who is able to use his good things.*
> *But if someone wastes away over his counting-stones, ever*
> *Striving to heap one wealth upon another;*
> *He will labor like a bee in many-holed hives,*
> *While others will harvest the honey.*
<note>This Greek epigram, often attributed to Lucian of Samosata, uses the "bee" metaphor to mock the miser who hoards for his heirs.</note>

Where I observe: this comparison of the miser with bees, who make honey not for themselves but for others, seems to have been taken by Lucian from Democritus <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher known as the "laughing philosopher."</note>. For thus says he in Stobaeus's <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors.</note> chapter *On Frugality*: "Misers have the fate of a bee; they work as if they are going to live forever." But what forbids me from adding here some Latin elaborations of these excellent poems? In our youth, we used to compete with these and with Sleidanus’s version <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a famous humanist historian and translator.</note> among ourselves as close friends and fellow students <note>original Greek: συμφοιτηταὶ (symphoitētai)</note>—myself and Solomon Rysinius Pantherus <note>Solomon Rysinius (Solomon Rysiński, c. 1560–1625) was a Polish-Lithuanian scholar and paremiologist.</note>, who is now a counselor and tutor to the most Illustrious Prince, Lord Christopher Radziwiłł <note>A member of the powerful Radziwiłł family of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.</note>. Sleidanus, therefore, translated it thus:

> *Noble is the treasure of the mind, noble is he,*
> *Whoever shall place his wealth in that final part.*
> *Truly rich will he be, who among faithful friends*
> *Generously pours out the goods acquired by labor.*
> *But whoever defrauds his own spirit, and piles up wealth*
> *Into a grasping jar, so that he may count it,*
> *Just like a bee, he will fill his little vessels in vain with greedy zeal,*
> *Until soon the drone plunders the honeycombs.*

**Solomon Rysinius Pantherus** translated it in a double manner; thus:

->**I.**<-

> *The riches of the mind alone are true and perennial riches:*
> *Other forms of wealth hold a great deal of ruin.*
> *But the man powerful in many resources and much metal,*
> *I call him rich who himself uses the goods he has acquired.*

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

*But he who wastes away by counting with anxious little stones,* <note>original: "sollicitis... lapillis." The "little stones" or "calculi" were used on a counting board to calculate wealth.</note>
*Ever striving to heap riches upon riches:*
*He, like an Attic bee in many-holed hives,*
*Toils away, leaving the honey to be harvested by others.*

### II.

*Only the treasures of the mind are worthy of the name of treasures:*
*Alas, how much harm the rest bring with them!*
*But he alone deserves the praise of both Pelops and Midas,* <note>Pelops and Midas were legendary figures of Greek myth famous for their immense—and sometimes cursed—wealth.</note>
*Who has the strength to use his own riches.*
*But he who is consumed by the wasting sickness of counting talents,* <note>A "talent" was a large unit of weight and currency in the ancient world.</note>
*And anxiously adds one set of riches to another:*
*He is tormented like a bee, who leaves his honey*
*To be gathered by others in many-holed hives.*

I thus varied the poetic style <note>original: "metricum stylum." Rittershusius is demonstrating his skill at "variatio," or rewriting the same idea in different Latin poetic meters.</note> four times:

### I.

*True wealth is situated in the mind. For the goods of the common crowd*
*Are trifles, and often harmful to their masters.*
*He is rightly called wealthy who has learned how to use*
*Riches, and does not wickedly condemn wealth to the chest.* <note>That is, he does not simply lock his money away in a strongbox where it serves no purpose.</note>
*He who always grows thin by calculating his accounts,*
*And hastens to heap riches upon riches—*
*To whom shall I compare this man? Unless to the bee, who stores up*
*Honey in hives for the use of mortals, and not for himself.*

### II.

*No possession is nobler than the riches of the mind:*
*For other goods always contain more of evil.*
*I would call this man truly rich, and rightly blessed:*
*He who well knows how to make his riches useful.*
*But the wretch, if he wastes away over his coins, and the more gold*
*He has, the more he busies himself in seeking more,*
*He is like the busy bee, who labors in making honey:*
*Soon to have his sweet honeycombs plundered by another.*

### III.

*The riches of the mind are the truest riches: but other goods*
*Often bring more of harm than of solid fruit.*
*This man deserves to be called truly opulent and wealthy,*
*He who knows how to have a good use for his riches.*
*But he who is consumed only by the counting of gold,*
*And always craves to add something to what he has gained;*
*Like the flower-gathering bee, a vain labor occupies him,*
*Who fills the cells with honey for others, not for himself.*
