# ON PORPHYRY

## IV.

->*The solitary mind possesses true wealth;*<-
->*The riches of the crowd often bring heavy loss.*<-
->*For he is truly worthy of the name "wealthy"*<-
->*Who puts good things to honorable use.*<-
->*But he who wastes away in counting his coins,*<-
->*Hurrying to pile new riches upon the old,*<-
->*I would say he is like the bees, who in their many-holed*<-
->*Hives, make honey for others, and not for themselves.*<-

But enough of this: I thought this digression would not be unpleasant for the reader.

<margin>31</margin> **Emphatic** <note>original: "᾿Εμφατικὰ"</note>] Thus it appears in our Manuscript. But in Iamblichus, at the end of chapter 15, it is read as "expressive" <note>original: "ἐμφαντικὰ"</note>.

**According to the inhabitants of the opposite earth** <note>original: "Κατὰ τοὺς ἀντίχθονας"</note>] By a more common word, these are called the **Antipodes** <note>From the Greek for "opposite feet," referring to people living on the other side of the globe.</note>. Diogenes Laërtius says in his *Life of Pythagoras*: "There are also Antipodes; and what is 'down' for us is 'up' for them." Nevertheless, there was no lack of very distinguished men among the teachers of the church who utterly denied that the Antipodes existed: such as St. Augustine and Lactantius Firmianus. The following are the words of Lactantius from Book 3 of *On False Wisdom*, chapter 24: *“What of those who think there are Antipodes opposite our footsteps? Are they saying anything? Or is anyone so foolish as to believe there are men whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that the things which lie on the ground here, there hang upside down? That crops and trees grow downward? That rain, snow, and hail fall upward onto the earth?”* etc. Then, after he examined the reasons of those who, following the doctrine of the spheres, establish the existence of Antipodes (whom he does not hesitate to say fall into many ridiculous things and defend monstrosities), he finally adds this <term>epiphonema</term> <note>A striking concluding sentence or "finishing touch" to an argument.</note>: *“Thus the roundness of the heavens invented these hanging Antipodes.”* And toward the end of the chapter: *“But I (he says) could prove by many arguments that it is in no way possible for the sky to be lower than the earth,”* etc.

In Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* Book V, I find that among the Pythagoreans, heaven itself was called "Antichthon" <note>Literally "Counter-Earth."</note>: *The Pythagoreans call the heaven the counter-earth.*

**Comparison** <note>original: "Σύγκρισιν"</note>] I think it should be read as "blending" or "tempering" <note>original: "σύγκρασιν."</note>.

<margin>32</margin> **To avoid the company of the many** <note>original: "᾿Εκτρέπεσθαι τὰς μετὰ τῶν πολλῶν ὁμιλίας"</note>] Pythagoras also warned that the commerce of the common crowd must be fled in that symbolic precept: *Do not walk on the highways* <note>original: "Τὰς λεωφόρους μὴ βαδίζειν." This was a "symbol," a metaphorical rule meant to encourage independent thinking over following the herd.</note>; of which we shall speak below. The reason is found in the heroic verses of Cleanthes in Clement of Alexandria.

**Tuning his soul to the lyre** <note>original: "῾Αρμοζόμενος πρὸς λύραν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν"</note>] Regarding this custom of Pythagoras in settling his mind to tranquility—

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...[tranquill]ity through the song of the lyre, and concerning the praises and benefits of music, besides those things I mentioned above, these observations from Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note>, chapter 28, will also be useful: “He also believed that music contributes greatly to health, if one uses it in the proper ways.” <note>original: "Ὑπελάμβανε δὲ καὶ τὴν μουσικὴν μεγάλα συμβάλλεσθαι πρὸς ὑγείαν, ἄν τις αὐτῇ χρῆται κατὰ τοὺς προσήκοντας τρόπους."</note> The same author says in chapter 25—and in almost as many words in chapter 32: “There were certain melodies among them composed for the passions of the soul, for despondency and distress, which were designed to be most helpful. And again, others for anger and for wrath, through which, by intensifying or relaxing them to a moderate degree, they achieved a balance suited to courage.” <note>original: "Ἦν δέ τινα μέλη παρ’ αὐτοῖς πρὸς τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς πάθη πεποιημένα, πρός τε ἀθυμίας καὶ δηγμοὺς, ἃ δὴ βοηθητικώτατα ἐπινενόητο. Καὶ πάλιν αὖ ἕτερα πρὸς τε τὰς ὀργὰς, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θυμοὺς, δι’ ὧν ἐπιτείνοντες αὐτὰ καὶ ἀνιέντες ἄχρι τοῦ μετρίου σύμμετρα πρὸς ἀνδρείαν ἀπειργάζοντο."</note> Again, the same Iamblichus at the end of the said chapter 25 writes: “In this way, Pythagoras established the correction of human character and lives through music as something extremely beneficial.” <note>original: "Οὕτω μὲν οὖν πολυωφελεστάτην κατεστήσατο Πυθαγόρας τὴν διὰ τῆς μουσικῆς τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ἠθῶν τε καὶ βίων ἐπανόρθωσιν."</note> One should note in passing a correction to the text of Iamblichus in that same chapter 25: where it is published as “toward every variation of such a soul,” <note>original: "Καὶ πρὸς πᾶσαν παραλλαγὴν τοιαύτης ψυχῆς"</note> it should be read as “such a variation.” <note>original: "τοιαύτην"</note> Even the most learned geographical writer, Strabo, did not remain silent about this utility of music; his words in Book 10 are: “And for this reason Plato, and even earlier the Pythagoreans, called philosophy 'music'; and they say that the universe is composed according to harmony, assuming that everything musical is the work of the gods. Thus, they also assign the formation of character to music, since everything that corrects the mind is close to the gods.” <note>original: "Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μουσικὴν ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Πλάτων, καὶ ἔτι πρότερον οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι, τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, καὶ καθ’ ἁρμονίαν τὸν κόσμον συνεστάναι φασὶ, πᾶν τὸ μουσικὸν θεῶν ἔργον ὑπολαμβάνοντες. οὕτω δὲ καὶ τὴν τῶν ἠθῶν κατασκευὴν τῇ μουσικῇ προσνέμουσιν, ὡς πᾶν τὸ ἐπανορθωτικὸν τοῦ νοῦ τοῖς θεοῖς ἐγγὺς ὄν."</note>

**Homer and Hesiod]** Iamblichus testifies to this same thing in the aforementioned chapter 25, where a correction should be made: “with selected phrases.” <note>original: "λέξεσιν ἐξειλεγμέναις"</note> It is truly strange that Pythagoras did not shrink from the poetry of Homer and Hesiod, since he boasted that he had seen the souls of those authors being tortured in the underworld because they invented such absurd fables about the gods. Specifically, he claimed that Hesiod’s soul was bound to a bronze pillar and emitted a certain wretched screeching, while Homer’s soul was hung from a tree and surrounded by serpents. Unless, perhaps, someone might argue that Pythagoras had not yet penetrated to the underworld at the time when he valued their poems so highly as to sing them to the lyre; but that after returning to the upper air, he abstained from them. See Diogenes Laërtius in his *Life of Pythagoras*, page 580, where the correction by the illustrious Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned Renaissance classical scholar.</note> is most true: “in exchange for the things they said about the gods.” <note>original: "ἀνθ’ ὧν εἶπον περὶ θεῶν"</note>

**He performed certain dances]** <note>original: "Ὀρχήσεις δέ τινας ὑπωρχεῖτο"</note> Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> discusses the various types and benefits of dances most learnedly in Book 10, which is worth looking into.

**Enviously]** <note>original: "Ἐπιφθόνως"</note> Perhaps it should read “unstintingly” <note>original: "ἀφθόνως"</note>, that is, copiously, in great number, etc. In this place, there are passages clearly identical to Malchus <note>The original name of Porphyry.</note>, which Cyril relates from Porphyry's book *On Pythagoras* in Book 3 *Against Julian*, translated into Latin here by Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius, a leader of the Protestant Reformation in Basel.</note>.

# ON PORPHYRY.

Nor did he himself take his walks with many people, but with two or three companions he sought out the most pleasant and especially the most silent places in temples or groves. He loved his friends greatly, being the first to say that among friends all things are held in common: and that a friend is a second self. And while he associated with those who were healthy, he also took care of the bodies of those who were suffering: and he also consoled languishing souls, as we have said—the former <note>original: "haec quidem" referring to bodies</note> by means of incantations and magic; the latter <note>original: "illas autem" referring to souls</note> by music, etc. It seems the translator read, "the former" (meaning <term>bodies</term>) and "the latter" (meaning <term>souls</term>). For more on Porphyry and Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Syrian name of Porphyry, meaning "king."</note>, see our notes above.

**He loved his friends exceedingly**] Diogenes Laertius <note>An 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note>, book 8, page 577, line 33, concerning the same Pythagoras: "He was a capable maker of friendship." <note>original: "Ἱκανὸς ἦν φιλίας ἐργάτης."</note> Iamblichus, book 1, chapter 33: "Pythagoras handed down the practice of friendship most clearly of all to everyone." <note>original: "Φιλίας δὲ διαφανέστατα πάντων πρὸς ἅπαντας Πυθαγόρας παρέδωκε."</note> See that whole truly remarkable chapter. But it should be noted here that the Pythagoreans cultivated friendship only among themselves, not with outsiders: as will be explained more fully below. Furthermore, for preserving friendship safe and sound <note>original: "sartam tectam," a Latin legal idiom for a building kept in good repair.</note> among themselves, that institution of which Plutarch writes in his commentary *On Having Many Friends* <note>original: "περὶ πολυφιλίας"</note> was most useful. For the Pythagoreans were accustomed, if perhaps some offense or quarrel had arisen between them during the day due to anger, to return to each other’s grace before the setting of the sun, by extending their right hands and adding mutual greetings. The words of Plutarch are these: "Then they should imitate the Pythagoreans, who, though not related by birth but sharing in a common reason, if they were ever led into insults by anger, before the sun went down, they would join right hands, greet one another, and be reconciled." <note>original: "Εἶτα μιμεῖσθαι τοὺς Πυθαγορικοὺς..."</note> This is very much in accord with the apostolic precept in Ephesians 4:26: "Be angry, and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down on your wrath." <note>original: "Ὀργίζεσθε, καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε. Ὁ ἥλιος μὴ ἐπιδυέτω ἐπὶ τῷ παροργισμῷ ὑμῶν."</note>

**Friends’ things are to be in common**] Diogenes Laertius, page 573: "He was the first to say (as Timaeus says) that friends' things are common; and that friendship is equality." <note>original: "Εἶπέ τε πρῶτος... κοινὰ τὰ φίλων εἶναι· καὶ, φιλίαν ἰσότητα."</note> And on page 587: "Friendship is a harmonious equality." <note>original: "φιλίαν τε εἶναι ἐναρμόνιον ἰσότητα."</note> So too Aristotle in book 9 of the *Ethics*, chapter 8, in a heap of other proverbs which are circulated in common speech concerning friendship, also records these two just mentioned: "And all the proverbs agree; such as, 'One soul'; and 'Friends' things are common'; and 'Friendship is equality'; and 'The knee is closer than the shin.'" <note>original: "Καὶ αἱ παροιμίαι δὲ πᾶσαι ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν..."</note> From which he says it can be inferred "that each person is most a friend to himself; and one must indeed love oneself most." <note>original: "ὅτι μάλιστα φίλος ἕκαστος ἑαυτῷ· καὶ φιλητέον δὴ μάλιστα ἑαυτόν."</note> Saint Jerome in his *Apology against Rufinus*: "Those are also Pythagorean precepts: *Among friends all things are common; and, A friend is a second self.*" See also Iamblichus, chapter 19. Euripides too expresses the same sentiment...

### NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSIUS

on the community of all things which exists among friends, he wove into his most "philosophical" <note>original Greek: φιλοσοφωτάταις (philosophōtatais)</note> tragedies more than once: as in *Orestes*: **For the things of friends are common.** <note>original Greek: Κοινὰ γὰρ τὰ τῶν φίλων (Koina gar ta tōn philōn)</note> And in *Andromache*:

> For friends have nothing of their own, those who
> Are rightly friends, but their possessions are common.

Terence <note>A Roman playwright of the 2nd century BCE.</note> (or he who is believed to have been Laelius) held the same in high regard, as appears from *The Brothers* <note>Latin: *Adelphi*</note> Act 5, Scene 9, line 3, where Micio says: *This is indeed an old saying, that all things are common among friends.* Yet know that there are those who abuse this most beautiful saying: such as that Candidus in Martial's <note>A Roman poet known for his satirical epigrams.</note> second book, Epigram 43, whom the poet snubbed thus:

> *Candidus, "friends' things are common," these are all yours, Candidus,* <note>original: "Candide, Κοινὰ φίλων [Koina philōn], haec sunt tua, Candide, πάντα [panta]"—mixing Latin and Greek.</note>
> *Which you grandly proclaim night and day,*

Then, after he had shown by a sixfold contrast the great and most overflowing abundance of that man, but his own slenderness and poverty, at the end he cries out concerning the unworthiness of the matter—that he does everything contrary to that Pythagorean dogma and (as the <term>pragmatici</term> <note>Legal experts or practitioners of the law.</note> say) acts in a way contrary to his protestation, not bestowing even a farthing upon a friend:

> *From such great wealth to an old and faithful companion*
> *You give nothing: and yet you say, Candidus, "friends' things are common"?*

For these lines must be read as a question, as if to say: are you not ashamed of your words, which your deeds contradict?

**And a friend is another self]** <note>original Greek: Τὸν δὲ φίλον ἄλλον ἑαυτὸν (Ton de philon allon heauton)</note> A friend was first called "another self" by Pythagoras. Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> in his commentary on the *Handbook* of Epictetus, page 63 of the Venice edition, where he speaks on the duty of friends toward one another: *One should consider nothing as one's own that does not belong even more to our friends; and one should gladly yield the first place, as if yielding to oneself, if indeed a friend is "another I" according to the ancient saying.* Thus that which was related a little earlier from Aristotle and Laërtius—that *friendship is equality*—the same Simplicius testifies in the said commentary on page 47 to be Pythagorean. There, after he taught that those who do not seek the goods of the rational soul (by which a human is a human) but follow other desires are both ungrateful and unequal, he adds this, explaining both parts: *They are unequal, because they are also friendless. For friendship is equality, as the Pythagoreans used to say, etc.* Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek lexicon and encyclopedia.</note> says: *Equality is friendship; this is a maxim showing that equality maintains friendship.*

**Songs also for diseases of bodies]** <note>original Greek: Μέλη καὶ πρὸς νόσους σωμάτων (Melē kai pros nosous sōmatōn)</note> Thus Athenaeus <note>A 3rd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> in book 14 writes, from the book of Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> *On Enthusiasm*, that sciatic pains...

### ON PORPHYRY

[...Physi]cians <note>The original text is cut off, likely beginning with "Physicos" or "Medicos."</note> [claim that] through the benefit of musical harmony, the pains of the soul are relieved:
"That music also heals diseases, Theophrastus recorded in his work *On Inspiration*, saying that those suffering from sciatica remain free of pain if one plays the flute over the affected area in the Phrygian mode." <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι δὲ καὶ νόσους ἰᾶται μουσικὴ..." The Phrygian mode was an ancient musical scale often associated with intense emotion or religious excitement.</note> Thus, those who have been bitten by the tarantula, a small venomous creature, are healed by dancing when musical modes are applied: on this matter, see the work of the Illustrious and most Distinguished Man, Master Philippus Camerarius, *Historical Meditations*, Century 2, chapter 18, and Century 3, chapter 97, where more is said on the power of music. <note>Tarantism was a historical phenomenon where victims of spider bites were said to dance uncontrollably to music to "sweat out" the venom.</note>

**And he soothed angers]** <note>Referring to Porphyry's description of Pythagoras's character.</note> Thus we have heard that Clinias the Pythagorean, a man of harsh manners and a quick temper, if ever he was stirred to anger, used to take up his lyre and play; to those asking the reason for this, he would reply that he was thus becoming mild. Athenaeus in Book XIV, citing the historian Chamaeleon of Pontus: "Clinias the Pythagorean, distinguished in both his life and character, if it ever happened that he was harsh due to anger, would take up his lyre and play the cithara; and to those who inquired the cause, he would say, 'I am being soothed.'" <note>original Greek: Πραΰνομαι (Praünomai)</note> Thus in Homer, Achilles grows mild by the song of the cithara when he had been inflamed with anger.

<margin>34</margin>
**Regarding his diet]** <note>Continuing the commentary on Pythagoras's lifestyle.</note> Regarding the frugal diet or way of living used by Pythagoras, there is an excellent passage in Athenaeus, Book X, where he praises Lycon of Iasus in his book *On Pythagoras*: "And Pythagoras of Samos used a moderate amount of food, as Lycon of Iasus records in his work *On Pythagoras*. But he did not abstain from living creatures <note>i.e., meat; this was a point of historical debate among ancient authors</note>, as Aristoxenus has said." And shortly after: "Pythagoras was also a small drinker and lived most simply, so that he was often satisfied with honey alone. Similar things are recorded about Aristides, Epaminondas, Phocion, and Phormion, the generals." To this belongs the fact that the Pythagoreans especially applied themselves to that part of medicine called <term>dietetics</term> <note>original Greek: διαιτητικὴ (diaitētikē), the study of health through diet and lifestyle</note>, which deals with an accurate regimen of living, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> testifies concerning them in more than one place. See him in chapter 29, number 136, and chapter 34, number 244. I shall add his very words, not only so that we may learn from them the methods of Pythagorean medicine, but also so that certain variations in the reading or emendations may be noted in Iamblichus, which we observed by comparing the parallel passages in numbers 163 and 244. "Of medicine, they say they especially approve of the dietetic branch, and are most accurate in this, and try first to understand the signs of symmetry <note>balance or proportion</note> in drinks (Number 163 has 'labors' <note>original: πόνων (ponōn)</note>, which is perhaps more correct) and foods and rest. Then, regarding the very preparation of the things consumed (read: 'things consumed' <note>original: προσφερομένων (prospheromenōn)</note>), they were perhaps the first to attempt..."

...the same expression, since no change occurred in the mind by which it is formed, etc. Simplicius <note>A 6th-century philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists.</note> on page 81. b. regarding that precept of Epictetus <note>A Stoic philosopher who taught that we should focus on what is within our control.</note> in which he wishes everyone to establish for themselves a certain character and model which they should constantly maintain throughout their whole life, whether living alone or interacting with others, brings forward the same Socratic example: "This means, I think, that one must always, as far as possible, remain in a state of identity, living one's own life always as one and the same, and not flowing along like the Euripus <note>original Greek: "Εὐρίπου δίκην." The Euripus is a strait in Greece famous for its violent and frequently reversing currents, used here as a metaphor for an unstable person.</note> according to the various things that happen from the outside. It was said, then, that Socrates was always seen in the same state of composure, and seemed to be moved neither by pleasures nor by what seemed painful, because he lived his own life always as one and the same. And perhaps this is the 'one character' which one must arrange and define, which he indicated briefly by saying that one must guard the same self, whether being by oneself or meeting with other people." <note>original: "Τοῦτο δὲ, οἶμαι, σημαίνει..."</note> To this is related, in a way, what is written about Socrates using the same clothes in both summer and winter: a fact which Antiphon the Sophist <note>A contemporary and rival of Socrates.</note> once threw at him as a reproach in the hearing of his students, so that he might alienate them and draw them away from him. This is found in Xenophon, Book I of the *Memorabilia*: <note>original: "Apomnemoneumatum."</note> "You eat the poorest food and drink the poorest beverages, and you are dressed in a cloak that is not only poor, but the same one in both summer and winter, and you go through life without sandals and without a tunic." <note>original: "Σιτία τε σιτῇ..."</note> Responding to him, Socrates says that the fewer things one needs, the closer one is to the divine. The same Simplicius, in his commentary on the *Enchiridion* <note>The "Handbook" of Epictetus's teachings.</note> of Epictetus, page 84, says: "It is a blessed thing to have been so nourished and accustomed from the beginning; for in this way a natural, simple, and unadorned diet will be tolerable, beneficial, and pleasant even to the body; and it is likewise good to have such a habit regarding clothing. For Socrates was said to use the same garments in both summer and winter." <note>original: "Μακάριον καὶ τὸ ἐξαρχῆς..."</note>

...so that their minds would not become more dull, but also so that men might strive rather to use foods that are more easily obtained, and practice temperance; then, so that they might become gentler toward their fellow kin. For he who is touched by compassion toward beasts will certainly be much more merciful and gentle toward men: as is also found in Solomon <note>Referring to Proverbs 12:10: "The righteous man has regard for the life of his beast."</note> and Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who integrated Greek philosophy with biblical exegesis.</note>. Plutarch observes this in his *Commentary*, *Whether animals are more intelligent* <note>original Greek: "πότερα τῶν ζώων φρονιμώτερα," a work also known as *On the Cleverness of Animals*.</note>, writing these things: "Just as, on the other hand, the Pythagoreans made kindness toward beasts a practice leading toward love for mankind and pity. For habit is a powerful thing, and when it gradually settles into our passions, it leads a man far forward." <note>original Greek: "Ὥσπερ αὖ πάλιν οἱ Πυθαγορικοὶ..."</note> And the same author in the *Commentary on how to profit from one's enemies*: "Pythagoras did rightly when, by training people to abstain from cruelty and greed toward irrational animals, he discouraged bird-catchers, and by buying up the fisherman's haul, he ordered them to release the fish, and he forbade the killing of any domesticated animal," <note>original Greek: "Ὀρθῶς δ' ὁ Πυθαγόρας..."</note> etc.

In order that Pythagoras might more easily achieve what he wanted, he tried to persuade men that human souls sometimes pass even into the bodies of beasts, and therefore they are held and joined with us by a common law. *Diogenes Laertius* <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note>, page 575: "For he forbade killing, let alone touching animals, since they have a soul in common with us. And this indeed was the pretext." <note>original Greek: "Τοῦτον γὰρ καὶ τὸ φονεύειν..."</note> (Ambrogio <note>Ambrogio Traversari, a 15th-century monk and translator.</note> incorrectly translates this as *fabulous*; it should rather be translated: *and this indeed was the pretext.*) "But the truth is that he forbade touching living creatures while training and habituating men toward an easy way of life, so that their food would be easy for them to obtain, as they took it uncooked and drank plain water."

*Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous "Life of Pythagoras."</note>, chapter 24: "Furthermore, he also commanded the lawmakers of the states <note>The Greek says "political ones," but the author prefers "constitutions" or "states" (πολιτειῶν).</note> to abstain from living creatures. For since they wished to act with the highest justice <note>reading "highest" (ἄκρως) instead of "top" (ἄκρους)</note>, they surely ought not <note>Corrected by D. Heraldus <note>Desiderius Heraldus, a 17th-century French scholar.</note></note> to do any injustice to kindred animals. For how could they persuade others to act justly if they themselves were caught in a greed toward their kin through the consumption of animals? For these animals, through the fellowship of life and the same elements, and the mixture composed from these things, are joined to us as if by a brotherhood." <note>original Greek: "Ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν πολιτικῶν..."</note> *Behold*, says Iamblichus, *because animals participate with us in both life and the same elements, therefore a certain right of brotherhood, as it were, exists between us and them; and accordingly, a certain justice must also be practiced toward them.* The same Iamblichus, chapter 30: "And he legislated the abstinence from living creatures" (the punctuation should be corrected thus, and accordingly the Latin translation as well, which is of no value there) "for many other reasons, and so that they might make peace..." <note>The original Greek ends mid-word: "ἐπιτή-", likely "suitable" (ἐπιτήδειοι).</note>

...training <note>The Greek text begins with the end of the word *paideuma*, meaning "instruction" or "training."</note>. For those who are accustomed to loathe the slaughter of animals as something unlawful and contrary <note>original Greek: "παρὰ (που περὶ) φύσιν," meaning "contrary to (or perhaps 'concerning') nature."</note> to nature, will consider it much more impious to kill a human being, and would no longer wage war. For war is the provider and lawgiver of slaughter. **And again in chapter 31: It is decreed that all disproportionate things are to be cut away with fire and iron. To the same category belongs abstinence from all living things, and furthermore from certain intemperate foods, etc.** <note>original Greek: "Πυρὶ καὶ σιδήρῳ τὰ ἀσύμμετρα πάντα ἀποκόπτειν..." This is a common Pythagorean maxim regarding the purging of excess from the body and soul.</note> **Clement of Alexandria dares to say even more in the *Miscellanies* <term>Stromata</term>, book 2, page 172.** It seems to him that Pythagoras derived that gentleness toward irrational animals from the divine law itself; for while the Law forbids the offspring to be snatched from the mother for sacrifice within the first seven days of birth, it intended to instill a mild disposition in humans toward other humans, beginning with that very gentleness which it commands to be exercised toward beasts. I will provide the words of the most learned writer themselves, so that I may at the same time remove an error from them: **"And it seems to me that Pythagoras also received his gentleness toward irrational animals from the Law. For instance, <note>Rittershusius suggests the Greek should read "ὃς αὐτίκα" (who for instance) or "αὐτίκα γὰρ" (for instance).</note> regarding the young born among the flocks, the goats, and the cattle, the Law forbade their immediate enjoyment, even under the pretext of sacrifice, for the sake of the parents and mothers, thereby nursing humanity in man from the level of irrational animals upward, etc."** <note>original Greek: "Ἐμοὶ δὲ δοκεῖ καὶ Πυθαγόρας τὸ ἥμερον..." Clement is arguing that Greek philosophy borrowed its best ideas from Moses.</note> **Where, instead of "from parents" <note>original Greek: "ἐκ γονέων"</note>, I think it should be read as a single word: "offspring" <note>original Greek: "ἐκγόνων"</note>. For this is what Clement means: that the Lawgiver had regard for both the young themselves (which are the *ekgona*) and their mothers. The same Clement, in *The Tutor* <term>Paedagogus</term>, book 2, page 63, gives a physical reason for that abstinence from the flesh of animals; namely, because the vapors ascending from the eating of meat cast a cloud over the soul.** **"Therefore, it is good not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, as he himself (Paul) <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Romans 14:21.</note> and the followers of Pythagoras agree. For this is more like a wild beast; and the exhalation from them, being more turbid, obscures the soul."** <note>original Greek: "Καλὸν μὲν οὖν τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν κρέα..."</note> **Here I do not understand what that word "wild beast" <note>original Greek: "θηρίον"</note> is doing; perhaps it should be read as "of wild beasts" <note>original Greek: "θηρίων" or "θηρίου"</note>. See similar views in Plutarch in his *Commentary on the Eating of Flesh*. In another place, however, the same Clement rebukes the false hypothesis of Pythagoras and his "irrational reason," namely the idea that one should abstain from eating living things because of the migration <term>metendesis</term> of human souls into the bodies of beasts.** **"If any of the righteous does not burden the soul with the ingestion of meat, he uses a certain reasonable argument—not like Pythagoras and his followers, who dream of the reincarnation <note>original Greek: "μετένδεσιν," literally a 're-clothing' or 'transmigration'</note> of the soul, etc."** **In place of a brilliant commentary on these words of Clement, we can apply what Origen writes in Book IV of *Against Celsus*, page 271 of the Augsburg edition, where he shows the distinction between Christians who sometimes abstain from meat, and between...**

Here, the focus shifts to the theological differences between Pythagorean abstinence and Christian asceticism, as well as historical debates about whether Pythagoras was a strict vegetarian.</meta>

->## ON PORPHYRY. 207<-

**Pythagoreans.** We do not <note>original Greek: "Οὐ," though the author suggests "οὐδὲ" (neither).</note> pride ourselves on not eating meat, nor do we come to eating out of gluttony. Therefore, as far as we are concerned, let those followers of Pythagoras who abstain from living things be well <note>original Greek: "χαιρόντων," literally "let them rejoice," but used here as a parting wish or "farewell to them."</note>. But look also at the difference in the reason for abstaining from living things between the followers of Pythagoras and the ascetics among us <note>Rittershusius notes: "Thus he calls the Monks, as do very often Basil the Great, Chrysostom, and others."</note>. For that man <note>referring to Pythagoras</note> and his followers abstain from living things because of the myth concerning the transmigration of the soul <term>metempsychosis</term>—and someone, lifting up his own dear son to slaughter him while praying, is a great fool <note>This is a reference to a fragment of Empedocles, describing the horror of accidentally killing a reincarnated relative.</note>. We, however, if we do such a thing <note>original Greek: "κἂν τὸ (malim τι) τοιοῦτο πράττωμεν," meaning "if we practice such [abstinence]."</note>, do it because we strike the body and lead it into slavery, and we wish to put to death the members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, passion, evil desire; and we do everything so that we might kill the deeds of the body. *Similarly, Saint Jerome in book 2 against Jovinian (on my page 166, column 1) says: "Before I come to the scriptures and show from them the fasts pleasing to God and acceptable continence, I shall compare the arguments of the philosophers with our own arguments. I will prove that we do not follow the dogma of Empedocles and Pythagoras, who, because of reincarnation <term>metempsychosis</term>, think that nothing which moves and lives should be eaten. They consider those who cut down a fir or an oak tree to be guilty of the same crime as parricides and poisoners. Instead, we venerate our Creator, who created all things for the use of humans," etc.*

However, that Pythagoras did not abstain entirely from all living things is hinted at here by Malchus <note>Malchus is the original Syrian name of Porphyry, the author of the biography being commented upon.</note>, and is expressly reported from Aristoxenus by Athenaeus in book 1: "He did not abstain from living things, as Aristoxenus has said." Plutarch also proves this in book 1 *On Homer*, using the authority of Aristotle, stating that the Pythagoreans did not abstain from eating animals, except for a few specific types of meat. See also Aulus Gellius, book 4, chapter 11. Finally, regarding the Pythagorean abstinence from living things which we have discussed thus far, there exists an Epigram by Diogenes Laërtius on this sentiment, which seems to me rather "cold" <note>In the sense of being a weak or trivial joke.</note>: It says that it is not only Pythagoras who abstained from eating living things, but that he has many companions in the same practice: since there is none of us who does not feed on the cooked meat of animals that have first been slaughtered and deprived of life; but we all abstain from animals while they are living, vibrant, and raw.

**Of pigs, the most tender]** I apply here those words from Aulus Gellius in the same chapter 11 of book 4: *Aristoxenus also reports that Pythagoras used to live on very small young pigs and tender kids.*

<summary>Rittershusius distinguishes between Pythagorean vegetarianism, based on the fear of eating reincarnated souls, and Christian monastic fasting, aimed at subduing bodily passions. He also cites ancient authorities like Aristotle and Aristoxenus to argue that Pythagoras may not have been a total vegetarian.</summary>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

**"A dough ox, as they say, the more precise [authors]"**] I think the order of the words here is somewhat disturbed, and should be restored as: **"as the more precise authors say, an ox"**; or: **"a dough ox, as the more precise authors say."** For the word **dough-made** <note>original Greek: σταίτινον (*staitinon*)</note>, I previously guessed it should read **made of fat** <note>original Greek: στεατινὸν (*steatinon*)</note>, that is, "fatty": for **fat** or **suet** <note>original Greek: στέαρ (*stear*)</note> is **grease** <note>original Greek: λίπος (*lipos*)</note>, as the lexicographer Hesychius explains. However, **dough-made** specifically refers to something fashioned from kneaded flour. I do not find the word for **dough** <note>original Greek: τὸ σταῖς (*to stais*)</note> used with the same meaning as "fat." Does Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry, the author being commented upon</note> mean for us to understand a "dough ox" as one that Pythagoras fashioned from flour and water and then sacrificed? I am more inclined to believe this: I will note the reason shortly, drawn from the example of Empedocles.

**"Having discovered the [property] of the right-angled [triangle]"**]. Plutarch also mentions this **ox-sacrifice** <note>original Greek: βουθυσίας (*bouthysias*)</note> in Book VIII of his *Table Talk* <note>Symposiaca</note>, problem 2; as does Diogenes Laertius in Book VIII, page 575, where he even recites a two-line poem <term>distichon</term>. It is helpful to provide the words of both authors so that the comparison is ready at hand. Plutarch writes: **"For among the most geometric theorems—or rather, problems—is this: given two figures, to construct a third equal to the one and similar to the other; upon the discovery of which, they say Pythagoras sacrificed."** Diogenes Laertius says: **"Apollodorus the Calculator says that it was when he discovered that the square of the side subtending the right angle <note>the hypotenuse</note> is equal to the squares of the sides containing it; and there is an epigram that goes like this:"**

->When Pythagoras found that famous figure,<-
->For which he offered a glorious ox-sacrifice.<-

This epigram also appears in Book I of the *Greek Anthology* under the title **"On Philosophers."** One may also compare these with Athenaeus, Book X, where the second line begins: **"Glorious, for which..."** However, Cicero, in Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, cast doubt on this sacrifice of Pythagoras with his own counter-argument, writing: *No one ever vowed a tenth to Hercules if he should become a wise man; although Pythagoras, when he had discovered something new in geometry, is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses. But I do not believe it, since he would not even sacrifice a victim to Delian Apollo, lest he sprinkle the altar with blood, etc.* I easily agree with Cicero that it was not a real, living ox sacrificed by Pythagoras, but rather an artificial one made of kneaded flour. I am moved by what Athenaeus writes in Book I regarding Empedocles, a student of Pythagoras: that when he emerged victorious in the Olympic games, he distributed an ox fashioned from myrrh, frankincense, and other precious spices among those who were present in that assembly of all Greece...

<summary>Rittershusius examines the legend that Pythagoras sacrificed an ox to celebrate a geometric discovery, concluding that the sacrifice was likely a bloodless, symbolic effigy made of dough or spices, consistent with Pythagorean non-violence.</summary>

<keywords>Pythagoras, geometry, Pythagorean theorem, sacrifice, dough ox, Cicero, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, Empedocles, bloodless sacrifice, Greek Anthology</keywords>

### ON PORPHYRY.
<sig>O</sig>
<meta>Volume II. Part II.</meta>

...should run. And for this reason, he sacrificed a fashioned ox <note>an ox made of dough or clay rather than a living animal</note>, because Empedocles was a Pythagorean and abstained from eating living things.

<margin>37</margin> **"For his teaching was twofold]"** Just as his method of teaching was twofold, so too Pythagoras had two classes of listeners. On one hand, the method of teaching was **discursive** <note>original Greek: διεξοδική (*diexodikē*), meaning detailed or step-by-step</note>; on the other, it was **symbolic** <note>original Greek: συμβολική (*symbolikē*) — using riddles or signs</note>. The former was clearer and easier, while the latter was secret and mystical. Among the listeners, some were called *Listeners* <note>original Greek: Ἀκουσματικοί (*Akousmatikoi*)</note>, others were *Learners* <note>original Greek: Μαθηματικοί (*Mathematikoi*)</note>. However, Agellius <note>the Roman author Aulus Gellius</note> adds a third class in Book I, Chapter 4, who were named *Naturalists* <note>original Greek: Φυσικοί (*Physikoi*)</note>. Those whom Agellius calls *Acoustics* are the same as those called *Akousmatikoi* by Iamblichus, Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note>, and others. Yet, in his description of each class, Agellius differs somewhat from Malchus and the others. See Iamblichus, Book I, Chapter 18, who—having a little earlier distinguished between *Pythagoreans* and *Pythagorists* <note>original Greek: Πυθαγορείους vs Πυθαγοριστὰς</note>, much like one distinguishes between *Attics* and *Atticists* <note>those who are native to Athens versus those who merely imitate Athenian style</note>—adds the following: *“In another way, there were two forms of philosophy. For there were also two classes of those who practiced it: the Listeners and the Learners.”* Then, after he described who both groups were (namely, that the *Listeners* were those to whom their master delivered **oral teachings** <note>original Greek: ἀκούσματα (*akousmata*)</note> that were **unproven and without explanation** <note>original Greek: ἀναπόδεικτα καὶ ἄνευ λόγων</note>), he divided these **oral teachings** into three types: 1. Concerning what each thing is. 2. Concerning what is most [significant]. 3. Concerning what must be done. Indeed, the teaching of the Seven Sages of Greece was of a similar character. The *Learners*, however, were those who possessed knowledge not only of **the fact** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι (*to hoti*)</note> or bare precepts, but also **the reason why** <note>original Greek: τὸ διότι (*to dioti*)</note>—that is, the reasons, principles, and causes of every matter: why, I say, a thing is so and not otherwise, or why something ought to be done or not done. He then indicates the reason for this distinction or inequality among Pythagoras's listeners, which was established by the master himself: because, when he had crossed over from Ionia and Samos into Italy while fleeing the tyranny of Polycrates (as mentioned above), he had the leaders of most of the cities of **Magna Graecia** <note>Great Greece — the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note> as his associates and disciples. These men, however, were not only of an advanced age but were also occupied with the business of the state and lacked the **leisure** <note>original Latin: *otium*, the time for contemplation and study</note> necessary for learning; thus, it seemed they could only with great difficulty be instructed through **mathematical studies** <note>original Greek: μαθήματα (*mathēmata*)</note> and **demonstrations** <note>original Greek: ἀποδείξεις (*apodeixeis*)</note>—that is, by a deeper and more precise reasoning. For this reason, he judged that they should be educated and shaped by bare precepts, thinking that even in this way he would benefit them significantly, even if he did not demonstrate the reasons why each thing should be done or omitted. For it is not necessary for the sick to know why they must do this or that; it is enough if they obey the physician's orders...

<summary>This page explains Pythagoras's division of his students into two tiers: the Listeners (Akousmatikoi), who received simplified moral rules, and the Learners (Mathematikoi), who studied the underlying scientific and logical reasons. This distinction was a practical necessity, as many of his students were elderly politicians in Italy who lacked the time for rigorous academic study.</summary>

From this, therefore, the Pythagorean **Hearers** <note>original Greek: Ἀκουσματικοί (*Akousmatikoi*)</note> were born, if Iamblichus is to be believed. But from where did the **Learners** <note>original Greek: Μαθηματικοί (*Mathematikoi*)</note> come? From the younger ones, who were more fit for both enduring labor and for learning. Iamblichus writes: "As for those who happened to be younger, and were able to work <note>original Greek: πονεῖν (*ponein*). Rittershusius notes that the text should certainly read 'work' or 'labor' rather than 'do' (*poiein*)</note> and to learn, with such men he dealt through demonstration and the mathematical sciences." With these men, therefore, he engaged through proof and mathematical studies.

This too is memorable, which Iamblichus writes: that the listeners of the first type were considered instructed in wisdom <note>original: *prudentia*</note>: "They themselves supposed among their own that those who had received the most 'hearings' <note>original Greek: ἀκούσματα (*akousmata*) — oral precepts or rules</note> were the best prepared for wisdom."

This agrees with what Epictetus writes in chapter 76 of his *Handbook* <note>also known as the *Enchiridion*</note>: that the first and most necessary place in philosophy is that which deals with the use of dogmas, or decrees, or precepts (these are the **hearings** <note>original Greek: ἀκούσματα</note> of Pythagoras); for example, "That one must not lie." The second place treats demonstrations: such as, "Why one must not lie." The third confirms and distinguishes the demonstrations themselves: such as, "How does it happen that this is a demonstration? What is a demonstration? What is a consequence? What is a contradiction? What is true, and what is false?" From these, the third place exists because of the second, and the second because of the first, which is the most necessary and in which one should find rest. He then reproaches those who invert this order, so that they linger in the third place, consuming all their zeal there, and completely neglect the first; namely, they lie vigorously, while in the meantime they have at hand the reason and the way of demonstrating: "That one must not lie," etc. I would think, moreover, that the reason for that double instruction and the two types of Pythagorean listeners can be rendered as being sought from nature itself: because it is natural to know *that* a thing is so <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι (*to hoti*)</note> before knowing *why* it is so <note>original Greek: διότι (*dioti*)</note>; to know that the matter stands thus, before knowing why it stands thus. Clement of Alexandria also mentions those two types of Pythagorean listeners in Book V of the *Stromata* <note>meaning "Miscellanies"</note>, page 246, in these words: "Indeed, the society of Pythagoras and the two-fold communion with his associates—calling the many 'Hearers' and certain others 'Learners' (perhaps 'Companions') <note>The original Greek uses *heterous* (others), but the editor suggests it should be *hetairous* (companions)</note> who were genuinely attached to philosophy. But that one part was spoken plainly, and the other part was hidden, was a riddle meant for the many." Regarding the different kinds of Pythagorean listeners—

# ON PORPHYRY.
### PAGE 211

It is also useful to bring in here what Photius writes in the *Excerpts of an Anonymous Author on the Life of Pythagoras*, page 214 of the *Library*: "Of the followers of Pythagoras, some were occupied with contemplation, who were called the **Venerable** <note>original Greek: Σεβαστικοί (*Sebastikoi*)</note>; some with human affairs, who were called the **Political** <note>original Greek: Πολιτικοί (*Politikoi*)</note>; and others with the mathematical sciences, geometry, and astronomy, who were called the **Mathematical** <note>original Greek: Μαθηματικοί (*Mathematikoi*)</note>. Furthermore, those who associated with Pythagoras himself were called **Pythagorics** <note>original Greek: Πυθαγορικοί (*Pythagorikoi*)</note>; those who were disciples of these were called **Pythagoreans** <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόρειοι (*Pythagoreioi*)</note>; and those from the outside who were otherwise emulators were called **Pythagorists** <note>original Greek: Πυθαγορισταί (*Pythagoristai*)</note>." Behold, this writer too has his own way of listing and describing Pythagoras’s listeners, and he differs from others, as is evident in itself.

From this Pythagorean institution, unless I am mistaken, **Aristotle** also borrowed his most noble distinction of works, by which he intended his writings to be of two types: some were **Esoteric** <note>original Greek: Ἐσωτερικά (*Esoterika*) — intended for an inner circle of advanced students</note>, that is, **Acroamatic** <note>original Greek: ἀκροαματικά (*akroamatika*) — designed for oral delivery to serious students</note>; others were **Exoteric** <note>original Greek: Ἐξωτερικά (*Exoterika*) — intended for the general public</note>. And the rest of the **Peripatetics** <note>The "Walkers," followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> followed the same example, establishing their discourses partly as **Probable** <note>original Greek: ἐνδόξους (*endoxous*) — based on common opinion</note>, and partly as **Scientific** <note>original Greek: ἐπιστημονικούς (*epistemonikous*)</note> or **Demonstrative** <note>original Greek: ἀποδεικτικούς (*apodeiktikous*)</note>. 

Moreover, we have learned which or what kind of writings Aristotle’s **Exoteric** works were, and by contrast which were the **Acroamatic** ones, from **Aulus Gellius** <note>The text uses the variant "Agellius"</note> book 20, chapter 4. There, a letter is also recorded from **Alexander the Great**, which he sent from way out in Asia—amidst the very battles and victories by which he was pressing **Darius**—to complain to his master <note>Aristotle</note> for having published the **Acroamatic discourses**. The most powerful and most studious king did not think these should be shared with just anyone. He was clearly afraid that if others knew the same things, he himself would have nothing special in which to excel above the rest. 

Regarding these same two types of Aristotelian commentaries, **Clement of Alexandria** writes thus in the fifth book of the *Stromata*, page 245: "And the followers of Aristotle say that some of his writings are **Esoteric**, while others are **Common** and **Exoteric**." Then, Clement’s words regarding the double type of Peripatetic discussions are these on page 246: "And perhaps that two-fold form of the Peripatetic school—the one called **Probable** and the other **Scientific** in their discourses—does not refrain from distinguishing <note>Rittershusius suggests the Greek should be read as 'distinguishing' rather than 'to distinguish'</note> **Opinion** from **Renown** and **Truth**." 

**Ammonius** also, in his *Commentary on Aristotle’s Categories*, where he provides a very beautiful division of Aristotle’s writings, writes among other things: "Of the systematic works, some are **Dialogic** <note>written in the form of a conversation</note>, and others are **In his own person** <note>original Greek: αὐτοπρόσωπα (*autoprosopa*) — direct teaching or monologues</note>. Those are 'In his own person' in which he provided the teaching from his own persona, which they also call **Acroamatic**, because he delivered the discourse to genuine listeners. But the **Dialogic** ones..."

...those things which he did not write from his own persona, but rather like Plato, assuming the characters of others, which they also called **exoteric** <note>original Greek: ἐξωτερικά (*exoterika*)</note>, because they were written for the benefit of the masses. There is a vast difference between the dialogic works and those written in his own person. For in the works written in his own person, since he is delivering his discourse to genuine students, he says what he truly thinks, using the most precise arguments which the common people are not able to follow. But in the dialogic works, since they were written for the common benefit and that of the masses, he says what he thinks, yet not through demonstrative arguments, but through simpler ones which the common people are able to follow.

To this same point belongs that mockery or derision of **Lucian** <note>A 2nd-century satirist known for mocking philosophers</note>, who, just as he held the philosophers of every sect—and indeed both gods and men—up to ridicule, so also he mocked this division of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for their habit of walking while discussing philosophy</note> in his dialogue titled *The Sale of Lives*: where, when Mercury the salesman said, as if in praise of his merchandise, that he was "double"—that is, he was a twofold man—and the merchant asked in wonder, "How so?" <meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the works of Porphyry, focusing here on correcting the text of Iamblichus concerning Pythagorean precepts on law, innovation, and proper religious conduct, comparing these ancient Greek traditions with biblical precedents and Latin poetry.</meta>

# ON PORPHYRY
### PAGE 213

...the people for the law, just as for the wall. <note>original Greek: τὸν δῆμον ὑπὲρ τοῦ νόμου, ὅκως ὑπὲρ τείχεος—a famous fragment usually attributed to Heraclitus, suggesting laws are as vital for a city's defense as its physical walls.</note> Here I note in passing a famous sentiment of Pythagoras regarding the changing of laws, which appears in Iamblichus, chapter 30, but it seems to be not without errors. For the words were published thus:

> Generally, they thought it necessary to assume that there is no greater evil than anarchy. For man is not naturally suited to be preserved without someone presiding over him. Those men [the Pythagoreans] approved of staying within ancestral customs and laws, even if they were slightly worse than others. For to easily leap away from existing laws, and to be fond of <note>original: οἰκείους εἶναι, literally 'to be at home with'</note> "law-cuttings" <note>original: νομοτομίας (*nomotomias*)</note>, is in no way beneficial or a means of salvation.

These latter words were always suspect to me. Finally, a conjecture occurred to me—not absurd, I think—that one should read, **and swift innovations** <note>original: καὶ ὠκείας εἶναι καινοτομίας (*kai okeias einai kainotomias*)</note>. Indeed, I have never read the word **law-cuttings** <term>nomotomias: literally 'cutting of laws', a very rare or perhaps non-existent term Rittershusius believes is a scribe's error</term>, which **Frisius the interpreter** <note>referring to a previous translator of Iamblichus</note> nevertheless translated as *cuttings of laws*. But **innovation** <note>original: καινοτομία (*kainotomia*)</note> is a novelty, or a zeal for new things. The **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and lexicon</note> says: *He innovates, he creates new things. "To innovate" is used in the sense of "to rule."* He then brings forward a passage from Aristophanes in which *innovation* is also used. **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century lexicographer who compiled unusual Greek words</note> says: *To have innovated is to have made something new.* And shortly after: *Having created new things, having performed new deeds.*

**Worship the gods, but not as a side-task]** <note>original: Προσκυνεῖν δὲ μὴ ἐκ παρέργου τοὺς θεούς</note> Pythagoras speaks quite excellently and divinely in Iamblichus, chapter 23:

> One should neither enter a temple as a side-task of a journey, nor worship at all in that way, not even if you happen to be passing by the doors themselves. Sacrifice and worship unshod [barefoot].

See also the **2nd Symbol of Pythagoras** in the same Iamblichus, in the *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original: *Protrepticus*</note>, last chapter, and his explanation on page 135. I think, moreover, that regarding the instruction Pythagoras gives about worshiping while barefoot, he drew that from the history of Moses in Exodus, who approached the burning bush on the mountain in that way by the command of God himself. Furthermore, these things will be wonderfully illustrated through those words of **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) often called the 'Christian Cicero' for his elegant Latin</note>, which I transcribe here from Book V of *On Justice*, chapter 20, and at the same time I correct them in one or two places:

> Therefore, the worship of God, since it is of the heavenly service <note>Rittershusius corrects the Latin *militiae* to *militia* (service/warfare)</note>, requires the greatest devotion and faith. For how will God love the one who worships Him if he himself is not loved by that person? Or how will He grant to the one praying <note>Rittershusius corrects the text from *peccanti* (to the one sinning) to *precanti* (to the one praying)</note> whatever he has asked for, when he approaches the prayer neither from the soul nor with proper observance? etc.

**Sacrifice odd numbers to the heavenly gods, but even numbers to the earthly ones]** <note>original: Τοῖς μὲν οὐρανίοις θεοῖς περιττὰ θύειν, τοῖς δὲ χθονίοις ἄρτια</note> Hence that famous line in **Virgil** (who was a good Pythagorean) in the *Sorceress* <note>original: *Pharmaceutria*</note>, or Eclogue VIII: *The god delights in an odd number.* Where **Servius of Daniel** <note>An expanded 7th-century commentary on Virgil</note> says: *Or whichever...*

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

*...and of higher things, according to the Pythagoreans, who assign the perfect number three <note>original: "ternarium numerum"</note> to the highest god, from whom there is a beginning, a middle, and an end. Or indeed he refers to Hecate <note>A goddess associated with crossroads, magic, and the moon, often depicted with three faces or bodies</note>, whose power is said to be triple, etc. And presently: "Or by an odd number in whatever way." For there are 7 chords on a lyre; 7 planets; 7 days named after the gods; 7 stars in the North <note>The Big Dipper or Great Bear constellation</note>; and many things similar to these. And the odd number is immortal, because it cannot be divided into equal whole parts. Although Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> says that the Pythagoreans believe the odd number has a limit, while the even is infinite; therefore, for the sake of healing and many other matters, odd numbers are observed, etc. Regarding the number three being used in the sacred rites of the gods since ancient times, Aristotle also writes in Book 1 of "On the Heavens," chapter 1:* **Therefore, having received from nature, as if they were her laws, we also use this number for the holy rituals of the gods.** <note>original Greek: Διὸ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως εἰληφότες... Rittershusius uses Aristotle to show that the "rule of three" was considered a natural law in ancient religion.</note> *See also Turnebus, "Adversaria" 27, chapter 25, and Caelius Rhodiginus, "Ancient Readings" 22, chapter 9. Furthermore, the Greeks call an odd number "peritton" and an even number "artion." There is also an "even-odd" number <term>artioperittos: a number that, when divided by two, immediately results in an odd number</term>, from which, when divided into two, an odd number immediately emerges: for instance, if we cut 14 into two equal parts, the middle will be 7. An "even" number <note>specifically "even-even"</note>, however, is one which, when divided into two, the middle remains even: as if you divide 32 equally into two parts, the middle will be 16, which is an even number. Likewise, if you divide 16 into two parts, they become 8. If 8, they become 4. If 4, they become two. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia</note> says:* **An even number is 32; but an even-odd is one divided immediately into an odd number, such as 14, for half of this is seven.**

A passage from Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer</note> should by no means be overlooked here, which is found in his "Roman Questions," problem 102. Where he investigates the reasons why the Romans were accustomed to give names to males on the ninth day from birth, but to females on the eighth, he writes among other things about this Pythagorean division of numbers into even and odd: **The Pythagoreans considered the even number female, and the odd number male. For the odd is fertile, and it prevails over the even when they are combined; and when divided into units, the even number, like the female, gives way to an empty space between them, while of the odd number, a certain part always remains full.** <note>This refers to the visual representation of numbers. Even numbers (e.g., • •) have a gap in the middle; odd numbers (e.g., • • •) have a central "seed" or unit that fills the middle.</note> **For this reason, they think the one is suited to the male and the other to the female, etc.** For he philosophizes more extensively on the nature of numbers in that same place.

<margin>59</margin> **Unfruitful** <note>original Greek: Ἄκαρπον (*akarpon*)</note>] This is how the manuscript had it, but it should certainly be read as **fruitful** <note>original Greek: ἔγκαρπον (*enkarpon*)</note>, as it is expressly written in Iamblichus's mention of the same precept in chapter 21. Moreover, what Diogenes Laertius writes on page 581 agrees with this passage: **A cultivated plant should neither...**

# ON PORPHYRY

...to destroy, nor to harm. But not even an animal which does not harm humans. From which I am led to think that in the text of Malchus <note>The original name of the philosopher Porphyry was Malchus; Rittershusius is suggesting a correction to the Greek manuscript text here</note> as well, we should restore the word to "animal" <note>original: "ζῶον"</note> instead of "of animals" <note>original: "ζώων"</note>; although that genitive case indicating a part might seem tolerable, so that we understand "that one": that is, that one from among the animals, etc.

## **And regarding a deposit...** <note>original Greek: Παρακαταθήκη δὲ. A "deposit" in this context refers to something entrusted to another's care, creating a moral and legal bond.</note>

Here, two types of deposits should be carefully noted: of goods, and of words, or speeches (namely, secret ones), in both of which equal faithfulness must be maintained. Regarding the deposit of goods, the poet says:

> Return what was entrusted: let piety preserve its own covenants:
> Let fraud be absent, etc. <note>original: "Redite depositum..."</note>

On the same subject, the well-known decrees and opinions of the Civil Law <note>The body of Roman law used in the scholar’s time</note> state: In this contract, good faith must abound: and a contract arising from good faith must not be turned into betrayal. A deposit must be restored very quickly without any obstacle: so that deposited items or money may be returned at first sight. He who does not return a deposit (having been summoned and condemned in his own name) is forced to its restitution with the danger of infamy <note>A legal status of disgrace that stripped a Roman citizen of certain rights and social standing</note>. See especially the third-to-last and second-to-last laws in the Code under "On Deposits" <note>C. Depositi</note>. Regarding the deposit of words, or a secret, which is entrusted to someone and must not be made public, that saying of Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> is well-known:

> He who cannot keep silent on things committed to him,
> This man is black-hearted; you, O Roman, beware of him. <note>original: "Commissa tacere / Qui nequit, hic niger est..."</note>

Both types of deposit are also recommended by Isocrates <note>A famous Greek orator</note> and the comic poet Anaxandrides, who undoubtedly borrowed this from Pythagoras, from whose springs many have drawn—philosophers, poets, and orators. Thus, Pythagoras, in advising his friend Demonicus, says: **Guard the deposits of your words more than those of your money. For good men should show themselves to possess a character more trustworthy than an oath.** <note>original Greek: Μᾶλλον τήρει τὰς τῶν λόγων...</note> Anaxandrides, moreover, creates two classes of those who reveal a deposit of secret words: For they are either unjust, if they betray it for the sake of profit; or exceedingly lacking in self-control, if they do so with no hope of profit proposed. Both types, however, suffer from equal wickedness. Stobaeus <note>An anthologist of Greek wisdom</note> recorded his words in Discourse 34, "On Secrets" <note>original: "περὶ ἀποῤῥήτων"</note>:

> Whoever, having received words as a deposit,
> Discloses them, is either unjust or lacks all self-control.
> The one is unjust for the sake of gain; the other, without this,
> Is incontinent. Perhaps, indeed, both are wicked. <note>original Greek: Ὅστις λόγους γὰρ...</note>

Also worthy of mention is the Epigram of Lucian, which appears in Book 1 of the Anthology, title 51, "On a Mystery" <note>original: "εἰς μυστήριον"</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the ethical and legal obligations regarding "deposits," comparing the physical return of entrusted property in Roman law to the Pythagorean duty of keeping entrusted secrets. It draws on various classical authors to argue that betraying a secret is as morally bankrupt as stealing money.</summary>

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

<page-num>216</page-num>

->Let a seal be placed upon the tongue for unspoken words.<-
->For the guarding of speech is better than the guarding of possessions.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀῤῥήτων ἐπέων γλώσσῃ σφραγὶς ἐπικείσθω. / Κρείσσων γὰρ μύθων, ἢ κτεάνων φυλακή.</note>

That is:

->*Remember to seal the tongue for secret sayings,*<-
->*The deposit of words is greater than wealth.*<-
<note>original Latin: Arcanis dictis linguam obsignare memento...</note>

Or, as Vincent Opsopoeus <note>A 16th-century German scholar known for translating Greek classics</note> translated it:

->*Ensure the custody of a silent tongue suppresses secrets:*<-
->*To me, the guardian of speeches is greater than wealth.*<-

Finally, regarding the necessity of not revealing secrets, there are also many passages in the Book of Sirach <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of ethical teachings in the Apocrypha</note>.

**Of the glorious]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν εὐκλεῶν</note> In the manuscript, it was read here as "of the inglorious" <note>original: ἀκλεῶν</note>. This is a mistake. For who would believe that Pythagoras wanted effort to be devoted to such things?

**To the songs of the Sirens]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν Σειρήνων ᾠδαῖς</note> This is a golden passage concerning the two types of pleasures: some of which are impure and shameful, perceived through gluttony, the belly, and sexual matters; others are pure, which are taken from the study of honorable and just things and those otherwise necessary for life. Rightly and skillfully, Pythagoras made the pleasures of the soul—which are of the latter kind—similar to some most sweet harmony of the Muses; however, he made those former pleasures of the body, which are perceived from the belly and those things beneath the belly, similar to the murderous songs of the Sirens. In the same way, Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> calls idleness (which is almost a sibling and companion of pleasure) a "wicked Siren." He says, *The wicked Siren, Idleness, must be avoided*. And rightly so. For just as the Sirens destroyed men sailing past them, lured by the deceptive sweetness of their song, so too do these pleasures drag those devoted to them into destruction.

Therefore, Archytas of Tarentum <note>A mathematician and philosopher who was a student of the Pythagorean school</note>, and a disciple of Pythagoras, used to say truly and gravely that no more fatal plague than bodily pleasure has been given to men by nature. He demonstrated this clearly by its effects, as recorded in Cicero’s *On Old Age* <note>original: Cat. Maj., referring to "Cato Maior de Senectute"</note>. This mention of the Sirens reminds me of another memorable sentiment of Pythagoras, which Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian</note> preserved for us in the first book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: Stromata</note> and Theodoret <note>A bishop and influential theologian</note> in his *Cure of Greek Affections*. It says: "That one must prefer the Muses to the Sirens" <note>original Greek: Ὡς χρὴ τῶν Σειρήνων προτιθέναι τὰς Μούσας</note>.

Theodoret interprets this enigma thus: "I think he compared the Sirens to ornate and deceptive speeches; but the Muses to those speeches which have nothing artificial about them, but display the naked beauty of truth." Clement puts it this way: "Pythagoras advises (or used to advise) that one should consider the Muses sweeter than the Sirens, and practice wisdom without..."

<summary>Rittershusius argues that Pythagoras prioritized the "deposit" of secrets over material wealth and draws a sharp moral distinction between the noble pleasures of the Muses (truth) and the destructive pleasures of the Sirens (sensuality and deceptive rhetoric).</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Sirens, Muses, secrecy, ethics, pleasure, Archytas of Tarentum, Clement of Alexandria, Theodoret, philology</keywords>

...teaching [the soul's] pleasure, and exposing other forms of enchantment as deceptive. **In the works of Theodoret** <note>An influential 5th-century theologian and bishop</note>, anyone who compares the Greek with the Latin will surely notice the error of the translator **Acciaioli** <note>Zanobi Acciaioli, a 15th-century scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note>, where he translates: *an unlearned man* <note>original Latin: "idiotam hominem"</note>. For how could Pythagoras, as an "unlearned man," have endured and achieved so much for the sake of wisdom? Evidently, **Acciaioli** had read in his copy—or certainly had it in his mind—the phrase *as an unlearned man* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἰδιώτην / hōs idiōtēn</note>, whereas the true reading is *as the sweeter voice of the Muses* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἡδίω τὴν τῶν Μουσῶν φωνήν / hōs hēdiō tēn tōn Mousōn phōnēn</note>. I wanted to mention this in passing for the sake of those who trust translators everywhere, so they may better understand how often they are wretchedly and ridiculously deceived while they cling only to versions and despise the original sources.

**For the things regarding life]** <note>original Greek: Τοῖς πρὸς τὸ ζῆν</note> It seems the word **"and"** <note>original Greek: καὶ</note> was omitted before this phrase.

**Two times especially]** <note>original Greek: Δύο τε μάλιστα καιροὺς</note> **Saint Jerome**, in his *Apology against Rufinus*, writes: *Care must be taken of two times especially, morning and evening: that is, of those things we are about to do, and of those things we have done.* **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras</note> says it beautifully in chapter 35: *Do nothing without forethought or without being held accountable; rather, in the morning, set out what must be done, and at night, reflect on what has been managed, while at the same time training the memory through this examination.* **Cato the Censor**, as quoted by **Cicero** in his *Dialogue on Old Age*: *In the manner of the Pythagoreans, for the sake of exercising my memory, I recall in the evening whatever I have said, heard, or done each day, etc.* I will note more on this below.

**An accounting of what has happened]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν μὲν γενομένων εὐθύνας</note> This exercise—a kind of mental rumination and recollection of the past—will be useful not only for maintaining an accurate account of one's life but also for nourishing and increasing the memory, that treasure-house, storeroom, and pantry of learning and wisdom. **Iamblichus** teaches us this when he writes in chapter 29: *A Pythagorean man would not rise from his bed until he had first remembered the events of yesterday.* He describes the method of this remembrance in the same place: *He performed the recollection in this way: he tried to recover in his mind what he first said, or heard, or commanded the servants upon rising; then what was second, or third. The same logic applied to what was to come* <note>The author notes the Greek text might need correction here from "he who is to be" to "that which is to be" or "things that are to be," which he prefers</note> *and then again, upon going out, whom he met first or second, and what words were spoken first, second, or third. The same logic applied to everything else. For he tried to recover in his mind everything that happened in the whole day, eager to remember in this order—* <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the next page</note>.

He emphasizes that daily recollection is essential for both moral accountability and the strengthening of the memory.</summary>

->E i<-

**"A dough-made ox, as the more precise authors say"]** <note>original Greek: Σταίτινον, ὥς φασι, βοῦν οἱ ἀκριβέστεροι</note> I think the word order here is somewhat disturbed and should be restored as follows: *as the more precise authors say, an ox*; or *a dough-made ox, as the more precise authors say.* Regarding the term **"dough-made"** <note>original Greek: σταίτινον / staitinon</note>, I previously guessed it should be read as **"fatty"** <note>original Greek: στεατινόν / steatinon</note>, meaning a plump animal. For **"fat"** <note>original Greek: στέαρ / stear</note> means grease, as the lexicographer Hesychius explains. However, the word **"dough-made"** refers specifically to something crafted from kneaded flour. I do not find the word for **"flour-dough"** <note>original Greek: τὸ σταῖς / to stais</note> used with the same meaning as fat. Does Malchus <note>Porphyry</note> want us to understand that Pythagoras made an ox out of flour and water and sacrificed it? I am more inclined to believe this; I will note the reason shortly, drawn from the example of Empedocles.

**"Having discovered [the property] of the right-angled triangle"]** <note>original Greek: Ἐξευρὼν τοῦ ὀρθογωνίου</note> Plutarch also mentions this cattle-sacrifice <note>term: βουθυσία / bouthysia; the ritual slaughter of oxen</note> in Book 8 of his *Symposiacs* <note>Table Talk</note>, Problem 2, as does Diogenes Laertius in Book 8, where he even recites a two-line epigram. It is helpful to provide the words of both so that a comparison is easy for anyone. Thus Plutarch says: *For among the most geometrical theorems—or rather, problems—is the construction of a figure equal to one given figure and similar to another; and they say Pythagoras sacrificed when this was discovered.* Diogenes Laertius says: *Apollodorus the Calculator says that he sacrificed a hecatomb <note>a massive sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> because the square of the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is equal to the squares of the sides containing it; and there is an epigram that goes like this:*

> When Pythagoras discovered that world-renowned diagram,
> For which he performed a famous cattle-sacrifice.

This epigram also appears in Book 1 of the *Greek Anthology* under the title "On Philosophers." Let Athenaeus also be compared (Book 10), where the second verse begins: *Renowned, for which...* However, Cicero, in Book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, cast doubt on this sacrifice of Pythagoras with his own counter-argument when he wrote: *No one ever vowed a tenth-part to Hercules if he became a wise man; although Pythagoras, when he had discovered something new in geometry, is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses. But I certainly do not believe it, since he would not even sacrifice a victim to Delian Apollo, lest he sprinkle the altar with blood, etc.* I easily agree with Cicero that it was not a real, living ox sacrificed by Pythagoras, but rather a manufactured one made from kneaded flour. I am moved by what Athenaeus writes in Book 1 regarding Empedocles, a disciple of Pythagoras: that when he emerged victorious in the Olympic games, he distributed an ox fashioned from myrrh, frankincense, and other precious spices among those at that assembly of all Greece...
