<meta>This page continues the commentary of Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry’s *Life of Pythagoras*. The discussion transitions from the specific story of Pythagoras sacrificing a dough ox after a mathematical discovery to a broader explanation of his two distinct teaching styles and the two classes of students he cultivated in Italy.</meta>

-># ON PORPHYRY<-

...they had run. And indeed, for this reason, it was a **false ox**, because **Empedocles** was a **Pythagorean**, and he abstained from eating living creatures. <note>Empedocles followed the Pythagorean rule of vegetarianism, so he would not have sacrificed a real animal; a dough effigy was used instead.</note>

<margin>37</margin>
**[For his teaching was twofold]** <note>original Greek: Διττὸν γὰρ ἦν αὐτοῦ τῆς διδασκ. / Ditton gar en autou tes didask.</note> Just as his method of teaching was twofold, so too did **Pythagoras** have two types of students. One method of teaching was **discursive** <note>original: διεξοδική / diexodike; a comprehensive, step-by-step explanation</note>; while the other was **symbolic** <note>original: συμβολική / symbolike; using allegories and hidden meanings</note>. The former was clearer and easier; the latter was secret and mystical. Among the students, some were called **Acousmatics** <note>original: Ἀκουσματικοί / Akousmatikoi; "the Listeners"</note>, and others **Mathematicians** <note>original: Μαθηματικοί / Mathematikoi; "the Learners"</note>. However, **Aulus Gellius** <note>referred to here as Agellius</note> in Book 1, Chapter 4, adds a third group who were named **Physicists** <note>original: Φυσικοί / Physiki</note>. The same people who are called **Acustici** <note>the Latin equivalent of Acousmatics</note> by him are called **Acousmatics** by **Iamblichus**, **Malchus** <note>The original name of Porphyry</note>, and others. But Gellius also differs somewhat from Malchus and others in his description of each group. See **Iamblichus**, Book 1, Chapter 18, who—having just before distinguished between **Pythagoreans** and **Pythagorists** (in the same way one usually distinguishes between **Attics** and **Atticizers**) <note>The suffix "-ist" or "-izer" often implied someone who imitated a style rather than being a true member of the group</note>—adds these words: *In another way, there were two kinds of philosophy. For there were also two types of those who practiced it: some were **Acousmatics**, others **Mathematicians**.* Then, after he described who both of these groups were (namely, that the **Acousmatics** were those to whom the master passed down **oral precepts** <note>original: ἀκούσματα / akousmata</note> which were unproven and without rational explanations. These were divided into three types: 1. Concerning what each thing is; 2. Concerning what it most is; 3. Concerning what must be done. For the oral precepts were divided into these three categories, much like the teaching of the **Seven Sages of Greece** <note>A group of 6th-century BCE philosophers and statesmen famous for their brief, practical wisdom</note> was). The **Mathematicians**, however, were those who knew not only the **fact** <note>original: τὸ ὅτι / to hoti</note>, or the bare instructions, but also the **reason why** <note>original: τὸ διότι / to dioti</note>—that is, the *rationales, principles, and causes of each thing; why, I say, it is so and not otherwise, and whether something ought to be done or not.* He points out the reason for this distinction or inequality among Pythagoras's listeners, which was established by the master himself: because, when he had crossed from Ionia and Samos to Italy, fleeing the tyranny of **Polycrates** (as mentioned above), he had the leaders of most of the cities of **Magna Graecia** <note>The coastal areas of Southern Italy settled by Greek colonists</note> as his associates and disciples. These men, not only because they were of a more advanced age, but also because they were occupied with the business of the state, lacked the necessary leisure for learning. It seemed difficult to instruct them through **mathematical studies** <note>original: μαθήματα / mathemata</note> and **proofs** <note>original: ἀποδείξεις / apodeixeis</note>—that is, by a deeper and more precise method of reasoning. Therefore, he decided they should be educated and shaped by bare precepts, thinking that even in this way he would benefit them significantly, *even if he did not demonstrate the reasons why each thing should be done or omitted. For it is not necessary for the sick to know why they must do this or not do that, provided they obey the doctor's orders.*

->O<-
->Volume II. Part II.<-

<summary>This page explains the division of Pythagoras’s followers into two groups: the Acousmatics, who received practical rules without explanation, and the Mathematicians, who studied the underlying reasons and proofs. The author justifies this split by noting that Pythagoras’s influential students in Italy were busy statesmen who required quick, practical guidance rather than lengthy academic proofs.</summary>

It expands on the distinction between the two classes of Pythagorean students—the Acousmatics and the Mathematicians—drawing parallels with the writings of Iamblichus, the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, and the Christian theologian Clement of Alexandria.</meta>

-># NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS<-

...for them, it is enough to recover their health, even if they do not understand the manner or the method of the cure themselves. **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> uses this elegant comparison. From this, therefore, the Pythagorean **Acousmatics** <note>original Greek: Ἀκουσματικοὶ / Akousmatikoi; literally "the Listeners." These students were taught the "what"—the rules and conclusions—without the complex proofs.</note> were born, if Iamblichus is to be believed. But from where did the **Mathematicians** <note>original Greek: Μαθηματικοὶ / Mathematikoi; literally "the Learners." These students studied the "why"—the mathematical and logical demonstrations behind the rules.</note> come? From the younger ones, who were more suited to both enduring hard work and for learning. Iamblichus says: *As for those who happened to be younger, and were able to work* (it should definitely be read as "to work" <note>Rittershusius notes a correction in the Greek text from "to do" (ποιεῖν) to "to work/labor" (πονεῖν).</note>) *and learn, with such as these he dealt through demonstration and mathematical studies.* With these sorts of people, therefore, he conducted his business through demonstration and the mathematical sciences.

It is also worth remembering what Iamblichus writes: that the listeners of the first type [the Acousmatics] were considered better equipped in practical wisdom: *They themselves suppose that those who have heard the most "acousmata"* <note>Oral teachings or "sayings."</note> *are best disposed toward wisdom.*

This agrees with what **Epictetus** <note>A famous Stoic philosopher born as a slave.</note> writes in chapter 76 of his **Handbook** <note>The *Enchiridion*, a manual of Stoic ethics.</note>: that the first and most necessary place in philosophy is the one which deals with the use of doctrines, or decrees, or precepts (these are the *acousmata* of Pythagoras), for example: *One must not lie.* The second place deals with demonstrations: such as, *Why one must not lie.* The third is to confirm and distinguish the demonstrations themselves: such as, how it happens that this is a demonstration; what is a demonstration; what is a logical consequence; what is a contradiction; what is true, and what is false. Of these, the third place exists for the sake of the second, and the second for the sake of the first, which is the most necessary, and in which one should find rest. He then rebukes those who invert this order, so that staying in the third place, they consume all their study there and utterly neglect the first—lying vigorously, while in the meantime they have at hand the reason and the way of demonstrating *that one must not lie*, etc. I would think that the reason for this double education and the two types of Pythagorean listeners can be explained by nature itself: because by nature, it is prior to know **that** a thing is so <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι / to hoti; the fact of a matter.</note> than to know **why** it is so <note>original Greek: διότι / dioti; the cause or reason for the fact.</note>: to know that the matter stands thus, rather than why it stands thus. **Clement of Alexandria** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often compared Greek philosophy to Christian doctrine.</note> also mentions those two types of Pythagorean listeners in Book 5 of the *Miscellanies* <note>original Latin title: *Stromata*.</note>, page 246, with these words: *Indeed, even the assembly of Pythagoras, and his twofold association with his companions—calling many "Acousmatics" and certain others "Mathematicians"* (perhaps read as "companions") *who genuinely applied themselves to philosophy. Ноwever, the fact that some things were stated openly and others were hidden was a hint given to the many.* Concerning the different kinds of listeners of Pythagoras... <meta>catchword: iu- (likely iunioribus, "the younger ones")</meta>

<summary>This page explains the hierarchy of Pythagorean education, distinguishing between the Acousmatics (who learned rules by heart) and the Mathematicians (who studied the underlying proofs). Rittershusius uses Epictetus and Clement of Alexandria to argue that practical moral living is the ultimate goal, even if it precedes the understanding of complex logic.</summary>

<keywords>Pythagoras, Acousmatics, Mathematicians, Iamblichus, Epictetus, Enchiridion, Clement of Alexandria, logic vs. ethics, pedagogical method, ancient philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Rittershusius on the different classifications of students in the school of Pythagoras. Having previously discussed the distinction between "Listeners" (Acousmatics) and "Learners" (Mathematicians), the author now brings in further historical evidence from Photius and compares these traditions to the pedagogical methods of Aristotle and the later Peripatetic school.</meta>

-># ON PORPHYRY<-

It is also useful to compare here what **Photius** <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who preserved summaries of many lost ancient books in his *Bibliotheca*.</note> writes in the *Excerpts* of an anonymous author concerning the life of **Pythagoras** (p. 214 of the *Bibliotheca*):
*Of the followers of Pythagoras, some were occupied with contemplation, who were called the **Venerable** <note>original Greek: Σεβαστικοί / Sebastikoi; those focused on the sacred or theoretical.</note>; others with human affairs, who were called **Political**; others with the sciences—geometry and astronomy—who were called **Mathematicians**. And those who associated with Pythagoras himself were called **Pythagoreans**; their disciples, **Pythagoreioi**; and those who were otherwise outside imitators, **Pythagoristai**.* Behold, this writer too has his own way of listing and describing Pythagoras’s listeners, and he differs from the others, as is evident in itself.

From this Pythagorean institution, unless I am mistaken, even **Aristotle** borrowed his own most noble distinction of works, by which he intended his writings to be of two kinds: that some should be **Esoteric** <note>original Greek: Ἐσωτερικὰ; "inner" teachings intended for advanced students.</note> or **Acroamatic** <note>original Greek: ἀκροαματικά; from "hearing," referring to oral lectures.</note>; and others **Exoteric** <note>original Greek: Ἐξωτερικά; "outer" teachings intended for the general public.</note>. And the rest of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they held discussions.</note> followed the same example, establishing their discourses partly as **reputable** <note>original Greek: ἐνδόξους / endoxous; based on common or probable opinion.</note>, and partly as **scientific** or **demonstrative**. Furthermore, we have learned what or of what sort Aristotle’s exoteric writings were, and on the contrary, what sort the Acroamatic ones were, from **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of the *Attic Nights* (Noctes Atticae).</note> in Book 20, Chapter 4. There, a letter is even reported from **Alexander the Great**, sent from all the way in Asia amidst the battles and victories with which he was pressing **Darius**. In it, the king complained to his teacher [Aristotle] for having published the *acroamatic* books of his discourses. That most powerful and equally studious king did not think they should be shared with just anyone. He was clearly afraid that if others knew the same things, he himself would have nothing special by which to excel above the rest. Concerning these same two types of Aristotelian Commentaries, **Clement of Alexandria** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often blended Greek philosophy with Christian thought.</note> writes thus in the fifth book of his *Stromata* (p. 245): *They say that among the followers of Aristotle, some of his writings are **esoteric**, and others are **common and exoteric**.* Then, the words of the same Clement concerning the double kind of Peripatetic disputation are these (p. 246): *Perhaps also that double form of those from the Peripatos, the one called **reputable** and the other **scientific** in discourse, is not exempt from **dividing opinion from both renown and truth**.* **Ammonius** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote commentaries on Aristotle.</note> also, in his *Commentary on Aristotle's Categories*, where he hand downs a very beautiful division of Aristotelian writings, writes among other things: *Of the systematic writings, some are in the form of **dialogues**, others are **in his own person**. Those in his own person are those in which he delivered teaching from his own character <note>rather than through fictional characters in a dialogue.</note>, which they also call **acroamatic**, because the discourse was made for genuine listeners. But the dialogues...*

<meta>This page continues Rittershusius’s commentary on the pedagogical divisions of the Peripatetic school (Aristotle's followers), specifically examining the distinction between "esoteric" (inner) and "exoteric" (outer) teachings. It transitions from a discussion of Aristotle and Plato into a satirical critique by Lucian, before moving on to specific moral precepts of Pythagoras regarding parents, benefactors, and the law.</meta>

-># NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS<-

...those works he did not write in his own persona, but like **Plato**, assuming the characters of others, which they called **Exoteric** <note>original Greek: ἐξωτερικὰ; literally "outer" works intended for the general public.</note>, because they were written for the benefit of the many. There is a very great difference between the dialogic works and those written in the author's own person. For in the works written in his own person, as one addressing genuine listeners, he says what he actually thinks, and does so through the most precise arguments, which the majority of people are not able to follow. But in the dialogic works, as they were written for the common benefit of the many, he says what he thinks, yet not through demonstrative arguments, but through simpler ones, which the majority are able to follow. To the same point belongs that mockery <note>original Greek: χλευασμὸς; "chleuasmós"</note> or derision <note>original Greek: διασυρμὸς; "diasyrmós"</note> of **Lucian** <note>A 2nd-century Syrian satirist known for mocking philosophy and religion.</note>, who, just as he held the philosophers of all sects—and indeed gods and men—up to ridicule, so also he mocked this division of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> in the dialogue titled *The Sale of Lives*: where, when **Mercury** the seller had said, as if to recommend his merchandise, that the man was **"double,"** **that is, a twofold man,** and the merchant had asked in wonder, **"How so?"** Mercury is brought in to explain the force of the word with these words: **"One man is the one appearing from the outside, but another is the one who seems to be on the inside;"** (so I read it, not "he seems") **"so that if you buy him, remember to call the one esoteric and the other exoteric."** But let us now proceed to other matters.

<margin>38</margin> **The more extraordinary]** <note>original Greek: Τὸν περιττότερον; "the more excellent" or "superfluous."</note> See the notes above at Number 18.

**To be auspicious]** <note>original Greek: Εὔφημον εἶναι; "to be well-spoken" or "observe a holy silence."</note> By this, **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note> should be corrected in chapter 21, where we read: "and auspiciously." In place of **"and,"** I restore **"to be."** For I do not think it right to join "auspicious" to "intellect."

**Well-disposed toward parents and benefactors]** Iamblichus, in the same place, says: *Likewise also to think concerning parents and benefactors.* By "likewise," understand "well." For it was preceded by: **"To have a good intellect."**

**To obey the laws]** **Pythagoras** did not only command that the laws be complied with (as our **Malchus** <note>Malchus was the original Syrian name of Porphyry, the author of the text being commented upon.</note> writes here), but also that aid should be brought to the laws, and that war should be undertaken against injustice or the violation of laws: as others have handed down much more emphatically, testifying that this was his daily precept. Iamblichus, in chapter 21: **"To aid the Law, and to wage war against Lawlessness."** And more fully in chapter 30: *Since both insolence and luxury and the contempt of laws often incite men to injustice, for these reasons he daily commanded: To aid the Law, and to wage war against Lawlessness, etc.* Similarly **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> on page 581: **"To aid the Law. To wage war against Lawlessness."** So too **Heraclitus** in the same Laertius: **"One must fight..."**

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershusius’s commentary on the life and teachings of Pythagoras, as recorded by Porphyry. The previous page concluded a discussion on Aristotle’s public versus private teachings and Pythagoras’s views on social duties. Here, the focus shifts to the stability of laws and the proper, devoted manner of worshiping the gods.</meta>

-># ON PORPHYRY<-

"...the people [should fight] for the law as if for their city wall." <note>original Greek: τὸν δῆμον ὑπὲρ τοῦ νόμου, ὅκως ὑπὲρ τείχεος; a famous aphorism by the philosopher Heraclitus.</note> Here, I note in passing a famous sentiment of **Pythagoras** concerning the changing of laws, which appears in **Iamblichus** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note> in chapter 30, though it seems to be not without errors. For the words are published as follows:

*In general, they thought they ought to believe that there is no greater evil than anarchy. For man is not born to be preserved if no one is in charge. Those men approved of staying within ancestral customs and laws, even if they were slightly worse than others. For to leap away easily from existing laws, and to be fond of [law-cutting], is in no way beneficial or saving.*

These last words always seemed suspicious to me. At last, a conjecture occurred to me—not an absurd one, I think—that we should read: *and [rapid innovations]*. Indeed, I have never read the word "law-cutting" <note>original Greek: νομοτομίας; *nomotomias*</note>, which nevertheless the translator Frisius rendered as *cuttings of laws*. But "innovation" <note>original Greek: καινοτομία; *kainotomia*</note> is a making of something new, or a passion for new things. **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note> says: *He innovates, he makes new works.* He adds that *to innovate* is used in the sense of "to rule" <note>Presumably meaning to establish a new order or regime.</note>. He then brings forward a passage from **Aristophanes** <note>The famous Athenian comic playwright.</note> in which *innovation* is also used. **Hesychius** <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer.</note> says: *To innovate is to make something new,* and soon after: *Having made new works, having performed new deeds.*

**Do not worship the gods as a side-task** <note>original Greek: Προσκυνεῖν δὲ μὴ ἐκ παρέργου τοὺς θεούς; this refers to the Pythagorean rule that one should not stop to pray as an afterthought while busy with other errands.</note>] Most excellently and divinely, Pythagoras says in Iamblichus, chapter 23: *One should neither enter a temple nor worship at all as part of a side-journey, not even if you happen to be passing by the doors themselves. Sacrifice and worship barefoot.* See also the second Symbol of Pythagoras in the same Iamblichus, in the *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original Greek: *Protrepticus*</note>, final chapter, and his exposition on page 135. 

Moreover, I think that what Pythagoras commands regarding worship being done barefoot, he drew from the history of **Moses** in **Exodus**, approaching the bush burning on the mountain in such a manner by the command of God himself. Furthermore, these things will be wonderfully illustrated by those words of **Lactantius** <note>A 4th-century Christian author, often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> which I add from Book 5 of *On Justice*, chapter 20, and at the same time I correct them in one or two places: 

*Therefore the worship of God, since it is a heavenly service* <note>original Latin: "militiae"; Rittershusius corrects this to "militia."</note>, *requires the greatest devotion and faith. For how will God love the one who worships Him, if he himself is not loved by that person? Or how will He grant to the one praying* <note>original Latin: "peccanti" (one sinning); Rittershusius suggests reading "precanti" (one praying).</note> *whatever he has asked for, when he approaches the prayer neither from the soul nor with observance, etc.*

**To the heavenly gods, sacrifice odd numbers; to the gods of the earth, even ones** <note>original Greek: Τοῖς μὲν οὐρανίοις θεοῖς περιττὰ θύειν, τοῖς δὲ χθονίοις ἄρτια; this reflects the Pythagorean belief that numbers held mystical and moral properties.</note>] Hence that famous line in **Virgil** (who was a fine Pythagorean) in the *Sorceress* <note>original Latin: *Pharmaceutria*</note>, or *Eclogue* 8: *The god delights in an uneven number.* Where **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> in the edition of Pierre Daniel says: *Or whomever...*

<summary>Rittershusius explores Pythagorean rules for social and religious life, emphasizing the danger of "innovation" in law and the necessity of total focus and specific rituals—such as barefootedness—when worshiping the divine.</summary>

-># NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS<-

...and of those above, according to the **Pythagoreans**, who assign the **number three** <note>original Latin: *ternarium numerum*</note> to the highest god as a perfect number, from which there is a beginning, a middle, and an end. Or, he truly refers to **Hecate** <note>A goddess of boundaries and crossroads, often depicted with three faces or in triple form.</note>, whose power is said to be triple, etc. And soon: *Or by an odd number in whatever way.* For there are 7 chords, 7 planets, 7 days named after the gods, 7 stars in the North <note>The seven stars of the Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note>, and many similar things. The odd number is considered immortal because it cannot be divided into whole parts <note>i.e., it cannot be split into two equal integers.</note>; although **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note> says the Pythagoreans think that the odd number has a limit, while the even is infinite, and for this reason odd numbers are preserved for the sake of healing and many other things, etc. Regarding the number three being used in the sacred rites of the gods since ancient times, see also **Aristotle**, Book 1 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 1: <note>original Greek: Διὸ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως...; "Therefore, having received [these] from nature as if they were her laws, we also use this number for the sacred rites of the gods."</note> See also **Turnebus**, *Adversaria* 27, chapter 25, and **Caelius Rhodiginus**, *Ancient Lessons* 22, chapter 9.

Now, the Greeks call an odd number <term>perittos</term> <note>original: περιττὸν; literally "excessive" or "odd."</term> and an even number <term>artios</term> <note>original: ἄρτιον; literally "complete" or "even."</term>. There is also an <term>even-odd</term> <note>original: ἀρτιοπέριττος; *artio-perittos*</note> number, which, when divided in two, immediately results in an odd number: for instance, if we cut 14 into two equal parts, the middle will be 7. Moreover, an *even* number is one where, even after being divided in two, the middle remains even: for instance, if you divide 32 equally into two parts, the middle is 16—that is, an even number. Likewise, if you divide 16 into two parts, they become 8. If 8, they become 4. If 4, they become two. **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and lexicon.</note> says: *An even number is 32; an even-odd is one that is immediately cut into an odd number, such as 14, for half of this is seven...*

A passage from **Plutarch** <note>A famous Greek-Roman biographer and philosopher known for his 'Moralia'.</note> should by no means be overlooked here, which is found in his *Roman Questions*, Problem 102. Investigating the reasons why the Romans were accustomed to naming boys on the ninth day after birth, but girls on the eighth, he writes the following, among other things, concerning this Pythagorean division of numbers into even and odd: <note>original Greek: Οἱ Πυθαγορικοὶ...; "The Pythagoreans considered the even number to be female, and the odd number to be male. For the odd is generative, and it prevails over the even when added to it; and when they are divided into units, the even, just like the female, yields a void space in the middle, while of the odd, a full part is always left over."</note> Indeed, in the same place, he philosophizes at length on the nature of numbers.

<margin>59</margin> **[Fruitless]** <note>original Greek: Ἄκαρπον; *akarpon*</note> So the manuscript had it, but it should certainly be read as **[Fruitful]** <note>original Greek: ἔγκαρπον; *engkarpon*</note>, as it is explicitly written in **Iamblichus**'s <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note> mention of the same precept in chapter 21. This matches what **Diogenes Laërtius** <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> writes on page 581: *Neither [destroy nor harm] a cultivated plant...*

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershusius’s commentary on Porphyry’s life of Pythagoras. # ON PORPHYRY

...to destroy, nor to harm. But not even a living creature that does not harm humans. <note>original Greek: φθείρειν, μήτε σίνεσθαι. ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ζῶον, ὃ μὴ βλάπτει ἀνθρώπους</note> From this I am led to think that in Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Syrian name of Porphyry; the author is discussing a textual variant in Porphyry's manuscript.</note> as well, we should write "animal" <note>singular</note> instead of "animals" <note>plural</note>; although that genitive case signifying a part of a whole seems tolerable, so that we might understand it as: "that one from among the animals," etc.

**But regarding a deposit** <note>original Greek: Παρακαταθήκην δὲ</note>] We must rightly note here two types of "deposits": of goods, and of words or speeches (namely, secret ones). In both of these, an equal degree of faith and trust must be preserved. **On the deposit of goods, the poet says:**

-> Return the deposit: let piety keep its own covenants: <-
-> Let fraud be absent, etc. <-

On this same subject, the sanctions and rulings of Civil Law <note>Referencing the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the fundamental collection of Roman law.</note> are well known: In this type of contract, good faith must be abundant; and a contract arising from good faith ought not to be turned into a matter of treachery. **A deposit must be restored as quickly as possible without any obstacle:** Such that deposited items or money should be returned at first sight. **He who does not restore a deposit (having been summoned and condemned in his own name) should be compelled to its restoration under the threat of infamy.** See especially the third-to-last and second-to-last laws in the Code, under the title *On Deposits*. **Regarding the deposit of speeches, or a secret entrusted to someone that must not be published, that famous line of Horace is well known:**

-> He who is unable to keep silent about things committed to him, <-
-> this man is black-hearted; you, O Roman, beware of him. <-

Both types of deposits are also recommended by **Isocrates** <note>An influential Greek rhetorician.</note> and **Anaxandrides the Comic poet**, who undoubtedly borrowed the idea from **Pythagoras**, from whose fountains so many have drawn—philosophers, poets, and orators alike. Thus, Isocrates advising his friend Demonicus: "Guard the deposits of words even more than those of money. For good men ought to show a character more faithful than an oath." <note>original Greek: Μᾶλλον τήρει τὰς τῶν λόγων...</note> **Anaxandrides, however, identifies two types of people who reveal a deposit of secret words:** **For they are either unjust, if they betray it for the sake of profit; or they are utterly lacking in self-control, if they do it without any hope of profit.** Indeed, both types suffer from equal wickedness. **Stobaeus** <note>A 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors.</note> recorded his words in Sermon 34, *On Secrets*:

> For whoever, having received words as a deposit,
> blabs them out, is either unjust or excessively weak-willed.
> The one is unjust for the sake of gain; the other, without this,
> lacks self-control. But perhaps both are equally bad.

Also worthy of mention is an Epigram by **Lucian**, found in Book 1 of the *Anthology*, title 51, *On the Mystery*.

<summary>This page discusses the ethical duty of "deposits," expanding the concept from the legal obligation to return borrowed money to the moral obligation of keeping secrets. Rittershusius links these virtues to Pythagorean influence on later Greek orators, poets, and Roman law.</summary>

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

->Let a seal be placed upon the tongue for unspoken words.<-
->For the guarding of speech is better than the guarding of possessions.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀῤῥήτων ἐπέων γλώσσῃ σφραγὶς ἐπικείσθω. Κρείσσων γὰρ μύθων, ἢ κτεάνων φυλακή.</note>

That is:
> Remember to seal the tongue against secret sayings,
> The deposit of words is greater than riches.
<note>original Latin: Arcanis dictis linguam obsignare memento, Dictorum maius depositum est opibus.</note>

Or, as Vincent Opsopoeus <note>A 16th-century German humanist and translator known for his work on the Greek Anthology.</note> translated it:
> Ensure the custody of a silent tongue suppresses secrets:
> To me, the guardian of speech is greater than wealth.

Finally, there are many passages regarding the non-disclosure of secrets also found in the Book of Sirach <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of ethical teachings in the Wisdom tradition.</note>.

**Of the illustrious]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν εὐκλεῶν</note> In the manuscript, it was read here as **"the inglorious"** <note>original Greek: ἀκλεῶν</note>. This is incorrect. For who would believe that Pythagoras wished for effort to be devoted to such things?

**By the songs of the Sirens]** <note>original Greek: Τῶν Σειρήνων ᾠδαῖς</note> This is a "golden passage" regarding the two types of pleasures: some of which are impure and shameful, perceived through gluttony, the belly, and sexual matters; others are pure, which are taken from the pursuit of honorable and just things and those otherwise necessary for life. Rightly and skillfully, Pythagoras made the pleasures of the mind—the latter kind—similar to a most sweet harmony of the Muses; while those former pleasures of the body, which are perceived from the belly and those things below the belly, he made similar to the homicidal songs of the Sirens. In this way, Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> also calls Sloth (which is almost a sibling and roommate of pleasure) a wicked Siren. *The wicked Siren, Sloth, must be avoided*, he says. And deservedly so. For just as the Sirens used to destroy men sailing past them, lured by the deceptive sweetness of their song: so also do these pleasures drag those devoted to them into destruction. Truly and gravely, therefore, Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician, and friend of Plato.</note>, a disciple of Pythagoras, was accustomed to say that no more deadly plague than bodily pleasure was given to men by nature: which he demonstrated brilliantly by its effects, as is recorded in Cicero’s *Cato the Elder on Old Age*. The mention of Sirens here reminds me of another memorable saying of Pythagoras, which Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian who often synthesized Greek philosophy with Christian thought.</note> preserved for us in the first book of the *Stromata* (p. 127) and Theodoret <note>A bishop and influential theologian of the 5th century.</note> in *The Cure of Greek Affections* (Sermon 8, at the beginning): **"That one ought to prefer the Muses to the Sirens."** Theodoret interprets this enigma thus: **"I think he compared refined and overly-eloquent speeches to the Sirens; but to the Muses, those speeches which have nothing artificial about them, but display the naked beauty of truth."** Clement puts it this way: **"Pythagoras advised (or used to advise) that one should consider the Muses more pleasant than the Sirens, practicing wisdom not with..."** <note>The text breaks off here.</note>

<summary>Rittershusius comments on the Pythagorean virtue of silence and the distinction between the "pure" pleasures of the mind (Muses) and the "impure" pleasures of the body (Sirens).</summary>
<keywords>silence, secrets, pleasures, Muses, Sirens, Archytas of Tarentum, Cicero, Clement of Alexandria, Theodoret, ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on the life and teachings of Pythagoras as recorded by Porphyry. The previous page discussed the distinction between pure and impure pleasures, using the "songs of the Sirens" as a metaphor for deceptive allurements. On this page, Rittershusius focuses on the importance of checking original Greek sources against Latin translations and details the Pythagorean daily practice of morning and evening reflection to train the memory and maintain ethical discipline.</meta>

### ON PORPHYRY.

...teaching of pleasure, but exposing the other kind of soul-leading <note>The Greek term *psychagogia* refers to the leading or "persuading" of the soul, often through art or rhetoric.</note> as deceptive.
Truly, anyone who compares the Greek with the Latin in the works of Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century theologian and historian.</note> will not fail to notice the error of the translator Acciaiolus, when he translates the phrase as: *an ignorant man* <note>original Latin: "idiotam hominem." In this period, "idiota" referred to a private person or someone lacking professional skill, rather than its modern derogatory meaning.</note>. For how could Pythagoras, if he were an "ignorant man," have endured and accomplished so much for the sake of wisdom? Clearly, Acciaiolus had read in his own copy—or certainly had in his mind—**as an ignorant man** <note>original Greek: ὡς ἰδιώτην</note>; whereas the true reading is **as the sweeter voice of the Muses** <note>original Greek: ὡς ἡδίω τὴν τῶν Μουσῶν φωνήν. The translator likely confused the Greek words "idioten" (private/ignorant) and "hedio" (sweeter).</note>. I wanted to mention this in passing for the sake of those who trust translators implicitly, so they might better understand how often they are miserably and ridiculously deceived when they neglect the original sources and cling only to translations.

**For the things regarding life**] <note>original Greek: Τοῖς πρὸς τὸ ζῇν</note> It seems that the word **and** <note>original Greek: καὶ</note> has been omitted before "the things."

**And especially two times**] <note>original Greek: Δύο τε μάλιστα καιροὺς</note> **Saint Jerome** in his *Apology against Rufinus* writes: The greatest care must be taken of two times, *morning and evening: that is, of those things we are about to do, and of those things we have done*. Iamblichus explains this excellently in chapter 35: *One should do nothing without forethought or without being held accountable, but in the morning one should prepare what is to be done; and at night one should reflect on what has been accomplished, while at the same time examining oneself and exercising the memory.* **Cato the Elder**, as quoted by Cicero in his *Dialogue on Old Age*, says: *In the manner of the Pythagoreans, for the sake of exercising my memory, I recall in the evening whatever I said, heard, or did each day, etc.* I will note more on this below.

**Accounts of the things that have happened**] <note>original Greek: Τῶν μὲν γενομένων εὐθύνας</note> This exercise and "chewing over" <note>original Latin: "ruminatio," a metaphor comparing the recall of information to a cow chewing its cud.</note> and recollection of the past within the mind will be beneficial not only for maintaining an accurate account of one's life, but also for nourishing and increasing the memory—that treasure-house, store-room, and pantry of learning and wisdom. Iamblichus teaches us this when he writes in chapter 29: *A Pythagorean man would not rise from his bed until he first remembered what happened yesterday.* He also describes there the method of this remembrance: *He performed the recollection in this manner: he tried to recover in his mind what he first said, or heard, or commanded the household servants upon rising; then what was second, or third. And concerning what was to come* (or perhaps we should read "the things that happened," which I prefer, for "concerning other things" follows shortly) *the same logic applied; and again upon going out, whom he met first, or second; and what words were spoken first, or second, or third; and for all other things the same logic. For he tried to recover in his mind all the events that occurred in the whole day, striving to remember them in order...*

<meta>catchword: ...to remember</meta>

<summary>Rittershusius critiques a translation error regarding Pythagoras's status and details the Pythagorean discipline of daily reflection. This practice involved a rigorous morning and evening review of one's actions and speech to improve both moral character and memory.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, translation errors, Acciaioli, memory training, daily routine, Iamblichus, Saint Jerome, Cato the Elder, ethical reflection</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on the life of Pythagoras. Building on the previous page's critique of poor translations, Rittershusius now examines the specific Greek phrasing used to describe Pythagorean memory exercises and ritualistic "incantations" used to soothe the mind. He continues to cross-reference Porphyry (Malchus), Iamblichus, and the "Golden Verses" to reconstruct the daily discipline of the Pythagorean school.</meta>

-># NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS<-

...to remember, **so that** <note>original Greek: ὥστε. Rittershusius suggests he would prefer ὡς (as) or ὡς καὶ (as also).</note> **it happened that each of them occurred. But if they had more leisure during the process of waking up, they would try to recall the events of the third day in the same way, and they tried to exercise their memory even further. For nothing is greater for knowledge, experience, and wisdom than the ability to remember.** <note>This quote describes the Pythagorean practice of "morning memory," where a student would mentally review every action of the previous days in chronological order to cultivate mindfulness.</note> Where the text says **they tried** <note>original Greek: ἐπειρῶντο (plural)</note>, perhaps we should rewrite it as **he tried** <note>original Greek: ἐπειρᾶτο (singular)</note>: specifically referring to "the Pythagorean man." Unless, of course, one argues that there is a sudden leap from the singular to the plural number—a shift I have shown is not uncommon among good authors in my *Commentary on Oppian* <note>Oppian was a 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet; Rittershusius published a famous edition of his work.</note>. Furthermore, instead of **to exercise with the memory** <note>original Greek: τῇ μνήμῃ γυμνάζειν</note>, I would prefer **to exercise the memory** <note>original Greek: τὴν μνήμην</note>. Or should we retain the former and imply that they were exercising **themselves** by means of memory? <margin>1</margin> <margin>Let the youth take good note of this recommendation of memory and its exercise, and compare it with Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory*, Book 2, Chapter 2.</margin> Furthermore, in that same passage of Iamblichus, I will correct in passing the word **aiming at** <note>original Greek: ἐφιέντες</note> and rewrite it as **letting go** <note>original Greek: ἀφιέντες</note>, which means "dismissing." This is what the philosopher is saying: once the disciples of Pythagoras had decided that whatever was proposed to them must be fixed in the memory, they did not think that what the master taught should be **let go** until they had firmly grasped it. Therefore, the translator Frisinus <note>Frisinus refers to a previous Latin translator of Iamblichus.</note> translates it poorly: *And in learning they did not first seek after that which was taught, etc.* as if the text read **desiring** <note>original Greek: ἐφιέμενοι</note>, and as if "to desire" and "to let go" had the same meaning. Also, in the same place, one should read **in this way** <note>original Greek: τόνδε τὸν τρόπον</note> as two words, not one.

**To enchant**] <note>original Greek: Ἐπάδειν</note> Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Phoenician name of the philosopher Porphyry; Rittershusius uses it here to refer to the author of the biography.</note> alludes with this verb to the Pythagorean "incantations" or "charms" (epodes), about which Iamblichus writes throughout his work. See what I noted above at Number 59.

**Nor sleep**] <note>original Greek: Μηδ’ ὕπνον</note> These first three verses are found among the *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras <note>A collection of 71 moral exhortations; though attributed to Pythagoras, they were likely compiled later.</note>, which some ascribe to Philolaus <note>A Greek Pythagorean and contemporary of Socrates.</note>: verse 40 and following.

**Where did I transgress?**] <note>original Greek: Πῇ παρέβην</note> See also Iamblichus on this.

**First upon waking from sleep**] <note>original Greek: Πρῶτα μὲν ἐξ ὕπνοιο</note> I believe this verse and the one following exist nowhere else. I first published them some years ago in our *Pythagorean Ephemeris* <note>A "diary" or "almanac" of Pythagorean daily practices compiled by Rittershusius.</note>, expressing them in Latin meter as follows:

> *First, when waking from sleep you leave your bed,*
> *Arrange in your mind the things to be done in the coming light.*

The previous three verses I translated into this form:

> *When dark night comes and takes the color from things,*
> *You must not first grant rest to your eyes,*

# ON PORPHYRY.

> Before you allow sleep to settle on your eyes,
> Review the deeds of the day three times in your mind:
> What have I done wrong? What have I accomplished?
> What part of my duty was neglected in any matter?
<note>original Latin: "Elapsi quam ter repetas animo acta diei: / Quid feci secus ac debebam? quidue patraui? / Officii qua pars aliqua est neglecta mihi in re?" These lines are a Latin translation of the famous "Golden Verses" of Pythagoras, a set of moral exhortations.</note>

I also used to make translations of the Greek verses into German rhymes; although they are not of great literary merit, I will include them here as well for the sake of the youth:

> As soon as you wake early in the morning,
> Before you begin your chores and business
->thereupon,<-
> You should immediately set in your mind,
> With what matters you wish to spend the day well.
> When the black night now falls upon us,
> Take care that you do not fall asleep,
> Until you have first considered the day's work within yourself,
> And remembered three times what you have accomplished,
> Speaking thus to yourself: what have I done,
> That would have been better if I had let it be?
> Where have I not properly considered my duty,
> And what my office <note>The word "Ampt" (office) here refers to one's social or professional responsibility.</note> requires, have I neglected?
> Thus from the first thing in order to the last place,
> You should always stride forward with your memory.
> Then rejoice in what was handled rightly;
> Grieve, on the other hand, where you have fallen short.
> Upon this apply yourself, for this carry desire and love,
> And occupy yourself with such thoughts every day.
> If you will examine yourself according to the aforementioned measure,
> Then you will advance further in the path of virtue.

<margin>St. Jerome, Book 4, *Apology against Rufinus*.</margin>
**"Above all, to speak the truth. For this..."** <note>original Greek: Μάλιστα δ’ ἀληθεύειν. τοῦτο γὰρ. This refers to the Pythagorean command to prioritize truth above all else.</note> After God, truth is to be cultivated (for this is a Pythagorean precept), which alone makes humans most like God. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> in the *Exhortation to Philosophy*, chapter 20, page 114: "Indeed, one must also value freedom from falsehood highly. For speaking the truth—both toward the Gods according to divine truth, and toward humans according to human truth—is the leader for us of all divine and human goods." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ἀψεύδειαν δεῖ περὶ πολλοῦ ποιεῖν... </note> Thus Plato in the fifth book of *The Laws* (whom Iamblichus imitated quite clearly, both here and often elsewhere): "Truth is the leader of all goods for the Gods, and of all goods for men; he who is to be blessed and happy should partake in it from the very beginning, so that he may live out as much time as possible as a man of truth." <note>original Greek: Ἀλήθεια δὴ πάντων μὲν ἀγαθῶν Θεοῖς ἡγεῖται... </note> I could have noted even more on this same sentiment from the writings of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who blended Hellenistic and Jewish thought.</note>, which I intentionally omit, being content to have added only this one thing from his book *On Rewards and Punishments*...

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershusius's scholarly commentary on the life of Pythagoras. Following the previous page’s look at the "Golden Verses" and the practice of self-reflection, the author now explores the philosophical link between truth, light, and the nature of the divine. He moves from Greek philosophy into Persian theology and Hebrew tradition to explain why truth is considered the ultimate human virtue.</meta>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...truth: *Seekers of truth seek God, aided by God, and find light by the help of light*, etc. However, concerning what is said here and by St. Jerome: that men are made like and near to God **BY TRUTH ALONE**, we should not imagine that this excludes beneficence <note>Doing good works or acts of kindness.</note>. For it is well known, and we read elsewhere, that doing good is also the means by which we men approach most closely to the divine nature. Strabo says in Book 10 of his *Geography*: <note>original Greek: Ἐὖ μὲν γὰρ εἴρηται καὶ τοῦτο, τοὺς ἀνθρώπους μάλιστα μιμεῖσθαι τοὺς θεοὺς, ὅταν εὐεργετῶσιν· ἄμεινον δ' ἂν λέγοι τις, ὅταν εὐδαιμονῶσι.</note> "For it has been well said that men most resemble the gods when they do good; but one might say even better, when they are happy."

The Pythagoreans themselves also confessed this. Since they had observed three ways by which a man might be made better than himself, they established the middle way as the pursuit of doing good. Thus writes an unknown author of a life of Pythagoras, found in Photius on page 712, whose words I will add below among the various sayings of Pythagoras.

-> **From God** ] I believe it should read **With God**, <-
<note>The author is suggesting a grammatical correction to the Greek text from "Παρά τοῦ θεοῦ" (from God) to "παρά τῷ θεῷ" (with/beside God).</note>

**Oromasdes** ] John Stobaeus, in his eleventh Discourse *On Truth*, reports the same proverb from an unknown author: but in his work it is read as *Oromagdes*. <note>original Greek: Ὠρομάγδην</note> Pythagoras, when asked what men do that makes them like God, said: "If they speak the truth." <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόρας ἐρωτηθεὶς, τί ποιοῦσιν ἄνθρωποι θεῷ ὅμοιον, ἔφη· Ἐὰν ἀληθεύωσιν.</note> The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or sages.</note> declare that the greatest of the gods, whom they call Oromagdes, resembles light in his body and truth in his soul. <note>original Greek: Οἱ δὲ μάγοι ἀποφαίνονται τοῦ μεγίστου τῶν θεῶν, ὃν Ὠρωμάγδην καλοῦσιν, ἐοικέναι τὸ μὲν σῶμα φωτί· τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἀληθείᾳ.</note> But it should be corrected to *Oromasdes*. <note>original Greek: Ὠρομάσδην</note> In Agathias, Book 2 of the *History of Justinian*, page 58 of the Greek edition by Bonaventure Vulcanius, this is the surname of Zoroaster, or Zaradas: *Zoroaster son of Ormasdes*. <note>original Greek: Ζωροάστρου τοῦ Ὀρμάσδεως</note> Those learned in Eastern languages derive the name from *Ur chasdim*, which is said to mean *fire of the Chaldeans*, or *holy fire*, which the Chaldeans worshiped as a god because they had learned from the Holy Fathers that sacrifices were kindled by fire falling from heaven. He is also named Orimasda in Plutarch’s lives of *Alexander* and *Artaxerxes*. From this, the name was also given to men among the Persians: Hormisdas, or Ormista. See Paul Orosius and the *Tripartite History*, Book 10, chapter 31. Indeed, even among the Roman Popes there was one by this name: Hormisdas, around the year 514 AD. Furthermore, regarding what the Persian Magi thought—that the greatest god was like light in body and truth in soul—they seem to have drawn this from the *Urim* and *Thummim* of the Hebrews, by which Light and Truth are designated. However, they did not correctly assert that God has a body and a soul, which is the error of the <term>Anthropomorphites</term> <note>A group of early Christians who were accused of heresy for believing that God possesses a physical human body.</note>.

<summary>In this commentary, Rittershusius discusses the Pythagorean and Persian belief that truth-telling and doing good are the primary ways humans emulate the divine. He traces the name of the Persian deity Oromasdes (Ahura Mazda) through various Greek historians and links the Persian concepts of light and truth to the Hebrew Urim and Thummim.</summary>

### ON PORPHYRY

To this passage where Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus, meaning "king." Rittershusius uses the names interchangeably.</note> comments on that truth, there is conveniently offered a most excellent Alcaic ode <note>A lyrical verse form consisting of four-line stanzas, named after the Greek poet Alcaeus.</note> on the same subject. It was very recently published in Paris by the most distinguished Lord Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>A famous French historian, book collector, and statesman (1553–1617).</note>, President and Royal Counselor. I shall insert it here, as it seems it will add a great ornament to this little work, while also bringing remarkable utility and pleasure to its readers. Thus, the Parisian copy reads:

->*T R U T H*<-
<note>original Greek: ΑΛΗΘΕΙΑ</note>

>*Beloved of heaven, radiant Truth,*
>*Hated on earth, daunting Truth,*
>  *O goddess, where do you flee,*
>    *The anchor and fortress of the imperiled and the innocent?*
>*Shall I follow you as you withdraw*
>*Through the pathless, snowy Alps,*
>  *Over the inhospitable ridges of Rhodope <note>A mountain range in the Balkans.</note>,*
>    *Or through the sharp, high wilderness of the Pyrenees?*
>*Or shall I, a traveler, seek the seas*
>*Teeming with scaly monsters,*
>  *And the lands scattered wide in the Atlantic surge,*
>    *Or the Indians scorched by a changing sun?*
>*Wherever it is granted to take wandering steps,*
>*Wherever it is lawful to turn focused eyes,*
>  *You are nowhere; blind darkness has seized all things,*
>    *And a heavy decay has occupied everything,*
>*As soon as you withdrew your foot*
>*From this injurious soil. Whither do you hasten?*
>  *If it is denied to mingle prayers in your presence,*
>    *Be present, mild one, to him who calls from afar.*
>*O Goddess, leader to minds deprived of light,*
>*You scatter the clouds of deceptions*
>  *Which stand in the way, and you provide safe passage*
>    *Through the shadows, over the rough paths of ignorance,*
>*Lest the wretched fall, their hearts*
>*Broken by a panic terror;*
>  *Nor should they shake off from a just neck*
>    *The yoke of a ruler with stubborn defiance.*
>*Lest they deny the watchful divinity over us,*
>*Thinking all things are carried by an uncertain impulse,*
>  *With Fortune rolling our labors*
>    *And shifting the turns of affairs.*
>*You [uncover] the hidden [snares] of viper-like Slander...*

### ON PORPHYRY.

*The tossing wave of opinions in the deep,*
*Religious faith, struck by north-westerly winds, groans.*
*And everywhere the sacred bonds of charity*
*Lie scattered and profaned.*
*With an avenging hand, cut off the horns*
*Of the wanton, spiteful beast,*

*Which seizes all things; and from secluded minds*

*And a short hour will release those who have*
*Finished life’s dangers and served their time.*

**And thus far the "Truth" of de Thou <note>original: "Ἀλήθεια Thuani." Jacques Auguste de Thou was a contemporary of the author and a famous historian.</note>.**

**"He used to say that the sea was a tear" <note>original Greek: Τὴν θάλατταν μὲν ἐκάλει εἶναι δάκρυον</note>]** It seems that Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who viewed the world as a struggle between Love and Strife.</note> drew his own idea from this, when he called the sea the *sweat of the earth:* which Aristotle, in the second book of his *Meteorology*, chapter 3, criticized as being <gloss>unclear and metaphorical</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀσαφὲς καὶ μεταφορικὸν</note>. Aristotle says: "Similarly, it is ridiculous if someone, saying that the sea is the sweat of the earth, thinks he has said something clear, just as Empedocles did. For perhaps such a statement is sufficient for poetry—since metaphor is a poetic device—but it is not sufficient for understanding nature. For even here it is not clear how salty sweat is produced from a sweet drink, *etc.*" Of the same kind seems to be his calling wine "water rotted in wood," that is, "cooked" water: as in his own verse, which Plutarch has preserved for us:

->**Wine is water from the bark, rotted in wood.**<-
<note>original Greek: Οἶνος ἀπὸ φλοιοῦ πέλεται σαπὲν ἐν ξύλῳ ὕδωρ.</note>

**"The Nature of the Symbols" <note>original Greek: Εἶδος τῶν Συμβόλων</note>]** Before we illustrate the Pythagorean Symbols cited here by Malchus <note>Another name for Porphyry.</note> or Porphyry by comparing them to other authors who have dealt with the same subject, I will set forth two points to be observed above all: one regarding the origin of the Symbols, the other regarding their interpretation. As for the origin, they are indeed from the Egyptians. For Pythagoras borrowed from them "the method of teaching through symbols" <note>original Greek: τὴν διὰ συμβόλων διδασκαλίαν</note>, that is, the symbolic way of teaching, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note> testifies in chapter 5 of his *Life of Pythagoras*, in addition to Clement of Alexandria: *He attempted to make his style of teaching symbolic, and in every way similar to the teachings in Egypt in which he had been educated.* <note>original Greek: Τὸν τῆς διδασκαλίας τρόπον συμβολικὸν ποιεῖν ἐπεχείρει, καὶ πάντη ὅμοιον τοῖς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ διδάγμασι κατ᾿ ἐπαιδεύθη.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry’s biography of Pythagoras. While the previous page discussed the metaphorical description of the sea, this page transitions into the interpretation of the famous Pythagorean "symbols"—short, enigmatic moral precepts that require allegorical explanation to be understood correctly.</meta>

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

I think we should read "according to which" <note>original Greek: καθ' ἃ, vel καθ' ὃν</note> so that it refers either to the "teachings" or the "manner." Or perhaps we should read "by the teachings in which he was educated" <note>original Greek: διδάγμασιν, ἃ ἐπαιδεύθη</note>? See the same Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous life of Pythagoras.</note> in chapter 23, where we should read "by a clear expression" <note>original Greek: διαρθρώσει</note> or "he might express clearly" instead of "clear expressions"; and "of a model" instead of "a model." Furthermore, the entire interpretation by Frisius <note>Lambertus Danaeus Frisius, a 16th-century scholar.</note> in that passage is worth nothing, as is the case elsewhere throughout his work. 

We must then be warned about the proper interpretation of the **symbols**; for unless this is added, the symbols themselves will differ very little from <gloss>old wives' tales</gloss> and will be plainly ridiculous. Iamblichus repeats and emphasizes this point three times, and not without cause: namely in chapters 23 and 32, as well as in the final chapter of his *Protrepticus* <note>term: Protrepticus — An "exhortation" or introductory book designed to encourage students to take up the study of philosophy.</note> on page 131. A comparison of these passages shows that the first mentioned chapter should be read as follows: *“And unless someone, having selected these symbols, should unfold them and embrace them with a blameless explanation, the things said would seem ridiculous and like old women's talk to those who encounter them, being full of nonsense and idle chatter.”* <note>original Greek: Καὶ εἰ μή τις αὐτὰ τὰ σύμβολα ἐκλέξας διαπτύξειε...</note> In that same place, instead of "bright and pure," I suspect we should read "clear and distinct instead of obscure." And shortly after, instead of "to reveal," read "he reveals." 

Then, in the final chapter of the *Protrepticus*, page 131, I assert the entire passage should be restored thus: *“And unless someone, having selected these symbols, should unfold them and embrace them with a blameless explanation, the things said would seem ridiculous and like old women's talk to those who encounter them [rather than ‘to them’], being full of nonsense and idle chatter. Therefore, so that useful things [rather than ‘possessions’] might be revealed,”* etc. Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist who often looked for links between Greek philosophy and Christian truth.</note> testifies to the same thing in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, page 14: *“But Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, who set out the doctrines of his own philosophy mystically through symbols, as those who have written his life show, himself appears to think things worthy of his journey to Egypt concerning the one God,”* etc.

***Of such things***] This should be restored to *of such a kind*, as it appears in the manuscript.

***Do not overstep the balance***] <note>original Greek: Ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν</note> Saint Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father.</note> recounted the first few symbols with their expositions in the same order and with the same words, up to the 11th (which begins, “And to make libations,” etc.), omitting only two in the middle, namely the 6th and 7th, in Book IX of *Against Julian the Apostate*. I will transcribe the version by Oecolompadius <note>Johannes Oecolompadius, a Protestant Reformer and translator.</note> from the Basel edition: 

*“Pythagoras does not despise enigmatic manifestation, but highly prizes it, as Porphyry says of him in the first book of the history of philosophy. There was also another kind of symbol such as: **Do not overstep the balance** <note>term: balance — The Greek 'zygon' refers to the cross-bar of a weighing scale, symbolizing justice and moderation.</note>: that is, Do not be greedy. **Do not poke the fire with a sword**: which meant, Do not provoke an impudent and angry mind with harsh words. And, **Do not pluck the crown**: that is, Do not offend the laws. For the ‘crowns’ of cities were, of course, their laws. Besides these and certain others: **Do not eat your heart**: i.e., Do not consume yourself with worries.”*

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of allegorical interpretation for Pythagorean symbols, arguing that without a "key," these moral precepts appear nonsensical. Rittershusius cites both Neoplatonists and Christian Fathers to show that these riddles contain serious ethical and theological lessons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry’s biography of Pythagoras. Having previously warned that the Pythagorean "symbols" (enigmatic maxims) require careful allegorical interpretation to avoid appearing ridiculous, Rittershusius now proceeds to provide specific examples and their meanings, drawing on various Church Fathers and classical authors.</meta>

### ON PORPHYRY.

***Do not sit upon a bushel (or a grain-measure)***: <note>original Latin: *Ne super choenicem (vel modium) sedeas*</note> that is, *Do not live idly.* ***Swallows are not to be received into the house***: that is, loquacious people and those with an uncontrolled tongue should not be made housemates. And, ***A burden should be placed upon those already carrying one, but it should not be taken off at the same time***: by which he warns that one ought not to assist anyone in laziness, but rather in virtues and labors. ***Do not wear the images of the gods on rings***: that is, do not easily reveal or divulge your opinion and discourse concerning the gods. These interpretations are from Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note>, and it would be worthwhile to read the preceding and following sections in his ninth book *Against Julian*. For he provides memorable details there concerning the hieroglyphic writings of the Egyptians, which I would wish to be added to what I noted above. Does not this passage of Cyril also most clearly confirm my conjecture proposed above regarding the author of this little book—that he is Porphyry himself, who, according to Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>, had the surname *Basileus*, or rather *Malchus*? <note>Malchus was Porphyry's original Semitic name, meaning "King," which was translated into the Greek *Basileus*.</note> In my mind, at least, it confirms it most strongly.

Furthermore, the fact that Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius, a Protestant Reformer and humanist scholar.</note>, in his explanation of the second symbol, translates the word for ***swelling*** <note>original Greek: τὸν ἀνοιδοῦντα</note> as "impudent," is worthy of notice and remark. For it seems he either read the word for ***shameless*** <note>original Greek: ἀναιδοῦντα</note> in his own manuscript, or certainly had it in mind. But we must retain the word for ***swelling***, which means *turgid*; or, as Saint Jerome translates it in his *Apology against Rufinus*, *puffed up* <note>original Latin: *tumidum*</note>. It should also be noted from the aforementioned passage of Cyril that Porphyry wrote several books regarding the *Life* or *History of Pythagoras*. For he says, "in the first book of the history." Therefore, there must have been at least two books, following the legal argument that where there is a "number," there is more than one. <note>original Latin: *argum. l. 12. Vbi numerus. D. de Testibus.* Rittershusius is citing a principle from Roman Law (the Digest) to prove that "Book 1" implies a "Book 2."</note> From this it is gathered that not only is this first book by Malchus (or Porphyry), which we are now publishing for the first time, mutilated and imperfect at the end, but the entire second book has perished.

Again: ***Do not step over the balance (the scales).*** <note>original Greek: Ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν</note> Saint Jerome, in his *Apology against Rufinus* which I have praised so often, translates: *Do not leap over the scales*, that is, *Do not overstep justice.* Athenaeus, in his tenth book, explains it more fully: *To flee and loathe all greed, and to seek equality.* Plutarch, in his work *On the Education of Children*, says: *That one must make much account of justice and not overstep it.* Clement of Alexandria, in the fifth book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original Latin: *Stromat.* (Stromata)</note>, page 239, explains it thus: *That is, not to bypass equality in distributions, honoring justice; equality binds friends to friends, cities to cities, and allies to allies. For equality is natural law for men.*

<meta>This page continues Conrad Rittershusius’s philological commentary on the symbolic maxims of Pythagoras. The previous page discussed symbols related to idleness (sitting on a bushel), gossip (swallows), and assisting others in their labors. This page focuses on symbols concerning justice (the yoke/balance) and anger (poking fire with a sword), while also critiquing previous scholars who attempted to find forced parallels between these pagan maxims and Christian scripture.</meta>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

"The lesser is always an enemy to the greater, and it leads the way to a day of enmity," <note>original Greek: πλέονι δ’ αἰεὶ πολέμιον καθίσταται τοὔλασσον, ἐχθρᾶς θ’ ἡμέρας κατάρχεται</note> according to the poetic grace. The verses he cites are those of Euripides in the *Phoenissae*. <note>A tragedy by Euripides centered on the conflict between the sons of Oedipus.</note> However, when the same most learned writer subsequently compares this Pythagorean Symbol with the words of Christ: *Take my yoke upon me, for it is good and not heavy* <note>original Greek: Ἄρατε τὸν ζυγόν μου, ὅτι χρηστός ἐστι καὶ ἀβαρὴς. A reference to Matthew 11:29-30.</note>, if I am to say what I truly feel, it is a foreign comparison—a cold and inept adaptation. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note>, at the end of chapter 30, says: **Do not overstep the yoke (the balance)** <note>original Greek: Τὸν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν</note> is an exhortation to justice, commanding one to practice all things that are just. The same author in the last chapter of his *Exhortation to Philosophy* says: It commands us to act justly, and to honor equality and moderation in a wonderful way; it teaches that justice is the most perfect virtue, which the others complete and without which the others are of no use. One must not know this virtue superficially, but through contemplation and scientific proof. This is the work of no other art or science except for the philosophy of Pythagoras alone, which especially prizes mathematics above all else. Diogenes Laertius, in book VIII, page 578, adds this explanation to our symbol: that is, **not to overstep the equal and the just.**

**Do not poke the fire with a sword** <note>original Greek: Μὴ τὸ πῦρ τῇ μαχαίρᾳ σκαλεύειν</note>] Saint Jerome, in his *Apology against Rufinus*, writes: *Do not dig into the fire with a sword*: meaning, do not provoke an angry and swollen mind with cursing words. Theodoretus also mentions this in his 8th Sermon *To the Greeks*, but he does not explain it. Athenaeus, in the aforementioned book X, says: **One should not quarrel with an enraged man.** For anger is the fire, and the quarrel is the sword. Plutarch, in the same place as mentioned before, says: **Do not irritate one who is angry.** For it is not fitting; rather, one should yield to those who are in a rage. Iamblichus says: **Do not poke the fire with a sword** is an exhortation to prudence. For it awakens in us the proper thought that one should not oppose sharp words to a man full of fire and anger, nor should one quarrel. For often through your words you will stir up the ignorant person, and disturb him, and you will suffer terrible and unpleasant things. Heraclitus is a witness to these sayings. For he says: **It is hard to fight with passion.** <note>original Greek: Θυμῷ γὰρ, φησὶ, μάχεσθαι χαλεπόν</note> For whatever it wants to happen, it buys at the cost of the soul. And he spoke this truly. For many, by indulging their anger, have traded away their own souls and made death more welcome. From the act of restraining the tongue and remaining quiet, friendship arises out of strife, as the fire of anger is extinguished; and you yourself will not appear to be a fool. Although this saying of Heraclitus praised here by Iamblichus is not found in his extant letters, it is nevertheless famous from the citations of Aristotle, such as in book II of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, chapters 3 and 2; likewise in chapters 7 and 5, and in the *Politics*, book XI: **It is hard to fight with passion.** For the soul...

<summary>This page analyzes two Pythagorean symbols: "Do not overstep the yoke" (signifying justice and equality) and "Do not poke the fire with a sword" (warning against provoking angry people). Rittershusius critiques anachronistic Christian interpretations while drawing on a wide range of classical authors like Iamblichus, Plutarch, and Aristotle to explain the moral philosophy behind the enigmas.</summary>

...soul—for it buys [its desire at that price]. <note>original Greek: χῆς—γὰρ ὠνεῖται. This is the conclusion of a famous fragment by Heraclitus: "It is hard to fight with anger; for whatever it wants, it buys at the price of the soul."</note> A similar sentiment belongs to Democritus in Stobaeus, <note>Joannes Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved extracts from many Greek authors.</note> under the title *On Anger*: "To fight with anger is indeed difficult; but it is the mark of a well-reasoned man to conquer it." <note>original Greek: Θυμῷ μάχεσθαι μὲν χαλεπόν· ἀνδρὸς δὲ, τὸ κρατέειν, εὐλογίστον</note> The translator Frisius <note>Likely a reference to a previous Latin translator of these texts.</note> did not grasp the force of this most elegant maxim when he translated it thus: *Let Heraclitus be a witness with his words. For he says it is difficult to fight with anger. For whatever use demands it to be, that is profitable for the mind.* However, *oneisthai* <note>original Greek: Ὠνεῖσθαι</note> means "to buy" or "to purchase," not "to be profitable." And how could it be profitable for the mind, when an angry man would not hesitate to pay his own life, like a price, to obtain his desire?

Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> says in the aforementioned passage: "He also intended that one should not poke the fire with a sword, meaning one should not stir up the anger of rulers or a swelling heart." <note>original Greek: Ἤθελε δὲ αὐτῷ τὸ πῦρ μαχαίρᾳ μὴ σκαλεύειν, δυναστῶν ὀργὴν καὶ οἰδοῦντα θυμὸν μὴ κινεῖν</note>

**Do not pluck the crown** <note>original Greek: Στέφανόν τε μὴ τίλλειν</note>] Saint Jerome says in the same passage: *The crown is by no means to be plucked: that is, the laws of the cities are to be preserved.*

**Do not eat the heart** (perhaps *the heart* in the singular) <note>original Greek: Μὴ καρδίας (forte καρδίαν) ἐσθίειν</note>] Jerome in the same place: *The heart is not to be eaten: that is, sorrow is to be cast out from the mind.* Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata*, <note>Clement's "Miscellanies," a work of early Christian philosophy.</note> Book 5: "For envy, jealousy, and grief stand outside the divine chorus; or rather, the initiates forbid 'eating the heart,' teaching that one should never, through laziness or pains, bite and devour the soul because of things that happen against one's will." <note>original Greek: Φθόνος γὰρ ἔξω θείου χοροῦ ἵσταται... καὶ κατεσθίειν τὴν ψυχήν</note> Certainly wretched was that man whom even Homer says wandered alone, "eating his own heart." <note>Refers to the hero Bellerophon in the Iliad, who wandered the Aleian plain in grief.</note> Athenaeus in Book 10 explains this as "practicing freedom from sorrow." Plutarch in *On the Education of Children*: "Do not harm the soul by wearing it out with cares." <note>original Greek: Μὴ βλάπτειν τὴν ψυχὴν, ταῖς φροντίσιν αὐτὴν κατατρύχοντα</note> Iamblichus in Chapter 24: "He legislated for them the same thing: not to eat the heart, and not to eat the brain; and the Pythagoreans were to abstain from these entirely. For these are the ruling parts, and as it were the steps and seats of thinking and of living. He consecrated these because of the nature of the divine Word." <note>original Greek: Ἐνομοθέτησε δὲ τοῖς αὐτοῖς... διὰ τὴν τοῦ θείου λόγου φύσιν. Here, "divine Word" refers to the Logos or rational principle.</note> In Chapter 21 of the same work: "The phrase 'Do not eat the heart' means that one must not tear apart the unity of the whole and its shared harmony. And even more so: do not be envious, but rather philanthropic and social. From this, he exhorts us to practice philosophy. For philosophy alone of the sciences and arts neither grieves at the good of others, nor rejoices in the misfortunes of neighbors—since it shows that all humans are by nature kindred and house-mates, sharing the same passions and subject to a common fate, with an unpredictable future hanging over all equally. Therefore, it commands us to be sympathetic and to love one another, and to be a truly social and rational animal." Diogenes Laertius on page 579: "By the phrase 'Do not eat the heart,' he indicated that one should not waste away the soul with distress <note>original Greek: ἀνίαις; Rittershusius notes that some editions incorrectly print 'follies' (ἀνοίαις) here.</note> and grief."

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

**Do not receive swallows into your house]** <note>original Greek: Μηδὲ χελιδόνας ἐν οἰκίᾳ δέχεσθαι</note> *St. Jerome says in the passage mentioned: "A swallow should not be received into the house; that is, talkative and wordy men should not be kept under the same roof."* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 5, page 238: "Immediately following the 'barbarian' philosophy <note>Clement often used 'barbarian' to refer to non-Greek sources of wisdom, particularly the Hebrew or Egyptian traditions.</note> are the Pythagorean symbols, which are very deeply hidden. Thus the Samian <note>Pythagoras, who was a native of the island of Samos.</note> advises not to have a swallow in the house; that is, not to receive a talkative, whispering, and forward-tongued person. For the swallow and the turtle-dove, birds of the field, 'know the times of their coming,' as the Scripture says, <note>Jeremiah 8:7</note> and one should never live with idle chatter. Indeed, the cooing turtle-dove, displaying an ungrateful murmuring of complaint, is rightly cast out. 'Lest you chirp at me, sitting here one after another.' <note>A poetic fragment, likely from a lost comedy, mocking those who chatter like birds.</note> The swallow, however, either hints at the myth of Pandion <note>A reference to the tragic myth of Philomela and Procne, daughters of Pandion, who were transformed into birds after a cycle of vengeance involving Procne's husband, Tereus.</note>—it is right to avoid the passions spoken of regarding that story, from which we have received that Tereus suffered some things and did others—or it is because it chases the musical cicadas. Thus, the persecutor of reason is rightly pushed away. 'And regarding the scepter-bearing Hera watching over Olympus, I have a faithful storehouse upon my tongue,' as the poet says. And Aeschylus: 'But I have a key as a guardian upon my tongue.'" Iamblichus, *Symbol XXII*, page 150: "The advice 'do not receive a swallow in the house' counsels: do not admit a lazy person, or one who does not work continuously, nor an unstable partisan or acquaintance into your doctrines. For these doctrines require continuous and most intense attention and endurance, because of the <gloss>perhaps "the"</gloss> <note>original Greek: forte τὴν. The editor suggests 'the' (singular) instead of 'of the' (plural) for grammatical clarity.</note> varied transformation and complexity within them. He uses the swallow as an image of laziness and an interruption of time, because this bird visits us for only one part of the year, and as it were, stays as a guest for a short time. But for the greater part, it stays away and is unseen by us." Diogenes Laertius, page 578: "Do not have swallows sharing your roof." <note>original Greek: Ὁμοροφίους χελιδόνας μὴ ἔχειν</note>

One should note here the ancient custom of women, who used to drive swallows out of houses by rubbing them with ointment. See, among others, Theodoret, *Second Sermon on the Beginning.*

**Help people load a burden, but do not help them unload it.]** <note>original Greek: Φορτία συνανάτιθέναι μὲν τοῖς βαστάζουσιν· συγκαθαιρεῖν δὲ μή.</note> *St. Jerome, in the said Apology: "A burden should be placed upon those already loaded; one should not share with those putting it down: that is, precepts should be increased for those proceeding toward virtue; those handing themselves over to idleness should be left behind."* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book I, page 118: "In the Laws, Plato—the philosopher of Hebrew descent <note>Clement famously claimed that Plato and other Greeks borrowed their best ideas from Moses; he here refers to the 'Hebrew' character of Plato's logic.</note>—commands that farmers should not irrigate their land nor take water from others unless they have first dug on their own land down to what is called the 'virgin soil' <note>term: 'virgin soil' (parthenios), a geological layer that indicates a total lack of groundwater.</note> and found the earth to be waterless. For it is not just to help except in cases of actual need;" (Thus it is published; but either the negative particle "not" should be deleted:
