...or as it should be read according to our friend David Hoeschelius <note>David Hoeschel (1556–1617) was a noted German humanist and editor of Greek texts.</note>, "not to provide, not just.") It is not good to provide for idleness; although Pythagoras said it is reasonable to help someone put on a load, but it is not fitting to help them take it off. Iamblichus, in his *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original Greek: Προτρεπτικός (Protreptikos)</note>, Symbol XI, page 141, explains how this teaching kindles one's own "eye of the mind" toward contemplation, perhaps by instilling something new like a grafting farmer, or by stirring up what is already within. He writes: "To help lift a load together, but not to help lay it down, encourages courage. For everyone lifting up a load signifies an act of labor and energy; but he who lays it down signifies rest and relaxation. So this symbol has the following reasoning: Do not be the cause of laziness or a soft lifestyle, neither for yourself nor for another. For every thing is attainable by labor." The Pythagoreans called this symbol "Herculean" <note>original: Ἡράκλειον</note>, sealing it in honor of the deeds of Hercules. For when he lived among men, he often returned from fire and all the most terrible dangers, rejecting hesitation. Success comes from doing and working, but not from shrinking away. The same Iamblichus reports this Symbol more fully in this manner: *Help a man who is lifting up a load; do not help one who is laying it down.* The same author in chapter 18 says: *Do not help take down a load; for one must not be the cause of a lack of labor; but help lift it up.* Diogenes Laërtius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> on page 578 records it as: *To help take down a load, and not to help put it on.* If this reading is true, it contains a completely opposite meaning: *Namely, that one should help someone laying down a burden, but not help impose a burden on one who takes it up.* But perhaps this Diogenes also needs to be corrected by the work of other writers, as is the case elsewhere.

### Nothing according to ease]
I suspect it should be read "one must not" <note>original: μὴ δεῖν</note>; as it is written above: "as one must not live idly."

### Do not wear images of the gods in rings]
Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note>, Book 5 of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: Stromata</note>, page 239, says: "Pythagoras cautions not to wear a ring, nor to engrave images of the gods on them. Just as Moses long ago explicitly legislated that no sculpted or painted statue or likeness should be made; so that we do not cling to things of the senses, but pass over to things of the intellect <note>In Platonic and Pythagorean thought, "intellectual" or "intelligible" things are the eternal truths perceived by the mind, as opposed to "sensible" things perceived by the body.</note>. For the habit of having the divine ready for the eyes cheapens its majesty. To worship the intelligible essence through physical matter is to dishonor it through the senses. For this reason, even the wisest of the Egyptian priests set apart the seat of Athena in the open air, just as the Hebrews established their temple without a statue," etc.

<summary>This page explores the Pythagorean virtues of industry and spiritual focus, using the "burden" symbol to advocate for hard work and the "ring" symbol to argue against physical idols in favor of mental contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Iamblichus, Hercules, labor vs. idleness, Diogenes Laërtius, Clement of Alexandria, Moses, aniconism, spiritual contemplation vs. physical senses</keywords>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

**Just as Clement joins two related Symbols together**, so also does Iamblichus in his *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original: Protrepticus</note>, Symbols 23 and 24. Regarding the rule, **Do not wear a ring**, let us take it according to the Pythagorean preference as an exhortation in this way: since a ring surrounds those who wear it in the manner of a bond, having the unique quality of not strangling or causing distress, but somehow fitting and being naturally attached; such a bond is also the body to the soul. Therefore, the phrase, **Do not wear a ring**, means to truly practice philosophy <gloss>perhaps read: "practice philosophy" as a command</gloss> and separate the soul from the bond that surrounds it. For philosophy is the practice of death and the separation of the soul from the body. Pursue the Pythagorean study, then, with great zeal—the study which draws itself away through the mind from all bodily things, and occupies itself with the intellectual and immaterial through theoretical studies. But also release <gloss>perhaps read: "release"</gloss> yourself from your sins, and from the distractions of the flesh that pull back and hinder the practice of philosophy, such as excessive foods and untimely fullness, which seize the body like a bond and unceasingly produce sickness and lack of leisure.

**Regarding the rule, Do not engrave the image of God on a ring**, it uses the following exhortation according to the previously mentioned sense: practice philosophy, and believe above all that the gods are incorporeal. For this is the most important root of Pythagorean teachings—that is <gloss>I read this as two words: "this is"</gloss>—from which almost everything depends, and by which it is strengthened until the end. Do not think that they [the gods] use forms that are bodily; nor that they are received in a material substance, or as if in a material body as a bond, like other living creatures. The engravings in <gloss>perhaps the word "in" is missing</gloss> rings show the bond through the ring itself, as well as the bodiliness, the perceptible form, and the sculpted appearance of something like a specific living creature. The race of the gods must be separated from this appearance most of all, as they are eternal and intellectual, remaining the same and in the same way always, as is discussed specifically and most fully in the treatise *On God*.

*The same author says in the Life of Pythagoras, chapter 18, number 84:* **Do not carry the mark of a god's image in a ring, so that** <gloss>it seems the word "not" is missing</gloss> **it might not be defiled; for it is an image which must be planted in the house** (this is a corrupt passage, which Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius (1538–1604) was a Frisian scholar and editor of Iamblichus’s work.</note> passed over in silence).

**And to make libations to the gods by the 'ear' of the cups]** Iamblichus, chapter 18: To pour libations to the gods by the ear <note>The "ear" of a cup refers to its handle.</note> of the cup for the sake of an omen, and so that one does not drink from that same part.

<margin>43</margin> **He advised abstaining from beans]** Pythagoras says this of himself in Lucian's *Sale of Lives* <note>original: βίων πράσει (Vitarum Auctio), a satirical work by Lucian of Samosata where various philosophical lives are auctioned off.</note>, when he is questioned by a buyer—

# ON PORPHYRY,

...the interrogator asks, "And what is the manner of your diet?" <note>original: Τὰ δ' ἀμφὶ δίαιταν ὁποῖός τις εἶ;</note> that is: *in what manner do you sustain yourself?* He answers him in these words: "I eat nothing that possesses a soul; and of all other things, I eat anything except beans." <note>original: Ψυχῆϊον μὲν οὐδὲ ἕν τι σιτέομαι· τὰ δ' ἀλλα, πλὴν κυάμων.</note> But here, I see first that there is no consensus among all authors as to what Pythagoras wished to be understood by the name of "beans" when he commanded that they must be abstained from. Secondly, different reasons for this prohibition are provided by different people. There are those who think that Pythagoras himself abstained, and forbade his followers from eating beans—or (to speak playfully with Aulus Gellius) "bean-lets"—because this type of legume is not only excessively nourishing but also flatulent <term>flatulentum</term>, and it "pours darkness over the mind" <note>original: menti tenebras offundat</note>. For this same reason, they also abstained from eating living creatures. Thus, that anonymous writer of the life of Pythagoras found in Photius, page 713 of the *Library*, states: "Such foods (animal flesh) thicken the mind, being more nourishing and creating a heavy distribution in the body. For this reason, they also stayed away from the bean, because it is gassy and extremely nourishing; and they provide several other reasons which led them to abstain from beans." <note>original: Ὅτι τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν βρωμάτων (τὰ ἔμψυχα) παχύνει τὸν νοῦν... κ.τ.λ.</note> Pliny, besides the dulling of the senses and the causing of insomnia, brings forward another reason according to the opinion of others. Both of these reasons for the prohibition of eating beans can be understood from his words, which I shall transcribe from Book 18, Chapter 12: "The bean has a manifold use for every kind of four-footed animal, and especially for man. It is even mixed with grain among most nations, and especially with millet, whether whole or more delicately crushed. Moreover, by ancient rite, 'bean-mash' <term>fabacia</term> is offered in the sacred rites of his religion to the gods, being a substantial pottage; yet it is thought to dull the senses and cause bad dreams. For these reasons, the Pythagorean sentence condemned it; or as others have passed down, because the souls of the dead are within it; for which reason it is certainly used in making offerings to the deceased. Varro also reports that for these reasons the Flamen <note>A high-ranking Roman priest</note> does not eat it, because mournful letters <note>Patterns on the bean flower thought to look like letters of lamentation</note> are found in its flower. In this same plant there is a peculiar religious dread. For it is the custom to bring back a bean from the harvest for the sake of an omen, which is therefore called 'the retriever' <note>original: refrina; the author suggests reading referina</note>. It is also thought to be profitable to use it at auctions. It is certainly the only one of the crops that, even when eaten away, refills itself as the moon waxes," etc. Diogenes Laërtius, on page 588, citing Aristotle's book *On Beans*, brings forward five reasons for this rule: "That he commanded to abstain from beans either because they are like genitals; or because they are like the gates of Hades (for it is the only plant without joints); or because it is destructive; or because it is similar to the nature of the universe; or because it is oligarchic, since they are used in casting lots." <note>original: Παραγγέλλειν αὐτὸν ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν κυάμων... κ.τ.λ. — The 'oligarchic' reference relates to the use of beans as ballots in elections.</note> The same Laërtius on page 582 says: "He forbade touching beans (I think it should read 'abstaining from'), because they are windy and..."

<summary>This page explores the diverse historical and philosophical justifications for the Pythagorean prohibition against eating beans, citing authorities like Pliny, Varro, and Aristotle. The reasons range from biological effects (flatulence and mental dullness) to mystical associations with the souls of the dead and political symbolism.</summary>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...to participate more fully in the soulful; and otherwise to make the stomach more orderly when beans are not consumed, and because of this, to render the visions seen in sleep smooth and undisturbed. <note>original: λον μετέχειν τοῦ ψυχικοῦ... κ.τ.λ.</note> Similarly, Cicero writes in Book 2 of *On Divination*: *Pythagoras and Plato, most eminent authors, command that we go to sleep prepared by a certain diet and way of life so that we may see more certain things in our dreams. The Pythagoreans strictly abstained from the bean, as if the mind—rather than the belly—is inflated by that food. But somehow, nothing can be said that is so absurd that it has not been said by some philosopher, etc.* <note>original: Pythagoras et Plato locupletissimi auctores... etc.</note> Aulus Gellius recorded this same passage of Cicero in Book 4, chapter 11, but in far different words. I believe this happened because, trusting his own memory, he did not look up Cicero's text nor count his exact words. He says it thus: *Plato therefore orders that one go to sleep with the body in such a state that there is nothing to bring error or disturbance to the mind. For this reason, it is thought that the Pythagoreans were forbidden from eating the bean, a thing which causes great flatulence. It is well known that this food is contrary to the tranquility of the mind, etc.* <note>original: Iubet igitur Plato sic ad somnum proficisci... etc.</note> Plutarch, however, in his book *On the Education of Children*, explains the phrase "abstain from beans" <note>original: τὸ κυάμων ἀπέχεσθαι</note> this way: *One must not engage in politics. For in former times, voting was done with beans, by which terms of office were brought to an end.* <note>original: Οὐ δεῖ πολιτεύεσθαι... κ.τ.λ.</note> Iamblichus says in chapter 24: *Abstain from beans for many sacred, natural, and soul-related reasons.* <note>original: Κυάμων ἀπέχου... κ.τ.λ.</note> (Where a little further on in the text it was published as: "and beginning through food, to lead men to virtue" <note>original: καὶ διὰ τῆς τροφῆς ἀρχόμενος, εἰς ἀρετὴν δηγεῖν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους</note>, I correct this in passing to "he led" <note>original: ὡδήγει</note>, for the previous verb "he established laws" <note>original: διεθεσμοθέτησε</note> was in the past tense.) The same Iamblichus in the last chapter of his *Exhortation*, Symbol 37, says: *The command to "abstain from beans" advises one to guard against everything that is destructive* (perhaps it should be read as "is destructive") *to communication with the gods and to divine prophecy.* <note>original: Τὸ δὲ, κυάμων ἀπέχου... κ.τ.λ.</note> But Lucian also, in the place mentioned above, introduces Pythagoras responding to a merchant's question as to *why he so abhors beans* in this way: *I do not actually abhor or hate them; but because they are sacred and possess a certain wondrous nature, for that reason I abstain from them.* <note>original: Ego vero eas non abominor... etc.</note> He then explains that nature in this manner: *First, they are entirely composed of seed; and if you peel a bean while it is still green, you will see its growth is similar to the male genitals. If it is boiled and you expose it to the moonlight for a set number of nights, you will turn it into blood. More importantly, it is the law among the Athenians to choose their officials using beans.* <note>original: Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ τὸ πᾶν γονή εἰσι... κ.τ.λ.</note> Applauding these words, the merchant says: *You have said everything well and in a manner befitting a priest.* <note>original: Καλῶς πάντα ἔφης καὶ ἱεροπρεπῶς.</note> In these words, there is nothing but Lucianic mockery and ridicule, as is also found in the same author's second book of *True History*, where at a solemn banquet celebrated by some people after a victory, even though beans had been cooked and served, they [the Pythagoreans] abstained from them...

# ON PORPHYRY.

...he makes Pythagoras an abstainer. <note>The text continues a passage describing a specific event.</note> "Then, after boiling beans—as was their custom when they were successful in war—they feasted on the victory and held a very great festival. Only Pythagoras did not participate in this; he sat far away without food, loathing the eating of beans, etc." <note>original: Τότε δ᾽ οὖν κυάμους ἑψήσαντες... κ.τ.λ.</note>

Nor indeed did they wish Pythagoras and his followers to abstain only from the eating of beans; (no differently than we shrink from marriage and union with kin; hence the poet of Venusia <note>The Roman poet Horace, born in Venusia, famously called the bean "the kinsman of Pythagoras" (*faba Pythagorae cognata*) in Satires 2.6.63.</note> gracefully called the bean the **kinsman of Pythagoras**) but they also superstitiously guarded themselves lest they should accidentally trample or violate beans still growing in the field, even to the point that they preferred to be killed than to do this. "Better to be captured than to trample them," <note>original: Ἁλῶναι μᾶλλον, ἢ πατῆσαι</note> Pythagoras used to say, according to the testimony of Diogenes Laertius on page 592. When Pythagoras, fleeing from Croton, had reached a field planted with beans (Tertullian calls these **bean-patches** in his book *On the Soul*, chapter 31) and had stopped there, he preferred to be slaughtered rather than to trample through the beans to cross over. See also Iamblichus, chapter 31, where he writes of the Pythagoreans as religious cultivators of beans: "And they were already catching up to them; for being weighed down by their armor, those caught in the pursuit were left behind. Had they not turned away and encountered a certain field sown with beans and blooming well, and, not wishing to violate the doctrine which commanded 'Do not touch beans,' they stood still, etc." <note>original: καὶ ἐπετύγχανον δὲ ἤδη τούτου... κ.τ.λ.</note> Thus should the text be read and punctuated there. See also Saint Chrysostom, Homily 1 on John, a passage I have noted elsewhere.

However, Aulus Gellius <note>referred to here as Agellius</note> in Book IV, chapter 11, refutes this old opinion as false. Drawing from Aristoxenus, a student of Aristotle, he proves that Pythagoras did not abstain from the **bean** <note>Gellius uses the Latin *fabulo*</note> (which the Greeks call <term>kyamos</term>), but rather approved of it more than all other legumes, and was accustomed to use it most frequently, because that food would gradually purge and soothe the bowels; or, as the Greek words have it: "For it is both stimulating and dispersive." <note>original: Κινητικόν τε γὰρ εἶναι καὶ διαφορητικόν</note> Gellius also reveals in the same place the cause of the error regarding the avoidance of the bean: it is because in a poem by Empedocles the Pythagorean, this verse is found:

> Wretched ones, utterly wretched, keep your hands from beans!
> <note>original: Δειλοὶ πάνδειλοι κυάμων ἀπὸ χεῖρας ἔχεσθαι</note>

This verse was followed immediately by another, recorded by Clement of Alexandria in the third book of his *Miscellanies*, page 187:

> It is the same thing, you see, to eat beans and the heads of one's parents.
> <note>original: Ἶσόν τοι κυάμους τρώγειν, κεφαλάς τε τοκήων</note>

From this, many have been of the opinion that <term>kyamos</term> refers to the common legume. But Gellius adds that those who read the poems of Empedocles...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUIS

...thought they had observed more diligently and skillfully that **beans** <note>original: κυάμους</note> there signify **testicles**: and that they were called **beans** by Pythagoras in a riddling and symbolic manner because they are **powerful for procreation and the causes of procreation.** <note>original: εἰς τὸ κυεῖν δεινοὶ, καὶ αἴτιοι τοῦ κυεῖν</note> Therefore, they believe he wished to steer people away not from eating the vegetable, but from the outpouring of the venereal act.

Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who often integrated Greek philosophy.</note> gives another reason for this "bean-ban," so to speak, in the cited passage: that Pythagoras wished to forbid us from indulging in sexual matters merely for the sake of pleasure after the procreation of offspring, since the eating of beans makes women infertile. Just as they say hens become sterile from a steady diet of beans; indeed, on the authority of **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note>, if you pour bean-husks around the roots of young trees, you will cause them to wither away. The words of Clement are these: "They say that the Pythagoreans also abstain from sexual pleasures, but to me they seem, on the contrary, to marry for the sake of child-bearing, but wish to exercise self-control over the pleasure of sex after child-bearing. For this reason, they mystically forbid the use of beans; not because the legume causes flatulence and is hard to digest and causes disturbed dreams; nor indeed because the bean is likened to a human head, according to that famous verse: 'It is equal to eat beans [as to eat the heads of one's parents],' but rather because beans, when eaten, make women childless, etc." <note>original: Φασὶ καὶ τοὺς Πυθαγορείους ἀπέχεσθαι ἀφροδισίων...</note> Next follows what I have already mentioned from **Theophrastus**, as well as the point about bean-eating hens becoming sterile.

Finally, we must not omit here a new and unique explanation of that Pythagorean precept *on the abstinence from beans*, which I read in Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 27, *Ancient Readings, chapter 17.* For he believes that under the Pythagorean name **cyamus** <note>The Greek word for bean.</note> nothing other than an **egg** was understood, because within it is the <note>original: κύησις</note> *conception* or breeding of animals. "It was his decree," he says, "that eating beans was considered equal to eating the heads of one's parents." In the same place, he proves with testimony from *Ovid, Juvenal, and Lucian* that eggs were customarily used in purifications and expiations.

# ON PORPHYRY

**In the same place, *Aralephs*]** <note>original: Ἀραλήφης</note> This is how it was written by the scribe in our copy. However, it should be read as ***akalēphēs*** <note>original: ἀκαλήφης</note>. For in this passage, the *akalēphē* is a sea fish, called a **nettle** <note>original: *urtica*</note>. It is also written with the letter *y*, as ***Akalyphē***: as seen in the works of Aristotle and Plutarch, whose words Agellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author known for his miscellany *Attic Nights*.</note> recites in Book IV, chapter 11. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia and lexicon.</note> says: *“The akalēphē is the nettle, both of the land and of the sea, which is a type of small shellfish.”* Then, after he produced verses by Aristophanes and Pherecrates <note>Greek comic poets.</note> in which they wove in this name, he adds testimonies concerning the sea nettle from Aristotle’s *On Animals*, Book 1, and Theophrastus’s *Physics*, Book VII. Let the proverb from the verses of Pherecrates be noted in passing: *“I would rather be crowned with a stinging nettle than listen to a foolish singer.”*

And let these notes suffice for now regarding the **Pythagorean Symbols**, which Malchus (or Porphyry) <note>Porphyry was born with the name Malchus (meaning "king"), which he later Hellenized.</note> touches upon and explains. However, Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who also wrote a biography of Pythagoras.</note> has many more in the final chapter of his *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original: *Protreptico*</note>, which I intended to insert here with my own explanations and corrections. But when I realized that, with the **book fairs** <note>original: *nundinis*—referring to the major European trade fairs, like Frankfurt, which dictated publishing deadlines.</note> approaching, I would have to hurry to complete this small work, we will provide those at a more convenient time in a separate little book. In the meantime, I refer the reader to the material found in Erasmus at the beginning of his *Adages* <note>original: *Chiliadum*—referring to Erasmus’s vast collection of Greek and Latin proverbs.</note>, and Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, etc.

**First, Euphorbus]** <note>original: Πρῶτον μὲν Εὔφορβος</note> Very many authors have mentioned this Pythagorean migration of the soul into various bodies: some of whom I have produced elsewhere; here I will cite others. Relevant here are these verses of Horace from Book I, Ode 28:

> *And Tartarus holds the son of Panthous <note>Euphorbus, whom Pythagoras claimed to have been in a previous life during the Trojan War.</note>, sent down*
> *To Orcus a second time, although—by taking down his shield and*
> *Witnessing to his Trojan times—he had surrendered nothing more*
> *Than sinews and skin to dark death,*
> *In your judgment, no mean authority*
> *On nature and truth, etc.*

On this passage, see the commentary of the most illustrious Turnebus <note>Adrien Turnèbe, a celebrated 16th-century French classical scholar.</note>. Ovid, in Book I of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Though the OCR says Book I, this famous passage actually occurs in Book XV.</note>, introduces Pythagoras himself speaking thus:

> *Souls are free from death, and having always left their prior*
> *Seat, they live in new homes, and dwell there once received.*
> *I myself (for I remember it) in the time of the Trojan War*
> *Was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose breast once*
> *The heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus <note>Menelaus.</note> was fixed.*
> *I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand,*
> *Recently in the temple of Juno at Argos, city of Abas.*

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

->All things change: nothing perishes: and from there<-
->the Spirit comes; from here to there, it occupies whatever limbs<-
->it pleases, and from beasts it passes into human bodies,<-
->and our spirit into beasts, nor does it perish at any time etc.<-
<note>original: "Omnia mutantur: nihil interit..." These famous lines are from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book XV, summarizing the Pythagorean doctrine that the soul never dies but merely changes its "housing."</note>

**Lactantius Firmianus**, Book III, *On False Wisdom*, chapter 19: *Unless perhaps we believe that foolish old man <note>referring to Pythagoras</note> who lied about having been Euphorbus in a previous life. This man (I believe because he was born of noble lineage) adopted a family for himself out of the poems of Homer. O marvelous and singular memory of Pythagoras! O wretched forgetfulness of us all, who do not know what we were before! But perhaps it was brought about by some error or favor that he alone did not reach the whirlpool of Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, a river in the underworld; those who drank from it forgot their past lives.</note>, nor tasted the water of forgetfulness: evidently a vain old man, just as idle old women are accustomed to do, he made up stories for credulous infants. For if he had felt properly toward those to whom he spoke these things, if he had considered them human beings, he would never have claimed for himself such a petulant license for lying. But the vanity of this most frivolous man is to be laughed at, etc.* The same author in **Book VII**, *On the Divine Reward*, chapter 23: *Philosophers too have attempted to say something concerning the resurrection <note>original: "anastasi"</note>, though as corruptly as the poets. For Pythagoras argued that souls pass into new bodies: but foolishly, because they pass from humans into beasts, and from beasts into humans, and that he himself was restored from Euphorbus, etc.*

**Tertullian** also prolifically refutes this same vanity of <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>the transmigration of souls</note> or re-embodiment <note>original: "metensomatosis"</note> or rebirth <note>original: "palingenesia"</note> (for he called it by so many names) in his book *On the Soul*, especially in chapters 28, 31, and 32. He even calls it *the recurring return of souls, always revolving from the alternating substitution of the dead and the living. "Recurring return" [recidivatum], just as we call a recurring fever.* Of the many writings of Tertullian, I will write down a few here. Thus says that most learned African <note>Tertullian was from Carthage, in modern-day Tunisia.</note> in chapter 28: *Neither does truth desire antiquity, nor does a lie avoid novelty. I clearly hold that a lie is made noble by antiquity. Why shouldn't it be false, when its testimony is also from a falsehood? How can I believe Pythagoras does not lie, when he lies so that I might believe? How will he persuade me that he was formerly Aethalides, and Euphorbus, and Pyrrhus the fisherman, and Hermotimus, and then Pythagoras, so that he might persuade me that the living are made from the dead—he who lied again about being Pythagoras? etc.* See the same **Tertullian** in his *Apology against the Nations*, chapter 48, and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 1. Pythagoras actually drew this dogma concerning the transmigration of souls from the Egyptians: concerning whom it is helpful to hear **Herodotus** in *Euterpe*, or the second Muse: *The Egyptians were the first to state this doctrine: that the soul of man is immortal...* <note>original Greek: "Πρῶτοι δὲ καὶ τόνδε τὸν λόγον Αἰγύπτιοι εἰσὶ εἰπόντες, ὡς ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ ἀθάνατός ἐστι·"</note>

<summary>This page presents a collection of critiques by early Christian scholars Lactantius and Tertullian against Pythagoras's doctrine of metempsychosis. It dismisses his claims of past-life memories as "old wives' tales" and traces the origin of the belief back to ancient Egypt via Herodotus.</summary>

Having established that the Egyptians originated the doctrine, Rittershusius now cites the specific passage from Herodotus before tracing how the idea of the "recycling of souls" permeated Roman poetry and Renaissance scholarship.</meta>

<header>ON PORPHYRY.</header>

...and when the body perishes, the soul always enters into another living being as it is born. When it has circled through all the creatures of the land, the sea, and the birds, it enters again into the body of a man at birth; this cycle takes three thousand years. There are some among the Greeks who used this doctrine—some earlier and some later—as if it were their own. Although I know their names, I do not write them. <note>original: "τοῦ σώματος δὲ καταφθίνοντος..." This is a direct quote from the Greek historian Herodotus (Book 2.123), describing the Egyptian belief in reincarnation.</note>

Without a doubt, he means Pythagoras and his followers.

From this same most foolish belief flowed those words of Tibullus near the end of his *Panegyric to Messala*:

> Nay more, when the tomb has covered my bones,
> Whether a timely day hastens a swift death for me,
> Or a long life remains, yet having changed my form—
> Whether nature fashions me as a horse, taught to run through swift fields,
> Or if I be a bull, the glory of a slow herd,
> Or if I be carried through the liquid air on the wings of a bird—
> Into whatever man a long age receives me,
> I shall weave songs for you on the scrolls I have begun.

On this passage, the most famous and elegant Passeratius <note>Jean Passerat (1534–1602), a French political satirist and classical scholar.</note> noted these things among others in his most learned lectures: *Whether a long life awaits me.* But in another body, whether human or beastly. For he alludes to the <term>transmigration of souls<note>original: μετεμψύχωσιν (metempsychosis)</note></term> of Pythagoras, about which Plato writes near the end of Book 10 and the final part of the *Laws* <note>The author attributes this to Plato's *Laws*, but these specific examples are actually found in the "Myth of Er" at the end of Plato's *Republic*.</note>: where Orpheus chooses a life in the body of a swan, having turned away from a human body out of hatred for women; Thamyras <note>A mythical singer who challenged the Muses.</note> in the body of a nightingale; Ajax son of Telamon in the body of a lion; Agamemnon in the body of an eagle. So Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius, the "Father of Roman Poetry."</note> dreamed he was changed into a peacock, and that the soul of Homer had migrated into his own body. Concerning this dream of Ennius, see also what Paul Merula wrote in his *Commentary on Book I of the Annals of Ennius*, page 68 and following. Horace, in Book II, Epistle 1, writes:

> Ennius, both wise and brave, and a second Homer
> (As the critics say), seems to care little
> Where his promises and Pythagorean dreams might fall.

This means: he is so negligent and almost loose in writing his verses that he seems to have been little mindful of those things which he had professed and boasted concerning the migration of Homer’s soul into his own body. Passeratius then brings forward an Epigram of Ausonius, who wittily mocked a certain Marcus with this Pythagorean dogma:

> Pythagoras, [once] Euphorbus, you who restore the seeds of things,
> And give returning souls to new bodies:

# NOTES OF CUNRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

->*Tell me, what will Marcus become, now that he has met his final fate,*<-
->*If he should return again to the life of the air?*<-

Pythagoras responds to this inquiry, having first learned through his questioning how impure and wicked a man that Marcus was while he lived:

->*He will be no bull, no mule, no giraffe,*<-
->*No goat or ram: but he shall be a dung beetle.*<-
<note>original: "Non taurus, non mulus erit, non hippocamelus, / Non caper aut aries: sed scarabaeus erit." The beetle was a common symbol for filth and lowliness in satirical writing.</note>

The Pharisees among the Jewish people suffered from the same madness (though somewhat more moderately). I say "more moderately" because, according to the testimony of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> in the *Antiquities*, Book 18, chapter 2, and *The Jewish War*, Book 2, chapter 8, they held that while every soul is indeed immortal, only the souls of the good pass into other bodies, and for them, the return to life is easy; the souls of the wicked, however, are tortured with never-ending punishment. A trace of this Pharisaic <term>dogma</term><note>A set of principles or beliefs laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true.</note> even appears in the Gospel history, where that same opinion is said to have been held by Herod regarding John the Baptist (who had been beheaded by Herod's order), believing that John had returned to life in the person of Christ. See Matthew 14 at the beginning; Mark 6, verse 14 and following; and Luke 9, verse 7 and following. I had these points to add to my previous notes regarding that Pythagorean teaching on the <term>transmigration of souls</term><note>The movement of a soul into a new body after death; reincarnation.</note>.

Especially memorable, however, is what authors write concerning Pythagoras’s seven-year concealment and his wasting away in a subterranean cave, or <term>hypogeum</term><note>An underground chamber or vault, often used for burials.</note>, where he hid himself away. (Only his mother was in on the secret; she both secretly provided him with the necessities for food and reported back to him what was happening among men in the meantime.) He did this so that he might appear to be dead, and finally to have returned from the underworld to the world above when, after seven years, he emerged again from that underground chamber and presented himself to be seen by men. See Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note> in the aforementioned chapter 28. Diogenes Laërtius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> also mentions this same hiding, although he does not specify a definite time there after which Pythagoras emerged again. He only says indefinitely that he *returned after a time, thin and like a skeleton* <note>original: "μετὰ χρόνον ἀνελθεῖν ἰσχνὸν καὶ κατεσκελετευμένον"</note>. The translator Ambrosius <note>Ambrogio Traversari (1386–1439), a monk and translator of Greek works into Latin.</note> should not have rendered this as *Pythagoras ascended after a year had passed*, etc., since the word "time" <note>original: "χρόνος" (chronos)</note> is never used specifically to mean "a year"; and it is likely that Diogenes, if not thinking of seven years, certainly intended more than one. Furthermore, that kind of deception and falsehood is also worthy of notice which Diogenes writes: that Pythagoras took the events which his mother had recorded in writing by her son's command, and then, after he had supposedly returned from the underworld, he recited them to his fellow citizens as if he himself, while absent, had observed and remembered them; which—

# ON PORPHYRY

...deceit won him a reputation for divinity among those people. Unless one were to say that these stories (like others of that kind) were fabricated and spread by malicious people out of hatred and envy toward Pythagoras. I lean more toward this opinion than to believing that he was an impostor or a forger of this sort, especially since I read his holy teachings elsewhere, which seem like they could hardly have come from a mere deceiver.

But leaving these matters aside—about which everyone may think what they wish—let us return for a moment to the <term>dogma</term><note>A set of established beliefs.</note> of <term>Palingenesia</term><note>Ancient Greek for "rebirth" or "regeneration."</note>, <term>Metempsychosis</term><note>The migration of a soul into a new body.</note>, and <term>Metensomatosis</term><note>A more specific term for the soul taking on a new physical body.</note>. This doctrine was not only rejected as being full of vanity (which it is) by the Church writers, but the satirist Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Greek rhetorician known for his witty sarcasm.</note> also mocked it, as can be seen in his dialogue titled *The Dream*, or *The Cock*; and likewise at the very beginning of his *Sale of Lives*. In the first dialogue, he introduces a cock who tells his story to Micyllus (for that cock had once been Pythagoras):

> Since I became Euphorbus, I fought at Troy, and having died at the hands of Menelaus, after some time I came into the person of Pythagoras. For a while I waited around homeless, until Mnesarchus <note>Pythagoras's father.</note> could finish building a house for me [meaning, his body]. etc.
<note>original Greek: "Ἐπείπερ Εὔφορβος ἐγενόμην, ἐμαχόμην ἐν Ἰλίῳ, καὶ ἀποθανὼν ὑπὸ Μενελάῳ, χρόνῳ ὕστερον ἐς Πυθαγόραν ἧκον. τέως δὲ περιέμενον ἄοικος ἑστὼς, ἄχρι δὴ ὁ Μνήσαρχος ἐξεργάσηταί μοι τὸν οἶκον."</note>

In the other passage, he promises the same transformation to a wondering merchant:

> Now you are this man, but long ago you appeared in another body and under another name, and in time you will pass into another again.
<note>original Greek: "Νῦν μὲν οὗτος, πάλαι δὲ ἐν ἄλλῳ σώματι, καὶ ἐν ἄλλῳ ὀνόματι ἐφαντάζεο, χρόνῳ δὲ αὖθις ἐς ἄλλο μεταβήσεαι."</note>

To which the Merchant responds:

> Are you saying this—that I shall be immortal, changing into many forms?
<note>original Greek: "Τοῦτο φὴς, ἀθάνατον ἔσεσθαί με, ἀπαλλαττόμενον ἐς μορφὰς πλείονας;"</note>

<margin>46 \</margin>
**Whose goal is to rescue and set free**
Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a biography of Pythagoras.</note> indicates in chapter 32 that the primary goal of Pythagorean philosophy was the same: namely, the liberation of the soul from bodily chains, using these words:

> The greatest of all commands toward courage is to set before oneself the most sovereign goal: to rescue and set free the intellect [nous] that has been held captive since infancy from such cages and bonds.
<note>original Greek: "Μέγιστον δὲ πάντων πρὸς ἀνδρείαν παράγγελμά ἐστι, τὸν σκοπὸν προθέσθαι τὸν κυριώτατον, ῥύσασθαι καὶ ἐλευθερῶσαι τῶν τοσούτων εἱργμῶν καὶ συνδέσμων τὸν κατεχόμενον ἐκ βρεφῶν νοῦν." Note: Rittershusius notes minor word variations in the manuscript of Malchus (Porphyry).</note>

Iamblichus also proposes the same goal in chapter 13 with these words:

> Philosophy appears to us to provide an escape from human bonds and a release from the cycle of birth, and a turning <note>original: "περιαγωγὴν"—a term famously used by Plato to describe the soul "turning around" from shadows to the light of truth.</note> toward that which truly is, and a knowledge of true reality, and a purification for souls. If true happiness is found chiefly in this, we must strive for it, if we truly wish to be blessed. etc.
<note>original Greek: "Φαίνεται ἡμῖν φιλοσοφία ἀπαλλαγὴν τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων δεσμῶν παρέχειν καὶ λύσιν τῆς γενέσεως, καὶ περιαγωγὴν ἐπὶ τὸ ὂν, καὶ γνῶσιν τῆς ὄντως ἀληθείας, καὶ κάθαρσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς. εἰ δὲ ἐν τούτῳ μάλιστα ἐστὶν ἡ ὄντως εὐδαιμονία, σπουδαστέον περὶ αὐτὴν, εἴπερ ὄντως βουλόμεθα μακάριοι εἶναι."</note>

To this same point belongs what Pythagoras used to say: that philosophy is a "meditation on death." Plato later borrowed this idea from him. Porphyry, quoted in Stobaeus's *Sermon 117* regarding death, says: "What nature has bound, nature looses; and what..."

<meta>Continuing from page 240, Rittershusius concludes his critique of the more superstitious interpretations of Pythagorean reincarnation, moving now into a more respectful analysis of the philosophical definitions of the soul’s relationship to the body, as found in the works of Neoplatonist commentators like Ammonius and Simplicius.</meta>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

Whatever the soul has bound, the soul itself looses. Nature binds the body within the soul, but the soul binds itself within the body. Therefore, nature looses the body from the soul, but the soul looses itself from the body. Consequently, death is twofold: one is the well-known kind, where the body is loosed from the soul; the other is the death of philosophers, where the soul is loosed from the body; and the one does not necessarily follow the other. <note>original Greek: "ἔδησεν ἡ ψυχή... οὐ πάντως ἕτερος ἑτέρῳ ἕπεται." This passage distinguishes between biological death and the philosophical discipline of detaching one's mind from physical desires.</note> Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae (c. 440–520 AD), a philosopher who taught in Alexandria and wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle and Porphyry.</note> in his *Commentary on the Five Voices* <note>A commentary on Porphyry’s *Isagoge*, an introduction to logic.</note> places this among other definitions of philosophy and explains it with a brilliant commentary:

> There is also another definition based on the goal, which says: Philosophy is the practice of death. <note>original: "Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλος ὁρισμὸς... Φιλοσοφία ἐστὶ μελέτη θανάτου."</note>

Lest anyone wrongly interpret this to mean that a person ought to physically remove themselves from human affairs (as did that Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who, after reading Plato's *Phaedo*, threw himself headlong from a wall and met his death), <note>Cleombrotus was a student who famously committed suicide not out of despair, but because he was so moved by Plato’s arguments for the immortality of the soul.</note> he teaches that the bond between the body and soul is twofold. One is natural, by which the soul is bound to the body and gives it life; the other is voluntary, or <term>proairetikon</term><note>original: "προαιρετικόν"; relating to "proairesis" or moral choice and the will.</note>, by which the soul is enslaved to the body and brought under its power (the voluntary bond, according to which the soul is bound in service to the body itself, and held by it: for this is how it should be read, or "subdued," not "held fast," as it was published in the Venice edition on page 6. b.). 

Thus, the dissolution of this bond, or death, is also twofold. One is natural and necessary, common to all people, by which the body is separated from the soul. The other is voluntary death, which is proper to philosophers who strive to separate the soul from the body. The first is the <term>separation of the body from the soul</term><note>original: "χωρισμὸς τοῦ σώματος ἀπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς"</note>. The second is the <term>separation of the soul from the body</term><note>original: "χωρισμὸς τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος"</note>. Thus Ammonius discusses this beautifully and at length. Plato also defined philosophy differently based on its goal as <term>becoming like God as far as possible for man</term><note>original: "ὁμοίωσιν θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἀνθρώπῳ"</note>: which the same Ammonius also explains beautifully in the same place.

For the sake of comparison, we shall also add the goal of Aristotelian philosophy, about which Ammonius writes in the preface to his *Commentary on the Categories*, page 11, b., Venice edition:

> What is the goal of Aristotelian philosophy? We say it is to know the principle of all things, the creative cause of all, which exists eternally and in the same way. For he demonstrates that the principle of all things is incorporeal, and that all things are produced from it.

I believe the passage should be read and punctuated in this way.

Nor should we overlook here a brilliant passage from Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), one of the last great Neoplatonists who wrote extensively on Epictetus and Aristotle.</note> in his *Commentary on the Handbook of Epictetus*, page 48, Venice edition, where he discusses the duty of the philosopher and the position they hold in the state, quite consistently with what has been said above:

# ON PORPHYRY

But we must ask, what place shall the philosopher hold in the city? Above all, he should be a maker of humanity, and a creator of faithful and modest citizens. For he will have no other task than to purify both himself and others for the life that is naturally fitting for a human being. He shall be a father common to all, a teacher, a corrector, and a counselor, offering himself as a guardian to everyone. As a helper in every good thing, he rejoices with those who prosper and suffers alongside those in pain, comforting them. Simply put, he will do those things that someone would do who considers his own work and his place in the city to be the care of all people for their own good, as far as he is able, and so on. <note>This Greek passage outlines the social responsibility of the philosopher, portraying him not as a hermit, but as a moral pillar of the community.</note>

But let us return to Pythagoras. Since he set such a goal for himself in his philosophy, and found the appropriate means to reach it—those being the best within his grasp—and diligently impressed them upon others through the most sacred rules of living, by which he might make all kinds of men better to the extent he could, how was it possible that he was simultaneously called a *sorcerer, an impostor, and a magician*? <note>original Greek: "γόης, πλάνος, μάγος" (goēs, planos, magos). These were common insults hurled at Pythagoras by his critics to dismiss his influence as mere trickery or dark arts.</note> Or should we believe that these titles were born from slanders? For whom have these universal slanderers not defamed? Not Socrates? Not Pythagoras? Not Plato? So says Dio Chrysostom <note>A Greek orator and philosopher of the 1st century AD.</note> in his *Corinthian Oration* (XXXVII, page 463 in my edition). But because we have spoken of the goal of Pythagorean philosophy, let us also note its fruit, which is: TO WONDER AT NOTHING. <note>original Latin: "NIHIL ADMIRARI." This is a famous philosophical stance of equanimity—not being shocked or overly impressed by the world because one understands the underlying causes of things.</note> Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening*, says: "For that man (Pythagoras) said that from philosophy he had gained the ability to WONDER AT NOTHING." <note>original Greek: "ΜΗΔΕΝ ΘΑΥΜΑΖΕΙΝ" (mēden thaumazein).</note> For philosophical reasoning removes the wonder that arises from doubt and ignorance by providing knowledge and an account of the resources behind every thing. Democritus called this by a single name, *athaumastia* <note>meaning "the state of not wondering" or "imperturbability."</note>, as Petrus Victorius <note>Piero Vettori (1499–1585), an Italian Renaissance humanist who edited many classical texts.</note> teaches in his *Various Readings* (Book XXXV, chapter 6), citing the first book of Strabo. Horace also begins his letter to Numicius in this way:

> To wonder at nothing is almost the one thing, Numicius,
> And the only thing, which can make and keep a person happy.

Therefore, the wise man or philosopher has this in common with the "magnanimous" or great-souled man. For, as Aristotle testifies in the fourth book of his *Ethics* (chapter 3), the great-souled man is not *given to wonder*, for nothing is great to him. <note>original Greek: "θαυμαστικός. οὐδὲν γὰρ μέγα αὐτῷ ἐστίν." The idea is that if you understand the vastness of the universe, nothing on earth seems surprisingly "large" or "important."</note>

**Separated]** <note>original Greek: "Κατακεχωρισμένον" (Katakechorismenon).</note> I think this should be read as *buried* or *overwhelmed*, <note>original Greek: "κατακεχωσμένον" (katakechosmenon).</note> from the verb meaning to be buried or covered with earth.

**Nothing healthy]** <note>original Greek: "Ὑγιὲς οὐδὲν" (Hygies ouden).</note> Everyone knows this is a proverb. See the *Adages* of Erasmus. <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), whose "Adagia" was a massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs. This phrase usually means "nothing sound" or "nothing trustworthy."</note> Close to this is that other one, "Nothing..."

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUIS

**Sacred:** Regarding this term, Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> noted the following: "Hercules, upon seeing a wooden cult-image of Adonis, said: 'Since only those who have benefited humanity ought to be honored,' or perhaps he said it because slaves who fled to that statue for sanctuary were not granted safety." Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian and lexicographer</note> explains it this way: "It is a proverb used for those who are completely useless at helping or sufficing for themselves or their acquaintances. They say that Hercules, when he first saw the image of Adonis, said, 'nothing sacred,' perhaps because it was not firmly established, or because it was useful for nothing."

**For the Mind by itself sees all:** This is a noble sentiment which Epicharmus <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher</note> expressed in trochaic verse, having drawn the idea from his predecessor Pythagoras, as he was often exceedingly delighted by this type of poetry:

->The mind sees, and the mind hears; everything else is deaf and blind.<-

That is:

->*The mind alone sees, the mind alone hears. All other things are deaf and blind.*<-

The same poem also appears in Clement of Alexandria, Book II of the *Miscellanies*, page 159 (or 142 in other editions), and in Theodoret’s *First Discourse on Faith against the Greeks*, page 15. Cassius also alludes to it in his 22nd *Problem*, saying, "The Mind sees, as one of the ancients says." Iamblichus also mentions it in Chapter 32 of his *Life of Pythagoras*, where certain parts of this passage can be restored—errors which both Arcerius and Heraldus <note>Previous editors of the text</note> passed over in silence. The most glaring error there is the phrase "through which that which is diseased" <note>original Greek: "δι’ ἧς τὸ νοσοῦν" (di' hēs to nosoun)</note>, which even misled the translator into wrongly rendering it as: *by which sense that which is morbid might operate.* In fact, the true reading is "through whichever [mind] is diseased" <note>original Greek: "δι’ ἥστινοσοῦν" (di' hēstin-osoun)</note>. Furthermore, in the same passage of Iamblichus, "according to them" is read instead of "by itself," "so many" instead of "such," and "connection" instead of "bonds." This sentiment of Pythagoras and Epicharmus is celebrated and occurs in many authors. Out of all that could be said about the excellence and speed of the mind (about which I also provided some notes in my commentaries on Oppian), let it suffice to quote what Philo says in his book *On Dreams Sent from God*: *The Mind, like the sun in the universe, holds the sovereign power within us, extending its rays everywhere.* But let us add to this "Hebrew Plato" <note>Philo of Alexandria was often called the "Hebrew Plato" because he blended Jewish scripture with Greek philosophy</note> the "Attic Plato" <note>The original Athenian Plato</note>, who in the *Philebus* introduces Socrates speaking thus: "All the wise agree, thereby exalting themselves, that Mind is our king of heaven and earth. And perhaps they speak well."

**Lame and blind:** Consider whether "deaf" <note>original Greek: "κωφὰ" (kōpha)</note> should be read instead of "lame" <note>original Greek: "χωλὰ" (chōla)</note>, since it is written that way in Clement of Alexandria, Iamblichus, and others. Certainly, "deafness" is the natural opposite to "hearing."

<summary>This page contains scholarly commentary on various Greek proverbs and philosophical fragments, focusing on the supremacy of the Mind (Nous) over physical senses, citing ancient authorities like Pythagoras, Plato, and Philo.</summary>

# ON PORPHYRY

...to be, not to be lame, or to limp, as is manifest to anyone.

**When one has been purified, then one should introduce something of the beneficial matters]** Pythagoras desired the soul to be purified before any useful doctrine was committed to it. For, as Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet (65–8 BC)</note> sings:

> *Unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour in turns sour.* <note>original: "Sincerum est nisi vas, quodcunque infundis, acescet."</note>

And the *Wisdom of Solomon* <note>A book of the biblical Apocrypha</note> denies that the spirit of wisdom will enter a malicious soul, or dwell in a body subjected to sin.

**Gently, and [page-part] little by little]** The same author a little later calls this "by degrees." *It should be noted here that the human mind must be led away from familiar things toward the contemplation of truth gradually, lest it recoil if it were done suddenly. For those who are brought out into the open air from some dark place in which they have long been held cannot bear the sudden glare of the sun with their eyes. In short, any sudden change is usually full of danger.* What wonder is it, then, if also **the mind, disturbed by a sudden and total change, should turn away and give up?** *as Malchus <note>The original name of Porphyry</note> most elegantly says here. The most wise Aristotle recognized the same when he judged that the human mind should be prepared by* **dialectical study—that is, through probable reasoning** <note>original: "πραγματείᾳ διαλεκτικῇ, ἤγουν τοπικῇ, δι’ ἐνδόξων"</note> *before it could grasp and endure* **rigorous demonstrative and analytical accuracy.** <note>original: "ἀκρίβειαν ἀποδεικτικὴν καὶ ἀναλυτικήν"</note> *See what I shall bring forward a little later from Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century philosopher</note> in his commentary on the* Categories, *where on page 12* **to journey in an orderly fashion** <note>original: "τῷ εὐτάκτως ὁδεύειν"</note> *he opposes* **placing the foot beyond the threshold,** <note>original: "τὸ πέμπειν πόδα ὑπερβάθμιον"</note> *following a proverbial phrase from an oracle.*

<margin>47</margin> **Through mathematical sciences]** *Mathematics exists, as it were, on the border between physical and non-physical things. Hence Ammonius, in his commentary on the* Five Voices <note>Porphyry’s introduction to Aristotle's logic, also called the *Isagoge*</note>, *where he establishes three species of theoretical philosophy—the theological, the physiological <note>meaning natural philosophy or physics</note>, and the mathematical—places the* **mathematical** *in the middle between the* **theological** *and the* **physiological, since it also possesses a middle rank by its very nature.** *He adds:* **Some of the ancients, however, placed this before the physiological. Those following Plato did so in order that, as they say, we might recognize the Ideas already stored in the soul—that is, that we might remember those things observed in particulars, using mathematics as a certain path and ladder. Those following Aristotle, however, assigned it the middle rank, wishing to habituate us to recognize the intelligible substance—which is invisible, but has a fuller and more distinct <note>The text suggests "enargesteran" (clearer) instead of "energesteran" (more active)</note> existence—starting from material substance.** etc. *Concerning these same mathematical studies and their use, it is well worth...*

<summary>This page discusses the Pythagorean and Platonic requirement of purifying the soul and training the mind through mathematics and logic before attempting to understand higher divine truths. It emphasizes that the transition from material concerns to spiritual contemplation must be gradual to avoid overwhelming the seeker.</summary>

# NOTES OF CUNRAD RITTERSHUSII <note>Cunrad Rittershusius (1560–1613) was a German classical scholar and jurist noted for his commentaries on ancient texts.</note>

...and to note another passage of Ammonius <note>A 5th-century philosopher in Alexandria who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> from his *Commentary on the Categories*. “What are the things that lead us to this end (of Aristotelian philosophy, which is to know the principle of all things)? We say it is the teaching of things that exist in time and change. Such are the things in the realm of generation and decay; for from these, through the medium of mathematics, we lead ourselves to the things that are always the same; such are the heavenly bodies. And so, after the incorporeal substances, we reach the first cause of all things. For since every motion is either of substance, or quantity, or quality, or place, things in the realm of generation move according to every motion; but the heavenly bodies move only according to place. Therefore, it is necessary to travel in an orderly way from things moving in many ways to things moving with only one motion, and thus to the motionless and eternally unchanging principle, and not, according to the oracle, to send forth a **step beyond the threshold.** <note>original: "ὑπερβάθμιον πόδα πέμπειν" — a Pythagorean maxim warning against overextending oneself or skipping necessary steps in spiritual progression.</note> For if we suddenly wished to leap from bodies to the first principle of all things, we might imagine that the principle itself is a body and has a shape.” <note>original: "Τίνα δὴ τὰ ἄγοντα ἡμᾶς... ἐσχηματίσθαι."</note> This is why Plotinus says that **mathematics should be handed over to the young to accustom them to incorporeal nature.** <note>original: "παραδοτέον τοῖς νέοις τὰ μαθήματα, πρὸς συνεθισμὸν τῆς ἀσωμάτου φύσεως."</note> A certain passage of Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue* he held with Trypho the Jew, also pertains here. But I will note that below.

**The contemplation of the truly real**] <note>original: "Τὴν τῶν ὄντως ὄντων θεάν"</note> This is what is called "first philosophy" or "metaphysics": named by Ammonius and other interpreters of Aristotle as **the theological species of theoretical philosophy.** <note>original: "τὸ θεολογικὸν τῆς θεωρητικῆς φιλοσοφίας εἶδος."</note> Moreover, the phrase **the truly real** <note>original: "τὰ ὄντως ὄντα"</note> is very common in Plato, signifying those things which are eternal. For he maintained that these truly exist, whereas the fleeting things of this lower world do not so much "exist" as "become," being in constant motion.

<margin>48</margin>
**Moderatus of Gades**] <note>original: "Μοδέρατος ὁ ἐκ Γαδείρων" — Moderatus (1st century AD) was a Neopythagorean philosopher from Gades (modern-day Cadiz, Spain).</note> Saint Jerome also mentions this writer in his *Apology against Ruffinus*, calling him most eloquent, whom Iamblichus partially imitated. Yet, surprisingly, Iamblichus never names him. Porphyry also numbers him among the eloquent men who wrote commentaries on the Pythagoreans, which Origen studied. See the words of Porphyry reported by Eusebius in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19. Stephanus, in his work *On Cities* <note>original: "de Urbibus"</note> under the entry "Gadeira," praises his five books of *Pythagorean Lectures*. But there it is erroneously read as **Moderatus of Gadara**, when the truth is **of Gades**. I say he was from Cadiz, not from Gadara. For the homeland of Moderatus was not Gadara (which was a city of Palestine, called by another name...

## ON PORPHYRY

...Antioch and Seleucia, which Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> mentions more than once: as in *The Jewish War*, Book 1, chapter 5, where he says it was restored by Pompey the Great in favor of his freedman Demetrius; and in Book 5 of the same work, chapter 3, where he calls it a most powerful metropolis that was inhabited by wealthy men.) But **Gadeira** <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain.</note> was both a city and an island in the Ocean, or the Atlantic sea, beyond the pillars of Hercules: so called as if it were a "neck of land" <note>original: τῆς γῆς δειρά (tēs gēs deira)</note>; the Latins call it Gades. From those things which I shall subjoin, the distinction between **Gadara** and **Gadeira** will be clearly manifest. Stephanus, in his cited book *On Cities*: "Gadeira, a city and island in the Ocean, being a narrow and very long strip, like a 'neck of land.' Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath and chief librarian at Alexandria.</note> refers to Gadeira in the feminine; the citizen is a Gadirean. For thus are titled the five books of the Pythagorean schools by **Moderatus the Gadirean**." (For so it must be read in that place, as I just said.) <note>Rittershusius is correcting a manuscript error where "Gadarene" might have been written instead of "Gadirean."</note> "It is also called Gadirite, according to Alexander Polyhistor. It is also called Gadeiraian, as if from the feminine Gadeira. And Gadiranans (perhaps Gadiran), and the possessive Gadiric, etc." And shortly after: "Gadara, a city of Palestine. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> mentions it in the third book of his *History of Philosophy*. The ethnic name is Gadarene, etc."

Hesychius: "Gadeira, an island outside the pillars of Hercules."
Suidas: "Gadara, a city of Coele-Syria, which was also called Antioch and Seleucia. The ethnic name is Gadarene. And Gadaris, referring to both the woman and the region."

"Gadeira, a place in the western region, the end of the sea, and as it were an outflow from our sea into the Atlantic sea—the Ocean—which it was not possible to sail through because it was rocky and dark. Gadeira is named from the 'land' and the 'neck' <note>original: δειράν (deiran)</note>, which is a throat. Having come this far, Hercules, being unable to cross, took pillars from the locals and set them up, showing through them that the land and sea are passable only up to this point." Strabo, Book 3: "Outside the pillars lies Gadeira," etc. Where he also brings forward more details about the founding of that city by the Tyrians <note>People from Tyre, a major Phoenician city-state.</note> according to an oracle. Dionysius in his *Description of the Habitable World*, verse 450 and following:

> Indeed, in the midst of the western pillars,
> Remote Gadeira appears to men,
> On a sea-girt island, at the ends of the Ocean.

He adds then that the city is inhabited by Phoenicians (that is, colonists from Tyre) who worship Hercules, and that it was previously called Cotinusa. See there Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and bishop known for his commentaries on Greek poetry.</note> in his *Commentary on Gades*. See also Pomponius Mela, Book III, *On the Situation of the World*, chapter 6, at the beginning. And these things [I have treated] a little more diligently...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

...should be recorded in grateful memory of Moderatus and his homeland: and also of another city, similar in name but located far away.

**To the men]** <note>original: Τοῖς ἀνδράσι (Tois andrasi)</note> I believe the "men" mentioned here are the Pythagoreans by way of eminence <note>Latin: *κατ’ ἐξοχὴν* (kat’ exochen), meaning "pre-eminently" or "par excellence."</note>: just as the followers of Pythagoras, wishing to indicate their great master, used to say "that man" <note>original: ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἄνδρα (ekeinon ton andra)</note>. They did this as a tribute of veneration to their teacher, so as to abstain from using his proper name; as attested by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras (c. 245–325 AD).</note> in chapters 10 and 35.

**For not being able, he says]** <note>original: Μὴ δυνάμενοι γὰρ, φησίν (Mē dynamenoi gar, phēsin)</note> Malchus <note>The birth name of Porphyry, the author being commented upon.</note> himself sufficiently indicates that these words were excerpted from Moderatus when he adds the word "he says" (*phēsin*).

**They turned to numbers]** <note>original: Παρεγένοντο ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς (Paregenonto epi tous arithmous)</note> However, Aristotle criticizes this Pythagorean method of philosophizing through numbers in his *Metaphysics*, Book 1, chapter 8 (page 227 in my edition). It will not be out of place to relate here what happened to Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note> when he wished to entrust himself to the friendship and teaching of a certain Pythagorean of great reputation. Justin writes that he was rejected by the man because he admitted he was not practiced in music, astronomy, and geometry when questioned. I will transcribe the words of that holy man from his *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, page 169:

"I went to a highly esteemed Pythagorean man, who took great pride in his wisdom. And then, when I spoke with him, wishing to become his student and associate, he said: 'What then? Have you studied music, astronomy, and geometry? Or do you think you will perceive any of the things that contribute to happiness, unless you are first taught these things, which draw the soul away from the world of the senses and prepare it to be useful for the world of the mind <note>original: τοῖς νοητοῖς (tois noētois) – refers to "intelligible" things that can only be understood by the intellect, not the physical senses.</note>, so that it may see the Beautiful itself and the Good itself?' After praising these subjects much and calling them necessary, he sent me away, since I confessed to him that I did not know them. I was therefore distressed, as is natural, having failed in my hope—all the more because I thought he actually knew something. Then, considering the time I would have to waste on those subjects, I could not bear to put it off for so long. In my helplessness, it occurred to me to meet with the Platonists. For their fame was also great, etc."

**The grammarians]** <note>original: Τοὺς γραμματιστὰς (Tous grammatistas)</note> Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian lexicographer of the 5th or 6th century AD.</note> defines *Grammatistes* as a "teacher of letters." Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> is more complete: *Grammatistes*, one who teaches the first elements. And he brings examples from histories, including this among others: "Not even having thoroughly learned the first elements from the grammarians." Likewise: "For nothing else regarding gram-

# ON PORPHYRY

...attending [a teacher], he learned nothing except how to write letters, and those poorly. <note>original: τιστοῦ φοιτῶν ἔμαθεν, ὅτι μὴ γράμματα, καὶ ταῦτα κακῶς, γράψαι</note>

Others, therefore, distinguish the *Grammatistae* <note>A basic literacy teacher</note> from the *Grammatici* <note>A more advanced scholar of literature and language</note>, as Suetonius elegantly puts it in his book *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 4: *There are some who distinguish a man of letters (literatus) from a teacher of letters (literator); just as the Greeks distinguish a 'Grammaticus' from a 'Grammatista': they consider the former to be perfectly learned, and the latter to be only moderately so. Orbilius <note>A famous Roman teacher known for being a harsh disciplinarian</note> even confirms this opinion with examples. For among our ancestors, he says, when a man's slave-household was being put up for sale, it was not common to rashly describe someone as 'literatus' in the title, but rather 'literator'; as if to imply he was not perfected in letters, but merely seasoned by them, etc.* 

Thus Julius Capitolinus, Aelius Lampridius, and others use the term *literatores*. Capitolinus says regarding Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher: *He utilized as masters for his first elements Euphorion the 'literator' and Geminus the comic actor, etc.* Then he names four Grammarians of both languages <note>meaning Greek and Latin</note> who were instructors to the same man. Lampridius says of Alexander Severus: *In his earliest childhood he had as 'literatores' Valerius Cordus and Lucius Veturius, etc.* Then, separately from these, he commemorates several Grammarians, both Greek and Latin. The same author says regarding Commodus: *He had a Greek 'literator', Onesicritus; and a Latin one, Capella Antistius, etc.* In our laws, the *Grammatistae* are noted by this phrasing: *Those who teach boys their first letters* <note>original Latin legal phrase: Qui pueros primas literas docent</note> or *Those who introduce boys to their first letters.* <note>Citing the Digest of Roman Law: l. II. §. vlt. D. Vacat. et excusat. muner. l. XI. vt gradatim §. vlt. D. De muner. et honor.</note>

**It was then]** <note>original: Εἶναι δ᾽ τότε (Einai d' tote)</note> Understand the figure of a triangle.

**The One]** <note>original: Τὸ ἕν (To hen)</note> To see how the Pythagoreans distinguished between *The One* and *The Monad* <note>original: τὴν μονάδα (tēn monada)</note>, see Justin Martyr in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*. They used to say that the **Monad** existed among the *intelligibles* <note>original: ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς (en tois noētois)</note>—that is, among those things grasped by the intellect—whereas **The One** existed among numbers. Similarly, the anonymous author of the *Life of Pythagoras* found in Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and encyclopedist</note>, page 722, says: *The followers of Pythagoras said that the Monad and The One differ; for among them the Monad was considered to be that which exists among the intelligibles; but The One is that which exists in numbers. Similarly, the number Two exists among things that can be counted; but they called the Monad (or rather the Dyad) 'indefinite'.*

**Preserving]** <note>original: Διακρατικά (Diakratika)</note> This is a typographical error. In the manuscript, it is correctly written as *diakratetikas* <note>meaning "holding together" or "preserving"</note>.

**Led from this]** <note>original: Ταύτης ἤγαγον (Tautēs ēgagon)</note> I conjectured this should be: *introduced by this way.* <note>original Latin: Diuinabam, ταύτη εἰσήγαγον (tautē eisēgagon)</note>

<header>NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS</header>

<margin>52</margin> **The Decade, as if it were the "receptacle" [dechada]. And shortly after: That the number ten is a perfect number, or rather, the most perfect.** <note>original Greek: Δεκάδα, οἷον δεχάδα. Et mox: Τέλειον ἀριθμὸν τὸν δέκα εἶναι, μᾶλλον δὲ τελειότατον</note> This same etymology belongs to Philo, the most learned of the Hebrews, in his treatise *On the Ten Words* <note>The Decalogue or Ten Commandments</note>: where he beautifully philosophizes on the number ten, and similarly argues that the "decade" is so called as if it were a *dechada* <note>a "receiver" or "receptacle"</note>, from the word "to receive" <note>original: παρὰ τὸ δέχεσθαι</note> and because it has accepted all kinds of numbers, and the ratios related to number, as well as proportions, harmonies, and musical chords. The first givers of names, he says, who were wise men, seem to have deservedly called this the "decade" as if it were the "receptacle," because it contains and encompasses all types of numbers, and of arithmetic ratios and proportions, and furthermore of harmonies and chords. These are the things that make the <term>denary</term> <note>the number ten</note> admirable, for it embraces a nature that is both without dimensions and subject to dimensions. *That which is without dimension pertains to the single point alone. That which has dimension has three species: the line, the surface, and the solid, etc.* The same author said a little before: **This occurs as something to be admired above all else (in the Decalogue, or ten summary precepts) that they are completed in the number ten, the most perfect of all, encompassing all the differences of numbers: of the even and the odd, of the two evens, of the three odds, of the five even-odds, etc.** Again, the same Philo, in his book *On the Preliminary Studies for the Sake of Education*, writes: **The whole framework of wisdom has been allotted the perfect number ten.** Furthermore, regarding the perfection of both the <term>septenary</term> <note>the number seven</note> and the denary, one may see many excellent things in Macrobius, Book I, *On the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 6, and in Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 10, from Varro’s *Hebdomades*; and in Alexander [of Aphrodisias] in the second book of *Problems*, 47, where he asks why infants born in the seventh month are viable <note>meaning they are able to survive</note> (which pertains to the law in the *Digest* 1.5.12, *On the Status of Men*: and Paul’s *Sentences*, Book IV, Title 9, where it is added: *For the ratio of the Pythagorean number seems to admit this.*), while those born in the eighth month are not. Among other things, he says: "That the number seven is perfect by nature, as Pythagoras, the mathematicians, and the musicians testify." <note>original Greek: Ὅτι ὁ ἑπτὰ ἀριθμὸς τέλειός ἐστι τῇ φύσει, ὡς μαρτυρεῖ Πυθαγόρας, καὶ οἱ ἀριθμητικοὶ, καὶ οἱ μουσικοί.</note> And shortly after: "That the number seven and the number ten are perfect by nature," etc. <note>original Greek: Ὅτι τέλειος ὁ ἑπτὰ καὶ ὁ δέκα τῇ φύσει ἀριθμός</note> And a little lower: "In the same way, the number ten, according to Aristotle and the philosophers, encompasses all things in the realm of generation and decay; and every number is generated through the ten according to a cycle," etc. <note>original Greek: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ δέκα ἀριθμὸς παρὰ Ἀριστοτέλει καὶ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις συμπεριλαμβάνει τὰ ἐν γενέσει καὶ φθορᾷ, καὶ πᾶς δὲ ἀριθμὸς διὰ τοῦ δέκα γεννᾶται κατὰ ἀνακύκλωσιν</note> In the same place, Alexander also noted this as a memorable fact: that those ancient mortals, who were most observant of justice, introduced the custom of joining right hands for the sake of strengthening a pledge; by which joining the number ten—the most perfect of numbers—is created, namely by adding five fingers to five fingers, etc. Anonymous author

<header>ON PORPHYRY.</header>

From the *Life of Pythagoras* found in Photius, page 712: <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ ἀριθμὸς συμπληροῦται τοῖς δέκα. ὁ δὲ δέκα σύνθεσις τῶν τεσσάρων, κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς ἀριθμούντων ἡμῶν· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὸν ἀριθμὸν πάντα τετρακτὺν ἔλεγον.</note> "The number is completed at ten. And ten is a composition of the [first] four, counting them in order; and for this reason they called every number the <term>Tetraktys</term> <note>The 'Tetraktys' was a mystical symbol for the Pythagoreans consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the sum 1+2+3+4=10</note>." St. Maximus the Confessor in the *Mystagogy*, chapter 5: <note>original Greek: Δεκάς δυνάμει ἐστὶν ἡ τετράς, ἀπὸ τῆς μονάδος εἰρμῷ κατὰ πρόοδον συντιθεμένη.</note> "The Decade is the tetrad in potential, composed from the unit in a sequence of progression." That is, *The decade is potentially the <term>quaternio</term> <note>the number four or a set of four</note>, composed from unity through a series of progression.* For if you join by adding one, two, three, and four, you will see the <term>denary</term> <note>the number ten</note> number is produced. And Ammonius, in his commentary on Aristotle's *Categories*, when he investigates the reasons why ten categories were established by the philosopher, writes this among other things: <note>original Greek: Μέλλων τὴν εἰς δέκα διαίρεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων ἡμῖν παραδοῦναι...</note> "Intending to hand down to us the division of things into ten, he first sets out the division into four. For having first handed down the division of speech into two, he proceeds quite reasonably to this fourfold cut. For the number two, multiplied by itself, makes four. After this division, he will hand down the division into ten. For the number beginning from the unit, when added up to four, makes ten: 1, 2, 3, 4; and it becomes ten." To this belongs that mockery <note>original Latin: χλευασμὸς</note> by Lucian in *The Auction of Lives*: where, when Pythagoras had promised a merchant the doctrine of the art of numbering, and the merchant replied that he already knew how to count, and was ordered by Pythagoras to give a specimen of his art, he said: "One, two, three, four." Interjecting and interrupting, Pythagoras said: "Do you see? Those things which seem to you to be four are actually ten, and the perfect triangle, and our sacred oath, etc." <note>Lucian is satirizing the Pythagorean belief that the Tetraktys was the source of all nature and the "oath" by which they swore.</note> And so that I may join a most holy and serious man to a profane and most frivolous jester, St. Jerome alluded to the same thing when he wrote in book 12 of his *Commentary on Ezekiel* (on page 456 in my Plantin edition): *Ten is a perfect number, and is contained either in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> or in the Sacrament of the four Gospels, which, beginning from one, reaches four in such a way that it fulfills the number ten.* And again in book 13 (page 466): *Ten, which is itself a perfect number, either because of the Decalogue or because of the Sacrament of the Gospel. If you come from one through two and three to the fourth number; the ten-fold number of the Gospels is produced,* etc. See similar things in the same author, book 14 (page 491). Concerning the same, he says in book 2 of the *Commentary on Isaiah* (page 19): *That the number ten in the Holy Scriptures is mystical and perfect.* The same in book 6 of the *Commentary on Jeremiah* (page 303): *That ten is a mystical number is shown by the Decalogue, which was written on stone tablets by the finger of God.* Where in the following parts he also treats the number seven, likewise showing that it is mystical.
