...deformed: as when it is read in Number 245: *that the "Dora" is the oldest of the dialects* <note>original Greek: to presbytaten einai tōn dialektōn tēn Dōra</note>; where either *Dorida* [Doric] should be read, or *Dorion* [Dorian]; as it was written shortly before: *and that the Dorian dialect is harmonious.* Indeed, he traces the antiquity of this dialect in the same place even from the myth of the nymph Doris, daughter of Oceanus and wife of Nereus, etc. Finally, he brings this forward as an argument for its antiquity: that Orpheus (who is known to be the oldest of all poets among the Greeks) used this dialect: *And that Orpheus, being the eldest of the poets, also used the Doric dialect* <note>original Greek: Kechrēsthai de tē Dōrikē dialektō kai ton Orphea, presbyteron onta tōn poiētōn</note>, etc. Even schoolboys would notice that one should read *Orphea*, not *Orphethon*.

**To appropriate the fruitful parts** <note>original Greek: Ta men karpima spheterisasthai</note>] To this "appropriation" <note>spheterismon</note>, by which some people steal the doctrines or the divine and famous discoveries of others and transfer them to themselves, we can give the elegantly composed name **word-theft** <note>original Greek: logoklopian</note> along with Diogenes Laertius in his life of Empedocles, page 602. There, quoting Timaeus, he says: *That having been convicted then of word-theft (just as Plato was), he was forbidden from participating in the discourses.*

**Mockery of the school** <note>original Greek: Chleuasmon tou didaskaleiou</note>] An ancient glossary translates <term>didaskaleion</term> <note>literally a place of learning</note> as "Doctrine." However, it actually refers to a school of letters. Furthermore, what Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus; Rittershusius uses them interchangeably</note> says here about the mockery, calumny, and **sycophancy** <note>malicious false accusation</note> with which the envious and malevolent attacked Pythagoras along with his school and followers, is also confirmed by other authors. They record that he was held and proclaimed by many to be an impostor, a juggler, and a vagabond <note>Latin: plano</note>. But Iamblichus refutes this calumny in chapter 32: *Far from it—one ought not to consider Pythagoras a sorcerer, he who taught these things* <note>original Greek: Pollou ge edei, goēta nomizein Pythagoran, ton tauta paideuonta</note>; (namely, when he taught, *that all things depend upon and are governed from heaven* <note>original Greek: ouranothen ērtēsthai kai oikonomeisthai ta panta</note>; a sentiment which Seneca the Tragedian also employed, expressing it thus: *Whatever we do, O mortal race, whatever we suffer, comes from on high*) *so much so that he [Abaris] marveled at him as if he were a supernatural god.* I have also removed several errors from that same chapter, to be presented elsewhere along with a new edition of Iamblichus himself. Regarding the calumnies with which Pythagoras was sprinkled, I have noted a passage from Dio Chrysostom elsewhere.

**He himself was admired, as were those with him** <note>original Greek: Ethaumazeto autos te, kai hoi synontes</note>] How much the Pythagoreans were admired by men, even in the age of Isocrates, can be understood from these words of the most pleasant rhetorician in his *Busiris*: *And it is not possible to disbelieve these things (namely, those which are proclaimed about Pythagoras); for even now, those who pretend...*

<meta>Continuing the commentary of Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry's Life of Pythagoras. This page follows the discussion of the Doric dialect and the school's reputation, transitioning into the extraordinary authority Pythagoras held over his followers and the origins of the famous phrase "He himself said it."</meta>

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

"...being his disciples, we admire them more for their silence than those who have the greatest reputation for speaking." <note>original Greek: menous ekeinou mathētas einai, mallon sigōntas thaumazomen, ē tous epi tō legein megistēn doxan echontas</note> He says that those who carried themselves as disciples of Pythagoras even in that age were held in greater admiration, even while they remained silent, than others who had attained the greatest glory of eloquence. From this, it can be easily estimated and proved how willingly young men followed Pythagoras, and how much the elders desired their children to associate with him—so much so that they even placed the care of their family property and business second to his instruction. To this same point belongs the proverb: *They are among the number of the Pythagoreans* <note>original Latin: De numero sunt Pythagoreorum; original Greek: tōn Pythagoreiōn eisi</note>, which Iamblichus writes in chapter 33 was still in use in his own time. Furthermore, to demonstrate the great esteem and authority of Pythagoras, there is the fact that it passed into a proverb: **He himself said it** <note>original Greek: Autos epha; original Latin: Ipse dixit</note>. Cicero, in the first book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: *In a dispute, one should not seek the weight of authority as much as the weight of reason. Indeed, the authority of those who profess to teach is often a hindrance to those who wish to learn. For they cease to use their own judgment; they take as certain what they see has been judged by the one they approve. Nor am I accustomed to approve of what we have heard about the Pythagoreans: who they say, if they affirmed anything in a dispute and were asked why it was so, were accustomed to answer: HE HIMSELF SAID IT.* That "he himself" was Pythagoras. Such was the power of a preconceived opinion that authority prevailed even without reason, etc. St. Cyril, in the third book of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 32—as translated by the most learned English scholar, Laurence Humphrey—writes: *They say it was the custom, when Pythagoras's disciples spoke things that were sometimes dull, or ridiculous, or incredible to many, to say this: HE HIMSELF SAID IT: that is, "Be silent, and have faith in the inventor of the doctrine, even without examination,"* etc. Suidas differs somewhat from these authors, suggesting that it was not the disciples of Pythagoras who were accustomed to say **He himself said it** <note>Autos epha</note> about their master, but rather Pythagoras himself saying it about God. For these are the words of that Lexicographer: ***He himself said it*** <note>Autos epha</note>. *This proverb entered into common life from (or perhaps because of) Pythagoras the philosopher. For he, dignifying his own speech and life, would say in his conversations: "He himself spoke," instead of just "he said." As if to say: "The word is not mine, but God's."* While Erasmus thinks that Pythagoras adopted this manner of speaking from the Egyptians, it might be more correctly said that he took it from the Hebrews, whose prophets are familiar with these formulas: *Thus saith the Lord*, and likewise: *The mouth of the Lord hath spoken*, etc.

**Cylon**] Concerning this Cylon, and his power, wealth, and tyrannical pride, and how and why he was rejected by Pythagoras—

<meta>Continuing the commentary of Conrad Rittershusius on Porphyry's Life of Pythagoras. # ON PORPHYRY

...had suffered [rejection], against whom for that reason he conceived a deadly hatred, which he also instilled in other conspirators; see also Iamblichus chapter 35. However, the same Iamblichus calls Cylon the **leader of the Sybarites** <note>original Greek: Sybaritōn exarchon; Sybaris was a city famous for its luxury and excess</note>.

**Using the power of wealth for the strength of wrongdoings** <note>original Greek: Tē tou ploutou dynamei pros ischyn adikēmatōn chrōmenos</note>] This is not "use" <note>original Greek: chrēsis</note>, that is, a legitimate use, but rather an abuse of wealth, when according to Isocrates in his *Exhortation* <note>original Latin: Paraenesi</note>, **wealth becomes the servant of vice** <note>original Greek: ho ploutos tēs kakias hypērētēs</note>, whereas it ought to be the servant of **true nobility** <note>original Greek: kalokagathia; a classical Greek ideal of being both "beautiful and good"</note>.

**He deemed himself worthy of all things that seemed noble** <note>original Greek: Hapantōn, ha edokei kala, heauton ēxiou</note>] This is indeed a mark of the magnanimous man according to Aristotle in his *Ethics*: to judge oneself worthy of the highest honors and rewards. However, not everyone who does this (for even the unworthy can do so) is immediately to be considered magnanimous. Certainly not this Cylon; Pythagoras was so far from judging him magnanimous that he rather deemed him unworthy to be admitted into his discipleship and intimacy.

**He approaches** <note>original Greek: Proseisi</note>] A conjunction <note>original Greek: syndesmos</note> seems to be missing from the speech here, and **at any rate** <note>original Greek: goun</note> should be supplied.

In the same place, **Praising himself** <note>original Greek: Heauton epainōn</note>] Here belongs the proverb in Suidas: **He plays the flute for himself** <note>original Greek: Autos hauton aulei</note>. To praise and extol oneself is **coarse** <note>original Greek: phortikon</note>, **ignorant** <note>original Greek: idiōtikon</note>, odious, and foolish, whether it is done by private citizens or by princes and kings. I am personally accustomed to laugh whenever I read that **self-glorification** <note>original Greek: periautologia</note> in Herodotus, Book IV, on the pillar which Darius erected for himself at the springs of the Tearus river, with this inscription: **DARIUS THE SON OF HYSTASPES, THE BEST AND MOST BEAUTIFUL OF ALL MEN.** I also laugh at that Acamatius of Heliopolis, of whom Suidas writes: **He was so unlearned that, having learned nothing beforehand nor afterward of anything pertaining to discourse, he nevertheless demanded to be called a philosopher. And by this name he revealed himself to everyone. Nor did any other of the people of Heliopolis call him anything but 'the philosopher.' Let this then be a reproach to human lack of education. But when we arrived in Heliopolis, this fabrication of Acamatius’s philosophy nearly fell apart. He even wanted to be one of the inspectors of sacrifices. This, however, is worthy of some forgiveness, because he was somehow able to encompass such things, especially before unlearned people.** Rightly did Cicero say in Book I of *On Duties*: *It is also shameful to boast about oneself, especially false things, and—to the laughter of the audience—to imitate the "Braggart Warrior," etc.* Not only.

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

Moreover, such people who are heralds of their own praises are usually not only laughed at, but even held in hatred. For men are burdened by those who praise themselves, because they think they are being accused by them, and are being reproached by a certain comparison, as if they themselves lacked those virtues which are present in others. Simplicius, in his *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Epictetus*: **For men are burdened by those who praise themselves, as they think they are being accused by them through these things, and being reproached by comparison.** <note>original Greek: Barountai gar hoi anthrōpoi tois heautous epainousin, hōs autoi dia toutōn hyp' autōn katēgoroumenoi, kai oneidizomenoi kata synkrisin. etc.</note> Plutarch, however, in a commentary written specifically on this subject, teaches in what way one may praise oneself without envy. Furthermore, just as this Cylon is described here and in Iamblichus, we can estimate that Lucius Cornelius Sulla <note>A Roman general and dictator known for his absolute power and the title 'Felix' (The Fortunate)</note> was also such a man, **who, having made an account of his own deeds, called himself "The Fortunate" and wrote so** <note>original Greek: hos epilogismon tōn heautou praxeōn poiēsas, Eutychē heauton ekalei kai egraphe</note> as found in Suidas; from which it is also helpful to add this memorable story about Laberia and Sulla:

**And once Laberia, a Roman woman of no small standing, walking behind Sulla, reached out her hand and plucked a thread from his cloak. When he turned around, she said, "It is nothing bad, Emperor; but I too wish to partake a little of your good fortune." He was greatly delighted by what was said, and a little later took her as his wife, Metella being already dead.** <note>original Greek: Kai pote Laberia, Rhōmaia gynē ouk aphanēs, exopisthen tou Sylla poreuomenē, epiballei tēn cheira, kai krokidy tou himatiou spa. tou de epistraphentos, Ouden deinon, eipein, Autokratōr; alla boulomai kagō tēs sēs mikron eutychias metalabein. ton de hyperēsthēnai te tō rhēthenti, kai meta mikron agagesthai tautēn gynaika, tēs Metellēs ēdē tethnēkyias.</note>

### Having judged the man by his appearance <note>original Greek: Physiognomōnēsas ton andra</note>

For Pythagoras held this art—which makes an inference about each person's nature and character from the features of the face—almost as a touchstone <note>literally "Lydian stone," a stone used to test the purity of gold</note> for testing suitable listeners and associates. As Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> said above in section 13 (see the Notes there); and add these things from Aulus Gellius, book 1, chapter 9: **Immediately from the beginning, he used to judge the appearance** <note>original Greek: ephysiognomonei</note> **of the young men who offered themselves for learning.** That word means to investigate the habits and natures of men by a certain conjecture from the character of the mouth and face, and from the build and habit of the entire body. He would immediately order that the one who had been tested and found suitable be received into instruction, and to keep silent for a certain fixed time, etc. Add also these things from Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, book 6 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 1: **Physiognomy is that part of divination which conjectures the habits of men from the face of the mouth and all the members of the body, from movement, and from the physical build,** etc. In this category are the **metoposcopists** <note>literally "forehead-watchers," who claimed to read a person's character from the lines on their brow</note>, whom Pliny interprets as those divining from the face.

<margin>55</margin> ### In the house of Milo <note>original Greek: En tē Milōnos oikia</note>

"Milo" is correct. Therefore, the writing of Iamblichus in chapter 35, "Myllon," is to be rejected. Nor is the spelling of Diogenes Laertius, "Mylon," or his transcriber Suidas, "Melon," any better. Concerning this most famous athlete, and his discipleship under Pythagoras, and his unusual and almost Samson-like strength...

# ON PORPHYRY

And concerning his death, the things which Strabo writes in Book VI are worth remembering; I subjoin his very words:

->“And Milo, who became the most illustrious of athletes, and was a disciple of Pythagoras, who lived in the city (Croton) for a long time. They say that once, during a communal meal of the philosophers, when a pillar gave way, Milo went underneath it and saved them all, then pulled himself out. Relying on this same strength, it is likely that he met the end of his life that is reported by some. For it is said that while walking once through deep woods, he wandered off the path quite a bit; then, finding a large log into which wedges had been driven, he thrust both his hands and feet into the split, attempting to force it completely apart. But he only had enough strength to make the wedges fall out, whereupon the parts of the log immediately snapped back together; left caught in such a trap, he was devoured by wild beasts.”<- <note>original Greek: Kai Milōn, epiphanestatos men tōn athlētōn gegonōs... thērobrōton genesthai.</note>

**Had traveled**] It should be read as, **He had traveled**. <note>The commentator is suggesting a grammatical correction to the Greek text: from "Peporeuto" to "Epeporeuto," adding the "e" augment to the verb to properly denote the past tense.</note>

In the same place, **having fallen into**] In Iamblichus chapter 30, where the same matter is discussed in almost the same words, it is published as, **having become distressed**. But I think **having fallen into** should be read in both places. <term>Peripetēs</term> <note>peripetēs</note> is one who falls into something. Suidas <note>An influential 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and lexicon</note> says: **To have become "peripetē" is to have fallen into completely.** (Read "to have fallen into"). And a little before: **peripeteis, those falling into.** The same Suidas explains the phrase **"peripetes" spear**, which is found in Sophocles' *Ajax*, as **fixed in him, that is, that which Ajax fell upon.** From this also comes the word <term>peripeteia</term>, that is, a *sudden and unexpected turn of events*. Suidas says: **Peripeteia, a headlong fall, or a misfortune, or a coincidence.** Concerning the same horrible disease and death of Pherecydes <note>Pythagoras's teacher, rumored to have died of a gruesome skin disease</note>, and concerning Pythagoras’s loyalty toward him, and his dutiful care and burial which he performed for his teacher, it has also been spoken of above.

**They burned everyone everywhere**] The sentence contains an <term>anacoluthon</term> <note>A grammatical term for a sentence that loses its structural consistency, often switching mid-thought</note>: unless one says the particle **as** or **that** was omitted by the scribe before **everyone**. For the parenthesis "some say" preceded it. Therefore, an infinitive "to have burned" or an indicative statement should have followed, but not without "as" or "that." These notes concern the establishment of the correct reading. As for the matter or the history itself, many authors remember this fire, by which the house where the society of the Pythagoreans had gathered was burned down along with them. Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> writes on page 591: **“Pythagoras died in this manner: while he was meeting with his associates in the house of Milo** (it should be written *Milo*, as in Malchus <note>Malchus is another name for Porphyry, the author of this biography</note>) **this house was set on fire by those who were not deemed worthy of admission”** (by these words Cylon is indicated, about whom Iamblichus and Malchus speak, as...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUSIUS

I noted at number 55) **that it happened that the house was set on fire due to envy.** <note>original Greek: dia phthonon hypoprēsthēnai tēn oikian synebē</note> He then adds that it was handed down by some that the people of Croton themselves threw fire into the buildings because they feared the Pythagoreans were aiming for a tyranny. Trogus Pompeius was also of this opinion, as can be seen in the work of his epitomator <note>An epitomator is a writer who creates a summary or "epitome" of a larger historical work.</note> Justin, Book 20: *Three hundred of the young men, bound by a certain oath of their brotherhood, lived a life separate from the rest of the citizens, as if they held meetings for a clandestine conspiracy. They turned the city against them; and when they had gathered into one house, the city intended to burn them. In that riot, about sixty perished; the rest went into exile.*

See also Polybius, Book II of his *Histories*, page 126 in Casaubon’s edition (a most precious gift which that most Illustrious Man generously gave to me: **great thanks to him** <note>original Greek: megalē charis autō</note>), where he suggests that even more colleges were burned—unless one prefers to understand the **meeting places** <note>Greek: synedria</note> as referring to a single large house (which Malchus <note>The original Syrian name of Porphyry, the author of this biography.</note> and Iamblichus elsewhere call the **Homakoeion** <note>A term for the Pythagorean communal assembly hall, meaning a "place for hearing together."</note>). The words of this most venerable author are:

->For at the times when, in the regions of Italy, in what was then called Greater Greece <note>Magna Graecia</note>, they set fire to the meeting places of the Pythagoreans. After this, a wholesale movement occurred regarding the governments—as was likely, since the leading men from each city had been so unexpectedly destroyed—it happened that the Greek cities in those places were filled with slaughter, factionalism, and every kind of turmoil. In those times, when ambassadors from most parts of Greece were sent to settle the disputes, they made use of the Achaeans and their good faith to lead them out of their present evils.<-

The asterisk placed after **called** <note>Greek: prosagoreuomenēn</note> indicates either that some words are missing—namely, who was the author of the fire—or that instead of **they set fire** <note>Greek: eneprēse</note> it should read **was set on fire**. Iamblichus, in the aforementioned chapter 35, writes that only two escaped from that fire, Archippus and Lysis (whom Malchus also names here), while the others were burned and perished. *While the Pythagoreans were meeting in Croton and deliberating on matters of war, having set the house on fire, they burned the men, except for two, etc.*

Ausonius says even more in his 15th Idyll, stating that the entire school was consumed by that fire:

->*Live, and always cultivate friendships: for because of this crime*<-
->*The entire school of Pythagorean Sages perished.*<-

But we accept this as written in a **more poetic and hyperbolic** <note>original Greek: poiētikōteron kai hyperbolikōteron</note> way. Beware, however, of thinking that what Cicero writes in Book II of *On the Laws* should be understood as referring to this same Cylonian conspiracy against the Pythagoreans: *The Athenians, from the Cylonian crime...* <note>Rittershusius is distinguishing between Cylon of Croton (who attacked the Pythagoreans) and Cylon of Athens (who attempted a coup in Athens in the 7th century BCE).</note>

# ON PORPHYRY

...once purified, and on the advice of Epimenides of Crete (whom we mentioned above was a disciple of Pythagoras), he built a shrine to Insult and Impudence. <note>original Latin: Contumeliae et Impudentiae. These personified vices were sometimes given altars in the ancient world to appease them.</note> (However, Cicero criticizes this same act in his own writings as a fault, since it is proper to consecrate virtues, not vices.) For that Athenian Cylon, the Olympic victor and seeker of tyranny over his fellow citizens, was far different from this man of Croton; regarding him, see Thucydides, Book I, and Adrianus Turnebus’s commentary on the aforementioned passage in Cicero’s Book II of *On the Laws*.

### And of himself]
<note>original Greek: Autou te</note>
I once thought this should be read as "there" <note>original Greek: autothi</note>. But I retracted this as soon as I returned to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who also wrote a biography of Pythagoras.</note> in the mentioned chapter 35 (from which it is clear these details were taken). There I read, "and they themselves" <note>original Greek: autoi te</note>; and not only this, but I noticed that certain things were missing from Malchus <note>The birth name of Porphyry, the author of the text being commented upon.</note>, and that instead of "they stoned," we should restore the word to "they were stoned." The words of Iamblichus are: *Then those who had been rejected by them (clearly meaning the Pythagoreans) and publicly shamed, attacked them and set fire to everything everywhere; and they themselves were stoned for this by the Italians and cast out unburied.* Summarizing this, Iamblichus says: although the Pythagoreans were oppressed by ambush and wickedly burned by those whom they had provoked by repelling and marking them as unworthy of their company, the dead did not go unavenged. Indeed, the Italians <note>Specifically the "Italiots," the Greek-speaking inhabitants of Southern Italy.</note> stepped forward as the avengers of their murder, overwhelming those arsonists of the Pythagoreans with stones and casting them aside without burial, **making them a prey for dogs**, to speak with Homer. I truly do not understand why a previous translator wanted to stuff in those words of which "neither a footprint nor a trace" appears in the Greek text: namely, calling the Italians "impudent and Greek men because they inhabited Italy." And why should they be branded with such a mark of insult as to be called "impudent men," when it is likely they were no less cultivators of all honesty, sanctity, modesty, and virtue than they were students of Pythagoras and his followers—which they declared more than enough by avenging their deaths?

### Of Archippus and Lysis]
St. Jerome also mentions these two students of Pythagoras together in his *Apology against Rufinus*; and indeed, he writes that both held schools in Thebes. Others, however, deny that Archippus ever reached Thebes.

### He lived with Epaminondas, whose teacher he also was]
It is well known that Lysis the Pythagorean came to Thebes and became the teacher of Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman known for his integrity and for transforming the Greek city-state system.</note>...

Diogenes Laertius was a 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> Iamblichus also testifies in chapter 35, who indeed adds that he was held in such great honor by his student that he was even accustomed to call him father. *For which reason Epaminondas became his listener, and called Lysis father.* <note>original Greek: Οὗπερ ἐγένετο Ἐπαμινώνδας ἀκροατής, καὶ πατέρα τὸν Λύσιν ἐκάλεσεν. Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the spiritual lineage between teacher and student.</note> Cicero says the same regarding Lysis and Epaminondas at the end of book I of *On Duties* <note>original Latin: *de Officiis*, a hugely influential work on ethics and civic responsibility.</note>: **"And those whose entire studies and lives were spent in the pursuit of knowledge nevertheless did not withdraw from increasing the usefulness and advantages of mankind: for they also educated many, so that they might be better citizens and more useful to their states, just as Lysis the Pythagorean taught the Theban Epaminondas"** (this should be read as *Lysis*, not *Lysias*, as it appears in some editions) **"and Plato taught Dion of Syracuse, and many others taught many."**

The same author in book III of *On the Orator*: **"Was it not by these arts (namely, all doctrines) that the Pythagorean Lysis instructed the Theban Epaminondas, who was perhaps the greatest man in all of Greece?"** etc. Cornelius Nepos (who is commonly known as Aemilius Probus) <note>For centuries, the biographies of Cornelius Nepos were wrongly attributed to Aemilius Probus, a late Roman editor.</note> mentions the same Lysis in the life of Epaminondas: **"As a teacher of philosophy,"** he says, **"he had Lysis (in some manuscripts it is written as Lysias, incorrectly. For Lysias was an Athenian orator; Lysis was a Pythagorean philosopher), a Tarentine Pythagorean: to whom he was so devoted that, as a young man, he preferred the company of the somber and severe old man to all his peers: nor did he let him go from him until he so far surpassed his fellow students in learning that it could easily be understood that he would likewise overcome all others in the remaining arts."** etc.

In this most excellent and brave leader of the Thebans (who also fell for his fatherland in the battle of Mantinea <note>The Battle of Mantinea (362 BCE) was a major conflict where Epaminondas won a tactical victory but was killed in action.</note>, and with whom the glory of Thebes died), leading men have something to imitate: both so they may judge that the study of literature and philosophy is by no means unworthy of their rank, and so they may be grateful toward their teachers, holding them in the place of fathers, mindful also of that saying, that more is owed to the teacher than to the father, because through the latter we have only received life, but by the benefit and instruction of the former we have also learned the honorable way of spending our lives. How well, successfully, and faithfully Epaminondas was instructed by Lysis, Plutarch introduces Theanores reporting to Simmias in the book *On the Daemon of Socrates*: **"And indeed, having met Epaminondas in the morning and hearing the manner in which he buried Lysis, I recognized that he had been well-educated by him even in the secret doctrines..."** <note>original Greek: Καὶ μέντοι καὶ συμβαλὼν ἔωθεν Ἐπαμινώνδᾳ, καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἀκούσας, ᾧ θάψειε Λύσιν, ἐπέγνων, ὅτι καλῶς ἄχρι τῶν ἀποῤῥήτων πεπαιδευμένος ὑπ᾽ ἐκείνου τἀν-. Plutarch's dialogue explores the "daemon" or guiding spirit of Socrates, here connecting the wisdom of Lysis to the character of Epaminondas.</note>

...it would be noble, and he would use the same guiding spirit for his life, if he were not evil; I judge the pilot by the voyage. For paths of life have been found, but few are those along which spirits lead men. etc. <note>original Greek: δρὸν εἴη, καὶ χρῷτο ταὐτῷ δαίμονι πρὸς τὸν βίον, εἰ μὴ κακός· ἐγὼ τεκμήρασθαι τῷ πλῷ τὸν κυβερνήτην. εὑρῆσθαι μὲν γὰρ ἀτραποὶ βίων, ὀλίγαι δὲ, ἃς δαίμονες ἀνθρώπους ἄγουσιν. etc. This fragment suggests that one's character is proven by the "voyage" of their life.</note>

Furthermore, that leader of Greece <note>referring to Epaminondas, Lysis's student</note> maintained among other Pythagorean customs this one as well: that he played excellently upon the strings, as Cicero testifies in the preface to the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. <note>The *Tusculan Disputations* is a series of books by the Roman statesman Cicero on Greek philosophy.</note> Nor can I restrain myself from recounting here an example of remarkable faith and observance of agreements which has been handed down in literature and memory regarding this same Lysis.

The story is as follows: Lysis had a certain close friend, Euryphamus of Syracuse. Once, when Euryphamus was seeking the temple of Juno for the sake of worship, he happened to meet Lysis near the vestibule of the temple just as Lysis was leaving, having finished his own ritual. Euryphamus asked Lysis to wait a little while for his companion's return until he himself had finished the same worship. Lysis agreed and took a seat upon a certain stone bench that was there.

What happened next? Euryphamus, becoming immersed in deeper meditations within the temple, forgot about Lysis and exited through another gate and part of the temple, returning home and leaving Lysis behind in the other section. But Lysis, mindful of the pact or agreement he had made with his companion, remained in that very spot, not moving himself from the place at all. He spent not only the remainder of that day there, but also the following night and the greater part of the next day, awaiting his companion’s return. Indeed, he would have remained there even longer had not Euryphamus, finally remembering him and coming to his senses, come back and led him away. 

For when Lysis was missed the next day in the common lecture hall by the other companions, Euryphamus finally remembered what had happened at the temple of Juno; he reported it and, setting out to bring Lysis back, found him sitting in the same place where he had left him. Excusing his forgetfulness, Euryphamus said, "Some god must have sent this forgetfulness upon me for the very purpose of proving, through this occasion, your constancy in keeping the faith of agreements." Iamblichus <note>a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> describes this incident <note>original Greek: σύμβαμα (*symbama*), an occurrence or event.</note> in chapter 30, but the reading there is corrupted (for instead of "agreements," <note>original Greek: συνθήκας (*synthēkas*)</note> the word "orders" <note>original Greek: συνταγὰς (*syntagas*)</note> is published), and the punctuation is even more at fault, which misled the translator into confusing different sentences and joining things that should not be joined.

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUISEN

...teaching. The same author, in his *Commentary on Job*, chapter 38, says: *The number ten is perfect, because by repeating it, every number is multiplied into infinity.* <note>original Latin: "Decimus numerus perfectus est, quia per ipsum iterando omnis numerus in infinitum multiplicatur."</note> Finally, let us note the warning of the same Jerome regarding chapter 19 of Job: *While this number remains solid and perfect, we should know that in the divine scriptures, sometimes a larger number and sometimes a smaller number is signified, depending on the diversity of the passages.* Philo, in his book *On the Change of Names*, page 1 of the Wechel edition, says: *The decad <term>decad: the number ten</term> represents progress; the century <term>the number one hundred</term> is a symbol of perfection.* <note>original Greek: Προκοπῆς μὲν δεκάς· ἑκατοντὰς δὲ τελειότητος σύμβολον.</note> The same Philo also philosophizes brilliantly on the perfection of the number seven in his book *On the Creation of the World* <note>original Greek: περὶ κοσμοποιΐας</note>; see that work. Macrobius, in the aforementioned chapter 6 of Book I, says: *When the decad, which is itself a most perfect number, is joined to a perfect number—that is, the septenary <term>the number seven</term>—so that either ten times seven or seven times ten years are counted, this is believed by natural philosophers to be the goal of living, and the perfect span of human life is bounded by this, etc.* <note>original Latin: "meta viuendi." This refers to the traditional "three score and ten" years of a human life.</note> Finally, regarding the mysteries and perfection of the number seven, one may also consult Gregory Nazianzen’s *Homily on Holy Pentecost*; as well as Maximus Margunius in an extemporaneous sermon <note>original Greek: αὐτοσχεδίῳ</note>—one which is indeed spontaneous, but equal to those of the most learned and ancient Fathers—on the same feast day, which was once given to me as an unpublished work and which I translated from Greek into Latin.

**All that has come to be**] This should be read as **all that is born**, <note>The commentator is suggesting a correction to the Greek text: from "γενόμενον" (happened/became) to "γεννώμενον" (born/produced).</note>

<margin>53</margin> **Such is the treatise on numbers among the Pythagoreans**] To the previous remarks already cited concerning Pythagorean numbers, this testimony from Cicero’s fourth book of *Academic Questions* should be added: *The Pythagoreans want all things to proceed from numbers and the principles of mathematicians, etc.* Furthermore, did not Pythagoras place the "highest good" in the perfect knowledge of numbers? For so says Theodoretus in Sermon 11, *On the End and Judgment*, in his *Cure of Greek Maladies*: *The much-famed Pythagoras supposed the most perfect knowledge of numbers to be the ultimate good.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ πολυθρύλλητος Πυθαγόρας τὴν τελεωτάτην τῶν ἀριθμῶν ἐπιστήμην ἔσχατον ὑπελάμβανεν ἀγαθόν.</note>

For Malchus <note>The author Porphyry, often called Malchus.</note> calls it "unclear" here. The entire passage regarding the Greek dialects is quite beautiful, but [is mentioned] once and again...

# ON PORPHYRY

...deformed: as when one reads in Section 245: *that the Doric is the oldest of the dialects* <note>original Greek: τὸ πρεσβυτάτην εἶναι τῶν διαλέκτων τὴν Δώρα</note>: where either *Dorida* should be read, or *Dorion*, as it was stated a little before: *that the Doric dialect is harmonious.* Indeed, he traces the antiquity of this dialect in the same passage back to the myth of the nymph Doris, daughter of Oceanus and wife of Nereus, etc. Finally, he brings this forward as an argument for its antiquity: that Orpheus (who is well known to be the oldest of all the Greek poets) used this dialect: *And that Orpheus, being older than the other poets, used the Doric dialect, etc.* <note>original Greek: Κεχρῆσθαι δὲ τῇ Δωρικῇ διαλέκτῳ καὶ τὸν Ὀρφέα, πρεσβύτερον ὄντα τῶν ποιητῶν</note> One must read *Orphea*, not *Orphethon*, as even a schoolboy would notice.

**To misappropriate the fruitful parts** <note>original Greek: Τὰ μὲν κάρπιμα σφετερίσασθαι</note>] This "appropriation" <term>appropriation: the act of taking something for oneself, specifically others' ideas</term>, by which some people stealthily gather the teachings or the divine and famous discoveries of others and transfer them to themselves, we can elegantly call "word-theft" <term>word-theft: literary plagiarism, from the Greek 'logoklopia'</term> following Diogenes Laertius in his life of Empedocles, page 602. There, quoting Timaeus, he says: *Because he was then convicted of word-theft (just as Plato was), he was barred from participating in the discussions.* <note>original Greek: Ὅτι καταγνωσθεὶς ἐπὶ λογοκλοπείᾳ τότε (καθὰ καὶ Πλάτων) τῶν λόγων ἐκωλύθη μετέχειν.</note>

**Mockery of the school** <note>original Greek: Χλευασμὸν τοῦ διδασκαλείου</note>] An old Glossary translates *didaskaleion* as "Doctrine." However, it properly means a school or a place of literary study. Furthermore, what Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Phoenician name of Porphyry</note> says here regarding the mockery, calumny, and malicious misrepresentation with which the envious and malevolent attacked Pythagoras along with his school and followers, is also confirmed by other authors. They recorded that he was regarded and proclaimed by many to be an impostor, a trickster, and a charlatan <term>charlatan: from the Latin 'planus', a wandering beggar or cheat</term>. But Iamblichus refutes this calumny in chapter 32: *It was far from the case* (I would prefer the word 'and' here) *that one should consider Pythagoras a sorcerer, he who taught these things* <note>original Greek: Πολλοῦ γε ἔδει, γόητα νομίζειν Πυθαγόραν, τὸν ταῦτα παιδεύοντα</note> (namely, when he taught that *all things depend on and are governed by heaven*: a sentiment which Seneca the Tragic also used, expressing it thus: *Whatever we do, as a mortal race, whatever we suffer, comes from above* <note>original Latin: "Quicquid faciamus, mortale genus, Quicquid patimur, venit ex alto." Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher and playwright.</note>) *so that even he* (namely Abaris) *marveled at him as if he were a god in a supernatural way.* From the same chapter I have removed several other errors, which will be brought forward elsewhere in a new edition of Iamblichus. Regarding the slanders with which Pythagoras was sprinkled, I have noted a passage from Dio Chrysostom elsewhere.

<margin>54</margin>
**He himself was admired, as were those with him** <note>original Greek: Ἐθαυμάζετο αὐτός τε, καὶ οἱ συνόντες</note>] How much the Pythagoreans were admired by men, even in the age of Isocrates, can be understood from these words of that most pleasant Orator in his *Busiris*: *And it is not possible to disbelieve these things (which are preached about Pythagoras); for even now, those who pretend...* <note>original Greek: Καὶ τούτοις οὐχ οἷόν τε ἀπιστεῖν... ἔτι γὰρ καὶ νῦν τοὺς προσποιου-</note>

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUISEN

...[being] disciples of that man, we admire more for their silence than those who hold the greatest reputation for speaking. <note>original Greek: μένους ἐκείνου μαθητὰς εἶναι, μᾶλλον σιγῶντας θαυμάζομεν, ἢ τοὺς ἐπὶ τῷ λέγειν μεγίστην δόξαν ἔχοντας</note> He says that those who conducted themselves as disciples of Pythagoras even in that era were held in greater admiration, even while they remained silent, than others who had attained the highest glory of eloquence. From this, one can easily judge and prove how willingly young men followed Pythagoras, and how much older men desired their children to associate with him—to such an extent that they even placed the care of their family estates after his instruction. To this same point belongs the proverb: *They are of the number of the Pythagoreans* <note>original Greek: Τῶν Πυθαγορείων εἰσί</note>; which Iamblichus writes survived even to his own time in chapter 33. Furthermore, to demonstrate the immense esteem and authority of Pythagoras, there is the fact that it passed into a proverb: *He himself said it* <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς ἔφα (Autos epha); Latin: Ipse dixit</note>. Cicero, in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: *In a dispute, one should seek the weight of reason rather than the weight of authorities. Indeed, the authority of those who profess to teach is often an obstacle to those who wish to learn. For they cease to apply their own judgment; they take as established whatever they see judged by the one they approve of.* And indeed, I am not accustomed to approving of what we have received concerning the Pythagoreans: of whom they say that if they affirmed anything in a dispute, when they were asked why it was so, they were accustomed to respond: HE HIMSELF SAID IT. "He himself," of course, was Pythagoras. *Preconceived opinion was so powerful that authority prevailed even without reason*, etc. Saint Cyril, in Book III of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 32, translated by the very learned Englishman Laurence Humphrey <note>Laurence Humphrey (1527–1589) was a prominent English theologian and President of Magdalen College, Oxford.</note>: They say it was the custom, when the disciples of Pythagoras spoke things that were sometimes cold, ridiculous, and incredible to many, to say this: HE HIMSELF SAID IT; that is, *trust and give faith to the inventor of the dogma, even without examination*, etc. Suidas <note>The Suda (or Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> departs somewhat from these views, suggesting that it was not the disciples of Pythagoras who used to say "He himself said it" <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς ἔφα</note> about their master, but Pythagoras himself saying it about God. For these are the words of that Lexicographer: *He himself said it. This proverbial expression entered common life from Pythagoras the philosopher. For he, dignifying his own speech and life, used to say in his lectures: "He himself said it," instead of simply "He said." Meaning: the word is not mine, but God's.* Whereas Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Northern Renaissance humanist and compiler of ancient adages.</note> thinks Pythagoras took this manner of speaking from the Egyptians, it might perhaps be more correctly said he took it from the Hebrews, to whose prophets these formulas are familiar: *Thus says the Lord*; likewise: *The mouth of the Lord has spoken*, etc.

**Cylon** <note>original Greek: Κύλων</note>] Concerning this Cylon, and his power, wealth, and tyrannical pride, and also how and why he was rejected by Pythagoras—

### ON PORPHYRY.

...he bore [this feeling], against whom he therefore conceived a deadly hatred, which he also instilled into other conspirators; see also Iamblichus, chapter 35. Yet the same Iamblichus calls Cylon "the leader of the Sybarites" <note>original Greek: Συβαριτῶν ἔξαρχον; the Sybarites were inhabitants of Sybaris, a city famous for its luxury and decadence</note>.

**Using the power of wealth for the strength of wrongdoings** <note>original Greek: Τῇ τοῦ πλούτου δυνάμει πρὸς ἰσχὺν ἀδικημάτων χρώμενος</note>] This is not a "proper use" <note>original Greek: χρῆσις</note>, that is, a legitimate use, but rather an abuse of opulence, when according to Isocrates in his *Exhortation* <note>original Latin/Greek: Paraenesi</note> **wealth becomes the servant of vice** <note>original Greek: ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς κακίας ὑπηρέτης</note>, which ought to have belonged to "nobility and virtue" <note>original Greek: καλοκαγαθίας; a term combining beauty and goodness</note>.

**He deemed himself worthy of all things that seemed noble** <note>original Greek: Ἁπάντων, ἃ ἐδόκει καλὰ, ἑαυτὸν ἠξίου</note>] This is indeed a mark of a "magnanimous" <note>literally "great-souled"</note> man according to Aristotle in the *Ethics*, to judge oneself worthy of the highest honors and rewards. However, not everyone who does this (for an unworthy person can also do so) should immediately be considered magnanimous. Certainly not that Cylon, whom Pythagoras was so far from judging magnanimous that he instead deemed him unworthy to be admitted into his discipleship and circle of friends.

**He approaches** <note>original Greek: Πρόσεισι</note>] A "conjunction" <note>original Greek: σύνδεσμος</note> seems to be missing from the sentence here, and "therefore" <note>original Greek: γοῦν</note> should be supplied.

In the same place, **Praising himself** <note>original Greek: Ἑαυτὸν ἐπαινῶν</note>] To this belongs the proverb found in Suidas <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>: "He himself plays the flute for himself" <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς αὑτὸν αὐλεῖ; similar to the English "blowing one's own trumpet"</note>. To praise and extol oneself is "vulgar" <note>original Greek: φορτικὸν</note>, "ignorant" <note>original Greek: ἰδιωτικόν</note>, "provokes envy" <note>original Latin: inuidiosum</note>, and is "foolish" <note>original Latin: ineptum</note>, whether it is done by private citizens or even by princes and kings themselves. I am accustomed to laugh whenever I read that "self-praise" <note>original Greek: περιαυτολογίαν</note> in Herodotus, Book IV, on the stone monument which Darius erected for himself at the springs of the Tearus river, with this inscription: **DARIUS SON OF HYSTASPES, THE BEST AND MOST BEAUTIFUL OF ALL MEN.** I also laugh at that Acamatius of Heliopolis, of whom Suidas writes: "He was so uneducated <note>original Greek: ἰδιωτικῶς εἶχεν</note> that, having learned nothing beforehand nor afterward of anything pertaining to learning of any kind, he demanded to be called a philosopher. And by this name he announced himself to everyone. And none other of the Heliopolitans called him anything else than 'the philosopher.' Let this then be a reproach to human ignorance. When we arrived in Heliopolis, this fiction of Acamatius' philosophy was nearly at an end. He also wished to be one of the inspectors of sacrifices. This, however, is worthy of pardon, because he was somehow able to grasp such things, especially among uneducated people." Cicero rightly says in Book I of *On Duties*: *It is even unseemly to boast about oneself, especially falsely, and to the derision of the listeners to imitate the "braggart soldier"* <note>the "Miles Gloriosus," a stock character of a boastful, cowardly soldier</note>, etc. Not only.

<meta>catchword: Non solum.</meta>

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUISEN

...Moreover, such men who are the heralds of their own praises are usually held not only in ridicule, but even in hatred. For men are annoyed by those who praise themselves because they feel they are being accused by them, and are reproached by a kind of comparison, as if they themselves lack those gifts which are present in others. As Simplicius says in his *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Epictetus*: "For men are burdened by those who praise themselves, as if they were being accused by them through these things, and reproached by comparison" <note>original Greek: Βαροῦνται γὰρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι τοῖς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπαινοῦσιν, ὡς αὐτοὶ διὰ τούτων ὑπ' αὐτῶν κατηγορούμενοι, καὶ ὀνειδιζόμενοι κατὰ σύγκρισιν</note>. etc. However, Plutarch, in a commentary written specifically on this subject, teaches in what way one might be able to praise oneself without [incurring] envy. Furthermore, we can judge that Lucius Cornelius Sulla was the same sort of man as this Cylon described here and in Iamblichus; Sulla, "who, having made a reckoning of his own deeds, called himself 'Lucky' and wrote it so" <note>original Greek: ὃς ἐπιλογισμὸν τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πράξεων ποιήσας, Εὐτυχῆ ἑαυτὸν ἐκάλει καὶ ἔγραφε</note>, as is found in Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. From this source, it is also pleasing to add this memorable story about Laberia and Sulla:

"And once Laberia, a Roman woman of no small renown, walking behind Sulla, reached out her hand and plucked a thread from his garment. When he turned around, she said, 'It is nothing bad, Emperor; but I too wish to share a little in your luck.' He was exceedingly pleased with what was said and a little while later took her as his wife, Metella having already died." <note>original Greek: Καί ποτε Λαβερία, Ῥωμαία γυνὴ οὐκ ἀφανὴς, ἐξόπισθεν τοῦ Σύλλα πορευμένη, ἐπιβάλλει τὴν χεῖρα, καὶ κροκίδα τοῦ ἱματίου σπᾷ. τοῦ δὲ ἐπιστραφέντος, Οὐδὲν δεινὸν, εἰπεῖν, Αὐτοκράτωρ· ἀλλὰ βούλομαι κἀγὼ τῆς σῆς μικρὸν εὐτυχίας μεταλαβεῖν. τὸν δὲ ὑπερησθῆναί τε τῷ ῥηθέντι, καὶ μετὰ μικρὸν ἀγαγέσθαι ταύτην γυναῖκα, τῆς Μετέλλης ἤδη τεθνηκυίας.</note>

**Having judged the man by his appearance** <note>original Greek: Φυσιογνωμονήσας τὸν ἄνδρα</note>] For Pythagoras held this art—which makes an inference about each person's nature and spiritual habits from the features of the face—as a kind of "Lydian stone" <note>a touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note> for exploring suitable students and associates. As Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> said above in section 13 (where you may see the Notes), and add these words from Aulus Gellius, Book 1, Chapter 9: "Right from the start, he would <note>original Greek: ἐφυσιογνωμόνει</note> the young men who offered themselves for learning. This word means to investigate the habits and natures of men by a certain inference from the character of the mouth and face, and from the thread and habit of the whole body. He would immediately order the one who had been tested by him and found suitable to be received into instruction, and to remain silent for a fixed time," etc. Add also these points from Lodovico Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 6 of *Ancient Readings*, Chapter 1: "Now <term>physiognomia</term> <note>physiognomy: the practice of assessing character from physical appearance</note> is that part of divination which infers the habits of men from the face and the appearance, movement, and 'thread' of all the limbs of the body," etc. In this category are the <term>metoposcopi</term> <note>metoposcopists: those who tell character or fortune by looking at the forehead or face</note>, whom Pliny interprets as "those divining from the face."

<margin>55</margin> **In the house of Milo** <note>original Greek: ’Εν τῇ Μίλωνος οἰκίᾳ</note>] "Milo" is written correctly here. Therefore, the spelling in Iamblichus, Chapter 35, "Myllon," is a trivial error. Nor is the spelling of Diogenes Laertius, "Mylon," any better; nor that of his transcriber Suidas, "Melon." Concerning this most famous athlete, and his discipleship under Pythagoras, and likewise his unusual and almost Samson-like strength...

### R

...and his destruction; the things that Strabo writes in Book VI are worth remembering, and I subjoin his very words: "And Milo, who had become the most famous of athletes, was a companion of Pythagoras, who stayed in the city (Croton) for a long time. They say that once in the dining hall of the philosophers, when a pillar was failing, Milo went under it and saved everyone, then drew himself back out. It is likely that, trusting in this same strength, he met the end of his life that is recorded by someone. At any rate, it is said that while traveling once through deep woods, he wandered quite far from the road; then, finding a great log that had been wedged open, he thrust his hands and feet together into the split, straining to pull it completely apart. He was only strong enough to make the wedges fall out, whereupon the parts of the log immediately snapped together; and being left caught in such a trap, he was devoured by beasts." <note>original Greek: Καὶ Μίλων, ἐπιφανέστατος μὲν τῶν ἀθλητῶν... θηρόβρωτον γενέσθαι.</note>

**"He had traveled"** <note>original: Πεπόρευτο</note>] This should be read as *He had traveled through* <note>original: Ἐπεπόρευτο</note>.

**In the same place, "having fallen into"** <note>original: περιπετῆ γενόμ.</note>] In Iamblichus, chapter 30, where the same matter is discussed in almost the same words, it is published as *having become full of suffering* <note>original: περιπαθῆ γενόμ.</note>. But I think *having fallen into* <note>original: περιπετῆ</note> should be read in both places. *Peripetēs* is one who falls into something. Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: "To become *peripetē* is to have fallen into [something] fully" <note>original: Περιπετῆ γενέσθαι, περιπεπωκέναι (lege περιπεπτωκέναι) πλήρη</note>. And a little before: "*peripeteis* means those falling into." The same Suidas explains the "falling-upon spear" <note>original: περιπετὲς ἔγχος</note>—which is found in Sophocles' tragedy *Ajax*—as "fixed around him, that is, the one upon which Ajax fell." From this also comes *peripeteia* <term>peripeteia: a sudden reversal of fortune, often the turning point in a Greek drama</term>, that is, *a sudden and unexpected event*. Suidas says: "*Peripeteia* means recklessness, or a coincidence, or a happening." Regarding the same horrific disease and death of Pherecydes, and concerning Pythagoras's loyalty toward him, his dutiful care, and the burial which he provided for his teacher, this was also mentioned above.

**"They set fire to all on every side"** <note>original: Πάντας πανταχῇ ἐνέπρησαν</note>] The sentence contains an *anacoluthon* <term>anacoluthon: a grammatical inconsistency where a sentence starts one way and ends another, common in ancient manuscripts</term>, unless someone says that the small word *as* or *that* <note>original: ὡς, vel ὅτι</note> was omitted by the scribe before the word "all." For the phrase "some say" <note>original: οἱ μέν φασι</note> preceded the parenthesis. Therefore, it ought to have been followed by the infinitive "to set fire" <note>original: ἐμπρῆσαι</note>, or an indicative statement, but not without "as" or "that." These notes concern establishing the correct reading. As for the matter or the history itself—this fire in which the house where the Pythagorean fellowship had gathered was burned down along with the members themselves—many authors mention it. Diogenes Laertius on page 591 says: "Pythagoras died in this manner: while he was meeting with his associates in the house of Milo <note>it should be written 'Milo' as in Malchus, rather than 'Mylon' as found here</note>, [the house was set on fire] by those who had not been deemed worthy of admission" (these words refer to Cylon, about whom Iamblichus and Malchus speak, as...

# NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUISEN

...I was noting at Number 55) **it happened that the house was set on fire through envy.** <note>original Greek: διὰ φθόνον ὑποπρησθῆναι τὴν οἰκίαν συνέβη</note> He adds thereafter that it is recorded by some that the Crotoniates themselves <note>The citizens of Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy</note> set fire to the buildings because they feared that the Pythagoreans were aiming at a tyranny. Trogus Pompeius was also of this opinion, as can be seen from his epitomizer <note>An editor who creates a summary or abridgment</note> Justin, in Book XX: **Three hundred of the youths, bound by a certain oath under the law of their fellowship, lived a life separate from the other citizens, as if they held a meeting for a clandestine conspiracy; they turned the city against them, which, when they had gathered in one house, wished to burn them. In this tumult nearly sixty perished; the rest went into exile.** See also Polybius, Book II of his *Histories*, page 126 of Casaubon’s edition <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar; Rittershuisen notes this was a gift from him</note> (with which most precious gift that most distinguished man generously presented me: **great thanks to him** <note>original Greek: μεγάλη χάρις αὐτῷ</note>), where he suggests that even more colleges <note>In the sense of organized groups or meeting halls</note> were burned: unless one prefers to understand **the meeting halls** <note>original Greek: τὰ συνέδρια</note> as referring to a single large house (which Malchus and Iamblichus elsewhere call the **homakoion** <term>homakoion: a Greek term for the common assembly hall or school of the Pythagoreans</term>). The words of that most serious author are:

**For during those times when in the places throughout Italy, in what was then called Greater Greece, the meeting-places of the Pythagoreans were set on fire. After this, a total upheaval of the governments occurred—as was natural, since the leading men of each city had been so unexpectedly destroyed—it happened that the Greek cities in those places were filled with murder, factionalism, and every kind of turmoil. At which times, with embassies being sent from most parts of Greece to mediate the disputes, they made use of the Achaeans and their good faith to expel the present evils.** <note>original Greek: Καθ' οὓς γὰρ καιροὺς... κακῶν ἐξαγωγήν.</note>

The asterisk placed after **called** <note>original Greek: προσαγορευομένην</note> indicates that either some words are missing—namely, who the author of the fire was—or that instead of **set fire to** <note>active voice: ἐνέπρησε</note> one should read **was set on fire** <note>passive voice: ἐνεπρήσθη</note>. Iamblichus, in the aforementioned chapter 35, writes that only two escaped from that fire, **Archippum and Lysidem** (whom Malchus also names here), while the rest perished in the flames. **While the Pythagoreans were meeting in Croton and deliberating on matters of war, they set fire to the house and burned the men, except for two, etc.** <note>original Greek: 'Εν τῇ Κρότωνι συνεδρευόντων... πλὴν δυοῖν</note> Even more is said by **Ausonius in Idyll XV**, that the entire school was consumed by that fire:

->*Live, and always cherish friendships: for on account of that crime*<-
->*the entire school of the Pythagorean Sages perished.*<-
<note>original Latin: Viue, et amicitias semper cole: crimen ob istud / Pythagoreorum periit schola tota Sophorum.</note>

But we take this as being written in a **more poetic and hyperbolic** <note>original Greek: ποιητικώτερον καὶ ὑπερβολικώτερον</note> manner. However, take care not to think that what **Cicero writes in Book II of *On the Laws***—**The Athenians, by the Cylonian crime**—should be understood as referring to this same **Cylonian** conspiracy against the Pythagoreans. <note>Rittershuisen warns the reader not to confuse Cylon of Croton, who attacked the Pythagoreans, with Cylon of Athens, who attempted a coup in Athens centuries earlier.</note>

# ON PORPHYRY

...after the purification, and at the persuasion of **Epimenides of Crete** (whom it was said above was a disciple of **Pythagoras**), he built a shrine to Insult and Impudence: (an act which **Cicero** nonetheless criticizes in that same place as a vice, since it is proper to consecrate virtues, not vices.) For that **Cylon the Athenian**, the **Olympic victor** and seeker of tyranny over his own citizens, was far different from this **man of Croton** <note>Cylon of Croton was the leader of the anti-Pythagorean faction; Rittershuisen is distinguishing him from the famous Athenian of the same name</note>: concerning whom see **Thucydides**, Book I, and **Adrianus Turnebus** in his *Commentary on Cicero* at the cited passage in Book II of *The Laws*.

**And of himself** <note>original Greek: Αὐτοῦ τε</note>] I once thought the reading should be *αὐτόθι* <note>Meaning "on the spot"</note>. But I retracted this as soon as I returned to **Iamblichus** in the cited Chapter 35 (from which it is clear these details were taken), where I read *αὐτοί τε* <note>Meaning "and they themselves"</note>; and not only this, but I noticed certain things were missing from **Malchus** <note>Malchus was the original name of Porphyry; the commentator uses the names interchangeably</note>, and that instead of *κατέλευσαν* <note>"They stoned"</note> it should be replaced with *κατελεύσθησαν* <note>"They were stoned"</note>. The words of **Iamblichus** are: *Then indeed those who had been rejected by them (clearly meaning the Pythagoreans) and publicly disgraced, attacked them and set fire to all of them everywhere, and they themselves were stoned by the Italiotes for this, and were cast out unburied.* <note>original Greek: Τότε δὴ οὖν οἱ ἀπογνωσθέντες... ἄταφοι</note> Wherein **Iamblichus** says this in summary: although the **Pythagoreans** were overwhelmed by treachery and wickedly burned by those whom they had provoked by repelling and marking them as unworthy of their company, nevertheless they did not die unavenged: since the **Italiotes** <note>The Greek-speaking inhabitants of Southern Italy</note> happened to be the avengers of their murder, who overwhelmed those arsonists of the **Pythagoreans** with stones and cast them aside unburied, *making them a prey for dogs*, <note>original Greek: ἑλώρια τεύξαντες κύνεσσιν</note> to speak with **Homer** <note>A famous phrase from the opening of the Iliad</note>. Here, why the translator wished to cram in those words—of which there is neither footprint nor trace in the Greek text—(*to shameless and Greek men, called Italiotes because they inhabited Italy*) I truly do not understand. And why should those who, it is likely, were no less cultivators of all honor, sanctity, modesty, and virtue than they were students of **Pythagoras** and his followers, be branded with such a mark of disgrace as to be called "shameless men," when they declared their character more than enough by the avenging of their murder?

**And of Archippus and Lysis** <note>original Greek: Ἀρχίππου τε καὶ Λύσιδος</note>] **St. Jerome** also mentions these two pupils of **Pythagoras** together in his *Apology against Rufinus*: and indeed he writes that both held schools in **Thebes**. Others, however, deny that **Archippus** reached **Thebes**.

**He both lived with Epaminondas, of whom he was also the teacher...** <note>original Greek: Ἐπαμινώνδᾳ τε συγγέγονεν, οὗ καὶ διδάσκ.</note>] That **Lysis** the **Pythagorean** came to **Thebes** and was the teacher of **Epaminondas**...

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUISEN

...was [at Thebes], as evidenced not only by **Diogenes Laërtius** (whose words in Book VIII, page 571 are: <note>original Greek: Λύσιδος τοῦ Ταραντίνου Πυθαγορικού φυγόντος εἰς Θήβας, καὶ Ἐπαμεινώνδα καθηγησαμένου</note> "of **Lysis the Tarentine Pythagorean**, who fled to **Thebes** and became the instructor of **Epaminondas**") but also by **Iamblichus** in Chapter 35. The latter adds that **Lysis** was held in such great honor by his disciple that he was even accustomed to call him "father." <note>original Greek: Οὗπερ ἐγένετο Ἐπαμινώνδας ἀκροατὴς, καὶ πατέρα τὸν Λύσιν ἐκάλεσεν</note> "Of whom **Epaminondas** became a pupil, and he called **Lysis** 'father'." **Cicero** writes of this same **Lysis** and **Epaminondas** at the end of Book I of *On Duties*: *And those whose entire life and studies were devoted to the pursuit of knowledge did not, however, withdraw from increasing the benefits and advantages of mankind; for they also educated many, so that they might be better citizens and more useful to their states, just as **Lysis** the Pythagorean (this is the correct reading, not **Lysias**, as it appears in some editions) <note>Rittershuisen is correcting a common scribal error where the philosopher Lysis was confused with the orator Lysias</note> taught the Theban **Epaminondas**, **Plato** taught **Dion of Syracuse**, and many others taught many more.* The same author says in Book III of *On the Orator*: *Was it by any other arts (namely, other than all the learned disciplines) that the famous Pythagorean **Lysis** instructed **Epaminondas** of **Thebes**, who was perhaps the greatest man in all of **Greece**? etc.*

**Cornelius Nepos** (who is commonly called **Aemilius Probus**) <note>In the Renaissance, the works of Cornelius Nepos were often mistakenly attributed to a 4th-century copyist named Aemilius Probus</note> also mentions this same **Lysis** in his *Life of Epaminondas*: *For his master in philosophy,* he says, *he had **Lysis** the Tarentine Pythagorean (in certain manuscripts it is written **Lysias**, incorrectly; for one was **Lysias**, the Athenian orator, and the other was **Lysis**, the Pythagorean philosopher). He was so devoted to him that, even as a youth, he preferred the company of that grave and stern old man to all those of his own age; nor did he let him depart until he had so far surpassed his fellow students in learning that it could easily be understood he would similarly excel all others in the remaining arts.*

In this most excellent and brave leader of the **Thebans** (who also died for his country in the **Battle of Mantinea**, and with whom the glory of **Thebes** perished), princes and great men have a model to imitate. They should realize that the study of literature and philosophy is by no means beneath their rank, and they should be grateful toward their teachers, holding them in the place of fathers. Let them remember the saying that one owes even more to a teacher than to a father, because from the father we received only life, but through the benefit and instruction of the teacher, we have learned the honorable way to live that life.

How well, successfully, and faithfully **Epaminondas** was instructed by **Lysis** is shown by **Plutarch** in his book *On the Sign of Socrates*, where he introduces **Theanore** reporting to **Simmias**: *And indeed, having met **Epaminondas** in the morning and heard the manner in which he buried **Lysis**, I recognized that he had been well-educated by him even in the secret doctrines...*

### ON PORPHYRY

...[he] would be [sturdy], and would use the same guardian spirit for his life, unless he were evil; I [think it right] to judge the pilot by the voyage. For broad are the paths of lives, but few are those along which spirits lead men. <note>original Greek: δρὸν εἴη... etc. This appears to be a fragment of a Greek quotation discussing the guidance of a "daemon" or guardian spirit in one's life.</note>

Furthermore, that leader of Greece <note>Epaminondas</note> maintained, among other Pythagorean customs, the practice of singing beautifully to the lyre, as **Cicero** testifies in the introduction to the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. I cannot restrain myself from sharing an example here of the remarkable loyalty and observance of agreements which has been handed down in writing and memory concerning this same **Lysis**. The story is as follows: **Lysis** had a certain close friend named **Euryphamus of Syracuse**. Once, when **Euryphamus** was heading to the Temple of Juno to offer a prayer, he happened to meet **Lysis** near the temple entrance just as **Lysis** was finishing his own devotions. **Euryphamus** asked **Lysis** to wait a moment for his companion’s return until he too had finished his worship. **Lysis** agreed and sat down on a stone seat that was there.

What happened next? **Euryphamus**, becoming deeply immersed in his meditations within the temple, forgot about **Lysis**. He left by another door and a different part of the temple and went home, leaving **Lysis** behind in the other section. But **Lysis**, mindful of the pact or agreement he had made with his friend, remained right there. He did not move from the spot, not only for the remainder of that day, but through the following night and most of the next day, waiting for his friend’s return. Indeed, he would have remained there even longer if **Euryphamus** had not finally remembered him and, coming back to his senses, led him away. For when **Lysis** was missed by the other companions in the common lecture hall the next day, **Euryphamus** finally remembered what had happened at the Temple of Juno. He set out to bring **Lysis** back and found him sitting in the exact same spot where he had left him. Excusing his forgetfulness to **Lysis**, he said: "Some god must have cast this forgetfulness upon me for the purpose of testing your constancy in keeping your word through this occasion." **Iamblichus** describes this <term>event</term> <note>original Greek: σύμβαμα (symbama)</note> in Chapter 30, but the reading there is corrupted (for it prints <term>instructions</term> <note>original Greek: συνταγὰς (syntagas)</note> instead of <term>agreements</term> <note>original Greek: συνθήκας (sunthekas)</note>), and the punctuation is even more flawed, which deceived the translator into confusing different periods and joining things that should not be joined.

**Dicaearchus]** <note>A student of Aristotle and a geographer/historian</note> See the previous note at number 18.

Whether, then, in the works of **Justin**...

### NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUISEN

Should the number also be changed, and **40** <note>Roman numeral: XL</note> be written instead of **60** <note>Roman numeral: LX</note>, merely by inverting the numeral letters? I would think so, had I not seen in John of Salisbury’s seventh book of the *Policraticus, or on the Trifles of Courtiers* <note>A 12th-century work of political philosophy</note>, Chapter 4, where that passage of Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian</note> is cited, written out in full and in the proper sequence of letters as *Sixty*. In that same compiler—who was quite learned for that era and a close associate of the Roman Pope—we read *of the law of fellowship* <note>original Latin: "sodalitii iuris"</note>; whereas in the current published editions of Justin, Book 6, it appears as *by the law of fellowship* <note>original Latin: "sodalitii iure"</note>. However, that reading by Salisbury is perhaps not to be dismissed, and based on it, even in Justin, we should rewrite the text so that we understand *fellowship law* <note>original Latin: "sodalitium ius"</note> to be used as an adjective, referring to a certain sacred oath of the fellowship law, <note>original Greek: οἱονεὶ τὸν ὅρκον τοῦ ἑταιρικοῦ δικαίου; "as it were, the oath of the law of companions"</note>, as the Greeks would call such a bond.

**[First, indeed]** <note>original Greek: Τὸ μὲν πρῶτον</note> There should follow: **to the harbor of Caulonia** <note>original Greek: εἰς Καυλωνίαν τὸν ὅρμον</note>; these words were omitted between the printing and proofreading of the text. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: *Caulonia, a region*. Malchus <note>A reference to Porphyry, who was also known as Malchus</note> here calls it a **harbor** <note>original Greek: ὅρμον</note>. Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note> identifies three cities by this name: one in Italy, another in the territory of the Locrians, and a third in Sicily. He says, however, that according to Hecataeus, it was called *Aulonia*.

**[We have nothing to find fault with in our own laws]** <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις νόμοις οὐδὲν ἔχομεν ἐγκαλεῖν</note> Just as here the Locrians <note>Inhabitants of Locri, a Greek city in southern Italy</note> find nothing lacking or blameworthy in their own laws, and therefore do not want them changed by Pythagoras, so too is the character of nearly all men: each tribe, nation, and city regards its own laws, rites, customs, and institutions as the best and prefers them above all others. **Herodotus** says it beautifully in *Thalia, or the 3rd Muse*: If someone (he says) were to offer all people the opportunity to choose the best from all laws, surely each one, after examining them all, would choose their own. He then adds, *Ancestral rites are not usually mocked except by the insane*; and he says that among other things, the fact that Cambyses <note>A Persian King</note> was violently mad is evidence of this. That everyone feels this way about their own laws—and that even here, "to each his own is beautiful"—he proves both with a certain story of Darius and by the testimony of the most wise Pindar. The story is as follows (**which Origen also chose to include in Book 5 of "Against Celsus", page 261**): Darius, having summoned the Greeks who were in his domain, asked how much money they would want to receive in order to eat their deceased parents; when they denied they would do this for any amount of money, Darius then—in the presence of the Greeks, who learned what was being said through an interpreter—asked those Indians known as the Callatiae, who do eat their parents, how much money they would want to receive to burn their deceased parents in a fire. The Indians...

### ON PORPHYRY

...vehemently protesting, they urged him to prophesy better omens. And so it was established by their customs. Next, this is the testimony of Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet from Thebes, active in the 5th century BCE</note> found in the works of Herodotus and Origen at the cited places: *It seems to me that Pindar did rightly to say that Law is the king of all.* Here, the Latin translator incorrectly translates the word as "custom." <note>original Latin: "morem"; Rittershuisen is distinguishing between mere social custom and the formal authority of Law</note> For the Greek text reads as follows: *And it seems to me Pindar acted rightly, saying that Law is the king of all.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὀρθῶς μοι δοκέει Πίνδαρος ποιῆσαι, Νόμον πάντων βασιλέα φήσας εἶναι.</note> Clement of Alexandria reports the sentiment of that Theban lyric poet more fully in his *Miscellanies* <note>The *Stromata*, a work of early Christian philosophy</note>, Book 1, page 154, and Book 2, page 158: *Law is the king of all, both of mortals and immortals, as the Boeotian Pindar sings.* <note>original Greek: Νόμος ὁ πάντων βασιλεὺς, θνατῶν τε καὶ ἀθανάτων, ὡς ὁ Βοιώτιος ᾄδει Πίνδαρος.</note> Nor do I doubt that Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his logic and ethics</note>, in his definition of law—which Marcian records in Book 2 of the *Digest on Laws* <note>A foundational collection of Roman legal rulings</note>—looked back to those words of Pindar when he said: *Law is the king of all things, both divine and human,* etc. <note>original Greek: Ὁ νόμος πάντων ἐστὶ βασιλεὺς, θείων τε καὶ ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων.</note> Similarly, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous life of Pythagoras</note> in his *Exhortation to Philosophy*, chapter 7, page 41, calls **Law** "ruler and master" when he writes: *For we all agree that while the most excellent and naturally strongest person should rule, law alone must be the ruler and master.* <note>original Greek: Πάντες γὰρ ὁμολογοῦμεν, ὅτι δεῖ μὲν τὸν σπουδαιότατον ἄρχειν, καὶ τὸν τὴν φύσιν κράτιστον, τὸν δὲ νόμον ἄρχοντα καὶ κύριον εἶναι μόνον.</note>

It is truly a wonder why the Locrians <note>Inhabitants of Locri, a Greek city in southern Italy</note> are said here to have so rejected Pythagoras that they openly declared they would abide by their own laws, and were unwilling to allow them to be reformed or corrected by him; especially since it is claimed by others that Pythagoras brought laws to them through Zaleucus. <note>Zaleucus was the legendary first lawgiver of the Locrians, often associated with the Pythagorean school</note> For thus Iamblichus clearly states in chapter 30: *The best lawgivers of all have been those who approached Pythagoras: first Charondas of Catania; then Zaleucus and Timaratus, who wrote the laws for the Locrians.* <note>original Greek: Νομοθέται πάντων ἄριστοι γεγόνασιν οἱ Πυθαγόρᾳ προσελθόντες, πρῶτον μὲν Χαρώνδας ὁ Καταναῖος· ἔπειτα δὲ Ζάλευκος, καὶ Τιμάρατος, οἱ Λοκροῖς γράψαντες τοὺς νόμους.</note> See also the same Iamblichus, chapters 7 and 27, and Seneca’s *Epistle 91* <note>Actually Epistle 90, where Seneca discusses the Golden Age and lawgivers</note>: *The laws of Zaleucus and Charondas are praised. These men learned the laws they would establish for then-flourishing Sicily and for the Greece throughout Italy, not in the marketplace, nor in the halls of legal consultants, but in that silent and sacred retreat of Pythagoras,* etc. 

Perhaps these things can be reconciled if we say that, at first, the Locrians calmly allowed laws to be imposed upon them by Zaleucus, a pupil of Pythagoras; but later, once those laws had long been received into use and custom, they were averse to any change to them—as such change is usually harmful to republics and often even fatal <note>original Greek: θανατηφόρος, "death-bearing"</note>. And when they feared Pythagoras as he approached them, lest he should innovate anything in the laws, they asked him to leave them be and allow them to use their own laws, to which they had already become accustomed.

<margin>57</margin> **Driven by despair to remove himself from life** <note>original Greek: Ἀθυμήσαντα ἑαυτὸν τοῦ βίου ἐξαγαγεῖν</note> If this story of Pythagoras's end is true—that out of sorrow of mind he withdrew himself from human affairs (which is called a "rational withdrawal" <note>original Greek: εὔλογον ἐξαγωγήν; a Stoic term for suicide under justifiable circumstances</note>)...
