### NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUISEN

...the Stoics called this "the leading out" <note>original Greek: *exagoge*. This refers to the Stoic doctrine of "rational suicide," where an individual chooses to leave life if circumstances make it impossible to live virtuously</note>, believing that it was permissible for anyone, when they no longer wished to live, to end their own life. In doing so, however, the individual acted against the very precept of Pythagoras, which stated:

> *All pious men must keep the soul in the custody of the body; nor should anyone depart from human life without the command of that commander who gave the soul to them, lest they seem to have fled the duty assigned to them by God.*

As found in Cicero’s *On Old Age* and Book 6 of *On the Republic*, and in Macrobius, Book 1, chapter 13. I have commented elsewhere with some diligence on this illustrious precept of Pythagoras, which stands in opposition to "self-handing" <note>original Latin: *autocheiria*, a term for suicide</note>.

**For there was no writing of Pythagoras**] I think the text should read **"For there was not any."** Other authors also testify that Pythagoras left no specific work written by himself to posterity. However, Diogenes Laërtius calls such people "mockers" (page 157) and refutes them on the authority of Heraclitus, who wrote three works in imitation of Pythagoras: *Wisdom*, *Much-Learning*, and *Bad Artifice*. Among other things, he says: *Some say Pythagoras left not a single writing, but they are mocking,* etc. Likewise, Lucian in his *Defense of a Slip of the Tongue in Greeting* (found in my Volume 3, page 198) says: *The divine Pythagoras, even if he did not deign to leave anything of his own behind, allows us to judge his work by Ocellus the Lucanian, Archytas, and his other associates,* etc. 

But if this is true, how could Plato—or Dion of Syracuse on Plato's orders—purchase three of his books for one hundred minae? <note>A "mina" was an ancient unit of currency; one hundred minae was a massive sum, equivalent to several years' wages for a laborer</note> There is a passage on this matter in Iamblichus, chapter 31 (which must be corrected in several places): *The precision of their secrecy is admired. For in so many generations of years, no one appears to have encountered <gloss>read: having encountered</gloss> any of the Pythagorean memoirs before the time of Philolaus. Rather, he <gloss>read: who, deleting "but"</gloss> was the first to publish those three famous books, which Dion of Syracuse is said to have bought for one hundred minae at Plato's request, when Philolaus had fallen into a great and severe poverty <gloss>read: having arrived</gloss>.* Since he (Dion, says Arcerius; on the contrary, I say, it was Philolaus. The Latin translator errs here in another way as well) was of the lineage of the Pythagoreans, he therefore shared in the books. 

Iamblichus says that Philolaus obtained the three most famous works of Pythagoras by right of kinship; these had been held in secret for a long time, so that no outsider to the Pythagorean philosophy could stumble upon them. Eventually, weighed down by a wretched and heavy burden of poverty, he sold them to Dion, who was Plato’s friend and <term>proxeneta</term> <note>A legal or financial agent; a middleman who acts on behalf of another party</note>. Diogenes Laërtius testifies to the same in Book 8, page 577: *Until the time of Philolaus, it was not possible to know any Pythagorean doctrine...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion by Conrad Rittershuisen regarding the written legacy of Pythagoras and the violent suppression of his followers. The previous page ended with a debate over whether Pythagoras wrote anything at all; here, Rittershuisen examines specific titles attributed to him and the accounts of the survivors of the attack on the Pythagorean school.</meta>

<page-num>265</page-num>

<header>ON PORPHYRY</header>

...doctrine. This man <note>referring to Philolaus</note> alone published the famous three books, which Plato sent instructions to buy for one hundred minas <note>original Greek: ἑκατὸν μνῶν ὠνηθῆναι; a mina was a significant unit of currency in ancient Greece</note>. The same Diogenes (page 170) also mentions these three works of Pythagoras. Pythagoras is said to have written three treatises: the *Pedagogical*, the *Political*, and the *Physical*; from which it would be easy to guess the subject matter of each. Regarding the *Physical* work of Pythagoras (the beginning of which Diogenes cites in that passage), I conclude from Pliny (Book 25, Chapter 2) that one part dealt with the medicinal powers of plants:

> *After Homer, Pythagoras, famous for his wisdom, was the first to compose a volume on the effects of herbs, attributing the discovery and origin to Apollo, Aesculapius, and the immortal gods in general.* 

See the same Pliny (Book 24, Chapter 17). Otherwise, how could those poems, which are titled the **Golden Verses of Pythagoras**, have Pythagoras as their author if he left no work behind?

**Lysis and Archippus escaped]** Plutarch, in his work *On the Sign of Socrates* <note>original Latin: *de Daemonio Socratis*</note>, names Philolaus instead of Archippus. In this, he differs from both Iamblichus and Malchus <note>Malchus is the original name of Porphyry, the author being commented upon here</note>, just as he does regarding the location of this fire, which he claims happened at Metapontum, rather than Croton. Here are his words:

> *For when the associations of the Pythagoreans in the various cities were expelled, having been overcome by factional strife, the followers of Cylon surrounded the house where those still remaining in Metapontum were meeting and set it on fire. They destroyed everyone in it except Philolaus and Lysis, who, being still young, pushed through the fire by their strength and agility. Philolaus fled to the Lucanians and was saved from there to join other friends who were already gathering again and overcoming the followers of Cylon. But where Lysis went was unknown for a long time,* etc. 

There follow some details about the divine spirit of the now-deceased Lysis. Diogenes Laertius (Book 8, page 577) also mentions this Philolaus: *Until Philolaus, it was not possible to know any Pythagorean doctrine. He alone published the famous three books, which Plato sent instructions to buy for one hundred minas.* To him belongs that noble but false opinion concerning the soul being sent into the body to pay the penalty of punishment, to which Cicero also alluded in his book *On Consolation*: *That the soul is joined to the body because of certain punishments, and is buried in it as if in a tomb.* He confirms this with the authority of ancient theologians and poets. See Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* <term>Stromata: a Greek word meaning "tapestries," used as a title for works of diverse theological reflections</term>, Book 3, page 186.

**As many as happened to be abroad]** Iamblichus says: *Some who happened to be in foreign lands at that time.* Which Arcerius <note>Johannes Arcerius, a 16th-century editor of Iamblichus</note> translates as: *Several...*

# NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUISEN

"...having been busy among other nations." I rewrite this as: **"while abroad"** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀποδηµίαις</note>, and I translate it as: *having then traveled abroad*.

<margin>58</margin> **"They perished from among men"** <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπώλοντο</note>] From this, Iamblichus must be restored, in whose text the word **perished** <note>original Greek: ἀπώλοιτο</note> is missing; this word must therefore be restored to him as if by a legal injunction for the restoration of property <note>original Latin: interdicto unde vi; a Roman legal term for recovering possession taken by force</note>, or if you prefer, according to the standard rules of textual reconstruction.

**"Having gathered together"** <note>original Greek: Συναγαγόντες</note>] In Iamblichus, the word is **"having assembled"** <note>original Greek: συναλίσαντες</note>. This is an elegant word, **to assemble** <note>original Greek: συναλίζεσθαι</note>, which Saint Luke also uses in *Acts 1:4*.

**"Each man left behind"** <note>original Greek: Κατέλειπεν ἕκαστος</note>] In Iamblichus, it reads: **"Each man left behind where they happened to be dying, charging etc."** <note>original Greek: κατέλιπον ἕκαστος, οὗ ἐτύγχανον. τελευτῶν ἐπισκήψ. etc.</note> But these should be corrected from the present passage of Malchus <note>Porphyry</note> in this manner: **"Each man left behind where he happened to be dying, they having charged etc."** <note>original Greek: Κατέλιπεν ἕκαστος οὗ ἐτύγχανε τελευτῶν, ἐπισκήψαντες. etc.</note>

**"To give to no one"** <note>original Greek: Μηδενὶ δοῦναι</note>] In Iamblichus, it is written as **"to be given"** <note>original Greek: διδοµέναι</note>; it should be corrected based on this text.

**"For a long time"** <note>original Greek: Μέχρι πολλοῦ χρόνου</note>] Iamblichus has: **"For a very long time"** <note>original Greek: Μέχρι παµπόλλου χρόνου</note>. In the same Chapter 35, instead of **"since he happened to be alone with his students"** <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ µόνοις ἐτύγχανε τοῖς µαθητοῖς</note>, I suggest the reading: **"he met with"** <note>original Greek: ἐνετύγχανε</note>. And shortly after: **"They were over three hundred"** <note>original Greek: ἦσαν ὑπὲρ τριακοσίους</note>; the particle **for** <note>original Greek: γὰρ</note> should be added after the word **they were** <note>original Greek: ἦσαν</note>. In the same chapter: **"The silent hatred broke out"** <note>original Greek: Ἐξεῤῥάγη τὸ σιωπούµενον µῖσος</note>; it should be read as **"being kept silent"** <note>original Greek: σιωπώµενον</note>, as we learned as boys <note>a grammatical correction regarding the proper spelling of the participle</note>. And, **"It is not fitting to allow them to speak"** <note>original Greek: Οὐ προσήκει ἐὰν αὐτοὺς λέγειν</note>: we should restore **"to allow"** <note>original Greek: ἐᾶν</note> instead of the word for **"if"** <note>original Greek: ἐὰν</note>. And for **"they have killed"** <note>original Greek: πεφεῖσιν</note>, read **"having killed"** <note>original Greek: πεfνεῶσιν</note>. In the same place, soon after, for **"it has been written"** <note>original Greek: ἀνάγραπται</note>, I restore not **"it has been crossed out"** <note>original Greek: διαγέγραπται</note>, but **"it has been recorded"** <note>original Greek: ἀναγέγραπται</note>. And again in the same place: **"not saying that even children should be torn away from their parents"** <note>original Greek: οὐ φάσκοντα δεῖν οὐδὲ τοὺς παῖδας ἀπὸ τῶν γονέων διασπᾷν</note>: let us not follow the editor Arcerius in reading **"saying"** in the feminine form <note>original Greek: φάσκουσαν</note>; the true reading is the masculine plural **"not saying"** <note>original Greek: οὐ φάσκοντες</note>. I also think that for **"he helped into exile"** <note>original Greek: συνεφυγάδευσε</note>, we should rewrite it as **"they helped into exile"** <note>original Greek: συνεφυγάδευσαν</note>.

But these matters are mentioned as if in passing. Another time will come when we shall provide the whole of Iamblichus properly purged of errors, unless we are beaten to it by someone else in this task—which has already happened to us more than once in other such undertakings.

**"Nicomachus says"** <note>original Greek: Φησὶ Νικόµαχος</note>] Porphyry (or Malchus) names this Nicomachus among other Pythagorean philosophers, even in the third book of his *Commentaries Against the Christians*. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History, Book 6, Chapter 19*.

**"To avoid foreign friendships"** <note>original Greek: Τὰς ἀλλοτρίας ἐκκλίνειν φιλίας</note>] Although the Pythagoreans placed the highest value on friendship—so much so that among friends all things were common, and they held that a friend was "another self" <note>original Latin: alterum eundem</note>, as we noted above in Number 33—they were mutually disposed toward one another just as an honorable father usually is toward his own children.

<summary>Rittershuisen provides a series of technical philological corrections to the texts of Porphyry and Iamblichus, comparing their accounts of the Pythagorean school's history and the specific wording of their doctrines on friendship and secrecy.</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, Nicomachus, Porphyry, Malchus, Eusebius, Pythagoreans, textual criticism, philology, friendship, Greek grammar corrections</keywords>

# ON PORPHYRY

(Iamblichus chapter 31: *All the Pythagoreans felt toward one another as a virtuous father would toward his children* <note>original Greek: Πάντας τοὺς Πυθαγορείους οὕτως ἔχειν πρὸς ἀλλήλους, ὡς ἂν πατὴρ σπουδαῖος πρὸς τέκνα ἔχοι</note>), indeed they even held their friends as gods, as the same Iamblichus testifies in chapter 35. However, they were friends only among themselves; they plainly rejected external friendships, no matter how splendid or even royal they might be. Iamblichus chapter 31: *Thus they were reluctant to enter into external friendships, even if they happened to be royal* <note>original Greek: Οὕτως δυσκατάθετοι πρὸς τὰς ἐξωτερικὰς φιλίας ἦσαν, εἰ καὶ βασιλικαὶ τυγχάνοιεν</note>. And, as the verses cited in the same author's 35th chapter have it:

> They held their companions equal to the blessed gods;
> But the others they held as nothing, and of no account.
<note>original Greek: Τοὺς μὲν ἑταίρους ἦγον ἴσους μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι· Τοὺς δ' ἄλλους ἡγοῦντ' οὔτ' ἐν λόγῳ, οὔτ' ἐν ἀριθμῷ.</note>

They had this law: that they were permitted to clasp the right hand only with fellow Pythagoreans, and with no one else (except for parents). Iamblichus, in the aforementioned chapter 35: *To offer the right hand only to Pythagoreans, and to no other of their household, except parents* <note>original Greek: Μόνοις τοῖς Πυθαγορείοις τὴν δεξιὰν ἐμβάλλειν, ἑτέρῳ δὲ μηδενὶ τῶν οἰκείων, πλὴν τῶν γονέων</note>. This might perhaps be more correctly rendered if the words are rearranged: *except for their own parents* <note>original Greek: πλὴν τῶν οἰκείων γονέων</note>. From this also came a proverb, which remained in use even in Iamblichus’s time; when people wanted to describe a state of the highest goodwill between certain individuals, they would say of them *that they are of the Pythagoreans* <note>original Greek: ὅτι τῶν Πυθαγορείων εἰσί</note>: that is, *that they belong to the number of the Pythagoreans*. Iamblichus chapter 33. But that very practice—this sort of disdain for other men who were not Pythagoreans—stirred up the greatest envy against them, and eventually brought about their ruin and almost **total destruction** <note>original Greek: πανωλεθρίαν; "utter ruin"</note>. This was also observed by Ausonius in *Idyll 15* regarding the difficulty of choosing a way of life, the verses of which I have already cited above.

As for the phrase here, **to avoid friendships** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλίνειν φιλίας</note>, the author soon uses the term **to turn away from them** <note>original Greek: περικάμπτειν αὐτάς</note> with the same meaning; these same words appear in Iamblichus, chapter 33. In that passage, a certain translator wrongly wishes to change the reading for us to **to cut off** <note>original Greek: περικόπτειν</note>, and translates it as *amputate*. He says (in his *Corrections*) that foreign and harmful friendships are not merely to be "turned away from," but should be plainly "cut off." On the contrary, I say we must retain the elegant word **to turn away** <note>original Greek: περικάμπτειν</note>, which has the same force as **to avoid** <note>original Greek: τῷ ἐκκλίνειν</note>. In the Gospel history, the word **to withdraw** <note>original Greek: ἐκνεῦσαι</note> is used with this same sense <note>Rittershuisen likely refers to John 5:13, where Jesus "slips away" or "withdraws" from a crowd</note>.

Furthermore, regarding what I noted above in Note 33 concerning friendship and how zealously the Pythagoreans cultivated it, I cannot help but add here an illustrious passage from Simplicius in his *Commentary on the Handbook of Epictetus*, page 65 of the Venice edition. There, among other memorable things, he says: the Pythagoreans called friendship the "bond of all virtues," and that no one is capable of such a great good unless they are endowed with every virtue, so much so—

### NOTES OF C. RITTERSHUISEN

even if one [virtue] should be lacking. 

Pure friendship, which brings friendly souls into a union, is the most beautiful preparation for union with God. For it is impossible for souls of the same kind to achieve a better union. And rightly did the Pythagoreans honor friendship more than the other virtues, and called it the bond of all the virtues. For if any one of the virtues is missing, friendship refuses to appear. For who that is unjust, or intemperate, or cowardly, or even more, foolish, could receive the good of friendship?
<note>original Greek: Ἡ καθαρὰ φιλία τὰς φίλας ψυχὰς εἰς ἕνωσιν συνάγουσα μελέτη καλλίστη γίνεται τῆς πρὸς Θεὸν ἑνώσεως. καὶ γὰρ ἀδύνατον πρὸς τοὺς ὁμοφύλους ψυχὰς κρείττονος ἑνώσεως τυχεῖν. καὶ καλῶς οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι περισσῶς τῶν ἄλλων ἀρετῶν τὴν φιλίαν ἐτίμων, καὶ σύνδεσμον αὐτὴν πασῶν τῶν ἀρετῶν ἔλεγον. Καὶ μιᾶς γὰρ ἡστινοσοῦν τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀπολειπομένης, οὐκ ἐθέλει παραγίνεσθαι φιλία. τίς γὰρ ἄδικος, ἢ ἀκόλαστος, ἢ δειλὸς, ἢ ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀνόητος; δύναται τὸ τῆς φιλίας ἀγαθὸν ὑποδέχεσθαι;</note>

**To have maintained unyielding**
<note>original Greek: Ἀνένδοτον διατετηρηκέναι</note>] In the edition of Iamblichus, it is published as *unyielding* <note>original: ἀνένδοτος</note>; which Arcerius <note>Theodorus Arcerius, a 16th-century editor</note> is eager to change into the adverb *unyieldingly* <note>original: ἀνενδότως</note>. But it should be restored there from Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> as the neuter *unyielding* <note>original: ἀνένδοτον</note>.

**From whom Aristoxenus**
<note>original Greek: Ἐξ ὧν Ἀριστόξενος</note>] A certain Aristoxenus is also praised by Aulus Gellius <note>Rittershuisen uses the spelling "Agellius," common in the Renaissance</note> (Book IV, chapter 11) as a musician and a man most diligent in ancient literature, a student of Aristotle, and one who left behind a book about Pythagoras. However, since Malchus writes here and above (Number 61) that he was an intimate of Dionysius of Syracuse <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant</note>, from whom he himself heard the story about Damon and Phintias; hence I doubt whether the same Aristoxenus could have been a student of Aristotle, or if there were two different men of the same name. The calculation of the dates makes the latter more likely.

**To teach letters in Corinth**
<note>original Greek: Γράμματα ἐν Κορίνθῳ διδάσκειν</note>] Thus it is in our manuscript. But it should be read as *he used to teach* <note>original: ἐδίδασκεν</note>, as it appears in Iamblichus, chapter 33. Cicero, in the 3rd book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, says: *Dionysius the tyrant, having been expelled from Syracuse, taught boys at Corinth; so much was he unable to be without power.* <note>original Latin: Dionysius quidem tyrannus Syracusis expulsus Corinthi pueros docebat: vsque eo imperio carere non poterat.</note> Ammianus Marcellinus, in Book XIV, writes: *Changeable and inconstant Fortune made Agathocles the Sicilian a king from a potter, and placed Dionysius—once the terror of nations—in charge of a grammar school in Corinth.* <note>original Latin: Fortuna mutabilis et inconstans fecit Agathoclem Siculum ex figulo regem, et Dionysium, gentium quondam terrorem, Corinthi ludo literario praefecit.</note> etc. This very well-known story gave rise to a proverb: *Dionysius in Corinth*. This is used to signify someone reduced from the highest dignity and the peak of power to a private and humble fortune—from a scepter properly so called, the emblem of royal majesty, to the *rods, the scepters of schoolmasters*, as Martial calls them. Regarding this proverb, see Erasmus, *Adages*, Volume 1, Century 1, Adage 83, where besides Plutarch’s *On Talkativeness* and Quintilian’s Book VIII, he also cites Cicero’s 9th book of *Letters to Atticus*. There is also another proverb: *Corinth of Zeus* <note>original: Διὸς Κόρινθος</note>, which Pindar uses.

<margin>60</margin>
**And he says that out of pities and tears etc.**
<note>original Greek: Φησὶ δ’ ὡς οἴκτων καὶ δακρύων etc.</note>] That these were the words of Aristoxenus himself is apparent from Iamblichus's *Life of Pythagoras*, Number 234.

### ON PORPHYRY.

**Once Dionysius** <note>original Greek: Ποτὲ Διονύσιος</note>] Here in the manuscript there were one or two gaps. The reader will easily see how these should be filled if he compares Iamblichus, chapter 33, where the same story of Damon and Phintias is related <note>This refers to the famous story where one friend stands as a hostage for the other under the tyrant Dionysius II of Syracuse</note>. See also Cicero, Book III of *On Duties* and Book 5 of the *Tusculan Disputations*; Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7; Lactantius, Book V, chapter 17; Plutarch, and others.

**Since it has been thus decided for you** <note>original Greek: Ἐπεὶ οὕτω σοι δέδοκται</note>] In the edition of Iamblichus, this is incorrectly written as *it has been shown* <note>original Greek: δέδεικται</note>; Arcerius <note>Theodorus Arcerius, a 16th-century editor</note> also correctly noticed this and advised that it be changed to *it has been decided* <note>original Greek: δέδοκται</note>. This brings to my mind that famous Agrippinus <note>Paconius Agrippinus, a Stoic philosopher</note> who, when he was about to dine and was informed of the sentence of exile imposed on him by Nero, said: "It is well; let us then go to Aricia and dine there." See the story described by Epictetus in Stobaeus, Discourse 7, *On Fortitude*. Regarding this Agrippinus, a most brave exile, our uncle Matthias Bergius—a most excellent and learned man <term>of pious memory</term> <note>original Latin: p. m., for piae memoriae</note>—wrote the following epigram during a certain calamity of his own:

> Every lot of life pleases Agrippinus: and as circumstances
> And chance have brought them, so he bears his mind and soul.
> With his liver scorched by fever, he sings his own praises to the fever:
> Bearing reproaches, he shows that honor dwells within them.
> When pressed by heavy poverty, scarcity dictates
> His praises, and the man opens his pen and mouth for them.
> Finally, Nero deprives him of his fatherland just as he is about to dine. Then he says:
> "Rightly so: we shall feed, then, in a cottage at Aricia."

->O singular equanimity and presence of mind!<-

**The rest of the day** <note>original Greek: Τὸ λοιπὸν τῆς ἡμέρας</note>] Iamblichus says the same in Malchus <note>Porphyry</note> number 235. According to these authors, therefore, the condemned Phintias sought a delay of only a few hours to undergo his death. Cicero differs from them in the passage cited just above, as he writes that Phintias requested a few days for himself.

**So that he might settle his affairs** <note>original Greek: Ὅπως οἰκονομήσηται</note>] To "arrange one's house" means to organize one's testament, or to establish one's last will. Thus in the Holy Scriptures: "Set your house in order" <note>original Greek: Ἔντειλαι τῷ οἴκῳ σου</note>, in the history of King Hezekiah, 2 Kings chapter 20, at the beginning, and Isaiah chapter 38.

**Having provided a guarantor** <note>original Greek: Ἐγγυητὴν παρασχών</note>] Legal interpreters debate whether a <term>guarantor</term> <note>original Latin: fideiussor</note> or <term>surety</term> <note>original Latin: vas</note> is permitted in capital cases. On this question, see the most lucid treatise on *Guarantors* by the most distinguished Lord Antonius Heringius, my old comrade-in-arms and honored friend, chapter 10, number 535, and many following sections.

He draws parallels between Pythagorean composure and Stoic resilience, citing the example of Agrippinus under Nero and discussing the legal implications of providing a hostage for a death sentence.</summary>

->### NOTES BY C. RITTERSHUSEN<-

**And he remained** <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἔμεινεν</note>] What is found in Iamblichus (Number 236), **And indeed he was** <note>original Greek: Καὶ μὲν ἦν</note>, is corrupt and should be corrected from this text; or perhaps one should read there **and to remain** <note>original Greek: καὶ μένειν</note>.

<margin>61</margin> **As one about to be abandoned** <note>original Greek: Ὡς ἐγκαταλειφθησόμενον</note>] In Iamblichus, there is an addition: **and mocking him, they said a deer had been substituted** <note>original Greek: καὶ σκώπτοντας, ἔλαφον ἀντιδεδύσθαι λέγειν</note>. No one will understand the force of this taunt who does not realize that the mockers were alluding to the myth of the deer that was substituted for Iphigenia and sacrificed in her place <note>In Greek mythology, Artemis saved Iphigenia from sacrifice by replacing her with a deer at the last moment</note>.

**Requesting that he be admitted as a third into their friendship** <note>original Greek: Ἀξιῶσαι τρίτον αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν φιλίαν παραδέξασθαι</note>] O, the great power and remarkable beauty of friendship, which even tyrants consider worth seeking for themselves! A passage from Cicero in Book III of *On Duties* is relevant here. They say that Damon and Pythias (though it should be read as **Phintias**) the Pythagoreans were so minded toward each other that, when the tyrant Dionysius had set a day for the execution of one of them, and the one sentenced to death had requested a few days to settle the affairs of his family, **the other became a surety for his return, so that if the first did not return, he himself would have to die.** <note>original Latin: vas factus est alter eius sistendi, ut, si ille non reuertisset, moriendum esset ipsi</note> When the condemned man returned on the appointed day, the tyrant, admiring their loyalty, asked that they enroll him as a third member in their friendship. The words of Cicero in Book II of *On Ends* also pertain to this: *Will you give yourself to a tyrant as a surety for your friend's death, as that Pythagorean did for the Sicilian tyrant?* Valerius Maximus also describes this same history beautifully in Book IV, chapter 7, "On Friendship," where he concludes it thus: *Such indeed was the strength of their friendship that it was able to breed a contempt for death, extinguish the sweetness of life, soften cruelty, turn hatred into love, and repay punishment with a kindness: to which almost as much veneration is owed as to the sacred rites of the immortal gods,* etc.

**To such a point** <note>original Greek: Εἰς τοιοῦτο</note>] I guessed the reading should be **to this** <note>original Greek: εἰς τοῦτο</note>. But in the edition of Iamblichus mentioned above, I see it is published as **to such a thing** <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ τοιοῦτο</note>. From this I am led to the conjecture that it is more correctly read in both places as **and to such a point** <note>original Greek: εἰς τε τοιοῦτο</note>.

**Hippobotus and Neanthes** <note>original Greek: Ἱππόβοτος δὲ καὶ Νεάνθης</note>] More research is needed as to who this Hippobotus was. Neanthes, however, was praised above by Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> as a writer on the history and doctrines of the Pythagoreans. Moreover, the narrative promised here concerning Myllia of Croton and his wife Timycha of Sparta is truly memorable; but since it has been lost from this point (as perhaps not a few other things are missing from the completeness of this little book—indeed, even the entire second book is missing)...

He also notes gaps in the surviving manuscript regarding other Pythagorean figures like Myllia and Timycha.</summary>

<header>ON PORPHYRY.</header>

...appears to have been lost, although we demonstrated above at Number 42—citing Cyril’s ninth book *Against Julian*, where he praises certain parts of Porphyry’s first book—that Porphyry (who is the same person as Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original Semitic name was Malchus, meaning "king"; his teacher later "Greektold" it to Porphyrius, referring to the royal purple color</note>) wrote several books on the history of Pythagoras. This lost section can easily be reconstructed from Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who also wrote a biography of Pythagoras</note>, chapter 31. The summary is as follows: When this Pythagorean couple was captured and brought before the tyrant Dionysius, he voluntarily offered them every luxury, even suggesting he might admit them into a partnership in his rule. But when they refused these magnificent promises from the tyrant, he asked first the husband, then the wife, what the reason was that the Pythagoreans preferred to face death rather than trample upon beans in a field <note>The Pythagorean prohibition against beans is one of the most famous and debated "taboos" of the ancient world; explanations range from religious reasons to the physical resemblance of beans to human embryos</note>. He promised that if he learned this from them, he would grant them an honorable release, since they did not wish to remain with him. Then, without hesitation, Myllias said: "Those men preferred to die rather than trample the beans; but I, lest I be forced to reveal the reason for this to you, prefer to trample the beans." After the man was removed, the tyrant attacked the woman, Timycha. He was confident that he would more easily squeeze whatever he wanted to know out of her, due to both the "weakness of her sex," the fact that she was pregnant at that very time, and his threats of torture. But his hope failed him by a wide margin. For Timycha, in an example of astounding persistence, bit off her own tongue with her teeth and spat it into the tyrant's very face, so that she would not accidentally reveal secrets that should be kept silent, even if she were overcome by the force of the tortures. See Iamblichus in the aforementioned chapter 31. In this matter, Timycha’s courage was similar to that of Leaena <note>The name means "Lioness"</note>, an Athenian courtesan. For she too, when the executioner was finally exhausted from inflicting tortures, spat her bitten-off tongue into the face of the tyrant Hippias (son of Pisistratus), so that she might "spit out her voice" as well, lest she betray the conspirators even if she had wanted to after being defeated. See Tertullian in his *Apology* and his *Book to the Martyrs*, Plutarch in the *Life of Hyperides* and the book *On Talkativeness* <note>original Greek: Περὶ Ἀδολεσχίας</note>, Pausanias in *Attics*, Pliny Book 7, chapter 23 and Book 34, chapter 8, Aulus Gellius Book 9, chapter 3 and Book 17, chapter 21, Athenaeus Book 13, and Lactantius Book 1, chapter 20. Similar stories about a certain Theodorus of Syracuse can be read in Livy, Book 24, and Valerius Maximus, Book 3, chapter 3, *On Patience*: where there are also examples of Anaxarchus and others of incredible persistence and hardiness.

Furthermore, in that same passage of Iamblichus, chapter 31, a little before, the word **refusing** <note>original Greek: ἀνανευόντων (ananeuontōn), literally "tossing the head back" in denial</note> is rendered as "nodding in agreement" <note>original Latin: annuentibus</note>. Correct this to **refusing** <note>original Latin: abnuentibus</note>: for this is what the Greek term means, just like the word **to turn away** <note>original Greek: ἀπονεύειν (aponeuein)</note>. To "nod in agreement," however, is a different word <note>original Greek: ἐπινεύειν (epineuein)</note>. From the same chapter, another error...

The author provides numerous historical parallels of heroic silence under torture, such as the Athenian Leaena.</summary>

I briefly correct this remarkable sentiment, which is similar to passages in Terence: <note>original: "Ὡς οὐδὲν δεῖται ἀνθρωπίνων συμπτωμάτων ἀπροσδόκητον εἶναι παρὰ τοῖς νοῦν ἔχουσιν, ἀλλὰ πάντα προσδοκᾷν, ὧν μὴ τυγχάνουσιν αὐτοὶ κύριοι ὄντες."</note> "That nothing of human accidents should be unexpected to those who have sense, but they should expect everything over which they themselves are not masters." It should be read "it is necessary" <note>original Greek: "δεῖ"</note> for the human [accidents]. For Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras</note> correctly has it this way in chapter 32, where the same precept is repeated in so many words, and is elegantly called the <term>greatest foundation of nobility</term> <note>original Greek: "μέγιστον τῆς γενναιότητος ἔρμα." The word "erma" refers to ballast or a foundation that keeps a ship steady</note>. For I would prefer to read it that way there, rather than as it was published, "and this was also the greatest [thing] toward the foundation of nobility," or, as Arcerius <note>Theodorus Arcerius, an earlier editor of Iamblichus</note> guesses, "the greatest <term>godsend</term> <note>original Greek: "ἔρμαιον" (hermaion), meaning a stroke of luck or a gift from Hermes</note> for nobility." You could also simply read, "the greatest foundation of nobility," omitting the word "toward."

# SUPPLEMENTS

## CERTAIN NOTES OF RITTERSHUISEN, TO BE INSERTED IN THEIR PROPER PLACES.

Regarding Number 1. Where you observe in how much esteem Pythagoras was held, not only by his own followers but also by foreigners, I would wish to add a passage from St. Augustine, Volume 1, page 495, at the very end of the second book of *On Order* to Zenobius. After Alypius <note>Augustine's close friend and student</note> had proclaimed the wonderful and truly divine discipline of Pythagoras, which was rightfully both held and approved, Augustine, taking up the discourse after other matters, speaks as follows:

> *As for your mention of Pythagoras, I believe it came to mind through that divine, hidden order. For a very necessary thing had entirely slipped my mind, which I am accustomed to admire and, as you know, extol with almost daily praise in that man—if anything is to be believed from written records (though who would not believe Varro? <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar renowned for his vast learning</note>). He used to pass down the discipline of governing the republic to his followers as the final stage, only when they were already learned, perfected, wise, and blessed. For he saw such great waves in politics that he did not wish to commit to them anyone except a man who, in governing, could avoid the reefs almost divinely, and if everything failed, would himself become a reef against those waves. For of the wise man alone can it be most truly said: "He stands unmoved like a rock in the sea," and the rest, which have been said in brilliant verses to this effect, etc.* <note>Augustine is quoting Virgil’s Aeneid (7.586) to describe the stoic stability of the Pythagorean wise man</note>

These are the words of Augustine (Vol. 1, page 5), which he nevertheless felt should be re-examined by him in the first book of the *Retractions*... <note>In his later years, Augustine wrote the "Retractiones" to correct or clarify points in his earlier works where he felt he had been too praising of pagan philosophers</note>

**To the same work, Number 1.** Where I discuss the statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades <note>An influential Athenian statesman and general</note> placed at Rome, I add the testimony of Pliny the Elder, **Book 34, Chapter 6** of his *Natural History*: *I find that statues of both Pythagoras and Alcibiades were placed at the corners of the Comitium <note>The open-air public meeting space in ancient Rome</note>. **To Number 15.** [Regarding the phrase "Those who eat figs"] Pliny, **Book 23, Chapter 7**: *Figs assist the body and its strength; for this reason, athletes were previously fed on this food.* Pythagoras the trainer was the first to transition them to eating meat, etc. However, Pliny here seems to imply, by the title of "trainer," a different Pythagoras from our philosopher; indeed, Diogenes Laërtius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> testifies in **Book 8** that several men—four, in fact—lived at the same time with the name Pythagoras.

**In the same place.** Regarding the idea that things which have once occurred happen again, and that there is absolutely nothing new, I add these words of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus, surnamed the Philosopher <note>Commonly known today as Marcus Aurelius</note>, from **Book 10** of his work *On His Own Life* <note>The *Meditations*</note>, page 284 of the Strasbourg edition: "Continuously reflect on how all such things happen now, just as they happened before, and reflect on them happening in the future; and keep before your eyes whole dramas and stages of similar form, as many as you have known from your own experience or from more ancient history—such as the entire court of Hadrian, the entire court of Philip, of Alexander, or of Croesus. For all those were just like these, only with different actors." <note>original Greek: "Συνεχῶς ἐπινοεῖν, πῶς πάντα τοιαῦτα νῦν γίνεται... μόνον δι’ ἑτέρων."</note> This is how the text there should be punctuated, which the most learned Xylander <note>Wilhelm Holtzmann, a 16th-century scholar</note> did not notice, incorrectly joining the phrase "through others" to the next word, "imagine." What the Emperor means is this: the actions were the same; only different persons were produced, as if on a stage, to perform the same play.

**To Number 20.** "The Tetractys, by which they used to swear." <note>The Tetractys was a mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</note> Lucian, in his book *On a Slip of the Tongue in Greeting*: "There are those who also consider the Tetractys to be their greatest oath, or that which completes their perfect number." <note>original Greek: "Εἰσὶ δὲ, οἳ καὶ τὴν τετρακτὺν..."</note> I read this as "or," and "it completes." <note>Rittershuisen is suggesting a textual correction to the Greek verbs.</note> Moreover, I have explained above—using other authors as well as Ammonius and Lucian himself in his *Sale of Lives*—how the Tetractys, or the "number four," produces the perfect number for the Pythagoreans, which is ten. See also Sextus the Philosopher <note>Sextus Empiricus</note> and Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, **Chapter 13, page 27.**

**To Number 26.** Regarding what I propose here as a conjecture about the name Malchus—namely, that Porphyry is identified by it—this is the absolute truth. It is confirmed not only by the testimony of Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, but also by Porphyry himself in the *Life of Plotinus* which he wrote. For he says: "Aemilius (whom Suidas also mentions as a disciple of Plotinus) dedicated this book to me, and in the inscription itself he named me *Basileus* (that is, King). For that was my name; in my native language I was called **MALCHUS**, which was also my father's name. But **MALCHUS**, when translated into the Greek language, is called *Basileus*, which means King." <note>Porphyry was born in Tyre, and "Malchus" is derived from the Semitic root *MLK*, meaning king.</note>

**To Number 35.** "Sometimes becoming fat..." <note>original Greek: "Ποτὲ μὲν πιαϊνόμενον"</note> What Malchus <note>Porphyry</note> writes here concerning Pythagoras, Iamblichus writes concerning the Pythagoreans in general in **Chapter 31**, a passage which I must take this opportunity to clear of more than one significant error. "For these men," he says, "took care that their bodies should always remain in the same condition, and never be at one time shriveled and at another time fleshy; for they thought this was a sign of an uneven life." <note>original Greek: "Προσεῖχον γὰρ οὗτοι, τὰ σώματα..."</note> He says: *These men (the Pythagoreans) gave effort so that their bodies were always in the same state, nor were they ever wrinkled*

...leanness, but at other times suffering from an excessive mass of flesh. For they took this as a sign of an inconsistent way of life. The scribes had handled this passage very poorly, as did the translator *Frisius*, who was far too trusting of them. For the text had been published with this most faulty punctuation and reading: "For they attended to their bodies, as if they were situated in the same state, and never worried, even when they were fleshy." <note>original Greek: "Προσεῖχον γὰρ οὗτοι τὰ σώματα, ὡσὰν ἐπὶ τῶν αὐτῶν διακεῖνται, καὶ μήποτε μεριμνᾷ, ὅτε δὲ πολύσαρκα."</note> This is how *Arcerius* <note>Johannes Arcerius, a 16th-century editor of Iamblichus</note> had translated it: "If indeed they applied bodies to these things, just as if they were fixed and attached in them, and not at all worried, even when they are heavy with flesh or fleshy, etc." But no one will doubt that I have correctly restored—to say nothing of the other points—the word **shriveled** <note>original Greek: "ῥικνά" (rhikna)</note>: a word which, besides Homer and Hippocrates, our *Oppian* <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet known for his works on fishing and hunting</note> also used in the *Halieutica* <note>A poem about fishing</note>, Book 5, verse 406: **shriveled of feet** <note>original Greek: "ῥικνὰ ποδῶν"</note>, where he speaks of a sea turtle wrinkled from lying in the sun. Furthermore, *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras</note> elegantly contrasts **shriveled bodies** with **fleshy ones**: that is, I say, lean and wrinkled versus those that are fleshy and well-conditioned. Next, after the word "but" and before "likewise," I think something is missing; or certainly the word "but" is redundant. In the same place, there is a faulty reading: "they called the admonisher *paidartan*"; for which I say we should substitute: **to admonish** <note>original Greek: "τὸ νουθετεῖν"</note>. I deny that "admonisher" <note>original Greek: "Νουθετὴν"</note> is a proper reading here. Let this work also be granted to *Iamblichus*, whom we have corrected in many other places in passing in this little book of Notes, intending to perform that task more fully elsewhere in a dedicated work.

**To Number 32.** Where the text discusses abstinence from living creatures, I add what is famously said about the **bloodless Delian altar** <note>An altar on the island of Delos, sacred to Apollo, where no animal sacrifices were permitted</note>, which only *Pythagoras* dared to approach, as he was polluted by no slaughter. *Clement of Alexandria* <note>A Christian theologian who often synthesized Greek philosophy with Christianity</note> writes in his *Stromata* <note>The "Miscellanies," one of Clement's major works</note>, Book 5, page 304: "But they have spread the story that the most ancient altar in Delos is holy, which they say only Pythagoras approached, since he was not defiled by slaughter and death." <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλὰ τὸν μὲν ἀρχαιότατον βωμὸν ἐν Δήλῳ ἅγιον εἶναι τεθρυλήκασι... φόνῳ καὶ θανάτῳ μὴ μιανθέντα."</note> He adds, however: "The truly holy altar is the righteous soul, and the incense rising from it is holy prayer." <note>original Greek: "βωμὸν ἀληθῶς ἅγιον τὴν δικαίαν ψυχὴν, καὶ τὰ ἀπ' αὐτῆς θυμιάματα τὴν ὁσίαν εὐχήν."</note>

**To Number 42.** Where the text discusses the **symbolic teaching** of *Pythagoras*, I add a passage from *Stobaeus* <note>A 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors</note> (Sermon 5, page 59) that should by no means be overlooked: "Indeed, nothing is so characteristic of the Pythagorean philosophy as its symbolic nature; it is a type of teaching mixed with voice and silence, as if in a mystery rite, so as not to say: *I will sing for those who understand; but shut the doors, you profane*; <note>A standard formula used in mystery religions to warn the uninitiated away from sacred secrets</note> but rather, the thing being expressed has light and character for those who are familiar with it, yet is blind and meaningless to the inexperienced. For just as the Lord at Delphi <note>The god Apollo, speaking through his oracle</note> neither speaks nor conceals, but signifies, according to *Heraclitus*; so also for the Pythagoreans..."

...of symbols, that which seems to be expressed is hidden, and that which is hidden is understood. <note>original Greek: "συμβόλων καὶ τὸ φράζεσθαι δοκοῦν, κρυπτόμενόν ἐστι· καὶ τὸ κρύπτεσθαι, νοούμενον."</note>

The verse **"I shall sing for those who understand"** <note>original Greek: "Ἀείσω συνετοῖσι"</note> etc. also appears in Stobaeus, *Discourse 39*. Similarly, Orpheus—as cited by Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, and others—says: **"I will speak to those for whom it is lawful; but shut the doors, you profane ones."** <note>original Greek: "Φθέγξομαι, οἷς θέμις ἐστί· θύρας δ’ ἐπίθεσθε βέβηλοι."</note> In imitation of these, Virgil wrote: **"Away, O away, you profane ones!"** <note>original Latin: "Procul o, procul este profani."</note> And Horace: **"I hate the profane crowd and keep them away."** <note>original Latin: "Odi profanum vulgus et arceo."</note>

**Regarding Number 48.** Where numbers are discussed, I add Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, chapter 2, page 2, and chapter 13, page 27. Also, Sextus the Philosopher <note>Sextus Empiricus, a Skeptic philosopher who wrote on Pythagorean mathematics</note>.

**Regarding Number 52.** Saint Augustine also emphasizes the mystery and perfection of the **denarius** <term>denarius: the number ten</term> in more than one place: especially in *Book II on the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 4, page 401; in *Gospel Questions*, Book II, chapter 6, page 339, Volume 4; in *Book XX of The City of God*, chapter 23; and in his single book *Against the Letter of Mani*, chapter 10. In the latter, he writes that the number ten signifies perfection, and that this perfection is achieved by adding the **trinity** of the Creator to the **septenary** <term>septenary: the number seven</term> by which all created things consist. He remarks: **"Regarding these matters, many things are discussed piously and cautiously among spiritual men."** <note>original Latin: "De quibus (inquit) rebus inter spiritales viros pie cauteque multa tractantur."</note> Furthermore, the Pythagoreans called not only ten a perfect number, but also the **senarius** <term>senarius: the number six</term>, which they also called **meseuthun** <note>original Greek: "μεσευθὺν"</note>: **because it is the middle of the "straight line"—that is, the midpoint between ten and two.** <note>The number 6 is the arithmetic mean of 2 and 10: (2+10)/2 = 6</note> Clement of Alexandria explains this more extensively in *Stromata*, Book 6, page 290.

**Regarding Number 56.** Saint Augustine also agrees with those who believe that Pythagoras wrote nothing. He says the following in *Book I on the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 7, Volume 4, page 376:

> When the pagans ask why Christ himself did not write anything, they seem prepared to believe about him only what he might have written about himself, rather than what others proclaimed about him according to their own judgment. I ask them: why have they believed such things about certain of their own most noble philosophers, which the written memory of their disciples has left behind, even though the philosophers themselves wrote nothing? For Pythagoras, than whom Greece then had nothing more illustrious in that contemplative virtue, is held to have written nothing, not only about himself, but about any matter at all. Socrates, moreover, etc.

Furthermore, where I mentioned in the Notes the shrine of **Insult** <note>original: Contumelia</note> and **Shamelessness** <note>original: Impudentia</note> consecrated at Athens, I add in passing that someone was also found who established two altars for performing divine rites: one to **Impiety** and the other to **Injustice**. This was Dicaearchus, a leader...

...a fleet established by Philip V, king of the Macedonians, against the Cyclades islands. Regarding him, Polybius writes the following, among other things, in Book XVII of his *Histories*: **"When he had moored his ships, he set up two altars: one to Impiety, and the other to Lawlessness; and upon these he offered sacrifices, and worshipped them just as if they were divine powers."** <note>original Greek: "Ὡς δ’ ὁρμίσειε τὰς ναῦς, δύο κατεσκεύαζε βωμούς· τὸν μὲν Ἀσεβείας, τὸν δὲ Παρανομίας· καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἔθυε, καὶ τούτους προσεκύνει καθαπερανεὶ δαίμονας." This refers to Dicaearchus, a commander under Philip V, who famously mocked the gods.</note> But Polybius adds that the same man also found a death worthy of his wicked life: **"Having established his life contrary to nature, it was fitting that he met an end that was also contrary to nature and fate."** <note>original Greek: "Παρὰ φύσιν ἐνστησάμενος τὸν αὑτοῦ βίον, εἰκότως παρὰ φύσιν καὶ τῆς εἱμαρμένης ἔτυχε."</note>

Regarding the Symbols, which are found in Malchus <note>the birth name of Porphyry</note> at Number 42, and in Iamblichus’s *Exhortation to Philosophy* on page 131 and following, other things could be added (which I shall look into at another time), as well as these:

**"Do not sail on land"** is a Pythagorean symbol. <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ γῆς μὴ πλεῖν"</note> Clement of Alexandria refers to this in Book II of his *Miscellanies*, page 239. <note>This maxim likely warns against pursuing "earthly" or material wealth through spiritual means, or engaging in business that is "unnatural" to one's station.</note>

**"Do not eat the black-tail."** <note>original Greek: "Μελάνουρον μὴ ἐσθίειν." The "black-tail" (melanurus) was a fish associated with the powers of the underworld or with "dark" emotions like grief and malice.</note> Cited by Theodoret in *Discourse 8 to the Greeks*, and Iamblichus in *The Pythagorean Life*, chapter 24.

**"One must prefer the Muses to the Sirens."** <note>original Greek: "Χρὴ τῶν Σειρήνων προτιθέναι τὰς Μούσας." This advises choosing the pursuit of knowledge and harmony (the Muses) over the destructive lures of physical pleasure (the Sirens).</note> Cited by Theodoret in the aforementioned *Discourse 8* at the beginning. Clement of Alexandria says the same in his *Miscellanies*: **"Pythagoras advises that the Muses are to be considered sweeter than the Sirens."** <note>original Greek: "Μούσας Σειρήνων ἡδίους ἡγεῖσθαι Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ."</note>

->END OF THE SUPPLEMENTAL NOTES.<-

<keywords>Philip V of Macedon, Polybius, Pythagorean symbols, Muses, Sirens, Clement of Alexandria, Theodoret, morality, impiety</keywords>

Music seemed to Pythagoras to be suitable for healing sick minds. 33.

# ON PORPHYRY

**Pherecydes** of Syros died on the island of Delos from a "disease of lice." **55.** <note>original: "phthiriasi." This was a common legendary death for ancient thinkers, often symbolizing a transition of the soul or a harsh physical end despite great wisdom.</note>
**Pherecydes**, the teacher of Pythagoras, was cared for by him while ill on Delos, and Pythagoras buried him after his death. **15.**
**Philosophers** in great numbers borrowed certain doctrines (indeed, the most fruitful ones) from Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans; the rest were later attacked by envious people and slanderers.
The goal of **Pythagorean Philosophy** is to set free the mind that is imprisoned by the bonds of the body. **46.**
Several reasons are offered as to why **Pythagorean Philosophy** eventually became extinct. **53.**
**Phintias**, having been condemned to death by Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily on the charge of conspiring against him, obtained a stay of a few hours after his friend Damon stood as a guarantor for his return. This allowed Phintias to arrange his and his companion's affairs; to the wonder of all, he returned before sunset to face his appointed death. **60.** <note>This famous story of Damon and Phintias illustrates the Pythagorean ideal of absolute loyalty in friendship.</note>
The **Phoenicians** have been students of numbers and proportions since ancient times. **6.**
How much Pythagoras attributed to **Physiognomy**. **13.** <note><term>Physiognomy</term>: The ancient practice of judging a person's inner character or soul by studying their outward physical features, especially the face.</note>
The **Physiognomy** of Cylon did not please Pythagoras, and for this reason, he rejected him from his school, to which Cylon had aspired. **54.** <note>This rejection is often cited as the catalyst for Cylon's later violent rebellion against the Pythagoreans.</note>
To **Fishermen** pulling a great weight in their net from the deep, Pythagoras predicted the exact number of fish they had caught; he then ordered them all to be released alive after a careful counting. **25.**
The **Planets** were called the "Dogs of Proserpina" by Pythagoras. **41.** <note>Proserpina is the Roman name for Persephone, queen of the Underworld; this metaphorical name likely relates to the planets' roles as "guardians" or "watchers" in the celestial spheres.</note>
**Plato** borrowed many things from the Pythagoreans. **53.**
The **Pleiades** were called the "Lyre of the Muses" by Pythagoras. **41.**
Fleeing the tyranny of **Polycrates** as something intolerable to a free-born man, Pythagoras departed from Samos for Italy. **9.** and **16.**
Equipped with letters of recommendation from **Polycrates**, the tyrant of the Samians, Pythagoras traveled to Amasis, the King of the Egyptians, so that he might then be recommended by him to the Egyptian priests. **7.**
Do not walk on the **Public** road. **42.** <note>original: "Populari via ne incedito." This is one of Pythagoras's "Symbola" (proverbial maxims), meaning one should avoid following the common or unthinking opinions of the masses.</note>
The **Teachers** of Pythagoras were Pherecydes, Hermodamas, and Anaximander. **2.**
In what way Pythagoras attempted to suggest to his listeners the difficulty of the **Primary** forms and first principles through the teaching of numbers. **48.**
For the **Dogs of Proserpina**, see Planets.
Pythagoras was once **Pyrrhus**. **45.** <note>This refers to the doctrine of metempsychosis (reincarnation). Pythagoras claimed to remember his previous lives, which included being the Trojan hero Euphorbus and, as noted here, a man named Pyrrhus.</note>
Concerning the **natural talent** of Pythagoras from his youth, and his aptitude for every kind of discipline. **1.** <note>original: "εὐφυΐα" (euphyia), meaning a natural goodness of shape or a well-disposed mind.</note>

# NOTES OF CONRAD RITTERSHUSIUS

...of symbols; that which seems to be spoken aloud is actually hidden, and that which is hidden is what is truly understood. <note>original: "συμβόλων καὶ τὸ φράζεσθαι δοκοῦν, κρυπτόμενόν ἐστι· καὶ τὸ κρύπτεσθαι, νοούμενον." This refers to the Pythagorean method of "Acousmata" or oral symbols where a simple statement masks a deeper philosophical truth.</note>

The verse *I shall sing for those who understand* etc. also appears in Stobaeus, Sermon 39. <note>Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved fragments of Greek literature.</note> Similarly, Orpheus is quoted in Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, and others: *I shall speak to those for whom it is lawful; but shut the doors, you profane ones.* <note>original: "Φθέγξομαι, οἷς θέμις ἐστί· θύρας δ’ ἐπίθεσθε βέβηλοι." This is a famous Orphic warning to keep sacred mysteries secret from the uninitiated.</note> In imitation of these, Virgil wrote: *Away, oh stay far away, you uninitiated ones.* <note>original: "Procul o, procul este profani." from the Aeneid.</note> And Horace: *I hate the profane crowd and keep them away.*

**Regarding Number 48.** Where numbers are discussed, I add Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, chapter 2, page 2, and chapter 13, page 27. Also Sextus the Philosopher. <note>Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic philosopher who recorded many Pythagorean mathematical theories.</note>

**Regarding Number 52.** Saint Augustine also emphasizes the mystery and perfection of the <term>denarius</term> <note>The number ten, which the Pythagoreans called the "Decad" and considered the most perfect number, containing the nature of all things.</note> in more than one place: especially in Book II of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 4, page 401; and *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, chapter 6, page 339, Volume 4; and Book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 23; and in his single book *Against the Epistle of Mani*, chapter 10, where he writes that the number ten signifies perfection. He explains it is created by adding the Trinity of the Creator to the number seven, which represents the entirety of the created world. Regarding these matters, he says:
> "Among spiritual men, many things are discussed concerning these subjects with piety and caution."

However, the Pythagoreans called not only the number ten perfect, but also the <term>senarium</term> <note>The number six.</note>, which they also named the "middle-straight" <note>original: "μεσευθὺν"</note>: because it is the middle point of the "straight" numbers—that is, between ten and two. <note>Six is the arithmetic mean of 10 and 2 (10+2=12, divided by 2 is 6).</note> Clement of Alexandria explains this more extensively in *Stromata*, Book 6, page 290.

**Regarding Number 56.** Saint Augustine also agrees with those who believe that Pythagoras wrote nothing, saying the following in Book I of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 7, Volume 4, page 376:
> "When the pagans ask why Christ Himself did not write, they seem prepared to believe about Him only what He might have written about Himself, rather than what others proclaimed about Him according to their own judgment. I ask them: why did they believe such things about certain of their own most noble philosophers, based on what their disciples left to memory in writing, when the philosophers themselves wrote nothing? For Pythagoras, than whom Greece then had no clearer light in that contemplative virtue, is held to have written nothing not only about himself, but about any matter at all."
But Socrates, etc. <note>The text cuts off as it moves to compare Pythagoras with Socrates, who also left no writings of his own.</note>

Furthermore, where I mentioned in the Notes the temple of Contumely and Impudence consecrated at Athens, I add in passing that a man was found who established two altars for performing divine rites: one to *Impiety* and the other to *Injustice*. This was Dicaearchus, a leader...

<summary>This page features scholarly commentary by Conrad Rittershusius, comparing Pythagorean secrecy and numerology with early Christian theology and Roman poetry. It specifically examines the mystical significance of the numbers six and ten and addresses the historical debate over whether Pythagoras ever committed his teachings to writing.</summary>

# ON PORPHYRY

...a fleet commander appointed by Philip, King of the Macedonians, against the Cycladic islands: regarding whom, after other details, Polybius writes thus in Book 17 of his *Histories*: *As he moored his ships, he established two altars: one to Impiety, the other to Lawlessness; and upon these he offered sacrifice, and worshipped them as if they were divine spirits.* <note>original: "Ὡς δ’ ὁρμίσειε τὰς ναῦς, δύο κατεσκεύαζε βωμούς· τὸν μὲν Ἀσεβείας, τὸν δὲ Παρανομίας· καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἔθυε, καὶ τούτους προσεκύνει καθαπερανεὶ δαίμονας." This refers to the admiral Dicaearchus, whose blatant sacrilege was cited by ancient historians as a peak of moral corruption.</note> But he adds that the same man also met an end worthy of his wicked life: *Having established his life contrary to nature, he reasonably met an end that was also contrary to nature and his allotted fate.* <note>original: "Παρὰ φύσιν ἐνστησάμενος τὸν αὑτοῦ βίον, εἰκότως παρὰ φύσιν καὶ τῆς εἱμαρμένης ἔτυχε."</note>

Regarding the Symbols which are found in Malchus <note>Malchus was the original Syrian name of Porphyry. The scholar uses it here to refer to Porphyry’s "Life of Pythagoras."</note> at Number 42, and in Iamblichus's *Exhortation to Philosophy* page 131 and following: while other things could be added (which I shall see to elsewhere), there are these:

*Do not sail on land.* <note>original: "Ἐπὶ γῆς μὴ πλεῖν."</note> This is a Pythagorean symbol. Clement of Alexandria records it in Book 2 of the *Miscellanies*, page 239. <note>Pythagorean "symbols" or acousmata were short, cryptic precepts. This one likely warns against engaging in work for which one is not naturally suited, or perhaps against seeking stability in moving things.</note>

*Do not eat the black-tail fish.* <note>original: "Μελάνουρον μὴ ἐσθίειν."</note> Theodoret, *Sermon 8 to the Greeks*. Iamblichus, *On the Pythagorean Life*, chapter 24. <note>The black-tail (melanurus) was a fish often associated by the Pythagoreans with "dark" or terrestrial spirits; avoiding it was a form of ritual purity.</note>

*One must prefer the Muses to the Sirens.* <note>original: "Χρὴ τῶν Σειρήνων προτιθέναι τὰς Μούσας."</note> Theodoret in the aforementioned *Sermon 8* at the beginning. Clement of Alexandria says the same in the *Miscellanies*: *Pythagoras advises thinking the Muses are sweeter than Sirens.* <note>In Greek mythology, the Sirens lured sailors to their death with beautiful songs, representing dangerous pleasure, while the Muses represented the divine harmony of the arts and sciences.</note>

Zamolxis, a Thracian youth, came to Pythagoras, and was beloved and educated by him. **14.** <note>Zamolxis was later worshipped as a god by the Thracian Getae; the text here links his wisdom to Pythagorean training.</note>
The double etymology of Zamolxis. **14.** and **15.**

Volume II. Part II.
Signature: T

Variant readings of Iamblichus’s third book **On the Common Mathematical Science** <note>original: "περὶ τῆς κοινῆς μαθηματικῆς ἐπιστήμης"</note>, noted from the Zeitz Manuscript <note>Latin: "Codice Cizensi"; a manuscript held in the library at Zeitz, Germany</note> and compared with the text of this book as it was first edited by Villoison in the *Greek Anecdotes*, Volume II, pages 188–225, from the Marcian Library <note>Venice</note> Manuscript 243, a 15th-century parchment in quarto. Prefixed are the summaries of the chapters transcribed from the same Zeitz Manuscript.

### CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD DISCOURSE.

1. **What the overall purpose of the present book is, and what the specific goals are within it; in how many ways and into what parts they are divided; from what source they derive the primary causes of their proper inquiry, and from what kind of essence.**

2. **What the common theory of all mathematics is, and concerning mathematical science: from where and from what sources its definition must be taken, how great a span it possesses, and over how many common classes it extends.**

3. **What the principles of mathematics as a whole are, and how they differ from other principles (specifically those that are principles of other types of being); and how these mathematical principles provide a common cause for all mathematical disciplines.**

4. **What the specific principles of each of the mathematical sciences are; what characterizes their unique identity and their difference from one another, as well as their difference from all other principles of all existing things.**

5. **What is the common subject matter for all mathematical studies—the things which those who love learning busy themselves with—and how it is possible to create a single, universal theory concerning them.**

## VARIANT READINGS <note>Latin: VARIETAS LECTIONIS</note>

**6.** What the best use of diligence regarding mathematical studies is, and toward what end one ought to direct the best action regarding these matters.

**7.** What proper object of knowledge <term>epistēton: a thing that can be known through scientific reason</term> underlies each mathematical science, and how it is possible to make a common distinction between them by means of division; this is done so that one may know what the nature of "the one" and "the many" <note>fundamental Pythagorean concepts of Unity and Plurality</note> is within mathematical subjects, and how one should define them.

**8.** What the common criterion for all mathematical studies is, and how it is discovered from the "section of the line" <note>a reference to the "Divided Line," a famous analogy for different levels of reality and knowledge</note> which the Pythagoreans hand down.

**9.** Concerning those who assign a defined essence <term>ousia: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> to mathematical objects; the first opinion presented is that of those who trace them back to the soul. Many reasons for such a hypothesis are given, as well as starting points for the whole contemplation <term>theōria</term> regarding them.

**10.** How the essence of the soul is composed of all the mathematical sciences, and by what demarcation the blending of these sciences within the soul might be defined; and whether the soul contains the entire subsistence <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or existence</term> of mathematical objects within itself, or if some other principle of them is also observed.

**11.** What the task of mathematical contemplation is and how it comes about, and why it is appropriately named "mathematical" <note>original: μαθηματικὴ; the Greek root implies "that which is learned"</note> in accordance with these facts.

**12.** What the powers of mathematical science are, what rank they hold among themselves, by how many differences they are divided, and in how many ways they are understood.

**13.** What the elements and genera of mathematical science are; how the same things can be both elements and genera; and how these differ from those elements found in other sciences and essences—both the intelligible essences and those that exist in the realm of generation <note>the physical world of change and becoming</note>.

**14.** Concerning similarity and dissimilarity in mathematics; what they are and how far they extend, how they exist within the mathematical essence, and in what way they differ...

**Vocabulary:** <note>original: μαθήματα, ψυχή, θεωρία, ἐπιστήμη, πυθαγόρειοι, οὐσία, στοιχεῖα</note>
mathematical studies, soul, contemplation, science, Pythagoreans, essence, elements.

# OF IAMBLICHUS, BOOK THREE <note>original Latin: IAMBLICHI LIBRI TERTII</note>

...the explanation of homonymous genera <note>terms that share the same name but have different definitions</note>, as many as are spoken of regarding both intelligible and sensible things.

**15.** How the entirety of mathematical science—including itself, its genera, its elements, and its principles—extends through the whole of philosophy and the various parts of philosophy, and how it communicates with them and toward what completion.

**16.** How many benefits it contributes to the arts, both to the arts as a whole and to those categorized by type, such as the theoretical, the productive, and the practical; and a summarized instruction concerning these matters.

**17.** What the order is within mathematical training, and whether it possesses an order according to nature and for the purpose of learning, and whether each order agrees with the other and the two with one another.

**18.** What the specific methods of the Pythagorean tradition of mathematical studies are, and how they were used and for whom; and how they always applied what was appropriate both to the subjects being studied and to the students themselves.

**19.** The division, according to the Pythagoreans, of the entire mathematical science into its most primary genera and species, while providing a common contemplation <term>theōria: deep, speculative study</term> regarding them.

**20.** What the definitional method <term>horistikē: the art of defining terms</term> of mathematics is and how it comes to be, what benefit it contributes to scientific knowledge, and that mathematics has a goal <term>telos: an ultimate purpose or end-point</term> and what the nature of that goal is.

**21.** Which leaders of the Pythagorean school of mathematics came first, what is exceptional about such science according to Pythagoras, and a general conception of how one must organize the arrangements of mathematical studies in accordance with him.

**22.** What the specific study <term>meletē: practice or disciplined exercise</term> of mathematical science was according to Pythagoras, how many useful things it looked toward for the soul and for humanity, and how they employed it throughout their entire lives.

# VARIETY OF READINGS <note>original Latin: VARIETAS LECTIONIS</note>

**23.** That it was not without reason that the Pythagoreans pursued mathematical studies at such great length, but rather for the necessary use of life; and what the reasons for this were, explained through several reminders.

**24.** What the custom was in the school of the Pythagoreans regarding their studies, and what their training <term>gymnasia: disciplined exercise</term> and systematic development in the sciences consisted of.

**25.** Who the "Mathematicians" were among the Pythagoreans and in what way they differed from the "Auditors" <note>original Greek: akousmatikoi; these were students who followed the rules of life without seeking the deeper proofs</note>, what their specific work was, and what kind of reasoning and demonstrations <term>apodeixeis: logical proofs</term> they employed.

**26.** Objections raised against mathematical studies, claiming they are worth nothing, and the counter-arguments and rebuttals made against these views, presented in several arrangements.

**27.** What one ought to demand from a mathematician who has been so educated, how their theoretical study <term>theōria: speculative or deep contemplation</term> should be judged, and by what standards its correctness is understood.

**28.** How to distinguish when a problem belongs to mathematics or to another science, and the scientific distinction regarding the manner of demonstrations.

**29.** Concerning mathematical syllogisms <term>syllogismos: a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> and mathematical divisions and definitions; how mathematical science employs them—whether in its own unique way, or by taking its principles from the art of dialectic.

**30.** That mathematics contributes greatly to the whole of philosophy and all its parts, serving it in all things—especially the Pythagorean brand of mathematics, which differs greatly from other forms of the discipline.

**31.** That the Pythagoreans used the same mathematical principles for many different matters, and used several different mathematical approaches to explain the same matter, and for what reasons they did so.

**32.** How we sometimes treat sensory objects <note>things perceived by the five senses rather than the mind alone</note> in a mathematical way, in how many ways this occurs, and how in mathematics many things are reduced to others, and for what reasons.

# BOOK THREE BY IAMBLICHUS <note>original Latin: IAMBLICHI LIBRI TERTII</note>

33. What is common to all of mathematical science; and what its specific nature is according to the differences observed in its many forms; and how one ought to divide these using the **diaretic science** <term>diaretic: the logical method of dividing a genus into its species</term> starting from one into two, and then into even more forms.

34. From where the science of mathematics received its name and what its character is, and what things one must pay attention to when judging the different forms of mathematics.

->**THE DIVISION OF QUANTITY**<-
-><term>Quantity</term> <note>original: τὸ ποσὸν; the fundamental category of "how much" in Pythagorean thought</note><-

| **Discrete Quantity** <note>original: διορισμένον; things that can be counted individually, like a group of people</note> | **Continuous Quantity** <note>original: συνεχὲς; things that are unbroken, like a line or time</note> |
| :--- | :--- |

<meta>This page continues the list of textual variations for Iamblichus's work, comparing the 1781 edition by Villoison with the "Codex Cizensis" (the Zeitz Manuscript). This section focuses on the later chapters of the third book, where subtle differences in spelling, grammar, and word choice often reveal how medieval scribes interpreted or accidentally altered the ancient philosophical text. These variants are crucial for scholars attempting to reconstruct the most accurate version of Iamblichus’s treatise on mathematical science.</meta>

| — | D. 2. "by that of the sesquioctave" <note>original: τῷ τοῦ ἐπογδόου; the ratio 9:8</note> | "those things of the sesquioctave" <note>original: τὰ τοῦ ἐπογδ.</note> |
| — | — 3. "and to these" <note>original: καὶ τούτοις</note> | "according to these" <note>original: κατὰ τούτοις</note> |
| — | — 5. "tradition" <note>original: παράδοσιν</note> | "they hand down" <note>original: παραδίδασιν</note> |
| 169. | A. 5. "it might become" <note>original: γίνηται</note> | "it becomes" <note>original: γίνεται</note> |
| — | — 7. "being judged" <note>original: κατακρινομένη</note> | "being tempered" <note>original: κατακιρναμένη; a term often used for mixing musical or physical elements</note> |
| — | B. 7. "after" <note>original: μετὰ</note> | "wherefore" <note>original: μεθὸ</note> |
| — | C. 2. "in the sesquialter" <note>original: ἡμιολίῳ; the ratio 3:2</note> | "of the sesquialters" <note>original: ἡμιολίων</note> |
| — | D. 2. "of the sesquitertial" <note>original: ἐπιτρίτου; the ratio 4:3</note> | "upon the third" <note>original: ἐπὶ τρίτῳ</note> |
| 170. | A. 5. "encompasses the" <note>original: ἐμπεριέχει τὰ</note> | "encompasses the [the] the" <note>original: ἐμπεριέχει τὰς τὰ; a scribal stutter</note> |
| — | B. 3. "the [interval] through" <note>original: τὸ διὰ; likely referring to the 'dia tessaron' or fourth</note> | "but the [interval] through" <note>original: τὸ δὲ διὰ</note> |
| 171. | A. 6. "thus greater [terms]" <note>original: οὕτω μείζονας</note> | "by this, greater [terms]" <note>original: τούτῳ μείζ.</note> |
| — | B. 2. "we omit" <note>original: παρίεμεν</note> | "we let pass" <note>original: παρίημεν</note> |
| 172. | A. 4. "already also upon" <note>original: ἤδη κἀπὶ</note> | "already however also upon" <note>original: ἤδη δὲ κἀπὶ</note> |
| — | — 5. "and wholly" <note>original: καὶ ὅλως</note> | "and wholly of the" <note>original: καὶ ὅλως τῶν</note> |
| — | — 8. "in those things" <note>original: ἔντα τοῖς</note> | "in those things" <note>original: ἐν τα τοῖς; likely a spacing error in the manuscript</note> |
| — | D. 4. "it is necessary" <note>original: δεῖ</note> | "but" <note>original: δὲ</note> |
| — | — 6. "having" <note>original: ἔχων; masculine</note> | "having" <note>original: ἔχον; neuter</note> |
| 173. | A. 1. "it might provide, which" <note>original: παρασχῇ, ὃς</note> | "it might provide as" <note>original: παράσχῃ ὡς</note> |
| — | B. 4. "it has" <note>original: ἔχει</note> | "**Is missing.**" <note>original: Deest.</note> |
| — | C. 6. "and neither has a third" <note>original: καὶ οὔτε τρίτον ἔχει</note> | "and has neither a half nor a third" <note>original: καὶ οὔτε ἥμισυ, οὔτε τρίτον ἔχει</note> |
| 174. | A. 6. "a concord. And again" <note>original: συμφωνίαν. Καὶ πάλιν</note> | "a concord being composed of the fourth and the fifth. And again" <note>original: συμφωνίαν σύνθετον οὖσαν ἐκ τῆς διὰ τεσσάρων καὶ διὰ ἐ. καὶ πάλιν; here the manuscript provides a fuller mathematical definition of a 'symphony' or concord</note> |

| — — 6. | "thus the" <note>original: οὕτω ὁ</note> | "thus the" <note>original: οὕτως ὁ; an alternative adverbial form</note> |

| — B. 6. | "more perfect for you" <note>original: ἐντελεσθέραν σοι</note> | "more perfect for you" <note>original: ἐντελέστερόν σοι; a variation in grammatical gender or case</note> |
| — C. 6. | "from these" <note>original: πρὸς τούτων</note> | "before these" <note>original: πρὸ τούτων</note> |
| — — 8. | "easier" <note>original: εὐμαρεστέρα</note> | "more cautious" <note>original: εὐλαβεστέρα</note> |
